### Continuation log — additional cognitive-architecture archaeology (2026-09-27)

An independent scan identified five cognitive mechanisms absent from the notebook's prior coverage: CHREST/EPAM, ICARUS, CLARION, SNePS, and GLAIR. I checked their core claims against primary papers or project-authored material. These enrich the archaeology map but do not change the broad-candidate decision.

#### AR-17 — CHREST / EPAM: attention-guided discrimination and chunk growth

- **Original computation and representation.** Incrementally route an attended pattern through a discrimination network. If no existing node captures the pattern, add a distinguishing test and node; if an existing chunk can be enriched, familiarisation updates it. CHREST adds recursive chunking, short-term-memory dynamics, perceptual mechanisms and retrieval structures to the EPAM lineage. It models how repeated chess positions/patterns become rapidly recognized. [Feigenbaum & Simon, EPAM (1984)](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog0804_1); [CHREST chess-memory paper](https://www.chrest.info/fg/papers/ModelChessMem/Chess%20Memory.html).
- **Learning, inference and memory.** Inputs are attended sensory/configural patterns; outputs are recognized chunks or predictions/skill-relevant associations. Learning appends discriminations or familiarisations to a long-term network; inference is indexed traversal and retrieval. The historical model makes network growth permanent, learning discrete, and avoids backtracking. Memory is the discrimination/chunk graph plus limited short-term references.
- **Why it struggled and what modern tech changes.** Large corpora and richer vision were expensive, so modern encoders, simulation and memory hardware could support much larger exposure and stimulus variation. But the architecture's structural risks remain: order-dependent irreversible growth, selecting the right perceptual tests, and brittleness when input features drift. Encoder upgrades can invalidate learned paths unless representations are versioned or memory is remapped.
- **Closest prior art / novelty.** Incremental decision trees, adaptive resonance, prototype/episodic retrieval, hierarchical sequence memory, and learned embeddings cover the broad mechanism. No unoccupied general model class remains. Potential component question: can a learned revision/merge operation relieve append-only memory growth while preserving fast chunk retrieval under drift? This directly modifies a defining CHREST assumption and likely overlaps tree pruning, memory consolidation and incremental clustering. **Novelty confidence: 0/5.**
- **Small falsifier and verdict.** CPU-only recurring-pattern task with controlled frequency shifts, noisy features and held-out combinations. Compare original append-only CHREST, bounded revision/merge, fixed-budget nearest-neighbor memory and a recurrent baseline under matched exposure and memory. Measure few-shot recognition, transfer, retrieval cost, memory size and catastrophic interference. Reject revival if any gain disappears with equal memory/input exposure or revision destroys useful chunks. **Worth a reproduction baseline, not a new architecture.**

#### AR-18 — ICARUS: recursive teleoreactive skill acquisition

- **Original computation.** Maintain concept rules over percepts and teleoreactive skill clauses. Start from a goal, select an applicable skill path, react to changing conditions, and execute a primitive action. If a familiar skill fails, use means-ends search over primitive skills; when search solves an impasse, compile its trace into a reusable, possibly recursive skill. This intertwines problem solving, control and skill learning. [Langley & Choi, JMLR 2006](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume7/langley06a/langley06a.pdf).
- **Unit, communication, knowledge, learning and inference.** The unit is a relational concept or skill clause with conditions, subskills/actions and effects. Concept inference maps observed objects/relations into a short-term belief store; top-down goal execution checks applicable skill paths; successful search traces create longer-term teleoreactive programs. It takes structured percepts/goals and emits subgoals/actions. The system requires primitive skills and concept predicates to seed reasoning; it learns new skills from traces, not raw sensory structure.
- **Historical issue and modernization.** Larger simulation/search budgets could find more solutions and modern learned perception could replace some manual predicates. Yet the 2006 paper explicitly notes search may fail under limited computation; scaling it does not remove combinatorial search, manually specified action effects/preconditions, or learned-program brittleness under unexpected effects. Recursive skills must remain reactive to be safe under changing environments.
- **Closest prior art / what might remain.** SHOP/HTN planning, Soar/PRODIGY impasse learning, programmatic RL, hierarchical RL/options and learned skill libraries overlap. ICARUS has direct prior art for extracting recursive reactive programs from successful problem-solving traces. A modern residual test is whether a learned concept interface and uncertainty-aware precondition repair makes these programs robust when perception/side-effects change; this is likely program repair plus skill learning, not a new class. **Novelty confidence: 0/5.**
- **Small falsifier and verdict.** CPU grid or Blocks World with keys, repeated subproblems, interruptions and randomized side effects. Compare ICARUS-style trace-compiled recursive programs, behavior-tree scripts, HRL options and search-only control under equal environment interactions and planning compute. Measure solve rate, search reduction, deeper-layout transfer, invalid skill executions and recovery after changes. Reject if compiled skills only speed near-identical layouts or their checks erase all gains. **Useful old-plus-modern skill-learning baseline.**

#### AR-19 — CLARION: reciprocal learning between implicit skill and explicit rule stores

- **Original mechanism.** Couple a bottom-level distributed/action-value learner (implicit procedural skill) to a top-level localist symbolic rule system (explicit knowledge). The 2001 account learns incrementally online; when implicit behavior succeeds under its criterion, it can construct a rule describing the current sensory state/action, while explicit information can also guide lower-level learning. The important mechanism is reciprocal learning across representations, not merely stacking a neural model before rules. [Sun, Merrill & Peterson, Cognitive Science 2001](https://homepages.hass.rpi.edu/rsun/sun.cs01.pdf); [Sun & Zhang, CLARION learning modes (2004)](https://homepages.hass.rpi.edu/rsun/sun-zhang-jcsr2004-f.pdf).
- **Unit, information, inference and memory.** The lower system stores distributed state-action values and learns by gradual reinforcement; the upper system stores explicit rules formed/refined from successful lower-level actions and instructions. Given a state/goal, the layers can propose or bias actions; feedback updates action values and rule confidence/structure. Intended uses include reactive skill learning, rule access/communication and explanation of how explicit procedures emerge from practice.
- **Historical limits and technological changes.** GPUs can enlarge the implicit network and simulation supplies more practice. The hard problem is evidential: many policies match sparse behavior, so extracting a compact correct rule is underdetermined; a symbolic rule can overgeneralize or be too narrow. Modern perception improves input grounding but can conceal whether reciprocal learning contributed. This was not mainly born before sufficient compute existed.
- **Closest work / residual novelty.** CLARION is direct prior art for implicit/explicit two-level learning, RER-style rule acquisition, and top-down/bottom-up interaction. Policy distillation, rule extraction, neuro-symbolic RL and hierarchical policies modernize the broad family. **Novelty confidence: 0/5.** A measurable open question is whether explicit rules improve transfer or calibrated intervention under distribution shift, rather than merely compressing a policy on the training task.
- **Small falsifier and verdict.** CPU minefield/navigation or changing-hazard task with online corrections. Compare implicit-only learner, explicit-rule-only, and CLARION-style reciprocal rule/skill updates at matched environment samples and compute; evaluate frozen rules on shifted layouts and ask the system to revise them after counterexamples. Measure reward, rule precision/coverage, transfer, sample efficiency and adaptation after a hazard change. Falsify any advantage if extracted rules fail to improve held-out transfer/intervention or destabilize the lower policy. **Keep as a baseline and possible reimplementation study, not a new hybrid claim.**

#### AR-20 — SNePS: proposition-centered term network and contradiction-tolerant belief revision

- **Original computation.** Represent terms and propositions as nodes in a semantic network with intensional semantics, support inference/acting, and tolerate contradictions without arbitrary explosion. Belief contraction uses support/assumption sets in an ATMS-like fashion; earlier versions asked a user to choose which inconsistent belief to remove, with later work adding automatic contraction under conditions. [Shapiro & Johnson, “Automatic Belief Revision in SNePS” (2000)](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0003011).
- **Information, operations and learning.** Its main persistent state is the propositional term network, inference links and belief support/origin sets. It receives assertions, queries and action requests; inference creates supported propositions, and contradiction detection/revision retracts or deactivates beliefs. This is knowledge representation/reasoning, not a learned parameter architecture; GPU capacity does not create the ontology or source-trust policy.
- **Historical issue, modernization and closest work.** Network memory and inference speed can improve, but the expensive parts are knowledge engineering, source choice, revision policy and managing justifications. Truth-maintenance systems, belief-revision logics, paraconsistent logic, provenance-aware knowledge graphs and incremental database maintenance directly overlap. The surviving value is a baseline for contradiction handling with explicit semantic support, not a new general learner. **Novelty confidence: 0/5.**
- **Small falsifier and verdict.** CPU benchmark with source-ranked, contradictory facts added and removed over time. Compare SNePS-style support contraction, an assumption-based truth-maintenance baseline and a provenance-aware graph store. Check answer consistency, correct reactivation/retraction, update work and memory growth. Reject a revival claim if explicit supports do not improve correctness or update efficiency. **Historical knowledge architecture, low priority for new-class search.**

#### AR-21 — GLAIR: layered symbol grounding with modality registers

- **Original computation.** GLAIR divides an embodied cognitive agent into a symbolic knowledge level, a perceptuo-motor level and a sensor-actuator level. Symbolic entity/action/time terms are aligned with perceptual feature descriptions and executable lower-level procedures. Deictic and modality registers record the agent, interlocutor, current time, gaze and ongoing modality activity; this lets reasoning inspect current embodiment and avoid reissuing actions such as looking at something already visible. Its Cassie instantiation was used in hardware and simulated robots. [Shapiro & Ismail, Robotics and Autonomous Systems 2003](https://cse.buffalo.edu/~shapiro/Papers/shaism03.pdf); [Shapiro & Bona, GLAIR (2009)](https://cse.buffalo.edu/~shapiro/Papers/shabon09a.pdf).
- **Learning, memory and hardware.** Knowledge is primarily symbolic; grounding depends on lower-level tuples/procedures and persistent register state, with perception/action modules updating them. There is no general learned grounding rule. Modern encoders, object tracking and simulators can increase sensory coverage, but do not guarantee persistent identity or confirm that a requested action succeeded.
- **Closest work / exact possible residue.** Symbol anchoring was already an explicit research program by 2000–2003; modern embodied multimodal models learn sensor-language-action relations directly, and robotics maintains object-symbol anchors. [PaLM-E (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.03378); [RT-2 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15818). A narrow empirical question is whether explicit modality registers catch perception/action-state errors that latent end-to-end policies miss. That is an auditability/control study, not a new architecture. **Novelty confidence: 0/5.**
- **Small falsifier and verdict.** CPU/simulator tabletop tasks with visually similar objects, occlusion, interruptions and concurrent speech/action. Compare explicit symbol anchoring/registers against an end-to-end policy with matched sensors and action budget. Measure identity retention, target errors, unnecessary repeated actions, action completion detection and recovery. Reject the revival if registers add no measurable reliability or auditability after perception quality is matched. **Useful embodied-grounding baseline, not new class.**

### Updated archaeology and hybridization ranking

- **No new architecture promoted.** AR-17–21 are old systems with well-described internal mechanisms and testable revivals, but their broad cores are prior art. The strongest prior-art lesson is that modern compute/data can make experience acquisition, retrieval, perception and search larger; it does not fix representational rigidity, evidence attribution, brittle skill preconditions, or the semantics of cross-layer grounding.
- **Most useful old-plus-modern falsifiers, in order:** (1) CLARION-style rule/implicit-policy coupling under task shifts, because the layers can be ablated and the claim is measurable; (2) CHREST memory growth versus revision under drift; (3) Polyscheme shared focus under fixed operations; (4) ICARUS skill compilation under side effects; (5) GLAIR registers versus learned embodiment. Each remains a reproduction/benchmark question, not a novel architecture candidate.
- **Resource record:** source review and notebook updates only; no code/model experiment ran. No GPU used, no GPU snapshot taken because no GPU experiment started. Any later GPU study must first inspect memory and process ownership, remain near 5.5 GB VRAM, and preserve the requested headroom without interfering with another user's workload.

#### HY-24 — CHREST pattern memory × CLARION bottom-up rule induction (demoted)

- **Source architectures.** CHREST contributes an attention-guided, incremental discrimination/chunk network that retrieves familiar perceptual patterns. CLARION contributes online implicit action learning plus explicit rule formation from successful behavior, with top-down and bottom-up interaction.
- **Proposed deep coupling.** A retrieved CHREST chunk would be a candidate predicate/condition for CLARION's explicit rule layer. Repeatedly successful actions in a chunked context would promote a rule whose antecedent references the chunk's discrimination path; prediction errors in similar contexts could refine or specialize the chunk test and attached rule together. The shared interaction is not just a CHREST front end feeding a CLARION controller: evidence from action outcomes would change both which perceptual distinction is stored and which symbolic rule becomes eligible.
- **Why this could behave differently.** Attention/chunk memory may supply sparse, reusable context conditions; reward learning can decide which distinctions deserve rule promotion; explicit rules could expose when an old chunk no longer predicts a safe action. The architecture would still depend on a manually specified object/percept vocabulary and a structured action task.
- **Closest prior art and novelty judgment.** CLARION already directly couples implicit learning and explicit rule formation. CHREST has been used with production-rule deliberation, though the retrieved patterns need not drive rule extraction. RuleNet already repeatedly extracts symbolic rules from learned neural representations, injects them back, and continues training; fuzzy ARTMAP has incremental rule extraction from learned categories. Thus the proposed co-refinement is closely surrounded by direct old prior art even if no exact CHREST–CLARION paper was located in this targeted search. Lack of an exact search hit is weak evidence. [RuleNet (NeurIPS 1991)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1991/file/cf67355a3333e6e143439161adc2d82e-Paper.pdf); [Carpenter & Tan, ARTMAP rule extraction (1995)](https://doi.org/10.1080/09540099508915655); [CHREST Tileworld agents](https://researchprofiles.herts.ac.uk/en/publications/the-effects-of-bounding-rationality-on-the-performance-and-learni/).
- **Likely advantage and failures.** Could improve sample efficiency and interpretability when the same perceptual motifs recur across tasks. Risks include rule overgeneralization, order-dependent CHREST growth, noisy success criteria, and feedback loops that stabilize a wrong chunk/rule pair. The extra symbolic layer may not beat simple policy distillation or a learned retrieval memory under equal compute.
- **Small falsifier.** CPU synthetic visual-maze tasks with recurring motifs, object-feature noise and mid-run layout changes. Compare CHREST+production rules, CLARION-style implicit/explicit learning, and the coupled promotion/refinement loop; include a neural policy with post-hoc rule extraction. Match observation exposure, memory and action-learning updates. Measure held-out layout success, rule validity, update cost, memory size and recovery after counterexamples. Reject if the coupling does not improve transfer or rule precision over CLARION alone, or if any gain disappears after matching memory capacity.
- **Decision.** Old-plus-old, deeply coupled in one possible implementation, but broad “implicit skill becomes explicit symbolic rule” and “neural representation yields rules” are established. **Novelty confidence: 0.05/5.** Keep only as an optional ablation/reproduction experiment; do not promote to the candidate slate.

### CLARION-style online rule/policy coupling — pre-registered CPU pilot (2026-09-27)

**Question.** In a controlled streaming Boolean task, does a CLARION-inspired coupling of a distributed implicit policy and a symbolic rule store improve recovery from a task-rule change over either representation alone? This is a small mechanism probe, not a faithful CLARION reproduction and not a novelty test; CLARION's architecture and rule extraction are established prior art.

**Protocol fixed before execution.** Use 6 binary input features and two phases of 800 uniformly sampled examples each. In phase 1, the target action is ((x_0 \land 
eg x_1) \lor (x_2 \land x_3)); in phase 2, it changes to ((x_4 \land 
eg x_1) \lor (x_2 \land x_3)). Use 20 paired seeds (4100–4119) and present the same stream to each learner. Three online learners: (A) implicit logistic policy with bias, single-feature and pairwise interaction features; (B) explicit signed-literal rule ensemble with all one- and two-literal conjunctions, Laplace-smoothed action estimates and a minimum support of 8; (C) coupled learner, which updates both from each labeled transition and averages their predicted action probabilities when the rule ensemble has support. Evaluate accuracy on all 64 contexts at 50-example checkpoints without updating. Report pre-change final accuracy, accuracy immediately after the switch, post-change learning-curve AUC, final accuracy, examples to sustain ≥0.85 accuracy at two successive checkpoints (censored if absent), and paired 95% t intervals for coupled-minus-best-single differences. CPU-only; NumPy 2.4.6 / Python 3.11.9. No GPU models or libraries are involved.

**Information limit.** This pilot supplies the correct action label on every context (supervised case feedback), so it isolates representation coupling and adaptation rather than partial-reward credit assignment. The context generator exactly matches the evaluation universe; the phase shift changes one rule feature but preserves the other disjunct. A follow-up would need noisy/perceptual inputs or sparse reward before making broader claims.

#### Pilot result — explicit rules did not improve the coupled policy

- **Implementation detail.** The implicit learner used online logistic SGD on bias, six bits and all 15 pairwise products (`η=0.10`, `L2=0.001`). The rule learner tracked target-label counts for every signed one- or two-literal conjunction, with Laplace smoothing; supported rules (at least 8 observations) voted by support-shrunk posterior, weighted by inverse conjunction length. The coupled system averaged implicit and explicit probabilities when at least one rule was supported, otherwise used the implicit score. Evaluation enumerated all 64 bit contexts at every 50 examples. This is a transparent CLARION-inspired proxy, not a reproduction of the original RER/arbitration algorithms.
- **Resource/runtime record.** Python 3.11.9, NumPy 2.4.6, CPU-only, 20 seeds, 1,600 training examples per seed, wall time 5.995 s. GPU use 0 GB; peak VRAM 0 GB; no other GPU process was checked because this experiment never initialized or queried a GPU. RAM was not measured.

| Learner | Pre-shift final accuracy | Immediately after rule shift | Post-shift mean checkpoint accuracy | Post-shift final accuracy | Examples to sustained 0.85 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Implicit pairwise logistic policy | 0.9977 ± 0.0057 | 0.8102 ± 0.0057 | 0.9533 ± 0.0081 | 0.9922 ± 0.0108 | 165 ± 28.6 |
| Explicit signed-rule ensemble | 0.8656 ± 0.0471 | 0.7453 ± 0.0283 | 0.7844 ± 0.0128 | 0.8063 ± 0.0326 | >800 in every seed |
| Coupled policy + rule ensemble | 0.9953 ± 0.0089 | 0.8125 ± 0.0072 | 0.9428 ± 0.0067 | 0.9805 ± 0.0133 | 185 ± 36.6 |

Values are mean ± standard deviation across seeds. Per-seed paired differences against the better single system were: pre-shift accuracy −0.0023 (95% t CI −0.0050 to 0.0003), immediate post-shift +0.0023 (−0.0003 to +0.0050), post-shift checkpoint mean −0.0105 (−0.0122 to −0.0088), and final accuracy −0.0117 (−0.0164 to −0.0070). Recovery took 20 more examples than the fastest single baseline (95% CI +6 to +34). The coupled system's short-term shift accuracy was statistically indistinguishable from the implicit policy, but it then adapted more slowly and finished lower.

- **Interpretation / falsification.** This pilot falsifies the narrow claim that this particular online rule-plus-policy coupling improves recovery on a simple compositional rule switch. The explicit component was itself weak and diluted a strong, well-specified pairwise policy; this may reflect the vote rule and full-information setting, not a general failure of CLARION. Do not retune on these seeds or infer that symbolic rules cannot help. The task was small, fully observed, supervised through case labels, and offered no transfer to larger input spaces.
- **Decision.** The result lowers the CLARION revival experiment's priority. Keep its architecture-level novelty at 0/5. Any follow-up must pre-register a new environment family and compare against calibrated rule extraction/distillation, not just repeat or tune this pilot. No broad candidate survives.
- **Updated next-action ranking.** First continue source-led candidate discovery and collision checks; then, if another small prototype is warranted, test the Polyscheme focus scheduler under matched specialist-operation budgets. Do not treat that test as a novelty demonstration.

### Continuation — Schema Mechanism archaeology and SHRUTI prior-art correction (2026-09-27)

This pass follows the new archaeology/hybrid track. It asks whether Drescher's developmental Schema Mechanism was merely limited by 1980s hardware and checks whether AR-09's oscillator-phase binding idea is distinct. Sources checked include Drescher's 1980 MIT working paper and 1987 AAAI paper, the 1991 MIT Press book record, Chaput's 2004 dissertation, the 1993 SHRUTI paper, the 2017 Schema Networks paper, and a 2025 direct schema-mechanism modernization in LIDA.

#### AR-22 — Drescher Schema Mechanism: constructivist sensorimotor schema growth (archaeology; not a new candidate)

- **Original computation.** Each schema is a partial-state transition assertion `(context, action, result)` with empirically tracked reliability. The learner attributes observed effects to actions, then spins off schemas by incrementally adding effect items and contextual conditions. Locally consistent but unreliable schemas can induce synthetic items for hidden, slowly changing conditions; schemas are composed into goal-directed compound actions. The original proposal aims to learn sensorimotor concepts such as persistent objects from interaction, not to fit labeled input/output pairs. [Drescher, 1980 MIT AI WP-198](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/b11149d3-f612-4c93-b9d0-6dde930ae382); [Drescher, AAAI 1987](https://cdn.aaai.org/AAAI/1987/AAAI87-052.pdf); [Drescher, *Made-Up Minds* (1991)](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262041201/made-up-minds/).
- **Unit, information and repeated operation.** The unit is an action-conditioned causal schema plus counters/estimates for activation, effect attribution, reliability and local consistency. It represents available sensory and motor items, partial conjunctions of those items, and learned synthetic state-elements for features not initially expressible. On each sensorimotor transition, update the statistics for active and inactive schemas; attribute candidate changes; create context/result spin-offs; update or bootstrap synthetic items; and try chains of reliable schemas when pursuing goals.
- **Input, output, learning, inference and memory.** Inputs are a structured sensor state, a performed action and the resulting state (the historical microworld has hand/eye primitives and explicit items). Outputs are predicted action consequences, learned state abstractions, and goal-relevant action sequences. Learning uses marginal attribution and empirical correlation rather than global gradient descent; inference is conditional transition prediction plus schema composition/search. Long-term knowledge lives in an expanding graph/table of schemas, synthetic items, action plans and statistics. The 1987 paper explicitly says a schema is predictive, not by itself a rule that commands the action; activation and goal valuation select behavior.
- **Use and possible advantage.** Most plausible for sensorimotor development, robotic affordance learning, hidden-object persistence, and learning reusable action effects from sparse interaction. Its potential advantage is explicit causal/action grounding and representation growth: a learner can invent a latent state item when existing sensory predicates cannot explain action success, and can exploit outcomes that are rare overall but reliable in context.
- **Was it bad or early?** Both factors mattered. The 1987 paper reports that MARCSYST had accumulated several hundred schemas when the Lisp Machine implementation slowed substantially, and Drescher proposed moving it to a massively parallel machine. Modern CPUs, memory and simulators would remove much of that immediate throughput bottleneck; modern visual encoders could also supply richer sensory features. But the 2004 analysis identifies a structural bottleneck that more hardware only postpones: every new spin-off is retained; intermediate context/result combinations proliferate; new synthetic items and composite actions add further correlations; and the original mechanism proposes no pruning. The dissertation describes exponential schema growth and resource exhaustion even in a 7×7 two-object microworld. This is not just a historically small-GPU problem. [Chaput 2004, efficiency analysis and CLASM](https://nn.cs.utexas.edu/downloads/papers/chaput.phdtr04.pdf).
- **Has it already been modernized?** Yes. Chaput's Constructivist Learning Architecture (CLA) and its CLASM implementation directly replace unbounded schema bookkeeping with finite SOM capacity, staged hierarchy and selectable input modes, then compare the reimplementation in Drescher's microworld. A 2025 paper directly implements a modified Drescher mechanism in LIDA's procedural-memory/action-selection modules, grounding schema learning through LIDA perception and adding hierarchical plans and exploratory behavior. This is evidence of active revival, not a forgotten architecture waiting for its first modernization. [Chaput, 2004 CLA/CLASM](https://nn.cs.utexas.edu/?cla=); [Kugele, 2025](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1389041725000014).
- **Closest modern adjacent work.** Schema Networks (2017) are an object-oriented generative causal physics model: local cause/effect relationships, multiple causes, uncertainty, and backward planning. They are not a direct reimplementation of Drescher's marginal attribution, open-ended synthetic-item creation, and schema spin-off process, but they substantially occupy the modern object-centric causal-transfer niche. [Kansky et al., Schema Networks, ICML 2017](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/kansky17a.html).
- **What might still differ.** A bounded, revisable schema store grounded in learned object-centric state features, where interventions nominate compact causal schemas and contradiction-triggered experiments decide which predicates or schemas to split/merge. A later prior-art audit below finds that Holmes & Isbell (2004) already extend Drescher's learner to POMDP hidden state and prediction-maintained synthetic items. The broad ingredients are established across CLASM, direct LIDA/developmental revivals, object-centric world models and active experiment design. No distinct general architecture claim is justified; novelty confidence is **0/5 as a class, 0.1/5 for this tightly specified update policy** until a full search shows a concrete uncrowded mechanism.
- **Small falsifiable experiment.** CPU-only 7×7 hidden-object microworld with touch/vision actions, occlusion, misleading transient cues and later novel action sequences. Compare a faithful marginal-attribution learner, finite-capacity CLASM-like prototype hierarchy, and an object-centric transition model with the same interaction budget. Measure persistent-object inference, prediction calibration, transfer to unseen action sequences, schema/prototype count, update time and recovery after feature drift. The modernization claim fails if bounded revisable schemas do not improve sample efficiency or transfer at matched interactions and memory, or if gains disappear against the object-centric model. The architecture revival is not worth pursuing if it needs hand-coded hidden-item labels or does not control growth without losing useful abstractions. **Not run; retained as a reproduction/benchmark plan, not a proposed breakthrough.**

#### Prior-art correction to AR-09 — temporal synchrony already implements dynamic variable binding

The previous AR-09 entry correctly cited LEGION as a phase-synchronization architecture for grouping image features, but it understated earlier binding prior art. SHRUTI (Shastri & Ajjanagadde, 1993) explicitly represents dynamic variable bindings as synchronous firing of the appropriate nodes, encodes rules as connectivity patterns driving rhythmic activity, and stores facts in temporal pattern-matching subnetworks. This precedes the 1997 LEGION paper and directly collides with any broad claim that “phase-coded binding” itself is a new architecture. [Shastri & Ajjanagadde, 1993, *Behavioral and Brain Sciences*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/abs/from-simple-associations-to-systematic-reasoning-a-connectionist-representation-of-rules-variables-and-dynamic-bindings-using-temporal-synchrony/A00CC41AFE06B361E644DAC5ED8F65A3).

This is a substantive correction to the earlier note: AR-09 is established prior art and should stay only as a possible hardware/robustness comparison. SHRUTI's binding capacity is itself constrained by oscillation frequencies and synchronization granularity, so translating the same mechanism to GPU software does not automatically preserve the biological timing semantics or remove binding-capacity limits. Any revival must identify a different mechanism than temporal synchrony and compare with SHRUTI directly.

#### HY-25 — Drescher schema growth × object-centric generative world model (demoted)

- **Source mechanisms.** Drescher contributes action-conditioned context/result schemas, outcome attribution and explicit synthetic state items. Object-centric generative world models contribute learned object/entity factors and action-conditioned state prediction; Schema Networks already provide a close causal, object-oriented model that supports backward planning.
- **Exact proposed coupling.** An object-centric learner proposes a compact set of candidate entities and state features from observations. After an action, the Schema Mechanism tracks context/effect evidence over those features. Persistent prediction residuals create a candidate synthetic item or split an existing predicate; successful and counterexample interventions update schema reliability and trigger bounded merge/prune decisions. The symbolic schemas feed back by choosing a targeted action or observation to distinguish competing object-state hypotheses, so the learned perception vocabulary and causal schema store co-adapt from interventions. This is more specific than placing a rule memory beside a world model, but all of its broad operations have close prior art.
- **Why it could behave differently.** It could yield interpretable, intervention-grounded causal factors while retaining learned visual object features, and it might allocate new state predicates only when prediction errors persist. The interaction changes representation growth and experiment selection, not just the choice of action model.
- **Prior-art collision / possible advantage.** Direct schema-mechanism integrations already exist in CLA/CLASM and LIDA; Schema Networks already learn object-level causes and plan backward; object-centric model-based RL and active experiment design cover learned entities, transition prediction and information-seeking. I found no evidence for this exact predicate-split/merge feedback loop in the checked sources, but that absence is weak evidence and the mechanism is an incremental combination. The likely advantage is transparent cause/effect accounting on partially observed tasks; likely failures are unstable slot identity, overproduction of predicates, noisy residual-driven splits, and added interaction cost.
- **Small falsifier.** Use the same hidden-object grid task as AR-22, with two visually similar objects, occasional false detections and an object that persists through occlusion. Compare the coupled learner with (a) object-centric world model alone, (b) finite-schema learner on oracle object states, and (c) a direct object-centric causal baseline; match environment steps and inference operations. Measure task success, object identity continuity, causal prediction, useful schema growth, compute and recovery from an object appearance change. Falsify the coupling if it fails to outperform the learned object-centric baseline on transfer/calibration, creates many unsupported predicates, or gains only with oracle object identities.
- **Decision.** Keep only as an optional CPU ablation comparing explicit causal schema bookkeeping with learned object-centric models. It is not promoted to the broad candidate slate. **Novelty confidence: 0.05/5.** Direct schema-learning extensions, object-centric causal models and causal object-centric RL crowd the proposed coupling; any residual is a benchmark question, not an architecture claim.

#### Further prior-art audit — schema descendants close the residual novelty (2026-09-27)

An independent auditor reported several direct descendants. I verified the central claims against proceedings/publisher-hosted primary papers before changing the verdict above.

- **Holmes & Isbell, NIPS 2004 — direct computational descendant.** Their “Schema Learning” extends Drescher's action-conditioned schema learner to arbitrary discrete sensors and POMDPs, improves schema discovery/refinement, and maintains hidden state using predictions. It compares next-action-effect prediction with predictive-state representations and reports approximately equal accuracy with faster convergence on the tested POMDPs. The paper specifically distinguishes schema learning from PSRs: schemas refine context and hidden-state items incrementally. This directly closes the proposed residual around synthetic-item creation and hidden-state discovery; it is stronger prior art than the generic object-centric comparison. [Official NeurIPS paper page and abstract](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2004/hash/18bb68e2b38e4a8ce7cf4f6b2625768c-Abstract.html); [full paper](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2004/file/18bb68e2b38e4a8ce7cf4f6b2625768c-Paper.pdf).
- **Georgeon & Ritter, 2011 — intrinsic-motivation and hierarchy.** Their Soar-based mechanism learns hierarchical interaction sequences driven by intrinsic proclivity rather than an externally supplied terminal reward. It explicitly reports hundreds of learned schemes per run, Soar working-memory limits, need for forgetting/merging, weak spatial regularity discovery and local optima. This is a useful example of both “born too early” and persistent algorithmic problems; the authors themselves identify memory organization and exploration as unfinished. [Primary paper](https://liris.cnrs.fr/Documents/Liris-5793.pdf).
- **Georgeon, Gay & Robertson, AGI 2025 — spatio-temporal schema mechanism.** The Springer proceedings describe a mobile-robot extension combining sensorimotor schemas with place/displacement graph structure inspired by place cells and episodic memory. This is a current physical-robot revival using basic range and inertial sensors, not a forgotten path. [Springer AGI 2025 proceedings](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-032-00686-8).
- **Neubert & Protzel, 2018 — schema/world-model hybridization.** This work explicitly combines Drescher's schema-mechanism inspiration with Schema Networks and proposes hypervector representations to relax shared-attribute and neighborhood restrictions in the latter. It is early/ongoing work, but demonstrates that the old-schema × modern-causal-world-model combination is already an investigated direction. [Author-hosted paper](https://www.tu-chemnitz.de/etit/proaut/publications/neubert18_hypervector_schemas.pdf).
- **Nishimoto & Matsubara, AAAI 2026 — close modern causal hybrid.** STICA couples object-centric slot dynamics with learned token-level causal relations used by policy/value attention. It does not reproduce Drescher's schema induction or symbolic synthetic-item reification, but it directly occupies the proposed “object-centric world model + causal policy feedback” territory. Any remaining experimental value of HY-25 is whether explicit, revisable, human-readable context/effect assertions help beyond this family, not the broad coupling itself. [AAAI proceedings entry and paper](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/39642).
- **Revised residual and decision.** The special ability to invent an explicit synthetic item for a hidden condition is itself part of Drescher's original mechanism; hidden-state prediction maintenance was then extended in 2004. Intrinsic exploration and hierarchical behavior have their own schema descendants and LIDA integration. I find no remaining new computational primitive here. Keep a small reproduction only if it isolates interpretability, controlled concept verification, or memory growth against Holmes–Isbell, CLASM, Schema Networks and modern object-centric causal RL. The new direct source audit downgrades AR-22 to established architecture archaeology and HY-25 to a low-priority baseline comparison.

#### SHRUTI capacity note — mechanism collision and hardware boundary

The 1993 SHRUTI paper establishes temporal synchrony as a binding mechanism. Wendelken & Shastri's 2004 multiple-instantiation analysis makes one key limitation explicit: under the paper's biological synchronization assumptions, fewer than about eight simultaneous dynamic bindings are available; accommodating more simultaneous relation instances can fail for lack of binding slots. This is a representational/timing-capacity constraint, not only slow 1990s simulation. Faster digital hardware can emulate phase events more quickly, but a software emulation no longer demonstrates the same biological mechanism; removing the binding cap would require a changed representation. The AR-09 phase-code proposal therefore stays rejected as a broad new architecture. [Wendelken & Shastri, 2004](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09540090412331311932).

- **Resource record for this audit:** literature review and notebook update only; CPU-side. GPU use 0 GB, peak VRAM 0 GB, and no GPU process snapshot because no GPU experiment was launched.

### AR-23 — ADAPT: concurrent robot schemas with goal-directed perception (2004 archaeology)

- **Original computation.** ADAPT (Adaptive Dynamics and Active Perception for Thought) was designed to combine four lines: Soar-style production matching, impasses, subgoals and learned chunks; ACT-R-style declarative memory and probability/cost-based action utility; EPIC-style parallel perceptual processors; and Robot Schemas (RS) for concurrent real-time perception/action. An ADAPT schema combines sensory conditions, motor behavior, variables and temporal constraints. Schemas can be instantiated, connected into networks, and execute concurrently. The cognitive executive remains focused on one architectural goal/action at a time, while multiple task goals/behaviors can be active together. [Benjamin, Lyons & Lonsdale, ICCM 2004](https://storm.cis.fordham.edu/~lyons/Papers2/ICCM2004.pdf).
- **Information, unit and repeated operation.** The unit is a parameterized declarative-plus-executable schema: perception predicates and time intervals specify when the motor behavior should run, and connected schemas share variables/state. Each cycle updates working memory from parallel sensory processing; the executive refines schemas, binds variables, starts/suspends/terminates schema instances, or enters an impasse. It then either searches over alternatives or uses stored goal-success and time-cost estimates. Search-control decisions can be chunked; schema variants can be generalized from execution history by replacing constants with variables or widening numeric intervals.
- **Input/output, learning, inference and memory.** Input is low-level sensor data, task goals, and motor/temporal feedback; the paper also seeks language integration. Outputs are concurrent sensor-processing choices and motor control schemas. Learning consists of Soar chunking for executive decisions, empirical probability/cost tracking for schemas, and inductive generalization of stored schemas. Inference combines symbolic subgoal search at the executive level with simultaneous execution of reactive behavior networks at the task level. Long-term general schemas and active instances are declarative structures in Soar working memory; learned search chunks reside in production memory.
- **Intended advantage and applications.** The paper targets robots that need to coordinate moving parts and sensors continuously without planning every low-level action interleaving. Its example catches a rolling ball by running grasp, arm-motion and tracking schemas together. Active perception is intended to direct camera orientation and even low-level image processing toward goal-relevant regions, rather than running a uniform recognizer first. Other plausible uses include navigation with sensor costs, manipulation under occlusion, and language-grounded task execution.
- **Was it bad or early?** The architecture addresses a real historical gap: the authors found cognitive architectures awkward for robot-native concurrency and active perception. Their 2004 implementation was described as initial; testing had just begun on a Pioneer P2. At the time described, the robot could use sonar and bump sensors for simple navigation/pushing, while vision and language integration were still planned. Modern GPU perception, simulation, robotics middleware and abundant replay data could make richer schema grounding and active visual selection more practical. The missing ingredient was not compute alone: executive schema management, conflict arbitration, action synchronization, and learning the right concurrent behavior hierarchy remain hard. The architecture also deliberately limits the executive to one architectural action and one active architectural goal to avoid uncontrolled goal multiplication.
- **Closest known work / what might be new.** ADAPT itself is already an explicit deep hybrid, so “combine Soar, ACT-R, EPIC and behavior schemas” is closed prior art. Subsumption/behavior-based robotics, behavior trees, active vision, hierarchical RL/options, and current robot task-and-motion systems cover its broad control organization. The 1999 active-perception integration paper predates ADAPT, and current Behavior Tree practice formalizes modular reactive hierarchies; a 2026 LLM/VLM-to-BT system is an example of adding modern perception/planning but remains a conventional robotics stack. [Wasson et al., 1999](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0921-8890(99)00050-0); [Ögren & Sprague, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-control-042920-095314); [AGRI-BT, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.atech.2026.102298). I found no unique broad computational primitive left in ADAPT; novelty confidence **0/5**.
- **Small falsifiable prototype.** CPU simulation of catching a rolling object while managing occlusion, camera pan/zoom cost, arm delay and occasional missed motor commands. Compare an ADAPT-like controller with parallel declarative sensorimotor schemas and goal-conditioned sensing against (a) a modern behavior tree with reactive controllers, (b) sequential Soar-style subgoal planning, and (c) a learned hierarchical policy. Equalize sensor calls and action/control operations. Measure catch success, collision rate, recovery after delay/disturbance, perception compute, replan latency and schema/behavior reuse across object speeds. The revival claim fails if concurrency and goal-conditioned sensing do not beat the best reactive baseline at equal resources, or if schema conflict resolution and executive bookkeeping erase their gains. This is a controller comparison, not a new model-class experiment.

#### HY-26 — ADAPT's old-old hybrid × modern learned perception (demoted)

- **Constituents and coupling.** ADAPT's established Soar/ACT-R/EPIC/RS combination places declarative-plus-executable perceptual/motor schemas under an executive that can deliberate or use probability/cost estimates, while active perceptual modules filter incoming data based on current goals. A modern version could let learned visual features feed schema predicates and send schema goals back into region selection, sensor settings and action-conditioned feature updates. The feedback would change which pixels or sensors are processed and which executable behavior is active; it is not a one-way encoder-to-planner interface.
- **Why it changes behavior / strongest case.** It couples perception allocation, representation and concurrent control: uncertainty about an active schema can request a targeted view, and the new view can refine the active schema or cause its suspension. This may give a robot a transparent, resource-bounded way to preserve fast behavior while directing expensive learned perception toward a task question.
- **Prior art and failures.** Active visual perception has long been integrated with autonomous robot architectures; active-inference/behavior-tree combinations explicitly handle reactive perception/action under uncertainty; modern BT and vision-language systems combine learned perception with hierarchical task execution. ADAPT already states the central goal-conditioned loop. Residual novelty is negligible. Risks include mismatched learned feature and schema identity, unsafe concurrent actions, stale estimates of sensor cost, and a one-at-a-time executive bottleneck. **Novelty confidence: 0.05/5; keep only as an ablation baseline.**
- **Falsifier.** Use the AR-23 simulation with controlled lighting, occlusion and sensor latency. Compare uniform perception, a standalone active-perception policy, an ADAPT-like schema-conditioned learned perception loop, and a behavior-tree active-sensing baseline. If the feedback loop cannot improve task success per sensor-operation budget and recover from novel visual conditions, discard the revival.

#### AR-24 — Selfridge’s Pandemonium (1959): parallel feature evidence with adaptive demons

- **Original computation and unit.** The 1959 design is a layered parallel recognition system. Data/image demons pass the input; computational subdemons apply primitive tests or composed feature functions; class-specific cognitive demons combine the resulting evidence; a decision demon chooses the largest score. Its basic unit is an individually evaluable feature program (“subdemon”), not a neuron with a shared global update. Input is an image or event sequence; output is a score for each pattern and a winner. [Selfridge, *Pandemonium: A Paradigm for Learning*, in the 1959 NPL symposium proceedings](https://cse.buffalo.edu/~rapaport/719/pandemonium.pdf).
- **Information, memory and repeated operation.** The source stores input samples/measurements, a hand-selected vocabulary of primitive operations, feature-program parameters and class-specific weights. Every pass evaluates available subdemons in parallel, sums weighted evidence by cognitive demon, then selects the strongest response. For Morse recognition, Selfridge specifies roughly 150 computational subdemons and operations for equality, ordering, maxima, tracking averages and recent dot/dash history. The historical proposal was richer than a static feature detector: after supervised score feedback, feature weights are adjusted by hill climbing; low-worth subdemons can be removed; survivors can be mutated (“fission”) or paired by simple logical/continuous combinations (“conjugation”). The paper also proposes adapting the mechanisms that govern their own changes, but labels this speculative.
- **Learning and deployment.** Learning is supervised at first: an external scorer reports errors, and the system searches weight vectors and candidate feature programs. Selfridge only tentatively suggests confidence/consensus as a later self-monitoring signal and says the system should first learn to perform well under supervision. It is not demonstrated as a mature unsupervised or post-deployment continual learner. Inference itself remains a straightforward evidence-aggregation pass.
- **Was it bad or early?** It was partly early: the paper describes a 704-era implementation and says design choices were bound by economy and space; modern vector hardware and memory make large banks of feature/template evaluations much cheaper. But hardware was not its only bottleneck. The primitive grammar and task representation were manually chosen; hill climbing has local optima and weak credit assignment for useful new features; the proposal itself discusses false peaks and the risk of unproductive mutations. Large data and GPUs can make candidate evaluation cheaper, but they do not automatically supply the right feature grammar or a stable structural fitness signal.
- **Modernized already? Closest prior art.** Yes, in a narrow and informative revival. Larsen and Bundesen’s 1996 template-matching Pandemonium combined stored handwriting templates with weighted evidence from multiple template analyzers and reported 95.3% recognition of unconstrained digits using a mean of 37 templates per digit. This demonstrates that a restricted demon/evidence mechanism could work well on a concrete task, but it does not validate open-ended demon evolution or a general architecture. [Larsen & Bundesen, 1996, publisher abstract](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03200876). The larger neighborhood includes nearest-template and prototype classifiers, feature ensembles, learned convolutional features, mixture-of-experts, genetic programming and neural architecture search. These occupy most of the proposed broad territory.
- **Potential advantage and failure modes.** Parallel modular evidence can preserve useful partial clues, explain which features supported a decision, and let a small set of new templates/features be added without retraining a deep model. This is most plausible in low-data or resource-limited recognition with interpretable feature evidence. Failure modes are template growth, correlated demons double-counting evidence, mutation/selection overfitting the validation signal, sensitivity to nuisance transformations, and slower evaluation as every detector competes. It is unlikely to beat learned hierarchical visual representations on broad perception.
- **Possible residual and novelty.** A bounded continual learner that invents transparent local feature programs from prediction errors and retains only features that improve held-out performance under resource limits is a specific experimental question. It still overlaps feature construction, evolutionary program search, prototype learning and online feature selection. Novelty confidence: **1/5 as a general class; at most 2/5 for a sharply defined resource-bounded online feature-program selection rule**, pending a direct search of that exact rule. No new C-number is assigned.
- **Small falsifier.** CPU-only, compare (a) weighted template-demons with a capped exemplar/feature bank, (b) nearest-template classification, and (c) a compact learned baseline on a few-shot handwritten-character task with a later style/noise shift. Match training examples, retained memory and number of candidate evaluations. Report accuracy, calibration, memory, update time and examples-to-recovery. The revival claim fails if weighted evidence gives no benefit over nearest-template at matched memory, or if demon growth only wins by consuming a larger bank. The test is a bounded revival benchmark, not a novelty demonstration.

#### HY-27 — Pandemonium × modern perception or program search (rejected as broad hybrid)

- **Constituents and exact coupling.** Selfridge contributes separately scored feature programs, evidence aggregation and selection/mutation; a learned perception encoder or modern program-search method would contribute robust primitive features or cheaper candidate generation. A nontrivial version would let prediction residuals nominate new feature programs over learned intermediate features, score the programs on held-out environments, and feed accepted programs back into the class demons and future feature search. The feedback changes representation growth and the learning rule, rather than simply putting a template bank beside an encoder.
- **Why it could behave differently.** It could combine invariant learned visual features with sparse, inspectable feature programs that adapt to new styles without full-model updates. Yet the encoder supplies much of the representation advantage, and the search/selection loop is directly adjacent to genetic programming, neuroevolution, differentiable architecture search and learned prototype systems. The 1996 Pandemonium already combines template matching and weighted feature evidence.
- **Failure modes and experiment.** Likely failures are search overfit, redundant programs, encoder drift invalidating stored programs, high scoring cost, and a learned encoder doing all useful work. Test on the same few-shot style-shift protocol as AR-24 with fixed encoder features; compare the coupled feature-program learner with the encoder alone, frozen templates and random program search. Reject if it cannot improve recovery or calibration at the same memory and scoring budget. **Decision:** retain only as a possible ablation inside AR-24; novelty confidence **0.05/5**. This is not “old architecture + modern model” novelty by itself.

#### AR-25 — AERA: executable causal-relational models in a resource-bounded runtime

- **Original computation.** AERA (first expanded as Autocatalytic Endogenous Reflective Architecture; now also called Autonomous Empirical Reasoning Architecture) is an implemented cognitive/control architecture, not a dormant idea awaiting GPUs. Its knowledge unit is an executable relational model: a left-hand pattern and right-hand pattern with guards encode a conditional causal relation. Matching a fact to the left pattern creates a forward-chaining prediction; matching a goal to the right pattern creates a backward-chained subgoal. Each match schedules a job. Model-execution traces and prediction/goal outcomes become new inputs, allowing self-modeling. A value/priority scheduler executes many jobs concurrently and can delay lower-priority work. [Nivel et al., 2013, *Bounded Recursive Self-Improvement*](https://people.idsia.ch/~steunebrink/Publications/TR13_bounded_recursive_self-improvement.pdf); [official AERA overview](https://openaera.org/).
- **Input/output, learning, inference and memory.** Inputs are timestamped, structured sensory or internal facts plus goals and action/device feedback. Outputs are predictions, subgoals, commands and learned causal-relational models. Prediction monitors update model reliability; unexpected prediction failures and goal successes trigger candidate pattern extraction. Candidate models are guesses guided in part by temporal precedence, then evaluated by later prediction evidence; unreliable models are phased out/deleted, and least-recently-used models/composite states can be garbage-collected. Inference runs forward prediction and backward goal decomposition in parallel. Memory is the shared, dynamically growing store of facts, models, composite states, traces and runnable jobs; the Replicode language/runtime was built to support pattern matching and dynamic code production. This is online learning during execution, not a separate training stage.
- **Historical results and limits.** The authors report a simulated interview demonstration: in E1 the agent learned from about 2.5 minutes / 17 observed turns and then made zero errors in the tested subsequent interaction; E2 used a 100-word vocabulary and six object categories, required about 20 hours of observation, and also reported zero errors in tested interaction. The paper attributes the E2 time increase to sentence combinatorics. These are substantive implementation results, but the task has a small seeded ontology, engineered perceptual inputs and a constrained interaction protocol; there is no matched comparison to modern learned world models or an independent broad benchmark. [Primary report, E1 results](https://people.idsia.ch/~steunebrink/Publications/TR13_bounded_recursive_self-improvement.pdf) and [E2 task/result details](https://people.idsia.ch/~steunebrink/Publications/AGI14_seed-AGI.pdf).
- **Was it bad or early? Has it been modernized?** AERA was explicitly designed to cope with limited time, memory and compute through resource-aware scheduling; its core demonstrations ran on CPU hardware. Faster CPUs, cheap simulation and modern encoders could widen the range of sensory inputs, but compute does not solve temporal confounding in causal induction, combinatorial model/job growth, dependence on seeded sensor/action primitives, or the substantial language/runtime complexity. The project publishes an implementation overview, and a 2020 paper formalizes autonomous cumulative transfer learning as an adjacent extension; neither makes AERA's known runtime a new architecture class. [Official implementation overview](https://openaera.org/implementation/), [ACTL paper](https://alumni.media.mit.edu/~kris/ftp/AutonCumulTransfLearn-SheikhlarEtAl-AGI-2020.pdf).
- **Closest prior art and possible advantage.** The broad class is established: NARS and other resource-bounded reasoning architectures, Soar/ACT-R and production systems, model-based planning such as Dyna, and executable-rule systems overlap with substantial parts. AERA’s exact integration of executable causal patterns, prediction monitoring, reflective traces and value-scheduled jobs is the known AERA architecture itself; it is not a new candidate for this notebook. Its plausible strength is transparent cumulative learning and graceful compute allocation in structured, interactive domains. Likely failures are causal confounding, uncontrolled combinatorics, brittle perceptual front ends, expensive matching and difficult independent reproduction. Novelty confidence: **0/5 as a new broad model class**.
- **Small falsifiable reproduction.** Use the public hand-grab-sphere learning example, then a CPU-only six-feature/three-action microworld with one delayed, confounded transition that changes regime. At a fixed job budget compare the AERA scheduler/model acquisition with FIFO scheduling, no failure-triggered acquisition, and a compact Bayesian/Dyna model-based baseline. Hold seed, input stream, actions, compute and memory cap constant; measure held-out transition prediction, novel goal compositions, recovery after regime change, deadline misses, job/model growth and CPU time. Falsify the proposed resource-bounded transfer benefit if the full loop does not improve held-out transfer/recovery at equal job budget, or if it needs the changed rule or feature supplied in the seed. This is a reproduction/ablation plan; it does not promote AERA as novel.

#### C031 adversarial correction — localized homeostatic reorganization is occupied prior art

An independent prior-art audit found a closer historical collision than the earlier C031 entry recorded. Powers, Clark and McFarland’s 1960 N-system senses error in critical intrinsic variables and explicitly considers reorganizing randomly across a hierarchy, localizing change in regions with error signals, or using a more efficient rule. The authors say they do not yet know the mechanism. This is already the central “violation → localize → reorganize” conceptual shape of C031. Ashby’s Homeostat supplies the earlier viability-triggered reorganization loop. [Powers et al., 1960, Part II](https://www.iapct.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Powers-et-al-1960-part2.pdf); [Ashby, *Design for a Brain*](https://www.ashby.info/Ashby%20-%20Design%20for%20a%20Brain%20-%20The%20Origin%20of%20Adaptive%20Behavior.pdf).

The engineering prior art is also direct. Boem et al. distribute local fault detection and active isolation over coupled subsystems, modify inputs to isolate faults under local state/input constraints, then reconfigure or disconnect the affected controller/subsystem using distributed tube MPC. This already captures local fault diagnosis plus constrained local recovery in a modern control setting. [Boem et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1109/TCNS.2019.2913557). Adaptive actuator diagnosis/accommodation and control allocation add further collision. C031 as a general architecture is therefore demoted to a fault-tolerant-control benchmark; estimated novelty is effectively zero (roughly **0.03/5** at most).

The original small C031 falsifier also needs a safety correction: a trigger that fires only after a hard viability bound is crossed cannot claim to preserve safety during diagnosis/recovery. Any comparison must include a shared predictive safety wrapper and matched probing/action budgets. A fair CPU study would compare localized reorganization with distributed active fault isolation plus local reconfiguration, adaptive actuator-effectiveness estimation/control allocation, and global Ashby-style reorganization on coupled plants with noisy sensors and hidden coupling changes. Track integrated bound violations, recovery time, unaffected-loop retention, false isolation, probe energy and CPU time. Keep only if it beats the strongest distributed fault-tolerant-control baseline at matched budgets; otherwise close C031 as an established control pattern.

#### AR-26 — Tierra/Avida digital evolution: computation as an ecology of self-reproducing programs

- **Original computation and unit.** In Tierra, organisms are instruction sequences that execute on virtual CPUs, reproduce by copying their code with errors/mutations, and compete for CPU time and memory in a shared “soup.” Avida kept the virtual-CPU / self-replicating-program substrate but gave organisms protected memory and explicit task rewards in additional CPU cycles; local population interactions can produce parasites, cooperation, specialization and ecological networks. The primitive is not a neural layer: it is a mutating executable population whose resource economy creates selection. [Ray, 1991, *An Approach to the Synthesis of Life*](https://tomray.me/pubs/alife2/Ray1991AnApproachToTheSynthesisOfLife.pdf); [Ofria, Bryson & Wilke, 2004, *Avida: Evolution Experiments with Self-Replicating Computer Programs*](https://cse.msu.edu/~ofria/pubs/2004OfriaEtAl.pdf).
- **Information, operations, learning and memory.** The genome represents a program, its executable behavior, and replication machinery; the environment stores the population, virtual registers/stacks, shared resources and task interfaces. Each execution step consumes virtual CPU; successful replication creates descendants with mutation; task reward may raise an organism's execution budget, allowing new computational traits to spread. Inference is whatever the evolved program computes. Learning is population-level variation, selection and ecological interaction across generations, not differentiable parameter fitting or an organism's explicit update rule. It can continue after deployment only if reproduction, mutation, selection and an environment remain active.
- **Was it bad or early?** More hardware clearly permits larger populations, longer runs, more heterogeneous worlds and richer measurements. Yet the strongest historical failure is structural and remains unresolved: the environment's instruction set and resource rules delimit what programs can do; narrow replication pressure selects short/fast replicators and parasites rather than generally useful intelligence; task rewards turn the experiment into externally designed evolutionary optimization; removing parsimony can produce larger but junk-filled genomes. Standish's Tierra experiments found no increase in measured organismal complexity in a size-neutral run, and later explored how strong parsimony favors simplification while relaxed parsimony inflates size without complexity. [Standish, 2002](https://arxiv.org/abs/nlin/0210027); [Standish, 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/nlin/0604026). The issue is not simply that 1990s CPUs were too slow.
- **Modernization, uses, and closest prior art.** Avida remains a public scientific platform, with a C++ implementation and a repository update in January 2025; researchers still use it to study evolution, complexity and computational life. [Avida repository](https://github.com/devosoft/avida); [recent Avida research overview](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7123229/). Modern CPUs/GPUs can accelerate ecological simulation and population experiments, but the core concept is already a mature artificial-life/evolutionary-computation family. The strongest use cases are experimental biology, evolved software, robust program synthesis and studying open-ended evolution—not general-purpose inference on ordinary data. Genetic programming, evolutionary algorithms, novelty search and quality-diversity search cover task-directed variants; artificial chemistries and digital evolution are direct substrate-level neighbors.
- **Possible residual and novelty.** A new AI architecture would need an explicit computational advantage from live ecological evolution—for example, learned executable organisms that compose, reproduce and compete for shared computation while retaining capabilities across nonstationary tasks. But the unresolved open-endedness problem, objective/selection design, and competition between survival and task utility make this speculative. Novelty confidence: **0/5 as an established architecture family; 1/5 for a precise modern coupling of ecology with useful lifelong program synthesis**, with no evidence yet of broad utility.
- **Small falsifier.** CPU-only digital-logic microworld with a fixed virtual ISA and multiple tasks that appear sequentially. Compare a Tierra/Avida-style reproducing population against genetic programming and a standard evolutionary strategy at equal total instruction budget and population memory. Reward old and new tasks after distribution shifts; measure retained skill, genuinely new program behaviors, complexity (not genome length alone), task coverage, and instruction cost. Reject the useful-continual-learning hypothesis if population ecology only improves in-world replication, if growth is junk/parasites, or if the task-fitness evolutionary baseline matches the result at lower cost. This is a research discriminator, not a proposed run until platform setup and operational complexity measures are specified.

#### HY-28 — digital-organism ecology × modern neural learners (demoted)

A hybrid in which executable digital organisms can call learned neural components, use shared compute as a resource, and reproduce only when their complete neural/program policy succeeds could change selection from weight optimization to ecosystem-level competition. The hoped-for gain is task-program diversity and survival of useful behaviors under task change; the likely failure is that externally designed rewards and mutation still do the essential optimization while adding simulation overhead and population collapse. Neuroevolution, genetic programming over differentiable modules, quality-diversity, population-based training and neural architecture search already occupy the broad combination. Small test: on sequential logic tasks with an abrupt reward reversal, compare the hybrid against the strongest neuroevolution and population-based baselines at matched forward-pass/instruction budgets, testing behavior retention, novelty and energy. If it does not beat them on held-out shifts or if the neural component masks the ecology's contribution, reject. **Novelty confidence: 0.05/5; no new candidate added.**
