### Additional computational-evolution archaeology (2026-09-27)

#### AR-27 — Barricelli’s symbioorganisms (1953–1954): local symbiotic reproduction without program genomes

- **Original computation and unit.** Barricelli’s substrate is a one-dimensional space-time lattice of signed integers and empty cells, not an explicit virtual machine. Each number is a heritable unit: a positive value moves that many cells right into the next generation; a negative value moves left. In the symbiosis rule, a number reproduces only when it lands below a *different* number; its copy is placed at an offset given by the partner. A conditional collision/mutation rule can create new signed values. Repeating the local lattice transition yields numerical “organisms,” recombination, parasites and ecological competition. The 1954 Italian paper was translated and critically edited in 2026; its editors state that it is the earliest published computational-evolution experiment they know of. [Barricelli, Bianchi & Taylor, 2026 English translation of the 1954 paper](https://www.tim-taylor.com/papers/barricelli2026numerical.pdf).
- **Input, output, memory and learning.** Input is a randomized initial row and an explicitly selected family of reproduction/mutation rules, including region-specific variants; output is the evolving lattice and the observed population/ecology of recurring numerical sequences. The lattice itself stores heredity and environmental context—there is no separate genotype interpreter, learned latent state or downstream task answer. Selection acts on viability and persistence under the local transition rules. Learning is therefore population evolution, not within-organism inference or a task-directed update.
- **Was it bad or early?** Compute was a real limit: Barricelli reports the longest Princeton run as 5,400 generations by 512 values, and says larger machines were needed for more complex organisms. But the paper also gives strong structural negatives. With the same rules everywhere, the lattice became homogeneous or disorganized within a few hundred generations; varying mutation rules across manually divided regions prolonged diversity, but most evolutionary runs still paused at local fitness maxima and all reported processes were short-lived. The 2026 editorial correction finds that the interpretation of the flagship random-start figure holds for only about 20% of comparable random starts; the other 80% settle into static or simple repeating states. More compute improves mapping and replication, but cannot by itself remove the need to hand-design a rule ecology that prevents collapse or make emergent organisms solve useful tasks.
- **Modernization, strengths and closest work.** Modern CPU simulation can repeat thousands of seeds, explore larger spaces, and report distributions rather than relying on a few hand-read runs. The substrate’s unusual strength is symbiotic assembly: reproduction itself can require useful interaction between distinct inherited units. But it sits within artificial life, cellular/automata chemistries, cooperative coevolution, Tierra/Avida and autocatalytic systems. It is an important computational-evolution substrate, not a broadly useful reasoning architecture. A still-open question is whether locally interdependent replicators produce scalable reusable computation without hand-authored regions and tasks; no such advantage was established in the checked source.
- **Small falsifier and decision.** Reimplement the exact signed-number update rules on CPU. Run 1,000 random initial states for 1,000 generations, then continue a stratified subset of 100 seeds to the 512×5,400 reference scale; compare uniform and region-varying mutation as separate arms. Measure persistent lineage count, occupancy, repeatable genotype diversity, complexity (not just sequence length), run duration and sensitivity to initial conditions. If the reported variety is rare, or survives only with externally specified regional mutation, reject the claim that the architecture was mainly waiting for hardware. **Decision:** preserve as a high-value negative archaeology case and possible substrate benchmark; novelty as a substrate is historical, novelty as a general intelligence class is **0/5**.

#### HY-29 — Barricelli symbiosis × Avida task evaluation (rejected as a new architecture)

- **Constituents and coupling.** Barricelli contributes locally interdependent reproduction, where different numerical units can reproduce only through a partner; Avida contributes executable genomes, virtual CPU budgets and task-dependent merit. A possible coupling would make each heritable component perform a subcomputation and let partner interactions yield both reproduction and task reward, so assemblies of components can become executable policies. This changes how programs assemble and reproduce, rather than merely combining a simulator with a classifier.
- **Why it might differ / why it is occupied.** It could allow task modules to assemble by mutually beneficial interaction instead of being fixed in a program tree, potentially supporting functionally specialized subpopulations. But the fitness/task interface remains designer-selected and each organism still adapts through evolutionary variation. Cooperative coevolution, symbiotic neuroevolution, genetic programming and Avida task rewards already cover these ingredients. No new learning rule or general architecture is evident.
- **Small disproof test.** In a changing Boolean-composition task suite, compare partner-required co-reproduction with ordinary Avida-style task-reward evolution and cooperative coevolution at matched instruction, population and memory budgets. Measure task coverage, reusable subprograms, lineage survival after reward shifts and simulator cost. Reject if symbiosis only boosts in-soup reproduction, harms held-out task performance, or matches cooperative coevolution at extra cost. **Decision:** close as a broad hybrid; novelty confidence **0.05/5**.

#### AR-28 — Stringmol automata chemistry and universal constructors (2010–2017 revival)

- **Original computation and unit.** Stringmol represents molecules as strings containing template symbols and functional opcodes. Molecules bind through complementary sequence matching; a bound pair executes a small program-like reaction that can read, write, split or transform strings. The same type of object can be both hereditary description and active machinery, so information and computation are physically coupled in the artificial chemistry rather than separated into a fixed genome and interpreter. Reactions, mutation-on-copy and molecule populations form the repeated operation. [University of York Stringmol language specification](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~ss44/bib/ss/nonstd/tr458.htm); [Hickinbotham et al., 2016, *Maximizing the Adjacent Possible in Automata Chemistries*](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/114475/1/alifej_16.pdf).
- **Learning, memory and output.** The system has no general task input or answer output. Its evolving strings store programs, templates and molecular state; stochastic binding/reaction and mutation create offspring or new species; selection comes from viability and resource competition. Learning is population-level evolution over molecules and their semantics. There is no task-conditioned inference mechanism unless an experimenter adds a domain and selection rule.
- **Modernization/prior art.** This was directly modernized in 2017: a Stringmol universal-constructor architecture co-evolved genome, copier and constructor, with viable offspring and observed shifts in what the genomic description meant. This is a real mechanistic result, but it is explicit artificial-life/semantic-closure prior art and does not demonstrate general-purpose useful learning. [Clark, Hickinbotham & Stepney, 2017, *Journal of the Royal Society Interface*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28515326/). The paper also makes the fragility measurable with repeated trial/extinction analysis. CPU simulation and better logging help explore seeds and mutation/decay regimes; GPUs or automatic differentiation do not address the lack of a task representation or selection mechanism.
- **Potential advantage, weakness and residual.** Same-substrate descriptions and machinery may enable semantic change, self-modification and compositional transitions that fixed virtual-machine instruction sets suppress. The biggest weaknesses are viability collapse, hard-to-control stochastic dynamics, arbitrary chemistry rules, no grounded task competence and very long search horizons. The exact UCA mechanism is already implemented; any novel claim would need a robust task-learning result beyond self-reproduction. Novelty confidence: **0/5 as a substrate family, 1/5 as an AI direction before a demonstrated task-evaluable coupling**.
- **Falsifier.** Re-run one published replicase/UCA seed under mutation and decay sweeps; compare co-evolving the copier/constructor with a fixed copier and genome. Track viable population lifetime, semantic transitions, task performance on a small external compositional task, and instruction/reaction budget. Reject a useful-learning claim if only self-replication survives, if behavior is not task-evaluable, or if coevolution has no robustness advantage at matched reaction counts. Keep as an archaeology benchmark, not a candidate.

#### AR-29 — Evochora: current thermodynamic/spatial digital-evolution platform (watchlist, not AI architecture)

Evochora is a current author-developed platform that makes digital-world physics a configurable experimental variable. Its documented mechanism uses code-bearing organisms in an n-dimensional spatial grid, local pointers, fuzzy label addressing, molecule ownership, and separate energy/entropy budgets; plugin points vary resources, mutation, death/recycling and instruction interception. The project reports a defensive self-replicator, long simulations and a first heritable selective sweep, while explicitly leaving cooperation, multicellularity and reaction chemistry as open experiments. [Project scientific overview](https://github.com/evochora/evochora/blob/main/docs/SCIENTIFIC_OVERVIEW.md).

This is useful as a modern response to historical scale and reproducibility limits: deterministic random seeds, parallel CPU execution, replay and telemetry make controlled physics sweeps possible. The important caveat is provenance: these performance and sweep claims are from the project’s own documentation, not yet an independent replication in the sources checked here. The platform studies digital evolution, not perception, reasoning or task generalization. It overlaps Tierra/Avida, spatial artificial life, thermodynamic agents and artificial chemistry; “energy+entropy” is an experimental control mechanism, not by itself a new intelligence architecture. The smallest worthwhile CPU study is to independently reproduce its published selective sweep, then ablate entropy accounting against energy-only mortality while holding mutation, population and instruction budgets fixed. Measure stable population time, viable lineage diversity, heritable adaptation and error catastrophe. If entropy offers no reproducible effect beyond tuned resource costs, the thermodynamic novelty is only a configurable selection rule. **Status:** watch the project and replication evidence; no candidate added.

- **Continuation/resource update:** This second pass checked the 2026 Barricelli translation, Stringmol’s 2017 peer-reviewed UCA paper, and Evochora’s own current technical claims. All were browser/CPU-side. No experiment or GPU process was started; GPU use attributable to this work remains 0 GB; live shared GPU usage is unknown. The newest archaeology answers the “born too early?” question in a useful way: compute was a real bottleneck for some old experiments, but their observed collapse, externally specified niches, objective gaps and weak repeatability remain after compute increases. AR-27 through AR-29 are not additions to C001–C031; HY-29 is rejected. Do not edit `04_RESEARCH_STATE.md` or any source files.

### Further early-learning archaeology — Minsky’s SNARC and random-net proposals

#### AR-30 — SNARC (1951–1954): stochastic pathways reinforced by recent-use traces

- **Original computation and unit.** Minsky’s 1954 dissertation calls the device a local-reinforcement circuit in a neural-analog network and includes a section describing SNARC, built with Dean Edmonds at Harvard in summer 1951. Its unit is a stochastic neuron-to-neuron pathway whose potentiometer controls the chance of signal transmission. A capacitor/magnetic-clutch mechanism preserves a short-lived trace of recent firing; an external reinforcement event mechanically changes the probability of currently eligible pathways. The network had roughly 40 neuron-like units, random connections, and a maze-light interface. Minsky’s 1952 technical-report title is “A Neural-Analogue Calculator Based upon a Probability Model of Reinforcement”; Minsky’s bibliography says it describes a reward signal facilitating recently used pathways. The report itself was not located as an accessible scan in this pass, so circuit details are cited to the dissertation and author bibliography rather than reconstructed from a photo or popular retelling. [Minsky, 1954 dissertation, especially §5.2 “The SNARC machine”](https://people.csail.mit.edu/brooks/idocs/Marvin_Minsky_PhD_Princeton_1953_1954.pdf); [Minsky’s publication bibliography](https://web.mit.edu/dxh/www/marvin/web.media.mit.edu/~minsky/Bibliography.html).
- **Represented information and repeated operation.** The path probabilities store what actions have tended to be selected and reinforced; temporary local activity traces identify which path segments were recently used. The system receives the maze’s sensory pattern, samples a route through its stochastic dynamics, and receives reward or extinction from a trainer after a result. It outputs movement behavior. Its persistent memory is distributed in connection probabilities, while short-term eligibility is physical state in the synapse-like element. It does not store an explicit maze map, predicted transition model, or symbolic plan.
- **Learning and inference.** Learning is local, online, and reward-modulated: local activity leaves an eligibility trace; later reinforcement increases or decreases the probability of the recently active pathway. Inference is stochastic propagation through the recurrent network; action selection is trial-and-error rather than search over a learned world model. The system can continue adapting during deployment if rewards continue. The task demonstration is a narrow embodied control loop, not evidence of generalization across maze families.
- **Was it bad or early?** Physical construction constrained size, repeatability, and the number of trajectories that could be tested; modern CPUs can simulate thousands of seeds and GPUs can batch network activity. That removes an implementation bottleneck, but the major algorithmic limits remain: random exploration wastes trials, terminal reward gives poor credit to long action sequences, stochastic path strengthening can overfit a single maze, and random wiring supplies no mechanism for learning reusable structure or planning. A larger random net does not itself invent abstractions. Minsky’s own 1961 analysis says operant reinforcement needs a trainer to select successful behavior, and identifies distribution of credit across a complex strategy as a serious problem; it suggests hierarchical partial-goal reinforcement and graded training as aids. [Minsky, “Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence,” 1961](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~barto/courses/cs687/Minsky60steps.pdf).
- **Modern status and nearest prior work.** The central learning primitive is now represented by reward-modulated Hebbian plasticity and three-factor learning rules: local eligibility plus a modulatory learning/reward signal. Williams’ REINFORCE formalizes connectionist reinforcement updates as gradient-following, while e-prop combines synaptic eligibility with learning signals for online recurrent spiking-network learning. These methods substantially generalize or analyze the local-trace idea, although e-prop is not a faithful SNARC reconstruction. Reservoir computing and stochastic neural networks separately occupy fixed/random recurrent substrate computation. A 2023 study evolves heterogeneous neuron parameters while leaving network weights random, showing a current random-network direction but not reviving SNARC’s reward-operated potentiometers. [Williams, 1992](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00992696); [Bellec et al., e-prop, 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-17236-y); [Pedersen & Risi, GECCO 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15945).
- **Use case, possible advantage, and weakness.** The plausible niche is cheap online adaptation in a small recurrent controller with delayed outcome signals and no backpropagation pipeline. Its strength is a physically local update with memory of recent causal activity. Its weakness is that a global reward pulse still does not determine which of many eligible actions caused the outcome; more hardware accelerates bad exploration just as readily as good exploration. It also lacks a competitive modern perception mechanism and meaningful evidence on transfer.
- **What could remain novel and novelty judgment.** No new architecture class remains in the described mechanism. A specialized physical implementation could matter under measured energy/latency constraints, but the architecture claim would then require matched joules, accuracy and adaptation tests against modern local-plasticity and control baselines. Broad class novelty: **0/5**. No direct modern faithful SNARC revival was located in this targeted search; this is a search result, not proof that none exists.
- **Small falsifiable prototype.** CPU-only stochastic maze family with held-out layouts, a mid-run obstacle change, sparse terminal reward and equal environment interactions. Compare a faithful eligibility-only stochastic recurrent controller, the same controller with a learned value/critic signal, tabular Q-learning where state size permits, and a small REINFORCE or actor-critic baseline. Match trainable state/parameter count and reward access; report success per episode, transfer to new layouts, post-change recovery, variance across seeds and computation per action. The useful-revival claim fails if local traces do not improve a practical latency/energy measure or if they lose on sample efficiency and transfer at matched interaction budget. **Not run; no novel-class claim.**

#### HY-30 — SNARC eligibility traces × Minsky’s learned secondary reinforcement (rejected as a new hybrid)

- **Constituents and exact coupling.** SNARC supplies stochastic action pathways with recent-activity eligibility. In his 1961 article, Minsky sketches an additional unit U that learns which environmental cues have been associated with primary reward; those cues can later produce substitute, “secondary” reinforcement signals. Coupled to the eligibility network, a learned cue would locally reinforce recently active paths before the original terminal reward arrives, potentially chaining useful subgoals. This changes the source and timing of the plasticity signal, rather than simply attaching an external reward predictor to a policy.
- **Why behavior might change.** The hoped-for effect is shorter temporal credit assignment under sparse reward: predictors of future reward become internal signals that reinforce upstream actions. The main failure is self-reinforcing error. A spurious cue can generate its own reward-like signal and stabilize a bad action chain; Minsky explicitly notes that recursive conditioned reinforcement risks a positive feedback loop that needs stabilization. Environmental correlations may also fail after layout or task changes.
- **Prior art and novelty.** This is not an unrecognized hybrid: Minsky directly describes the secondary-reinforcement extension and its stability concern in 1961. Temporal-difference learning, actor-critic value bootstrapping, conditioned reinforcement, learned reward models, and reward-modulated eligibility traces already cover the general way predicted outcome signals shape local action updates. The old-plus-old interaction is historically interesting but not a new class. [Minsky, 1961, secondary reinforcement discussion](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~barto/courses/cs687/Minsky60steps.pdf); [three-factor eligibility review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6079224/).
- **Small disproof test and decision.** If revisited as a benchmark, use two maze families where an initially reliable cue is later decorrelated from success. Compare terminal-reward SNARC, secondary-reinforcement SNARC, and TD(λ)/actor-critic under equal reward observations and action budgets. Measure early learning speed, false-reward lock-in after decorrelation, transfer, and recovery. Reject the useful hybrid hypothesis if faster early learning is purchased with severe instability, or if a TD baseline recovers faster with no more labels. Novelty confidence: **0.02/5**; keep only as a historical test case.

#### AR-31 — Minsky’s 1961 random-connection Bayes nets: stochastic feature sampling for classification

Minsky’s 1961 “Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence” gives a separate, more statistical use for random connectivity: if a task has many weakly informative properties, sample paths through a random connection net and weight the resulting evidence for class decisions. It explicitly relates the units to Selfridge’s data and cognitive demons. The paper derives connection-weight updates from observed property/class events and notes a speed–variance tradeoff controlled by the decay constant. This is an early random-feature/weighted-evidence proposal, distinct from SNARC’s reward-modulated action learning; it is not a claim that the same details appear in the separate 1961 Minsky–Selfridge paper. [Minsky, 1961, §§III-F–G](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~barto/courses/cs687/Minsky60steps.pdf); [Minsky & Selfridge, “Learning in Random Nets,” bibliographic record](https://web.mit.edu/dxh/www/marvin/web.media.mit.edu/~minsky/Bibliography.html).

The author’s own boundary is unusually clear: additive evidence can estimate a maximum-likelihood decision under conditional-independence assumptions, but randomly generated properties and weights will not capture relational figures such as “two separated parts,” normalize position and scale, or extract useful nonadditive combinations even with large nets and long training. In the same paper, Minsky says more complex visual discrimination needs recursive processing. Modern compute addresses the number of random features but not the missing invariance/relational representation. Random Fourier features, random kitchen-sinks models, reservoir readouts, and deep learned representations already cover sampled nonlinear bases and learned evidence combinations; this is historical lineage, not an open architecture family. No separate candidate is added.

- **Continuation/resource record:** This pass checked the 1954 dissertation’s indexed SNARC section, Minsky’s own publication bibliography and 1961 paper, plus primary modern references on REINFORCE and e-prop. Work was browser/CPU-side. **No experiment ran, no GPU process was started, GPU use 0 GB and peak VRAM 0 GB; live shared GPU use remains unknown because there was no reason to query it.** AR-30 and AR-31 are archaeology entries, HY-30 is rejected; C001–C031 remain unchanged. The finding reinforces the notebook’s skeptical pattern: 1950s hardware constrained scale, but Minsky already identified credit assignment, representation, invariance and training curriculum as deeper limits. ### Program-evolution archaeology — Friedberg’s instruction-reinforcement learner

#### AR-32 — Friedberg’s Learning Machine (1958–1959): evolve a program by reinforcing instruction slots

- **Original computation and unit.** Friedberg’s unit is an instruction slot in a stored-program computer. A generator samples whole candidate programs (Minsky reports 64 instructions for the discussed experiment), runs each on a small simulated machine, evaluates success, and increases the chance that instructions found at successful positions are selected again. Part II varies the generation and reinforcement operators and tests decomposition/priming. The primary Part I abstract explicitly describes trying many candidate programs and favoring instructions associated with success. [Friedberg, 1958, Part I](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.21.0002); [Friedberg, Dunham & North, 1959, Part II](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.33.0282).
- **Input, output, learning, inference and memory.** The input is a tiny programming task plus a success monitor; the output is an executable instruction sequence. Each evaluation is one complete trial. The candidate pool and instruction-position statistics store knowledge; learning is stochastic generate–execute–score–update, not differentiable fitting. Inference is execution by the target machine. The program persists after deployment, but it does not autonomously update unless evaluation and selection continue.
- **Was it bad or early?** More compute would make more program trials possible, and better virtual machines/evaluators would simplify reproduction. But the central failure is algorithmic credit assignment: success or failure of the full program is attributed to individual fixed positions even though instructions interact as subroutines and control-flow hierarchies. Minsky’s 1961 analysis reports that the Part I learner found extremely simple programs at around 1,000 times the random-search cost; he argues Part II’s modifications moved the search step size toward random behavior and did not demonstrate learning above chance. He identifies module/function-level credit as essential and notes that Part II’s clearest improvement came from solving subproblems sequentially without reinforcement. This is a contemporary critique, not a modern re-evaluation of all of Friedberg’s results. [Minsky, “Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence,” §III-D](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~barto/courses/cs687/Minsky60steps.pdf).
- **Modern status / closest prior art.** This is an early form of evolutionary program synthesis, and that family is not dormant: genetic programming adds structured trees and crossover; grammar-guided search and enumerative synthesis use task-appropriate program spaces; CEGIS uses counterexamples to constrain revisions; AutoML-Zero evolves learning algorithms from primitive operations. These methods address representation and search operators, but they do not make program synthesis generally cheap. Scaling still depends on a good DSL, efficient semantic tests, reward density, and search-space structure. [AutoML-Zero, ICML 2020](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/real20a.html).
- **Potential strength and failure modes.** It treats a task solver itself as the learned object and can discover procedures that are reusable at run time. With a small DSL and exact evaluator, candidate code can be inspectable and testable. Failure modes are sparse whole-program credit, destructive one-site updates, execution loops, brittle exact-task overfitting, and the combinatorial blowup of useful instruction sequences. Modern evaluation speed addresses throughput but not the credit/representation problem.
- **What could remain novel and novelty judgment.** The original mechanism is historical program evolution, not a new architecture. A modern case would have to change the search/learning interaction—e.g., use verified subprogram contracts as local credit and revise only modules whose counterexamples violate a contract. But module-level evolutionary operators, grammar-guided synthesis, counterexample-guided repair, and hierarchical task decomposition already cover most of that proposal. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 as a class; under 0.1/5 for the generic contract-credit hybrid below.**
- **Small falsifiable prototype.** CPU-only synthesis of short Boolean programs, then held-out compositions of learned subroutines. Compare Friedberg-style fixed-slot reinforcement, grammar-guided genetic programming, a CEGIS baseline, and a hybrid with typed modules and local contract tests. Match total candidate executions and memory; measure solve rate, evaluator calls to solution, held-out composition accuracy, retained module utility after task changes, code size and invalid-program rate. Reject the usefulness claim if local contracts fail to reduce search cost at matched execution budget or yield modules that do not transfer. **Not run; retained as an archaeology benchmark, not a candidate.**

#### HY-31 — Friedberg instruction-slot reinforcement × contract-guided modular repair (demoted)

- **Source mechanisms and exact coupling.** Friedberg contributes stochastic program generation and selection from execution outcomes. Contract-guided synthesis contributes typed module boundaries, executable postconditions and counterexamples. The proposed coupling would give local update credit to a module only when its contract is violated, then use the failing counterexample to change that module’s instruction distribution; passing modules would be frozen or reused when combining candidate programs. This replaces the original per-address, whole-program success signal with behavioral credit at module boundaries.
- **Why behavior might differ.** Credit could align with reusable semantic units, improving search over hierarchical programs and retaining correct subroutines across tasks. Unlike changing one instruction based on terminal success, a counterexample identifies an input and a failed contract for a specific module. Risks: the contracts are difficult to invent, overly narrow contracts produce no useful generalization, incorrect contracts freeze a bad decomposition, and test generation can dominate the whole search budget.
- **Prior art and disposition.** This is near grammar-guided genetic programming, modular evolutionary algorithms, hierarchical synthesis, CEGIS, and program repair. It is a more precise coupling than simply “use an evolutionary algorithm plus tests,” but its ingredients and loop are established. It also reuses mechanisms already explored in C027 and the candidate ledger’s program-search collisions. Do not add another candidate number.
- **Disproof test.** Use compositional Boolean circuits where module contracts are derived from task decomposition, then a second arm with learned contracts to expose contract cost. Compare against flat GP and CEGIS at equal interpreter calls, held-out composition accuracy and wall time. Reject if the module hybrid only wins when given oracle decomposition/contracts or if learned contract discovery costs more than the search it saves. Novelty confidence: **0.05/5; optional synthesis-method benchmark only.**

- **Continuation/resource update:** Source review verified Friedberg Part I’s publisher DOI/abstract and Minsky’s detailed contemporary account of the 1958–59 experiments; Part II’s exact full text was not independently inspected in this pass, so numerical and interpretation claims are attributed explicitly to Minsky’s review. No program prototype or GPU experiment ran. GPU use 0 GB, peak VRAM 0 GB; no current GPU occupancy check was needed. AR-32 is negative archaeology and HY-31 is demoted; C001–C031 remain intact. The main historical finding is that the central weakness—assigning whole-program success to unstructured instruction positions—was recognized before modern hardware and is precisely why modern program search relies on structured representations and richer counterexamples.

### Neural-architecture archaeology — the overlooked Gamba perceptron question

#### AR-33 — Gamba perceptrons (1960s–1971): multilayer linear-threshold networks before practical hidden-unit learning

- **Original computation and unit.** In Minsky and Papert’s 1971 report, a “Gamba perceptron” is defined plainly as several linear-threshold systems whose outputs feed a further linear-threshold system: a multilayer network of hard-threshold units. It is not a different primitive from a feedforward neural network; the historically interesting piece is that its computational capabilities and learning methods were still being debated. Their report says little was known and conjectures that this kind of network might do little more than low-order perceptrons. [Minsky & Papert, 1971 report](https://web.mit.edu/dxh/www/marvin/web.media.mit.edu/~minsky/papers/PR1971.html); [MIT Press record for *Perceptrons*](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262130431/perceptrons/).
- **What it represents and computes.** Inputs are binary stimulus properties; hidden threshold units compute conjunction-like or other linearly separable intermediate predicates; an output threshold combines those predicates. Parameters are connection weights and thresholds. Each layer repeatedly applies weighted summation and thresholding, mapping an input pattern to a class/action. Knowledge resides in the selected intermediate features and weights. Inference is a forward pass; training the hidden layer is the key issue, because output supervision does not directly say which hidden predicates to form.
- **Was the idea bad or early?** This is a clear case where the representation was underdeveloped as a learnable system, not simply too slow. Minsky and Papert’s formal limitations concerned defined perceptron classes; the 1971 report’s skepticism about Gamba networks was expressed as an unproved conjecture, not a theorem that multilayer nets cannot compute useful functions. The major change was credit assignment: Werbos’s 1974 thesis derived error back-propagation for multi-stage systems, and Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams’s 1986 paper demonstrated hidden units learning task-relevant features through back-propagated errors. GPUs, automatic differentiation and larger datasets later made the training loop practical at much larger scale. Smooth or piecewise-differentiable units also avoid the zero/undefined gradient of a literal hard threshold. [Werbos, 1974 thesis record/full text](https://gwern.net/doc/ai/nn/1974-werbos.pdf); [Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, 1986](https://doi.org/10.1038/323533a0).
- **Modern status, use, and prior art.** This path was revived directly and absorbed into standard MLPs and, with locality/weight sharing, CNNs. The useful modern lesson is not “Gamba is novel”; it is that a representational architecture can be present before a workable learning rule. More compute alone would not tell hidden units what to represent; differentiable optimization and error propagation supplied that missing assignment mechanism, then compute/data enabled scale. Depth, optimization pathologies and inductive bias still matter, but the old two-layer threshold class is not an unoccupied model family.
- **Potential advantage, weakness, and residual.** Layered thresholds can form increasingly abstract Boolean/visual predicates, and compositional depth can represent some functions more compactly than a single threshold layer. Exact threshold units are difficult to train with ordinary gradients; learned hidden predicates can be unstable or data-hungry; and the family has no architecture-level advantage over modern learned networks without a measured hardware/energy or interpretability claim. Novelty confidence: **0/5**.
- **Small falsifiable historical reproduction.** CPU-only parity/XOR and a relational-image toy (for example, two separated components under translation). Compare single-layer perceptron, random fixed hidden thresholds with a trained readout, hard-threshold two-layer search, and a smooth-activation multilayer network trained by backpropagation. Match examples and parameter/evaluation budgets; measure representation size, sample efficiency, generalization under transformations, and training time. The historical “only hardware was missing” hypothesis is falsified if the random/hard-threshold forms remain poor despite adequate evaluations while the differentiable learner succeeds, showing that the update rule and representation—not just arithmetic throughput—were decisive. This is a teaching benchmark, not new-candidate work.

- **Continuation/resource update:** This short pass checked Minsky and Papert’s own 1971 definition/conjecture and the primary Werbos and Rumelhart et al. learning sources. It corrects a common historical overstatement: their Gamba discussion is a conjecture about a two-layer threshold network, while the single-layer limitations in *Perceptrons* are formal results. No experiment or GPU work ran; GPU use 0 GB, peak VRAM 0 GB, live shared occupancy unknown. AR-33 is a direct modernized lineage, not a candidate. The candidate slate remains C001–C031; continue the archaeology search beyond neural networks and record cases where a missing learning rule, not just hardware, determined the outcome.

### Visual computation archaeology — Ullman’s visual routines

#### AR-34 — Visual routines (1984) and learned selective perception (1996–2024)

- **Original computation and unit.** Ullman proposed a two-level account of visual reasoning: broad early processing builds a base representation, then task-dependent visual routines apply sequences of elemental operations to selected image locations or objects to extract shape properties and spatial relations. The unit is an operation plus its current target and partial result, not a fixed feature vector or a single end-to-end mapping. Operations discussed in the later literature include visual search, curve tracing, grouping, and cueing. The same small set of operations can be composed in different orders to answer different visual questions. [Ullman, “Visual Routines,” 1984](https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0277(84)90023-4); [Mollard et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012030).
- **Information, repeated operation, input and output.** Information includes the scene’s early feature maps, selected locations or contours, the current task, and the result passed from one operation to the next. Repeated computation selects an anchor, shifts or propagates attention, traces/groups a relevant structure, and stores or exposes its result as the next operation’s input. The input is an image plus a task or query; the output is a spatial property, relation, or target action. Inference is a serial, task-dependent routine over a scene, with faster broad processing followed by more selective work.
- **Learning and memory.** Ullman’s 1984 account specified a computational hypothesis, not a complete training algorithm. McCallum’s 1996 U-Tree supplied one learning path: reinforcement learning grows a decision tree over selected perceptual features and short histories; leaves hold action values. It explicitly trades lower per-step perception for the need to remember context when a narrow view aliases distinct world states. In 2010, an object-based active-vision system used U-TREE to grow attention-control state and update action values from reward; a separate actor-critic model learned and readapted routines while documenting persistent difficulty learning an optimal visual exploration policy. In 2024, Mollard et al. trained recurrent convolutional networks with RELEARNN, a reward-modulated local learning rule, to learn curve tracing and search-then-trace / trace-then-search routines. Persistent enhanced activity in a retinotopic map acted as a blackboard: one operation’s selected location seeded the next. [McCallum, AAAI Fall Symposium 1996](https://cdn.aaai.org/Symposia/Fall/1996/FS-96-02/FS96-02-018.pdf); [Borji et al., 2010](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.imavis.2009.10.006); [Ognibene et al., 2010](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-15193-4_19); [Mollard et al., 2024](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012030).
- **Possible uses and advantage.** Visual routines could help with diagram relation queries, visually guided manipulation, search under occlusion, and robotics where processing every pixel at full resolution is wasteful. They offer a natural account of serial computation and explicit transfer of an intermediate result. Selective perception can cut work when a task needs only a small part of a large scene.
- **Was it bad or early?** Some constraints were technological: early active-vision systems had weak image features, slow processors, and little simulation data; current visual encoders, event/sensor simulators, and compute can make the low-level perceptual substrate much stronger. But insufficient hardware was not the main missing piece in Ullman’s proposal: it was not itself an executable learning architecture. U-Tree addressed a key conceptual problem—partial observability created by selective attention—before modern deep vision. The 2024 recurrent model is a direct modernization, but its inputs were tiny 15×15 four-color grids, its routines were a small set of known task families, and eye movements were represented as output choices rather than simulated sensor shifts. Its authors leave wider routine sequencing, richer region grouping, and deeper multi-task learning as future questions. More GPU capacity does not by itself discover a useful operation vocabulary, bind reusable operations, or prevent state aliasing and task-specific overfit.
- **Closest prior art / novelty judgment.** This is a productive historical idea but not an unoccupied architecture family. U-Tree already combines selective perception with history-dependent state; active object-based U-TREE and actor-critic models learn attention/routines; RELEARNN implements local recurrent propagation and between-operation transfer; modern recurrent visual attention and active predictive coding occupy the learned glimpse/action territory. Ullman’s central mechanism has been repeatedly revived rather than abandoned. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 as a broad class.**
- **Small falsifiable prototype.** If revisited, use CPU-rendered relational scenes with random shapes, locations, distractors, occlusion, and held-out combinations. Compare (a) a fixed full-image feature baseline, (b) a U-Tree-style history/attention learner, (c) a recurrent routine learner with persistent spatial focus, and (d) a coupled controller. Match visual operations, pixels inspected, action budget, and training episodes; report relation accuracy on held-out compositions, sensor work, sample efficiency, recovery from perceptual aliasing, and routine reuse. The revival claim fails if the sequential mechanism cannot improve held-out relational accuracy per pixel/compute or if its memory/tree growth and active-view costs erase the savings. The direct 2024 code is public, enabling a small reproduction before any larger redesign. [Reference implementation](https://github.com/samimol/Visual-Routines). **Not run.**

### Visual learning archaeology — Fukushima’s Neocognitron

#### AR-35 — Neocognitron (1980): local competitive feature planes with pooled position tolerance

- **Original computation and unit.** The Neocognitron alternates S-cell layers, whose local afferent weights become selective to recurring shape features, and C-cell layers, which pool over neighborhoods so deeper responses vary less with small translations and deformations. A cell plane is a spatial map of units sharing a receptive-field pattern. Cascading these planes builds progressively larger receptive fields and more abstract shape responses. This was a self-organizing hierarchical visual recognizer, not a modern convolutional network with a different name. [Fukushima, 1980](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00344251).
- **Information and operation.** The input is an image-like receptor array. S planes represent local oriented/shape features; C planes represent pooled evidence for those features across nearby locations. Each stage repeats local feature detection, competition/plasticity, and spatial pooling. The output is a set of class-selective responses whose strength should be stable under location changes. Inference is a forward cascade; learned synaptic weights and plane assignments store the visual repertoire.
- **Learning and use.** Repeated examples organize feature detectors without category labels, with competitive/local plasticity and inhibitory interactions. This could be useful where label budgets are tight and spatially local feature learning or local updates matter. Its strongest case is not broad general intelligence; it is a biologically constrained, potentially online visual feature learner with built-in transformation tolerance.
- **Was it bad or early?** Both architecture and hardware mattered. Fukushima reported that the 1980 simulation used 24 planes per layer and could not test larger banks because of memory limits. The same paper also says ten-pattern recognition was critically sensitive to small parameter deviations and presentation order. That sensitivity is an optimization/representation issue, not merely a shortage of RAM. Modern hardware removes the plane-count ceiling, but not competitive-learning instability, weak task-specific credit, or the difficulty of composing learned parts into new semantic structures.
- **Modernization and closest prior art.** CNNs absorbed the local feature hierarchy and pooling structure. LeCun et al. explicitly describe their shared-weight feature maps plus averaging/subsampling as reminiscent of Neocognitron, while identifying supervised backpropagation as an important difference. Fukushima himself then added top-down feedback to a Neocognitron-type hierarchy; the 1986 model used its interaction with afferent processing for selective attention, segmentation, and separate pattern recognition. The 1987 version improved segmentation with lateral inhibition and added associative recall. Later revisions added supervised competitive learning at the top and incremental learning across stages. This is a direct, actively revised historical lineage, not a novel revival. [LeCun et al., 1989](https://papers.baulab.info/papers/LeCun-1989.pdf); [Fukushima, 1986](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00363973); [Fukushima, 1987](https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.26.004985); [Fukushima, 2003](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0925-2312(02)00614-8); [Fukushima, 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14690705/).
- **Potential edge and failure modes.** Local self-organization might reduce annotation needs, support online adaptation, and yield interpretable spatial parts. Risks are unstable feature competition, poor calibration of plane capacity, forgetting, coarse invariance that removes useful location detail, and poor transfer to unseen compositions. There is no demonstrated advantage over modern convolutional self-supervision without a matched comparison. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 as a broad architecture; worth retaining only as a historical baseline.**
- **Small falsifiable prototype.** On CPU, train a tiny faithful S/C hierarchy and a variant with a modern view-consistency signal on procedurally generated glyphs and compositional shapes. Compare them against a parameter- and data-matched supervised CNN and a self-supervised convolutional baseline. Vary examples per class, then test translations, small warps, occlusion, and unseen part combinations. Measure label efficiency, robustness, feature reuse, stability across seeds, and compute. The local-self-organization claim fails if gains vanish against tuned modern controls, depend on handcrafted glyphs, fail on unseen compositions, or require top-layer labels to reach comparable performance. **Not run; retain as a historical baseline question, not a candidate.**

#### HY-32 — U-Tree state growth × recurrent visual routines with local reward learning (demoted)

- **Source mechanisms and exact coupling.** U-Tree contributes reward-tested growth of a history/feature decision tree for selective perception and action. The recurrent visual-routine network contributes local recurrent propagation that performs a visual operation and leaves its selected spatial focus available to the next operation. The proposed coupling makes the focus map and recent operation/action history eligible features for U-Tree state splits. A newly resolved branch gates which recurrent feature planes and routine transition learn from a reward-prediction error; the spatial map then writes the operation result that the next branch can read.
- **Why it could behave differently.** Narrow attention creates aliased observations. If two histories with the same current glimpse lead to different rewards, tree growth could add just enough context to distinguish them, while the recurrent spatial map retains the target location across operation boundaries. This is a concrete interaction between memory growth, routing, local credit assignment, and active inference; it is deeper than putting a decision tree beside a CNN.
- **Prior art and rejection.** McCallum’s 1996 paper is already titled “Learning Visual Routines with Reinforcement Learning”: U-Tree learns selective perceptual-action sequences and adds short-term memory for the hidden state caused by narrowed attention. The 2010 task-driven attention system grows object-conditioned state with U-TREE to control attention/action; Ognibene et al. learn and readapt active visual routines with actor-critic; Mollard et al. directly learn recurrent routine sequencing and blackboard-like transfer with a local reward rule. Active predictive coding and recurrent visual-attention work further overlap. [Active Predictive Coding, 2024](https://direct.mit.edu/neco/article/36/1/1/118264/Active-Predictive-Coding-A-Unifying-Neural-Model); [Mnih et al., recurrent visual attention, 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.6247). I found no evidence that the precise branch-conditioned local-plasticity loop has been evaluated, but the residual is a narrow controller-to-plasticity coupling, not an unoccupied model class. **Novelty confidence: 0.1/5; keep only as an empirical benchmark, not as a new class.**
- **Disproof test.** In a partially observable synthetic relation task, compare a U-Tree policy, a recurrent routine learner, and the coupled system with the same glimpse count, local operations, episode budget, and parameter/memory budget. Add latent cue changes so identical glimpses sometimes require different routines. Measure reward, held-out routine composition, state growth, sample cost, and interference after task changes. Reject the coupling if its advantage disappears at equal capacity, if tree growth grows roughly with history instead of resolving aliasing, or if branch-specific plasticity prevents useful routine reuse.

#### HY-33 — Neocognitron feature self-organization × task-selected visual routines (demoted)

- **Source mechanisms and coupling.** The Neocognitron contributes locally self-organized S-cell feature planes and C-cell pooling; visual routines contribute task-selected sequences such as search then trace. A tightly coupled version would let the selected routine focus gate which feature planes compete and update, while C-layer spatial responses provide the persistent anchor map read by the next operation. Reward for a relational answer would therefore shape both the reusable feature repertoire and the sequence that binds those features.
- **Why it might change computation.** It could allocate unsupervised feature learning to the parts of a scene actually used by a task, retaining translation tolerance while preserving the spatial anchor required for a subsequent operation. The intended gain is fewer labels and less interference than global self-organization or a fixed full-image pipeline.
- **Closest prior art and status.** CNNs already modernize the Neocognitron hierarchy. More directly, Fukushima’s 1986 Neocognitron-type model used top-down efferent feedback interacting with afferent processing for selective attention, segmentation, and separate recognition; his 1987 version improved segmentation through lateral inhibition and added associative recall. AGREL later coupled action-specific attentional feedback with a global reward-prediction signal to gate plasticity; RELEARNN made the reward/credit mechanism recurrent and spatially local and learned routine transfer. [Fukushima, 1986](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00363973); [Fukushima, 1987](https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.26.004985); [Roelfsema & van Ooyen, 2005](https://doi.org/10.1162/0899766054615699); [Brosch et al., 2015](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1004489); [Mollard et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012030). Thus routine-gated competitive S/C updating has substantial direct overlap and is not a new architecture class. A specific learning rule tying U-Tree state splits to S-plane competition may still be a controlled ablation, but would require a direct search of Fukushima’s selective-attention variants and attention-gated plasticity first. **Novelty confidence: 0.1/5; demote to a possible controlled ablation.**
- **Falsifier.** Reuse the AR-35 generated-shape benchmark with labels held sparse. Compare ungated Neocognitron, routine-gated local competition, modern convolutional self-supervision, and an active-attention CNN. Match feature-map capacity and image-pixel budget. If gated learning does not improve held-out relation and shape-part compositions per label or if it loses location information needed by routines, discard it.

- **Continuation/resource update:** This pass verified Ullman’s original paper record, McCallum’s 1996 AAAI paper, the 2010 active-attention U-TREE and actor-critic lineages, the 2024 recurrent visual-routine paper and its open implementation, Fukushima’s 1980 primary paper, LeCun et al.’s direct architecture comparison, and Fukushima’s later revisions. Work was literature review only. No prototype ran; GPU use 0 GB and peak VRAM 0 GB, and no GPU process snapshot was taken because no GPU experiment was started. AR-34 and AR-35 are archaeology entries; HY-32 and HY-33 are rejected/demoted; C001–C031 remain unchanged. The hardware hypothesis is mixed: Neocognitron’s feature-bank size hit a documented RAM limit, but the 2024 visual-routine revival still solves only tightly controlled visual tasks, showing that richer representation, compositional reuse, and state discovery remain open engineering and learning problems. Continue the broad archaeology and hybrid scan; do not edit protected research files.

### Symbolic problem-solving archaeology — Newell, Shaw, and Simon’s GPS

#### AR-36 — General Problem Solver (1957–1969): recursive difference reduction over symbolic operators

- **Original computation and unit.** GPS represents a task as a current symbolic situation, a goal situation, a set of operators, and connections associating recognizable differences with relevant operators. Each step identifies a difference, selects an operator meant to reduce it, and, when the operator’s preconditions are unmet, creates a subgoal to establish them. The unit is a goal/difference/operator relation in a symbolic problem space, not a learned hidden unit or a generic text completion. [Newell, Shaw & Simon, 1959 report](https://home.mis.u-picardie.fr/~furst/docs/Newell_Simon_General_Problem_Solving_1959.pdf); [Simon, “The General Problem Solver,” memoir](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/5737/chapter/11).
- **Information, repeated operation, input and output.** It represents objects, predicates/relations, the initial and desired states, operator preconditions/effects, and which differences each operator may reduce. It repeatedly compares the current and goal states, selects a relevant transformation, recursively resolves unmet preconditions, applies the operation, and checks progress. Input is a formal task description; output is a sequence of symbolic operations or a proof/search trace. Its inference mechanism is means-ends analysis plus operator subgoaling and backtracking when an attempted path fails.
- **Learning and memory.** The core system relies heavily on a problem representation, operator descriptions, and a table of connections supplied for the task. Work around GPS also studied generating operators from primitives and learning which operators reduce which differences, but this did not eliminate the need for representable state transitions and domain knowledge. Memory includes the symbolic state, current goal/subgoal stack, operator library, difference tests, and learned or supplied connection table. It can continue to update those tables if equipped with feedback, but the central solver is not a general continual learner of new domains.
- **Use, strengths and weaknesses.** GPS could apply one search framework to structured logic, puzzle, and transformation tasks. Its explicit goals and operator sequence are inspectable, and a goal difference can provide an interpretable search direction. Its generality is bounded by tasks that can be expressed through symbolic states and operators; poor difference measures or inaccurate relevance links still send search down unproductive paths. More compute expands a weak search, but does not invent the right state variables, operators, preconditions, or common-sense model.
- **Was it bad or early?** The general search/control idea was valuable and directly influenced later planning and cognitive architectures. Its broad “general solver” ambition was limited by representation and knowledge: GPS required a problem space and operator knowledge, and means-ends analysis does not suit every problem representation. John McCarthy’s 1996 critique explicitly separates GPS’s useful goal/subgoal strategy from its failure as a general solver; he argues that many problems do not take the expression-transformation form and that common-sense knowledge is not simply a set of transformation rules. Modern compute can make search cheaper, while learned world models, domain-specific heuristics, theorem provers and simulators can supply missing pieces, but the architecture itself remains a known weak-method planner. [McCarthy, “The GPS and Its Successors,” 1996](https://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc/generality/node2.html); [Ernst & Newell, 1969](https://books.google.com/books?id=xpNQAAAAMAAJ).
- **Closest prior art / novelty judgment.** STRIPS explicitly uses means-ends analysis over symbolic world models and operator sequences, providing a direct planning successor. GPS also sits in the lineage of Soar and hierarchical/goal-directed planning already covered in this notebook. Today, symbolic planners, model-based RL, and learned heuristic search are direct modern counterparts. This is important archaeology, not an unoccupied architecture class. **Novelty confidence: 0/5.**
- **Small falsifiable prototype.** If revisited, use CPU-only Blocks World tasks with held-out initial states, goal arrangements, and operator compositions. Compare a faithful GPS-style difference table, STRIPS/A* planning, and a version that updates operator relevance from execution outcomes. Match action-model knowledge and search expansions; measure solved fraction, expansions, replanning after failed preconditions, transfer to unseen layouts, and the cost of learning the relevance table. The “modern feedback revives GPS” claim fails if learned relevance does not improve transfer and solution cost over STRIPS/A* at equal search budget, or if its gains require hand-authored difference rules. **Not run; retain only as a historical planning baseline.**

#### HY-34 — GPS means-ends search × a learned causal action model (rejected as a new class)

- **Constituents and coupling.** GPS supplies explicit goal differences, operator preconditions, and recursive subgoals. A learned causal/action model supplies transition evidence from interaction. Rather than using a fixed difference-to-operator table, the solver would update operator-effect and applicability beliefs from observed results, then use those beliefs to propose or rank subgoals and operators.
- **Why it could change behavior.** Failures could revise the problem solver’s action model and its choice of the next goal-reducing step, reducing reliance on hand-built connection tables. This couples representation learning to search control: the solver’s action outcome changes both what an operator is believed to do and which future differences it is considered useful for reducing.
- **Prior art and disposition.** This is the ordinary convergence of symbolic planning with learned action models, heuristic learning, or model-based reinforcement learning. STRIPS already states planning as operator sequence search over world models and uses means-ends analysis; adaptive planning and learned dynamics already revise action knowledge from execution. I found no basis for treating the generic combination as new. **Novelty confidence: 0/5; reject as a class, retain as a baseline design pattern.** [Fikes & Nilsson, STRIPS, 1971](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(71)90010-5).
- **Falsifier.** In the AR-36 Blocks World setup, hide selected operator effects and let each system learn from execution. Compare GPS with a fixed operator table, the learned-model hybrid, STRIPS-style regression/search, and a model-based RL baseline under matched observations and search expansions. Reject any claimed benefit if model acquisition costs more than the search it saves or if the system cannot transfer the revised operator model to unseen arrangements.

- **Continuation/resource update:** GPS research checked the 1959 primary report record, Simon’s retrospective description of the operator/difference knowledge it requires, McCarthy’s contemporary-to-the-1990s critique of its limits, and STRIPS as direct successor prior art. No prototype ran. GPU use 0 GB and peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU process snapshot was taken because no GPU experiment was started. AR-36 is negative archaeology, HY-34 is rejected; C001–C031 remain unchanged. The persistent lesson is that faster hardware improves search throughput, while representation and domain-knowledge acquisition remain the bottleneck. Continue beyond symbolic planning and vision for less-covered old computational primitives.

### Source-check amendments to AR-34–AR-36

- **AR-34 / HY-32 — scope correction from the RELEARNN primary paper.** The 2024 model was trained on three specified visual tasks: curve tracing, search-then-trace, and trace-then-search. Its input was a 15×15 pixel grid, the eye movement itself and resulting retinal shift were not simulated, and credit propagation failed on sufficiently long curves when the local signal did not reach the far end. It did show some transfer to distractors and longer curves under its curriculum, so the result is meaningful within this controlled setting. It does not establish a general visual-program learner. Any follow-up comparison should reproduce this baseline and report generalization to unseen operation orders separately from task accuracy. [Mollard et al., 2024, task/model and failure analysis](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012030).
- **AR-35 / HY-33 — add Fukushima’s later Neocognitron learning updates.** Fukushima’s 2010 winner-kill-loser rule removes losing feature cells and creates a new cell when all are silent, explicitly addressing how competitive feature units occupy feature space. His 2018 margined winner-take-all rule changes training of the deepest layer. These papers show continued modernization of the original family and further reduce novelty for adaptive feature growth or competitive updating; their reported recognition gains do not by themselves establish an advantage over matched modern self-supervised CNNs. [Fukushima, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2010.04.008); [Fukushima, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2017.10.005).
- **AR-36 — clarify the actual GPS research and its control failure.** GPS’s standard use required a supplied problem space, operators, and relevance links, but GPS research also developed schemes that generated operators from primitives and learned which operators reduce which differences. Simon’s retrospective names a specific failure: nested subgoals could form a deep pit from which upper levels could not regain control, one motivation for production-system control. This strengthens the negative verdict: the issue was not only missing domain knowledge or insufficient search throughput. [Simon, “The General Problem Solver,” §§ GPS and production systems](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/5737/chapter/11).

### Nonlinear dynamical computation archaeology

#### AR-37 — Heteroclinic / winnerless computation and chaotic itinerancy (1990s–present)

- **What the architecture computes.** A heteroclinic network represents discrete states as unstable equilibria or periodic orbits in a continuous dynamical system. Couplings create directed trajectories from one metastable state to another; inputs perturb which transition wins, while noise can help or disrupt state traversal. “Winnerless competition” is a neural/population-dynamics realization of this idea. Chaotic itinerancy is related but not identical: it describes high-dimensional chaotic trajectories wandering among quasi-stable regions and is not, by itself, a finite-state computing or learning algorithm. Aihara-style chaotic neural networks are another related but distinct nonlinear family.
- **Unit, information and communication.** The computational unit is a saddle state together with its stable/unstable directions and outgoing transition structure. The topology and local eigenvalues/couplings encode the allowed states and transitions; units communicate through dynamical couplings. The current activity vector and its position in a basin/transient encode short-term state. Dwell time may carry temporal or confidence-like information, but it also creates a latency/error tradeoff.
- **Input, output, repeated operation and inference.** Input is a perturbation, cue, or initial condition. The system repeatedly flows toward a metastable state, then exits along an unstable direction into one of its successors. Output is the visited-state sequence, a finite-state decision, or a generated temporal pattern. Inference runs by integrating an ODE or physical circuit and reading the active state/transition sequence.
- **Learning and memory.** In early engineered examples the graph and parameters are designed. Later work learns couplings or infers topology/eigenvalues from a teacher trajectory, sometimes online while the learner is driven by the source signal. Memory is in the graph, coupling strengths/eigenvalues, and current dynamical state, not in a separate retrieved record. Continued adaptation is possible for the demonstrated template-learning rules, but they are not general representation-learning procedures.
- **Was it bad or early?** These systems were never simply abandoned for lack of GPUs: nonlinear dynamics remains an active research area, and finite-state computation through heteroclinic or excitable networks was explicitly developed in the 2010s. Faster simulation, automatic differentiation and differentiable ODE tooling can ease parameter fitting and search over graphs. Yet the known bottlenecks are structural: precise invariant subspaces or robust excitability, sensitivity of transition timing/order to noise and input, and the need to hand-specify or infer a useful state graph. A 2019 learning method can infer a simple network’s topology from generated time series, but requires a compatible template and sufficient visits to each saddle. Modern hardware does not supply useful state abstractions, reliable transitions under broad perturbations, or perception.
- **Scaling and hardware.** Sparse low-dimensional graphs are easy to simulate on CPUs; parallel ODE trajectories and parameter sweeps map to GPUs, but the serial sequence itself offers limited parallelism. Analog/neuromorphic circuits could exploit continuous-time dynamics, but an energy advantage must be measured against digital integration. State count and couplings grow with the graph; transition precision, trajectory length and calibration can dominate. The data need is demonstrated temporal sequences or a designer-specified graph, not large-scale raw perception.
- **Strength, failure modes and nearest prior art.** The plausible strength is a compact, naturally asynchronous temporal controller whose sequence and dwell times emerge from dynamics rather than clocked symbolic dispatch. Failure modes include noise-induced wrong transitions, long and variable dwell times, weak scaling to rich representations, brittle parameter sensitivity, and no established general-purpose learning objective. Ashwin’s 2005 network computes a multi-base counter; Ashwin and Postlethwaite (2013) show how to realize broad classes of directed graphs; their 2018 paper explicitly demonstrates sensitive finite-state computation with a noisy network attractor. A 2023 review catalogs hierarchical chunking, sequence memory, graph design, and the accuracy/speed/noise limits. Voit and Meyer-Ortmanns (2019) infer network topology and eigenvalues from data. Tsuda’s chaotic itinerancy and Aihara’s chaotic neuron precede these but do not make heteroclinic computing a new class. [Ashwin, 2005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physleta.2005.08.013); [Ashwin & Postlethwaite, 2013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physd.2013.09.006); [Ashwin & Postlethwaite, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1109/TNNLS.2018.2813404); [Voit & Meyer-Ortmanns, 2019](https://doi.org/10.3389/fams.2019.00063); [2023 review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10663269/); [Tsuda, 1991](https://doi.org/10.1080/02604027.1991.9972257); [Aihara et al., 1990](https://doi.org/10.1016/0375-9601(90)90136-C).
- **What might actually be new / novelty judgment.** “Heteroclinic computing,” “winnerless competition,” chaotic itinerancy, and learned sequential memory are established; there is no broad new architecture claim here. A narrower possibility would require a new rule that learns a reusable state graph from high-dimensional interaction and maintains robust transitions under distribution shift without supervised state labels. Existing demonstrations already occupy parts of that territory, so this is not promoted. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 as a class; at most 0.1/5 for unspecified robust online graph learning.**
- **Small falsifiable prototype.** CPU-only simulate a 4–8 state WLC network that must execute a cue-conditioned finite-state sequence with occasional skipped, repeated, or noisy cues. Compare a hand-built heteroclinic network, the learned-topology rule, a finite-state controller, and a small recurrent network. Match state count, training trajectories, and transition queries; measure sequence accuracy, adaptation samples after graph changes, latency variance, and recovery under noise and parameter perturbations. The practical claim fails if its robustness or adaptation does not beat the digital controller/RNN at matched state and data budgets, or if successful operation requires hand-tuning each transition. **Not run; no prototype needed to retain the prior-art rejection.**

### Automated discovery archaeology

#### AR-38 — AM / EURISKO: agenda-driven concept growth and meta-heuristic search (1976–1983)

- **Original computation and unit.** Lenat’s AM starts from a supplied body of elementary mathematical objects and heuristics. It represents concepts as executable LISP characteristic functions plus descriptive information, places specific tasks on an agenda, and applies heuristic rules to explore properties or define new concepts. EURISKO extends the representation into a richer slot language so that concepts and heuristics can be represented and changed; meta-heuristics propose and score modifications to other heuristics. The unit is a typed symbolic concept/heuristic plus an agenda item, rather than a learned neural feature.
- **Information, repeated operation, input and output.** The system stores objects, concept definitions, conjectures, descriptions, heuristic rules and their utility histories. It selects an agenda task, applies one or more heuristics to create or test a concept/conjecture, evaluates results, updates the agenda and heuristic priorities, and accumulates discoveries. Inputs are domain primitives, a vocabulary, and task/evaluation rules; outputs are candidate concepts, conjectures, designs or revised heuristics.
- **Learning, inference and memory.** Learning is symbolic accretion and meta-level rule revision rather than gradient descent. AM’s memory is its growing concept graph and agenda; EURISKO adds explicit descriptive slots and heuristics that can mutate or specialize other heuristics. Inference is heuristic search through executable symbolic transformations. The systems can change after deployment if the search/evaluation loop continues, but the change is bounded by supplied domains, primitive operations, descriptors and fitness tests.
- **Was it bad or early?** More compute and modern execution environments would let these programs test many more candidates and run safer, reproducible sandboxes. But the central historical limit was knowledge representation and heuristic acquisition. Lenat reports that AM could not discover strong domain-specific heuristics for new fields; EURISKO’s authors note that the LISP mutations useful for mathematical concepts did not transfer naturally to heuristic rules. Ritchie and Hanna also raise methodological/reproducibility concerns about whether the published rule set makes AM’s behavior sufficiently clear. This is a mixed case: compute improves search throughput, but does not choose the right ontology, useful meta-heuristics, or reliable novelty test.
- **Modernization and closest prior art.** Genetic programming, enumerative program synthesis and modern automated scientific-discovery systems occupy concept/program search. AutoML-Zero is a particularly clear modern parallel: it evolves complete learning algorithms from primitive operations, but searches ML algorithms rather than AM’s mathematical concepts. Modern sandboxes, formal checking, typed DSLs, simulators and cheap parallel execution improve candidate evaluation; they do not remove the need for representational bias and domain evidence. The broad architecture of self-modifying heuristic search is established. [Lenat, AM thesis, 1976](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/An_Artificial_Intelligence_Approach_to_Discovery_in_Mathematics_as_Heuristic_Search); [Lenat, EURISKO, 1983](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0004-3702(83)80005-8); [Ritchie & Hanna, 1984](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(84)90015-8); [AutoML-Zero, 2020](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/real20a.html).
- **Potential advantage, weakness and residual.** Explicit concepts and procedures can make generated knowledge inspectable and locally editable, while meta-heuristics could adapt search to new domains. The weaknesses are hand-built primitives/ontology, sparse and contestable discovery scores, heuristic overfitting, unbounded agenda growth, difficult verification, and poor transfer. The only plausible residual is a specific mechanism that learns portable search guidance across tasks and validates it out of domain; “the system edits its own heuristics” is not enough. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 as a class.**
- **Small falsifiable prototype.** CPU-only finite typed DSL for small graph properties. Compare mutable AM-style meta-heuristics, a fixed heuristic library, and evolutionary program search under equal evaluation budgets; hold out combinations of graph properties and vary evaluator noise. Measure valid novel rules, transfer accuracy, evaluations to first useful discovery, and invalid/redundant output rate. Discard the revival if meta-heuristic mutation does not improve held-out discovery per evaluation or mainly exploits the training evaluator. **Not run; retained as negative archaeology.**

#### AR-39 — BACON: empirical-law discovery through regularity detectors and derived attributes (1978–1987)

- **Original computation and unit.** BACON.1 represents observations as clusters of attribute–value pairs. Production rules detect constancies, direct/inverse trends, then propose derived attributes such as ratios, products or linear combinations; new attributes are recursively evaluated as candidate explanations. The unit is a data regularity/hypothesis cluster plus a production rule that reacts to it. Later BACON versions added richer symbolic structure and law types.
- **Input, output, repeated operation and memory.** Input is an experiment table or a controlled query to a domain, with independent and dependent attributes. The system repeatedly gathers or receives an observation, finds trends/constancies, creates a derived feature, tests candidate laws, and adds supported hypotheses to a description hierarchy. Output is an empirical relationship such as a power law or conservation law, sometimes with conditions. Memory stores raw and derived data clusters, hypothesis clusters and the production rules.
- **Learning and inference.** Heuristics are mostly hand-authored; learning is constructing higher-level attributes and hypotheses from evidence, not learning the discovery procedure itself. Inference and data collection are interleaved, but BACON.1’s original sampling used a straightforward factorial design. It does not autonomously invent arbitrary mathematical transformations or represent general relations between structured objects.
- **Was it bad or early?** Modern simulators, instruments and parallel compute make broader queries and large hypothesis checks cheaper. Yet Langley’s 1978 report explicitly identifies restricted attribute–value representation, perfect-data assumptions and inefficient factorial search as limitations; it suggests changing hypothesis tests and selecting data based on partial hypotheses. More compute does not fix a biased transformation vocabulary or the problem of distinguishing equations from sparse noisy evidence. Later BACON versions address some limitations, so claims about BACON.1 must not be generalized to every version.
- **Modernization and prior art.** BACON.3 and later systems extended term construction and law types; symbolic regression, AI Feynman, grammar-guided equation discovery, SINDy and autonomous “robot scientist” systems cover modern pieces of the same scientific-discovery problem. AI Feynman organizes formula search using symmetries, separability and compositional structure; current equation discovery includes active data queries and simulators. This is an established scientific-discovery family, not a new general architecture. [Langley, BACON.1, 1978](https://iiif.library.cmu.edu/file/Simon_box00013_fld00882_bdl0001_doc0001/Simon_box00013_fld00882_bdl0001_doc0001.pdf); [Langley, BACON.3, 1981](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1551-6708.1981.tb00869.x); [AI Feynman, 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7159912/); [2025 automated-discovery review](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-025-06955-2).
- **Possible use and residual novelty.** It is useful when variables are already meaningful, data are controlled, and interpretable empirical laws matter. The plausible residual is not “more compute” but a well-specified active experiment rule that chooses the cheapest intervention to separate competing transformations under noise and changing conditions. Active experimental design and modern equation search already overlap; no candidate is promoted. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 for the family.**
- **Small falsifiable prototype.** CPU-only generate small physical systems from a held-out equation grammar and expose them through a queryable simulator.
