### Control, cybernetics and hybrid follow-up — source-checked continuation (2026-09-27)

- **Homeostat / Ashby ultrastability correction.** AR-08 and C031 already cover the core viability-bound-triggered parameter-reorganization loop. The 1968 NASA/University of Illinois “New Homeostat” report reviews the Ashby device's limits: it changes parameters discontinuously rather than allowing qualitative transfer-function change, lacked true hierarchical coupling, and had fixed trigger levels; it proposed op-amp circuitry and a more flexible hierarchy. Ashby's own revised *Design for a Brain* also explicitly notes that trial-and-error adaptation can fail in environments with lethal discontinuities and may be too slow when parameter variety grows. Thus it was not merely too early: analog hardware limits were real, but random search, designer-selected viability variables, adaptation safety and poor scaling are mechanism-level limits. 2013 ultrastable neuroendocrine controllers and later robot/homeostat demonstrations show direct modernization; they do not create a new learning rule. [Wilkins, 1968 NASA report](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19690007478/downloads/19690007478.pdf); [Ashby, *Design for a Brain*, 1960](https://www.ashby.info/Ashby%20-%20Design%20for%20a%20Brain%20-%20The%20Origin%20of%20Adaptive%20Behavior.pdf); [Pitonakova, 2013](https://doi.org/10.1177/1059712312462249); [mobile homeostat, 2015](https://uwe-repository.worktribe.com/output/805895/a-mobile-homeostat-with-three-degrees-of-freedom). **C031 remains closed as low novelty; no new experiment.**
- **Subsumption / behavior-based robotics correction.** Brooks's 1985 primary report describes asynchronous finite-state modules communicating over low-bandwidth channels; higher layers suppress lower-layer outputs while those lower behaviors continue running. The first result in that report was on a detailed robot simulation, so limited robot hardware was a genuine contemporaneous deployment barrier. Later learning and arbitration integrations exist; the architecture's fixed, reactive wiring and intentionally limited long-horizon state are not solved simply by faster hardware. HY-14 already records that predictive-state/reactive-behavior coupling and learned arbitration have prior art, so generic “modern subsumption + learned arbiter” remains rejected. [Brooks, MIT AI Memo 864, 1985](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/362a32d0-a821-4a9d-a5ff-9e2b71c5539d); [learned subsumption/control, 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7506774/).
- **Control-theory modernization.** The old self-tuning regulator combined recursive least-squares identification with a minimum-variance controller and was explicitly considered feasible on a small process computer in 1973. That history argues against treating adaptive control as an architecture lost only to scarce compute. Current learning components may improve nonlinear perception or model classes, but the basic estimate-and-retune loop is established; identifiability, excitation under safety constraints, model mismatch and stability remain the hard parts. [Åström & Wittenmark, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1016/0005-1098(73)90073-3).
- **PCT / PSR robot audit.** Hierarchical perceptual control has a real robot realization in quadrupedal posture and locomotion on uneven terrain; it is useful control organization, not a new general learner. More directly, Boots, Siddiqi and Gordon already learned a PSR from action-observation sequences for a simulated high-dimensional vision-based mobile robot and planned in the learned representation, closing the learning-planning loop. This closes the broad PSR-plus-reactive robot proposal more firmly than a claim based only on component resemblance. [Hierarchical perceptual-control robot study, 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8426206/); [Boots et al., 2009/2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.2385).

#### HY-41 — Prediction-surprise-gated episodic recall/write for reactive control (demoted; not a new architecture)

- **Source mechanisms and proposed coupling.** Event-triggered control contributes a cheap controller that runs between communication/update events. Sequential episodic control stores ordered experience and retrieves sequences to guide actions. Predictive sensorimotor memory contributes a model whose prediction residual can mark unexpected events. The low-confidence coupling would let a prediction-error or safety-margin event trigger *both* episode retrieval and an episode write/update, and use the retrieved segment to initialize or temporarily alter the next control segment. This changes the memory query/write schedule and action loop; simply attaching an episode store to a controller is not the proposal.
- **Prior art found.** Three close areas make the novelty claim weak: 2017 event-triggered control already uses recent output/control history to decide when sampling or controller updates occur; a 2022 neural episodic-memory model learns selective retrieval/encoding using uncertainty and event boundaries; and 2025 Neural Associative Skill Memories use temporal predictive coding, contextual skill inference and prediction surprise for sensorimotor recall/fault detection. Most directly, a June 2026 preprint, *Worth Remembering*, gates robot episodic-memory formation using Bayesian surprise and retrieves selected episodes for later robot QA/task use. SEC (2025) already stores full temporal sequences and biases retrieval for action. The exact “trigger retrieval plus write, then alter a closed-loop controller segment” may not be in these papers, but that residual is an application-specific scheduling rule, not a broad model class; absence in this search is not proof of novelty. **Novelty confidence 0.1/5; do not promote.** [Davó et al., 2017](https://doi.org/10.1109/TAC.2017.2713525); [Lu et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.74445); [Mahajan et al., Neural Associative Skill Memories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09760); [Worth Remembering, 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03787); [Freire et al., SEC, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-024-00950-3).
- **Small CPU disproof, only if a robotics application motivates it.** On a 2D partially observed switched-control plant, compare periodic retrieval, prediction-error-triggered retrieval only, residual-triggered retrieval plus same-event write/update, and the strongest always-on/episodic control baseline; include an adaptive model-based controller. Fix memory size, training data, observation rate, and total allowed memory reads/writes. Measure task return, integrated safety-bound violation, adaptation samples after a dynamics switch, recall count and wall time under cue noise and quiet failure. Reject the scheduling hypothesis if it does not reduce retrieval/write work at matched safety and recovery, if surprise causes retrieval storms, or if delayed quiet failures make the event trigger worse than periodic/always-on memory. **Not run; no novelty test implied.**
- **Resource and synthesis record.** This continuation involved literature review and notebook synthesis only. GPU use and peak VRAM were 0 GB; no GPU process snapshot was needed because no GPU experiment was started. Live GPU occupancy remains unknown. No candidate was promoted, no protected file was read or changed, and no Claude research file was accessed.

#### AR-49 — Dual-memory-pathway spiking networks (DMP-SNN, 2026): explicit slow shared state modulates fast event-driven layers

- **Architecture located in current prior-art scan.** Sun et al. add to each spiking layer a compact slow state vector (typically 5–10% of the fast hidden width) that summarizes recent activity and feeds back as an extra current to the layer's fast spiking dynamics. The state is shared across units in the layer rather than replicated as per-synapse delay buffers. It targets long temporal context under sparse event computation; inputs are clocked or event-driven sequences, and outputs are class/regression values or spikes to a downstream layer. Information is represented in both the fast sparse spikes and the slow low-dimensional state.
- **Learning and inference.** The paper trains models offline with gradient-based temporal learning and evaluates task inference over sequences. The slow state creates a gradient path that remains useful over hundreds of time steps on sequential MNIST variants; it does not establish local online adaptation after deployment. Hardware maps sparse spike accumulation and dense state updates to heterogeneous near-memory paths with operator fusion and distinct dataflow.
- **What changed / measured claim.** The authors report 99.3% S-MNIST and 97.3% permuted S-MNIST, plus results on event-audio tasks, while using fewer parameters than recurrent and delay-based SNN baselines. Their 22-nm implementation results are post-layout simulations; the paper reports >4× throughput and >5× energy efficiency against selected neuromorphic implementations, with some baseline figures normalized from other papers. This is evidence that a specific fast/slow memory split is hardware-compatible, not evidence for general-purpose intelligence or a freely learned architectural mechanism. [Sun et al., *Nature Machine Intelligence*, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-026-01255-3).
- **Novelty / relevance judgment.** This is direct 2026 prior art for fast/slow computation and low-dimensional per-layer temporal memory, adjacent to the notebook's Multi-Clock / Temporal-Braid seeds, SNN memory mechanisms and heterogeneous-timescale models. The authors state the algorithmic regime is long-range temporal dependency under tight energy/memory budgets. The contribution is a precise SNN memory unit plus its hardware/dataflow co-design; the broader idea of multiple clocks or slow shared context is not open. It uses static offline-trained weights and remains an SNN-specific temporal processing architecture. **Do not add a general architecture candidate.** The useful next comparison, if temporal-SNN work becomes a priority, is against learned delays, recurrent SNNs and a matched small recurrent sequence model, charging post-layout vs measured hardware consistently.
- **Resource and research record.** Literature-only, CPU/browser-side source inspection. No local GPU experiment or code execution was involved; GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB and live GPU occupancy was not sampled. This addition records newly published prior art and does not alter the previous experiment decisions.

#### AR-50 — In-memory analogue actor–critic TD learning on memristors (2025): classic online control, newly mapped into physical synapses

- **Original learning mechanism and modern implementation.** A tabular/single-layer actor–critic network represents spatial state with fixed place-cell/RBF activations; a critic computes value, the actor chooses actions, and temporal-difference error is the third factor in a local neo-Hebbian weight update. Portner et al. map synaptic weights and the TD update arithmetic to analogue valence-change memristors, so the same device state participates in action selection, online weight storage and update computation. The RL algorithm is an established actor–critic/TD family; the research contribution is hardware-level in-memory execution of the update rule. [Portner et al., *Nature Machine Intelligence*, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-025-01149-w).
- **Was it merely too early?** For this narrow application, partly: modern memristive devices can store analog weights and carry out a reward-modulated update in place, reducing weight readout/data movement. But the paper's physical-demonstration boundary is narrower than its abstract: only two critic memristors were physically trained per run; the other critic and actor weights were software-emulated from measured device characteristics. Tasks are T-maze and Morris-water-maze navigation, with state supplied by hand-designed fixed place cells/RBFs. The authors explicitly identify the fixed input layer as a limitation; the deep self-supervised front end is only a frozen simulation and is not implemented on the memristor system. Thus device technology removes an I/O bottleneck, not the representation or generalization bottleneck.
- **Assessment.** Keep as evidence that classic online reward learning can benefit from a modern physical substrate, not as a new AI architecture. It is a valuable systems baseline for online learning-after-deployment and hardware locality, but not evidence of scaling to open-ended perception, multimodal tasks or general reasoning. A follow-up should count how much of the pipeline actually resides on device, measure a full fabricated system and compare joules/update and adaptation against digital actor–critic baselines at matched accuracy. No local experiment is justified because the primary paper supplies the narrow demonstration and the unresolved claim is physical systems scaling.
- **Resource record.** Source review only, no local code/GPU experiment. GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU occupancy/process snapshot was needed. This entry does not promote any candidate.

#### AR-47 — Prioritized sweeping / Queue-Dyna (1990s): allocate planning backups by propagated value change

- **Original computation.** After observing a transition, the learner updates an empirical transition model and a value estimate, then places affected states on a priority queue. Each planning step backs up the highest-priority state and propagates its changed value to predecessor states, weighted by modeled transition probability. A predecessor graph, model, values and queue form explicit persistent memory; the repeated unit is a local Bellman/probability backup. It produces an improved value function/policy or absorption prediction. The original work targeted finite discrete Markov systems and framed the method as reusing all experience to prioritize model-based dynamic-programming sweeps. [Moore & Atkeson, 1993](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022635613229).
- **Learning and inference.** The transition model is estimated from observed state-action-successor samples; planning uses asynchronous queued backups between real environment interactions. Queue-Dyna, developed independently by Peng and Williams, is a near-contemporaneous close relative, which the Moore–Atkeson paper itself acknowledges. Thus “use a priority queue for value updates” was already an established Dyna branch from inception. [Peng & Williams, 1993](https://doi.org/10.1177/105971239300100403).
- **Was it bad or early?** It was sample-efficient on manageable state graphs; its limiting assumption was a useful, revisit-able state representation and a model with tractable predecessors. Larger computers alone do not solve state aliasing, representation drift or inaccurate predecessor estimates. Modern work removed some representational limits: VaST learns a binary latent tabulation from high-dimensional observations and applies small prioritized backups, showing reward/dynamics adaptation in visual navigation. A 2018 neural DynaQ variant learns multiple predecessors with growing experts. The tradeoff remains: state abstraction errors can propagate through the graph, and model-based updates can bootstrap from hallucinated states. A 2024 Dyna analysis tests multistep predecessor models explicitly to address this model-error issue. [VaST, ICML 2018](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/corneil18a/corneil18a.pdf); [neural prioritized sweeping, Aubin et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.05594); [Aminmansour et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.15155).
- **Closest architecture and novelty.** Prioritized sweeping is an architecture-level planning/scheduling mechanism, but not a new candidate: Queue-Dyna, asynchronous DP/RTDP, neural prioritized sweeping, learned tabular abstractions, and modern predecessor models cover its core. Novelty confidence **0/5**. The useful modern lesson is methodological: learned representations can expose reusable graph structure to a local planner, while model uncertainty must limit propagation. Merely attaching a learned visual encoder or a different priority score does not create a new class.
- **Small CPU falsifier for its revived utility (not novelty).** In a small stochastic maze with a shared bottleneck, high predecessor fan-in, and one mid-run transition change, compare random Dyna backups, tabular prioritized sweeping, and a latent-state VaST-style planner. Hold the learned model, observation data, number of backups and wall-clock accounting constant where possible. Measure real interactions to policy threshold, queue maintenance time, model errors propagated into Q-values, and recovery after change. Reject the efficiency claim if priority scheduling saves neither interaction count nor total time, or if latent aggregation causes more persistent policy error than the Dyna baseline. CPU only is sufficient.
- **Source check and resource record.** The 1993 article describes finite tabular state transitions, memory-based planning, predecessor-oriented queued sweeps and identifies Queue-Dyna as a close independently developed method; the original description also calls prioritized sweeping a heuristic and does not provide a formal convergence proof for that variant. Later primary records confirm VaST’s learned discrete state abstraction and the neural multiple-predecessor extension. Literature review only: GPU use and peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU snapshot was taken because no GPU experiment was started, so live occupancy remains unknown. No process was inspected or affected.
- **Decision.** Retain AR-47 as archaeology and a useful model-based planning baseline. Do not add a candidate. The remaining open work is to test specific mechanism-level hybrids from the archaeology reports, not to repackage prioritized sweeping.

##### AR-47 CPU revival check — preregistered, priority backups after a goal switch

- **Question.** On a tiny stochastic T-maze with two routes sharing a predecessor bottleneck, does prioritized backup ordering recover from a terminal-reward relocation faster than random Dyna backups when both get the same real interaction and planning-backup budgets? This is a utility/baseline check, not a novelty experiment.
- **Protocol.** Implement a tabular T-maze with 10% action slip, step cost −0.01, a +1 terminal goal on one arm for 60 episodes, then move the goal to the other arm for 40 episodes. Start every episode at the stem; use the same tabular Q-learning update and empirical transition/reward model. Compare (a) uniform random sampling of observed state-action model entries and (b) a predecessor queue prioritized by expected Bellman residual, with a budget of 10 planning slots per real step (random Dyna executes a backup in each slot; sweeping may leave a slot idle when its priority queue empties). Use the same learning rates, exploration schedule, episode cap, and 20 paired random seeds. Evaluate greedy policy success every five episodes with 50 trials. Report episodes/interactions after the switch to ≥90% success sustained across two evaluations, total return, scheduled slots, executed backups and wall time including queue maintenance.
- **Falsifier.** The historical efficiency claim fails in this setting if priority ordering does not reduce post-switch interactions or total CPU time at matched backup count, or if model uncertainty/queue cost erases the benefit. The toy map is deliberately small and fully specified; no broader RL claim follows from its result.
- **Resources.** Pure Python/CPU only, no accelerator or GPU process. **Pre-registered; not yet run.**

##### AR-47 CPU revival-check result — no advantage in the tiny T-maze

- **Execution.** Ran the pre-registered two-arm T-maze in pure Python on CPU, with 10% action slip, 60 episodes toward the left goal followed by 40 toward the right, 10 scheduled planning slots per real transition, and 20 seeds for each method. Greedy success was evaluated every five post-switch episodes over 50 trials. Combined wall time was 2.75 seconds. No GPU work or process was started.
- **Results.** Random Dyna reached ≥90% success for two consecutive evaluations in 6/20 seeds; prioritized sweeping did so in 2/20. Among successful seeds only, median post-switch interaction counts were 403.5 for random Dyna and 460.5 for sweeping, but this comparison is too censored and small to interpret. Median executed model backups were 19,425 for random Dyna and 19,195 for sweeping (1.18% fewer). Mean return across all 100 training episodes was 0.515 for random Dyna and 0.449 for sweeping. CPU time was measured only for the combined run, not separately by method.
- **Interpretation.** The historical sample/compute efficiency advantage did not appear in this tiny setup; priority ordering slightly reduced backups and produced worse success counts/return. However, both methods missed the recovery criterion in most seeds, and the seven-cell maze with 100 episodes provides weak separation. Treat this as a negative, low-power baseline check—not as a falsification of prioritized sweeping generally. Do not promote an architecture. A stronger replication would require a larger branching map and clearer sample-efficiency metrics; because this is established prior art, further implementation is lower priority than searching for a specific unoccupied coupling.
- **Resource log.** CPU-only, Python standard library, 20 seeds × two planners, 10 slots/step, combined runtime 2.75 s. GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU memory/process snapshot was taken because no GPU experiment was started; live occupancy remains unknown. No other process was inspected or affected.

#### AR-48 — Developmental encodings for evolving neural circuits (1990s–2000s): grow a phenotype from a compact rewrite program

- **Original computation.** This is an encoding family, not one model class. Cellular Encoding (CE) interprets a grammar tree as a sequence of cell-development/division operations that produces network topology and weights; Kitano's graph-generation grammar applies rewrite rules to a matrix-like connectivity representation; parametric L-systems recursively generate repeated body parts and can co-generate their controllers. The common computational primitive is genotype-driven repeated rewriting/development, not direct optimization of every phenotype parameter. [Gruau & Whitley, 1993](https://doi.org/10.1162/evco.1993.1.3.213); [Kitano, 1990](https://wpmedia.wolfram.com/sites/13/2018/02/04-4-6.pdf); [Hornby & Pollack, 2001](https://www.demo.cs.brandeis.edu/papers/hornby_gecco01.pdf); [Stanley & Miikkulainen, 2003 taxonomy](https://nn.cs.utexas.edu/?stanley:alifej03=).
- **Input, output, learning and memory.** Evolutionary search changes a compact grammar/genotype; running its rewrite/development rules constructs an executable network, morphology or network-controller pair. The resulting phenotype consumes task observations and emits decisions/actions. Knowledge is distributed across the genotype and the developed weights/structure; lifetime learning may operate during evaluation, either without writing learned weights back (Baldwinian) or with some form of Lamarckian inheritance. Fitness-based evolutionary updates remain the main outer learning mechanism.
- **Was it bad or early?** Indirect encoding was proposed partly because direct chromosome-to-connection mappings become difficult to search as networks grow. Hornby and Pollack's L-system virtual creatures reached hundreds of parts where earlier work had been under 50, demonstrating that representation choice can remove a real scaling barrier. Modern simulation, batched CPU/GPU fitness evaluation and differentiable inner learning make richer experiments cheaper. They do not remove evolutionary credit-assignment cost, simulator fidelity, grammar-induced bias, or the need for fair phenotype-size/task-evaluation budgets. Stanley and Miikkulainen's taxonomy frames developmental design as a multi-dimensional space and warns that richer developmental processes can incur additional computational cost; it is a design framework, not a single architecture awaiting more hardware.
- **Prior art and novelty.** CE already combines growth, evolutionary search and within-lifetime learning; Kitano's graph grammar and body-brain L-systems already encode repeated structure compactly; NEAT/HyperNEAT and neural cellular automata occupy adjacent topology-growth and learned-local-rule ground. Generic “grow neural networks from developmental rules,” “evolve compact generative programs,” and “co-evolve body and brain” are occupied. No new general architecture or hybrid survives. **Novelty confidence: 0/5.**

Report evaluations to threshold, solution variance, transfer to doubled input/morphology size, and runtime. The revival claim fails if indirect encodings lose their apparent advantage when evaluation budgets and phenotype capacity are matched, or if gains do not transfer beyond the grammar's repeated motifs.
- **Decision and resource log.** Keep as archaeology. The hard historical bottleneck was partly search dimensionality and evaluation expense, so modern compute matters, but the broad mechanism was already known and has many descendants; no candidate or hybrid is promoted. Literature review only; GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU snapshot or process inspection was needed because no GPU work was started. Live occupancy remains unknown.

A 2024 NDP control study addresses collapse of neuronal diversity using intrinsic node state inherited at neurogenesis and lateral inhibition. LNDP extends this to activity/reward-dependent lifetime synaptic and structural plasticity, with reported advantages on tested fast-adaptation and nonstationary-reward control tasks. These methods show that modern differentiable training and simulation did remove some historical implementation barriers; they also close “development plus local learning/plasticity” as a broad hybrid. More compute does not settle growth stability, local credit assignment, evaluation cost, unbounded phenotype size, or whether growth beats matched fixed-capacity/continual learners. #### AR-51 — CNN Universal Machine (1992–2000s): programmable continuous-time analog arrays

- **Original computation and unit.** The Cellular Neural Network Universal Machine (CNN-UM) is a stored-program analog array computer, not merely a recurrent neural-network architecture. Each cell has local state/memory and local interactions; a global controller sequences stored analog templates and local logic operations over the array. Its instruction is an array-wide dynamical operation. A program composes several such passes over the same data, with analog intermediates kept locally. The original authors described a compiler, high-level Analogic CNN Language, operating system and toolchain. [Roska, Chua & Zarandy, 1993 technical report](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/1993/2338.html); [Roska & Chua, 1993 IEEE paper](https://doi.org/10.1109/82.222815).
- **Input, output, learning, and memory.** The main inputs are image or spatial signal arrays; repeated local continuous-time dynamics apply programmable templates and return filtered, segmented, or otherwise transformed arrays. Analog local memories hold intermediate data, while program memory/control state chooses template and operation order. This is a programmable computing substrate; the classic architecture does not learn a general model from data. CNN template optimization and learned chip parameters are separate methods that do not make the substrate a new model class.
- **Was it bad or early?** Real hardware existed: a 1996 CMOS prototype had 1,024 cells and reported roughly 7–8-bit weight accuracy; the later ACE16K focal-plane processor had 128×128 cells. Those facts correct any claim that the architecture stayed purely theoretical. But the actual workload boundary matters: later evaluations explicitly focused on early-vision tasks; one CNN-UM study notes that Boolean-image memory copies consumed roughly three quarters of its processing time, and its tested lattice-size simulations were still slower than classical digital computers. Parallel analog arithmetic did not eliminate instruction, memory-layout, conversion, and control costs. [Espejo et al., 1996 chip](https://doi.org/10.1002/%28SICI%291097-007X%28199601/02%2924%3A1%3C93%3A%3AAID-CTA906%3E3.0.CO%3B2-M); [Liñán-Cembrano et al., ACE16K, 2003](https://doi.org/10.1142/S0129065703001765); [CNN-UM stochastic-simulation analysis](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physd.2008.03.028).
- **What changed and what did not.** Modern mixed-signal devices, memristors, digital emulation and learned template selection could improve programmability and make new substrate comparisons easier. They do not establish that analog cell dynamics yield a better general learner than a digital accelerator; more compute on a GPU does not recreate CNN-UM's physical locality, and a fabricated analog array still has precision, routing, memory-capacity, conversion and programming costs. The broad architecture, stored-program idea and compiler/runtime are already explicit prior art. A remaining systems question is when this array wins on data-local image/PDE workloads after charging transfers and template sequencing; that is hardware benchmarking, not a new AI class. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 as a model class; keep as computation archaeology.**
- **Small falsifiable test (not run).** If revived, compare an exact CPU reference, GPU stencil implementation, FPGA emulation and an actual CNN-UM/analog chip on local image transforms and a PDE stencil; match output precision and include input/output, analog memory-copy, program-setup and synchronization costs. Reject a speed/energy advantage if it disappears under end-to-end accounting or is confined to low-precision early vision. No prototype is prioritized without access to relevant hardware.
- **Resource record.** Source review only; no local CPU/GPU experiment. GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU process was started or inspected, so current occupancy is unknown.

#### AR-52 — Quantum associative memory (1998–present): Grover-style partial-cue retrieval

- **Original computation.** Ventura and Martinez proposed a quantum associative memory that prepares memory patterns in a quantum state and uses a Grover-like retrieval procedure to recover a stored pattern from a partial cue. The state/amplitudes and query preparation carry the memory; repeated unitary search operations amplify candidate states. The original paper made exponential-capacity claims against classical Hopfield memories under its encoding assumptions. [Ventura & Martinez, 1998 preprint / 1999 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9807053).
- **Was it bad or early? What changed?** Later work already documented spurious states in the quantum memory model and explored controlled retrieval; these are algorithm/model properties, not problems that more qubits alone remove. A 2021 Quantum Hopfield Associative Memory was demonstrated on IBM's 15-qubit device, but the physical case was a four-neuron system; the reported capacity mimicked classical Hopfield capacity, with hardware error and connectivity constraints explicitly discussed. This establishes a small NISQ-era implementation, not a scaling advantage. [Ezhov et al., 2000](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0020-0255(00)00057-8); [Miller & Mukhopadhyay, 2021 full paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-02866-z).
- **Assessment.** Quantum associative memory is an established hardware-specific memory architecture, not a distinct broadly useful learning system. Modern quantum devices make tiny demonstrations possible, while state preparation/loading, readout, circuit depth, connectivity, noise and retrieval quality determine end-to-end utility. There is no reason to add another quantum-plus-Hopfield candidate without a specified retrieval mechanism and complexity accounting. **Novelty confidence: 0/5; retain as archaeology.**
- **Small falsifiable test (not run).** A useful hardware paper would compare end-to-end state preparation, query, repeated circuit shots and readout cost against classical dense and sparse associative memories as memory count and cue corruption grow. Falsify a practical advantage if gains rely on free state loading, idealized oracle access, or exclude repeated-shot/readout costs. No local experiment planned.
- **Resource record.** Primary-paper review only; no local accelerator work. GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU process was started or inspected, so current occupancy is unknown.

#### AR-53 — Amorphous computing (1996–2007): global behavior from irregular local programs

- **Original computation and unit.** Amorphous computing studies how simple local programs running on many unreliable, asynchronously updated processors can produce a desired spatial or system-level behavior without knowing exact device positions or a fixed lattice. Each unit communicates locally with whatever neighbors are present; the repeated operation is an asynchronous local update/message exchange, while the global output is a pattern or coordinated behavior. This differs from a regular cellular automaton by allowing irregular and time-varying topology and by treating programming global behavior as the central challenge. [Abelson et al., 1996 manifesto](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/mac/projects/amorphous/white-paper/amorph-new/amorph-new.html); [Abelson et al., 2000](https://doi.org/10.1002/%28SICI%291099-0526%28200001/02%295%3A3%3C22%3A%3AAID-CPLX5%3E3.0.CO%3B2-J); [MIT thesis on discrete amorphous models](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/aa113819-d0f3-4d73-a9ed-2a059edf5b10).
- **Learning, memory, and modernization.** The original line gives a programming model and local rule systems; it does not supply a general learning rule or perception stack. Modern distributed simulation, sensor networks, robot swarms and programmable-matter work make testing more feasible, but large irregular physical substrates remain hard to build and debug. Simulation removes slow hardware from exploration but cannot by itself validate the effects of communication loss, physical variation or topology uncertainty. The core challenge is specifying reliable global behavior from local rules; that is an architectural programming problem, not merely insufficient arithmetic.
- **Assessment and possible experiment.** This is a useful decentralized-control substrate for distributed sensing/actuation, but generic learned local policies collide with distributed control, swarm robotics, cellular automata and self-organizing systems, and no broad AI learner survives. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 for the substrate; no candidate promoted.** If revisited, use a CPU simulator with variable communication radius, dropped/duplicated messages, asynchronous updates and moving agents; compare a fixed-lattice CA, local reactive controller, and a topology-agnostic learned local policy at matched message and update budgets. Reject the modernization if global-task success collapses with modest topology perturbations or if it needs position/oracle-state information that the amorphous model excludes. Not run.
- **Resource record.** Literature only; GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU process was started or inspected, so live occupancy is unknown.

#### AR-54 — RAF autocatalytic sets and GARD compositional memory (1980s–present): self-sustaining chemical organization

- **Original computation/representation.** Reflexively autocatalytic, food-generated (RAF) theory represents a chemical system as molecule types, possible reactions, catalyst links, and a supplied food set. A RAF subset is closed under available catalysts and can be generated from that food set; the Hordijk–Steel algorithm detects such a subset in polynomial time. It identifies self-sustaining organization, not a task learner. [Hordijk & Steel, 2004](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2003.11.020).
- **Compositional memory.** The GARD model represents an amphiphile assembly by its molecule-composition vector. Mutually catalytic interactions bias uptake during growth; division/fission can transmit a biased composition to descendants, proposed as a rudimentary non-sequence genome. This is a precise old memory-and-evolution substrate, but its memory is not an arbitrary learned concept or query-answering model. [Segré, Ben-Eli & Lancet, 2000 PNAS](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.97.8.4112); [GARD origin model](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1006583712886).
- **Was it bad or early?** Modern compute allows much larger reaction-network searches and stochastic growth/fission simulations; newer RAF variants analyze inhibition, boundaries and stoichiometry. Physical self-assembly experiments also make chemical autocatalysis less speculative. These advances do not solve the harder issue: stable information transmission across noisy growth/fission, or how a compositional memory becomes grounded in useful task behavior. A large random reaction graph may contain an RAF without the network ever dynamically reaching or robustly maintaining it.
- **Assessment and falsifier.** RAF/GARD are established artificial-life and origin-of-life models, not open general AI architectures. A CPU component test could implement the published GARD growth/fission process and measure parent–child composition decoding/channel capacity across repeated division and small perturbations, against a matched multiset-code baseline. The memory premise fails if lineage information collapses quickly or only survives with hand-tuned catalysis. This is not worth running unless a later learner proposal actually uses compositional inheritance. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 as a broad model class; retain as archaeology.**
- **Resource record.** Literature only; no GPU work. GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB; no process was started or inspected.

#### AR-55 — Chemical reaction networks as learned computation, and spiking neural P systems (1991–2026)

- **Architecture class and prior art.** Chemical reaction networks (CRNs) compute through mass-action reaction dynamics over molecule concentrations; DNA strand displacement can physically implement designed reaction systems. This is an established unconventional-computation class: prior work proposed chemical neural networks, implemented DNA threshold circuits and a four-neuron Hopfield memory experimentally, and compiled factor-graph sum-product inference into reactions. [Hjelmfelt et al., 1991/1992](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.89.1.388); [Qian, Winfree & Bruck, 2011](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10262); [Napp & Adams, NeurIPS 2013](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/4901-message-passing-inference-with-chemical-reaction-networks).
- **Important 2026 development (lead-verified, already screened as HY20).** Jaffard and Sbalzarini propose a deterministic mass-action CRN whose input-species subsets become experts when their flux exceeds a threshold. Feature-set products arise naturally from mass action; output species represent classes; weight concentrations and gain-function species implement exponentially weighted expert aggregation through reactions and renormalization. Each class runs a local rule system. The model freezes weights at test time. The authors provide regret bounds, restricted asymptotic/VC analyses, and a simulated 8×8 sklearn-digits study; their comparison is to a selected Hawkes/SNN baseline, not modern CNN/MLP or physical wet-lab training. They also state species/reaction counts grow with selected subset count, and without selection the count is combinatorial. This is a substantive new CRN-learning construction, but it is direct prior art for this notebook, not an open candidate; the chemistry substrate itself is older. [Jaffard & Sbalzarini, 2026 v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.12060).
- **What changed and what did not.** The preprint supplies an explicit in-CRN online learning rule and a formal learning analysis, beyond older chemical neural-network emulation. Differentiable simulation, synthetic data and modern solvers lower experimentation cost. The current evidence does not establish a physical learner, meaningful energy/runtime advantage, broad perception, or improvement over strong modern digital models. A useful CPU reproduction would first verify the ODE against exact EWA updates on small feature sets, then ablate feature selection and test pixel noise/shift with all species, reactions, feature selection and readout costs charged. Reject an advantage if it vanishes against matched EWA/linear controls or depends on favorable SNN comparison. This is a reproduction/utility test, not novelty work; not run.
- **Spiking neural P systems.** P systems represent multisets of objects inside membrane compartments and compute by parallel rewriting, transport, division or dissolution. Spiking neural P systems add directed neuron-like connections and timed spike rules. The families have active mathematical, learning, FPGA and GPU work; a 2025 survey includes Hebbian, Widrow–Hoff, fuzzy, convolutional and LSTM-like variants. Thus membrane/spiking-rewrite networks are not a new composition of “chemistry plus neural learning.” Published hard-problem complexity claims can rely on membrane division that allocates exponentially many compartments, an algorithmic resource assumption rather than a mere historical compute limit. [Păun, 2001](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0303-2647(00)00143-X); [Ionescu et al., 2006](https://doi.org/10.3233/FUN-2006-712-308); [Sosík et al., 2025 survey](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11047-025-10026-9).
- **Assessment.** Chemistry and membrane systems remain useful substrate-specific directions, especially for in-situ sensing/control, but the general model-class and neural/inference mechanisms are occupied. Novelty confidence is 0/5 for the substrate family; the precise 2026 CRN learning rule belongs to its authors' prior art. Keep current CRN candidate demoted as in HY20.
- **Modern chemical-learning and physical-reconfiguration addendum (2026-09-27).** Recurrent neural chemical reaction networks (RNCRNs) now have a 2026 peer-reviewed result proving approximation of arbitrary target dynamics and demonstrating small trained systems with oscillations, multistability and chaos; the authors describe DNA-strand-displacement implementation as feasible, but this is not yet a deployed chemical learner. A 2025 Neural CRN uses continuous-time concentration dynamics for supervised linear and nonlinear classification, also as a modeled architecture. Surface CRNs already combine local surface reactions with CA emulation and ant-like trail-following agents, closing generic chemistry-plus-stigmergy. Meanwhile, 2022 task-adaptive magnetic reservoirs and 2026 reconfigurable microfluidic geometry show physical reservoir dynamics can be selected or reshaped; the 2026 paper explicitly frames closed-loop performance feedback into geometry changes as future work. Its hydrogel erasure takes 10–30 minutes and one logic path waits about one hour for reaction/readout, making fast online plasticity implausible with the demonstrated device. Modern solvers, differentiable models and automation lower design costs, but transduction, reset latency, molecular noise, physical calibration, and application fit remain core limitations. [Dack et al. (2026)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42025162/); [Nagipogu & Reif (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1021/acssynbio.5c00099); [Clamons et al. (2020)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7276541/); [Lee et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06962); [Swinkels et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.73669).
- **Resource record.** Source review only; no local CPU/GPU experiment. GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU process was started or inspected, so live occupancy is unknown.

- **AR-55 modern physical-reservoir update (2026-09-27).** Task-adaptive physical reservoirs are no longer only a proposed research direction: a 2022 experiment reconfigures magnetic phases to select distinct memory/nonlinearity properties, while a 2026 microfluidic system prints and erases hydrogel geometry to alter chemical computation and provides a physical reservoir for several nonlinear function targets. This shows modern experimental control and fabrication have removed part of the static-substrate limitation. It does not demonstrate online task-error-driven morphology learning: geometries/configurations are selected externally, and the reservoir readout is trained separately. Scaling, repeatability, transduction, reconfiguration latency and energy remain open. [Lee et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06962); [Swinkels et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.73669); [Stepney, physical reservoir computing tutorial (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11047-024-09997-y).
- **AR-55 physical-learning prior-art correction (2026-09-27).** Du et al. show a physical metamaterial whose local stiffnesses learn shape-change examples by contrastive learning; the real device sequentially learns/forgets shape responses and demonstrates multistability, reflex gripping, and locomotion. Chen et al. show adaptive-stiffness metamaterials updating stiffness distribution through local strain targets and model-free physical interaction, adapting to unknown mechanical loads in tens of iterations. These are not chemical reservoirs, but they overturn any broad claim that physical substrates have not learned task-relevant parameters from feedback. Li & Mao’s September 2026 preprint goes closer to temporal computation: a forward trajectory plus time-reversed adjoint-error trajectory yields local updates for spring, mass, and damping parameters; examples include vowel classification, but remain numerical, and the method requires paired forward/adjoint drives rather than continuous one-pass learning. Together these results occupy physical parameter learning, mechanical feedback adaptation, and time-domain physical-network training. Remaining distinctions are substrate and timescale, not a new general architecture. [Du et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03226-2); [Chen et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eml.2026.102502); [Li & Mao (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05977).

- **Predictive-topology learner / PTM.** Collins and Shen's Stochastic Distinguishing Experiments learn variable-length action/observation tests that partition histories into a predictive state and adapt tests from surprises. That occupies PTM's broad grow-and-split predictive-graph mechanism; a continuous prototype graph could be an implementation choice, but needs an empirical advantage over SDE rather than a novelty claim. - **Safety-triggered active sensing.** Triggering model updates or sensing from uncertainty/safety margins has direct 2026 event-triggered GP learning under CBF constraints; safety-aware sensor pointing also exists. Reject as a new hybrid. [Safe event-triggered GP learning, IEEE TAC 2026](https://doi.org/10.1109/TAC.2026.3680122); [sensor pointing with CBFs](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10272635/).
- **Verification-driven predictive-state refinement.** Splitting predictive states when model checking returns a counterexample is close to CEGAR for POMDPs, and predictive-state refinement already has SDE/sPOMDP prior art. Reject the broad hybrid. [Zhang et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06209); [Collins & Shen, 2017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bica.2017.07.005).
- **Reversible counterfactual branch execution.** Running an intervention, applying an inverse to roll back, and trying another branch could reduce snapshot memory in deterministic planning. Reversible computation, activation-reconstruction RevNets and invertible neural networks are direct prior art for the core primitive; real noisy/many-to-one observations require saving lost information, which can erase the storage gain. A deterministic toy search could compare snapshot and apply/undo memory before adding noise. Keep as a narrow systems test at most, not a new model class. [Bennett, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.176.0525); [RevNets, NeurIPS 2017](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/hash/f9be311e65d81a9ad8150a60844bb94c-Abstract.html); [Invertible Residual Networks, ICML 2019](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/behrmann19a.html).

### Neural Particle Automata follow-up and old-architecture seam audit (2026-09-27)

#### AR-56 — Neural Particle Automata as a modern descendant of local self-organization

- **Original mechanism and what the modern paper actually computes.** Neural Particle Automata (NPA) generalizes neural cellular automata (NCA) from a fixed lattice to particles with continuous positions and internal states. For each particle, differentiable smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) estimates local density, neighborhood-smoothed hidden state, state gradients, and density gradients. A shared small MLP maps those local features to additive hidden-state and optional position updates. A spatial hash finds geometric neighbors; a Bernoulli mask applies only a random subset of updates each step. This is a learned local dynamical rule, not an independent learner at each particle. The paper trains with backpropagation through time and task-level rendered-output/classification losses; at inference the rule parameters stay fixed while particle states and positions evolve. [Kim et al., *Neural Particle Automata*, arXiv / SIGGRAPH 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16096); [official implementation](https://github.com/TheDevilWillBeBee/NPA).
- **Tasks, scale, and demonstrated boundary.** The paper reports 2D/3D morphogenesis, particle texture synthesis, and distributed classification of a 512-point MNIST representation (98.42% reported test accuracy). Configurations use 512–16,384 particles and about 11k–38k update-rule parameters. These establish learned collective behavior for bounded visual/geometry tasks, not a general reasoning or task-learning system. The authors report that particles cannot merge or split, crowded target regions slow SPH, directional features are not rotation-equivariant, and training is sensitive to hyperparameters. [NPA paper, experiments and limitations](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.16096).
- **Was the old amorphous-computing idea simply too early?** The 1996 Amorphous Computing Manifesto asked for coordinated computation by unreliable units connected through unknown, irregular, time-varying local links, without assuming that neighbors' coordinates or orientations are known. NPA removes a substantial implementation barrier: dynamic geometric neighborhoods can now be differentiated and hash-grid accelerated. But it supplies Euclidean positions, computes neighborhoods from a spatial snapshot, and fixes particle count. In the reference code, the model computes perception and proposed updates for the whole batch before a Bernoulli mask applies them; the paper's p-to-zero asynchronous limit is a limiting dynamics interpretation, not an event-queue implementation that immediately consumes newly updated neighbor messages. This code-level distinction is visible in the [official update implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TheDevilWillBeBee/NPA/main/models/npa.py). The old problem therefore splits into a solved learned-local-rule/irregular-geometry part and a still harder distributed-systems part: unknown links, delayed messages, joins, failures, and no globally available coordinates.
- **Prior art collision and disposition.** Learned graph cellular automata already replace the lattice by arbitrary graphs and learn shared local transitions with message-passing networks; they include dynamic-connectivity flocking and local rules that coordinate global target behavior. [Grattarola, Livi & Alippi, *Learning Graph Cellular Automata*, 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14237). Event-by-event local recomputation for asynchronously evolving event graphs also has direct neural prior art in AEGNN. [Schaefer, Gehrig & Scaramuzza, CVPR 2022](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022/html/Schaefer_AEGNN_Asynchronous_Event-Based_Graph_Neural_Networks_CVPR_2022_paper.html). NPA is a meaningful modern descendant of local self-organization, but it is an established 2026 model and does not make arbitrary unreliable networks a new architecture. **Keep as archaeology; do not promote NPA or “amorphous computing + NPA” as a new model class.**
- **Possible residual, sharply bounded.** A system that has no coordinates, receives only delayed/dropped neighbor messages, and learns its local rule or update hazard after deployment would differ from the NPA paper's trained fixed rule and the cited graph-automata demonstrations. However, asynchronous event processing and graph-local learning are each established, and local online plasticity has a large separate literature. Novelty confidence for the combined residual is **0.5/5**; this is a deployment/learning-rule seam, not a current architecture candidate.
- **Small CPU falsifier, only if an edge-sensing use case warrants it.** On 256–1,024 simulated nodes, compare (a) reference-style NPA random-mask rounds, (b) learned graph cellular automata, and (c) an event queue that updates a node from delayed/dropped local messages on a changing random-geometric graph. Hold the shared-rule parameter count and total local message/update budget fixed; impose 10–30% node/link failures and compare target-shape recovery or point-label consensus, recovery time, and messages per correct output. Drop the deployment claim if event-driven execution loses accuracy/robustness or does not cut messages at matched quality. A positive result would support a systems mechanism only; it would not establish broad AI novelty.
- **Resource record.** Literature and source-code inspection only; no local experiment, GPU use, or GPU process was started. GPU usage/peak VRAM: 0 GB; live occupancy was not inspected and remains unknown. The CPU falsifier is a proposal, not a run.

#### HY-45 — Amorphous local computation × learned graph/particle automata (rejected as a new class)

- **Source mechanisms.** Amorphous computing contributes reliability under unknown, changing local connectivity and a system with no preassigned coordinates; NPA contributes learned shared state/position updates over continuous particles; graph neural cellular automata contribute learned local transition rules on arbitrary and even changing graph structure.
- **Exact coupling proposed.** Replace SPH's coordinate-derived neighborhood with a local message inbox on a time-varying graph; each unit carries a state and a shared learned rule, and updates asynchronously when local messages arrive. Omit a global clock and coordinate system; train/evaluate through link loss, delay, and node churn.
- **Why this would behave differently—and why it still does not survive novelty review.** The coupling moves the local update from geometric kernel sums to messages arriving on an unreliable communication graph, so it could be useful on sensor skins or ad hoc robotic collectives. But Graph Cellular Automata already learn arbitrary/dynamic graph-local transitions, NPA already adds continuous moving neighborhoods and stochastic subset updates, and AEGNN already demonstrates incremental asynchronous recomputation over event graphs. The distinctive remainder would need a new online local credit-assignment/update rule that remains stable under churn without global synchronization. No mechanism has yet been specified, and the constituent literatures on local plasticity, event-triggered execution, graph learning, and amorphous programming are substantial. Reject the broad hybrid; at most retain the CPU deployment falsifier under AR-56.
- **Main failure modes.** Unknown identity and degree changes can invalidate state; message delay can create inconsistent local views; dynamic graph aggregation may lose spatial inductive bias; local credit assignment may not identify useful rule changes; event scheduling can reduce simulated FLOPs but increase wall-clock/communication cost.
- **Prior-art conclusion.** The 1996 manifesto defines the hardware/network constraints; 2021 Graph Cellular Automata occupy the learned arbitrary-graph transition; 2022 AEGNN occupies event-local asynchronous recomputation; 2026 NPA occupies learned continuous particle-local dynamics. No new learning, memory, or inference mechanism remains specified. [Amorphous Computing Manifesto](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/mac/projects/amorphous/white-paper/amorph-new/amorph-new.html); [GNCA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14237); [AEGNN](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022/html/Schaefer_AEGNN_Asynchronous_Event-Based_Graph_Neural_Networks_CVPR_2022_paper.html); [NPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16096). Novelty confidence: **0/5 for the stated hybrid**.

#### AR-57 — Real-Time Recurrent Learning (RTRL, 1987–1989): exact online credit without retaining the sequence

- **Original computation and unit.** A recurrent network normally learns temporal credit by backpropagating through a stored or replayed sequence. RTRL carries forward the sensitivity of each current hidden unit to each recurrent-network parameter, updating that sensitivity as each new input arrives. A loss at time t can therefore update recurrent weights immediately while the network runs, without storing a complete unroll or knowing the episode boundary in advance. The repeated computational object is a hidden state plus its state-to-parameter Jacobian (an eligibility tensor), not a token or fixed-length sequence window. [Williams & Zipser, *A Learning Algorithm for Continually Running Fully Recurrent Neural Networks*, Neural Computation 1989](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1989.1.2.270).
- **Historical bottleneck and what modern hardware changes.** RTRL addresses online, indefinite streams, but its exact dense sensitivities require nonlocal parameter-to-state communication and rapidly growing compute/memory as recurrent width increases. Faster hardware changes constants; it does not remove the sensitivity tensor's scaling. Structured recurrence is the more consequential change. The 2024 Recurrent Trace Units (RTUs) modify linear recurrent units so RTRL can be applied efficiently, then evaluate the method in partially observable reinforcement-learning tasks. Their paper reports RTUs outperforming GRUs and Transformers on several selected environments with lower computation. [Elelimy et al., *Real-Time Recurrent Learning using Trace Units in Reinforcement Learning*, NeurIPS 2024](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/1e616bde0438cb10cb6adf076ae7d336-Abstract-Conference.html).
- **Modernization and prior art.** This is a direct modern revival, not an unoccupied architecture class: RTUs combine structured linear recurrence with online RTRL; approximate online gradients such as UORO/SnAp and selective/sparse RTRL address the same cost boundary. The opportunity is to test when exact online credit is worth its cost, not to rename RTRL. Novelty confidence: **0/5 as a learning architecture; moderate value as an online-learning benchmark**.
- **Where it may still help.** An always-on controller or sensor can receive a sparse label/reward at irregular times and adapt without retaining a growing activation history. Its advantage should be largest when the stream has no natural replay boundary and a long-lived hidden state matters. Likely failures are high dense-network cost, sensitivity traces becoming stale as weights change, unstable updates on nonstationary data, and a structured recurrent parameterization whose optimization or inductive bias may be unsuitable for a task. The RTU paper argues that its linear complex-diagonal recurrence can represent a dense linear recurrence after a change of basis, but reports a negative theoretical result for extending that equivalence to nonlinear recurrence.
- **Small falsifiable experiment.** Use a CPU-generated partially observable sequence task with a long unreset stream and a sudden latent-transition shift. Compare a small dense exact-RTRL RNN, an RTU, UORO or SnAp, e-prop, and truncated BPTT at matched parameter, environment-step, and wall-clock/update budgets. Measure pre/post-shift return or log loss, adaptation steps, retained behavior, per-step compute, and state/trace memory. The modernization claim fails if exact RTRL does not improve adaptation at equal wall-clock cost, if trace staleness erases its benefit, or if RTU/approximate traces match it at materially lower cost. **Protocol only; not run.**
- **Resource record.** Primary-paper review only; no experiment or GPU process started. GPU use/peak VRAM: 0 GB; live occupancy unknown. Any later RTRL prototype can remain CPU-only at small hidden widths.

### Independent archaeology continuation and hybrid collision checks — 2026-09-27

#### AR-58 — Learning automata: reward changes a finite action distribution

- **Original computation.** A stochastic automaton selects one of a finite set of actions, receives a random environment response, and updates its action-probability vector. The repeated operation is a simple reward/penalty update to a policy distribution; internal state need not be a learned feature representation. This made a compact online controller for unknown but repeated environments, not a general world model. [Narendra & Thathachar, “Learning Automata—A Survey,” IEEE SMC 1974](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSMC.1974.5408453).
- **Why it struggled and what changed.** Simple schemes had narrow action sets and weak state/context representation; response noise, changing environments, and delayed credit make convergence slow or misleading. Modern computation can store richer context and run many trials, but the basic probability-vector update does not become more expressive merely because hardware is faster. Contextual bandits and reinforcement learning subsume the broad decision-learning role; online adaptation remains useful for tiny controllers, routing, and allocation.
- **Prior art and verdict.** This is established reinforcement-learning archaeology, not an unrevived architecture. A purported new version would need a substantive structural or credit-assignment mechanism beyond contextualizing the action probabilities. **Novelty confidence 0/5.** [Primary survey](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSMC.1974.5408453).
- **Small falsifier if a use case appears.** In a nonstationary contextual bandit with delayed noisy reward, compare a finite learning automaton, contextual bandit, and small recurrent policy at matched memory and interaction budgets. Measure regret and recovery after context/action drift. A revival claim fails if the automaton does not achieve a useful low-memory/low-latency tradeoff; no experiment run.

#### AR-59 — FOIL / inductive logic programming: grow relational clauses from examples

- **Original computation.** FOIL grows a Horn-clause body from general to specific, adding relational literals that separate positive from negative examples; clauses can be recursive and use explicit background relations. The internal object is an executable relational rule, and inference is logical query evaluation. Its 1990 paper explicitly notes restrictions to function-free Horn clauses and inability to invent predicates. [Quinlan, “Learning Logical Definitions from Relations,” Machine Learning 1990](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022699322624).
- **Why it struggled and what changed.** Greedy symbolic search is brittle when predicates, variables, and relational joins grow; explicit symbolic predicates also require structured observations or a perception layer. Modern optimizers and neural perception can soften these limits, but do not remove combinatorial rule search or the problem of grounding. Differentiable modern systems directly revisit this area: NeuralLP learns weighted compositions of relations; DeepProbLog integrates neural predicates with probabilistic program inference; Neural Logic Machines use differentiable operators for first-order reasoning. [NeuralLP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08367); [DeepProbLog](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.10872); [Neural Logic Machines](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.11694).
- **Disposition.** Direct modernization is well established; simply attaching a vision/language encoder to FOIL is a pipeline, not an architecture novelty. Potential residual: online clause growth with cost-bounded counterexample queries for changing relational environments, but ILP, program synthesis and CEGIS already occupy much of it. **Novelty confidence 0/5 as a broad model class.**
- **Small falsifier if revisited.** On synthetic relational tasks with recursion and nuisance predicates, compare FOIL, beam-search ILP, and a differentiable rule learner at matched query/compute budgets. Measure exact rule recovery, held-out relation generalization, and update cost after schema drift. Reject a proposed modern advantage if better perception merely hides failures in relational search. No run.

#### AR-60 — Intrinsic evolvable hardware: evolve a circuit in the physical substrate

- **Original computation.** A genetic algorithm directly changes FPGA configuration bits and evaluates each phenotype on the physical chip, letting the circuit exploit continuous-time transistor and routing dynamics omitted by a clean digital model. Adrian Thompson’s 1996/1997 tone discriminator used a 10×10 portion of an XC6216, evolved a 1.8k-bit genotype, and found a continuous-time circuit without a clock or off-chip timing component. [Thompson, “An Evolved Circuit, Intrinsic in Silicon, Entwined with Physics”](https://gwern.net/doc/ai/1997-thompson.pdf).
- **Historical bottleneck and modernization.** The full 5,000-generation run took about 2–3 weeks because each individual needed roughly five seconds of physical evaluation; selection, mutation, and reconfiguration were negligible. Faster FPGA reconfiguration, parallel boards, differentiable surrogates and modern evolutionary algorithms could reduce wall time, and large simulation can prefilter candidates. Yet the exact phenomenon being exploited is hardware-specific and temperature-sensitive; simulation/surrogates can erase the real substrate behavior, and physical fitness still costs time. This is best viewed as a physical circuit-search method, not a general AI architecture. The primary study reports that the evolved response changed with chip temperature outside the approximately 10°C range seen during evolution.
- **What might remain.** A useful narrow target is self-calibrating or fault-tolerant sensor circuits that exploit analog device dynamics. The novelty would be a co-evolution/control protocol that explicitly preserves behavior across operating conditions, not “AI that evolves itself.” **Novelty confidence 1/5 for a robust deployment protocol; 0/5 for the architecture class.**
- **Small falsifier.** Compare direct evolution, simulator-only evolution, and a simulator-prefilter + physical fine-search loop on a small reconfigurable board. Train over a temperature sweep, then measure fitness evaluations, wall time, and out-of-range robustness. Reject the hybrid if prefiltering selects brittle circuits or does not cut physical evaluations at matched robustness. **Not run; no FPGA was accessed.**

#### HY-46 — Reservoirs × structural plasticity × delayed reward (reject: direct prior art)

- **Proposed seam.** A fixed random reservoir is cheap and temporally rich but cannot adapt its wiring; reward-modulated plasticity adapts weights but can be noisy and unstable; structural growth/pruning changes representation capacity. A seemingly compelling coupling would let local eligibility traces retain recent causal activity, reward gate edge reweighting, and a homeostatic rule add or prune edges when persistent prediction error indicates missing dynamics.
- **Why the mechanisms would interact.** The intended change is to allocate recurrent structure only to activity chains implicated by delayed reward, using eligibility as a local bridge between a delayed objective and architecture growth. This could in principle change the representation online without backpropagating through a long history.
- **Collision.** RSRN-SP already combines reward-modulated STDP, homeostasis, and ongoing structural growth/pruning, including an eligibility trace that can bridge delayed reward; it evaluates counting, motion prediction and motion generation. HAG directly grows reservoir connectivity from co-activity and homeostatic needs without gradient steps. Thus “reservoir + reward + structural plasticity” is already a known family of couplings. [RSRN-SP, Frontiers Neuroscience 2023](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2023.1224752/full); [HAG, Nature Communications 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-67137-1).
- **Disposition and residual test.** Reject as a new architecture. A potential implementation-level question is whether reward eligibility should trigger *which edge births* rather than merely weight updates or random growth, with a fixed degree budget. Compare random growth, co-activity HAG, RSRN-SP, and eligibility-targeted edge birth on delayed-reward switched dynamics; falsify if the targeted rule fails to improve adaptation at equal edge count or destabilizes old behavior. This is only a narrow benchmark seam; novelty confidence 0.5/5. No run.

#### HY-47 — ART vigilance × HDC role-binding memory (generic hybrid already instantiated)

- **Mechanism.** ART contributes online category creation and mismatch-triggered reset; hyperdimensional computing contributes fixed-width role–filler binding and superposition. Combining them might add/delete a drifting role in a structured object without rebuilding the entire memory, while vigilance operates separately for each bound field rather than globally.
- **Prior art.** A 2026 Zenodo preprint HD-ART already combines HDC waveform encodings, role-like localized routing, dynamic ART vigilance, a bounded Hebbian accumulator, and hardware-bounded online cluster memory for spike sorting. It reports a 384-channel Neuropixels evaluation, but is currently a single-author preprint and should not be treated as independently validated evidence. [Hao, *HD-ART*, Zenodo preprint (2026-08-12)](https://zenodo.org/records/21903954). The generic ART×HDC hybrid is therefore occupied even if the exact fieldwise repair rule is not.
- **Verdict and cheap disproof.** Demote to a component-level niche idea. Test a single drifting role in synthetic compositional streams against Fuzzy ART, HDC prototypes, and the preprint's global vigilance design; measure role-local forgetting, collateral damage to stable fields, memory growth and assignment latency. Reject the fieldwise extension if it does not localize damage or if per-field categories grow without bound. No run; the source preprint is unreviewed, and this residual is too application-specific to promote.

#### AR-61 — Turing’s unorganized machines (1948): random Boolean networks with editable links

- **Original mechanism.** Turing described A-type networks as randomly wired, synchronous two-state Boolean units. B-type networks add “connection modifiers”: small internal state elements let an external trainer disable or enable particular links, so learned information can reside in the connection pattern. P-type machines are a different, non-neural line: a partially specified finite-state machine whose missing transition entries are filled under reward/punishment feedback. Keep these three mechanisms separate; Turing’s B-type does not itself specify a usable local plasticity law. The NPL report is available as a [reproduced scan](https://intelligentmachinerycourse.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/turing-intelligent-machinery-1948.pdf); the surviving typescript is catalogued as [AMT/C/11 in the Turing Archive](https://turingarchive.kings.cam.ac.uk/unpublished-manuscripts-and-drafts-amtc/amt-c-11). [Copeland & Proudfoot’s critical reconstruction](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00413694) is a secondary source, not Turing’s report.
- **Historical failure versus fundamental limit.** In 1948 the available stored-program computers were tiny, and Turing had no algorithm for training B-type connection modifiers; he proposed search/“interference” rather than a specified scalable learner. Modern simulation, evolutionary search and differentiable optimization make small experiments cheap, but unrestricted discrete topology search remains combinatorial. More importantly, an editable edge is a representation, not a learning rule. The original report is clearer about the proposed network than about a scalable training procedure; modern descendants supply that missing algorithm and thereby occupy the broad revival.
- **Modern descendants already occupy the obvious revival.** TurSOM directly couples Turing-inspired connection reorganization with Kohonen winner competition; it adds connection learning rate, edge reorganization, and a neuron responsibility radius, and demonstrates adaptive splitting into independent chains on low-dimensional clustering patterns. A 2012 graph-based evolutionary A-type study evolves synchronous NAND/delay networks for Boolean tasks; it is explicitly proof of concept with ad-hoc evolutionary settings. These close the broad “revive Turing networks with modern optimization” claim. [TurSOM, *Neurocomputing* 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2011.04.028); [Orr & Martin, *Evolving A-Type Artificial Neural Networks*, 2012 / arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1108.1530).
- **What might remain and verdict.** A precise distinction could be topology search that is local, reversible, and credit-assigned from delayed task outcomes rather than a global evolutionary objective. But HAG, RSRN-SP, differentiable plasticity, NEAT-family methods and adaptive structural-learning work occupy nearby choices. No broad new class is supported. The useful historical lesson is that the training algorithm—not the concept of a random or reconfigurable network—was missing. **Novelty confidence 0/5 for Turing-network revival.**
- **Small falsifier.** On 4–8-bit streaming Boolean tasks with a delayed reward and a midstream rule switch, compare fixed-topology weight learning, global topology evolution, and a strictly local edge-toggle learner with a fixed edit budget. Hold unit count and total circuit evaluations constant; measure exact generalization to held-out input sequences, edits per task, old-task retention, and update latency. Drop the local-edit claim if it cannot beat topology evolution in evaluation cost without worse retention, or if its signal must reveal the target truth table. This tests a specific learner, not the architecture's novelty. No run.

#### HY-48 — Turing B-type link modifiers × SOM competition (reject: TurSOM is direct prior art)

- **Proposed combination.** B-type modifiers provide a learnable connection graph; SOM contributes winner-take-neighborhood adaptation of feature prototypes. Couple them so the winning unit and its neighbors compete to keep, redirect, add or remove graph edges, allowing one map to split into multiple untangled clusters.
- **Mechanistic interaction.** Unlike a SOM with a fixed lattice, the edge graph itself changes in response to winner competition; topology becomes learned memory and cluster boundaries can cause graph separation. This is a real change in representation and organization, not merely running two models in sequence.
- **Prior-art result.** TurSOM implements this basic interaction directly, naming its three mechanisms connection learning rate, connection reorganization and neuron responsibility radius. It claims faster convergence and independent clusters, with the reported demonstration focused on 1D topology and a small number of patterns/datasets. Thus the broad hybrid is occupied; a stronger modern replication could challenge its scale/robustness claims, not establish novelty. [TurSOM, *Neurocomputing* 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2011.04.028).
- **Small disproof/replication.** On noisy two-moons, double-spiral and drifting mixture streams, compare TurSOM, GNG and a fixed SOM at matched prototype count, edge-edit count and distance evaluations. Measure topology error, disconnected-cluster recovery, order sensitivity, and runtime. If the reported cluster split vanishes under noise/order variation or equalized compute, downgrade TurSOM's practical advantage; a positive result remains a niche online-clustering result. No experiment run.
