### Symbolic-memory and external-stack archaeology — 2026-09-27

#### AR-62 — K-lines (Minsky, 1979): reinstate a partial solver state

- **Original computation.** When a problem solution or memorable event is judged useful, create a K-line connected to some of the active “mental agencies.” Later activation reinstates a partial state, allowing prior procedures and dispositions to contribute to a new situation. Minsky adds two specific safeguards: a level band limits activation to intermediate agency levels so low-level old perceptions and high-level old solutions do not overwhelm current input/goals; cross-exclusion groups make competing agent states persistent; recursive K-lines can link to already-active K-lines, making memory compositional. This is a richer hypothesis than storing the old answer or replaying a full episode. [Minsky, MIT AI Memo 516 (1979)](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.803/pdf/aim-516.pdf).
- **Was it bad or early?** The bottleneck was mainly an underspecified mechanism, not insufficient computation. The memo describes agents, level bands, selective reinstatement and conflict behavior, but does not operationalize what counts as a solver agency, a memorable success, cue similarity, level assignment, or harmful/obsolete activation. More compute cannot choose those semantics. Narrow implementations exist for mood-conditioned music histories; broader episodic control, skill memory, Soar chunking and modular routing are adjacent descendants/components, but none alone is identical to the proposed partial solver-state reinstatement. [Toptsis & Dubitski, 2008](https://doi.org/10.2174/1874061800802010046).
- **Disposition.** Retain as cognitive-architecture archaeology and reject as a new general memory class until the selection, cueing, pruning and conflict rules are made algorithmic. Potential residual is cue-triggered reinstatement of a sparse bundle of rule/module activations, guarded by present context. Novelty confidence **0.5/5**; low-priority niche probe.
- **Falsifiable probe.** In a deterministic solver with reusable subroutines, surface variation and some obsolete routines, compare K-line activation bundles against exact trace replay, Soar-style chunking and a learned module router at matched memory and compute. Measure solver calls, transfer to recombined tasks, stale-rule harm and recall. Reject the mechanism if any benefit reduces to a macro/router or if old co-activations override current evidence. No run.

#### AR-63 — Rete (1974–1982): incremental rule matching with retained partial joins

- **Original computation.** Rete compiles the condition sides of many production rules into a shared network of feature tests and joins. Each node retains matching facts or partial matches; inserts, edits and deletions are propagated through affected paths to update the conflict set, instead of rescanning all rules against all facts every inference cycle. Forgy reports use with hundreds to over a thousand patterns and objects and notes observed systems spending over 90% of runtime in matching. [Forgy, “Rete: A Fast Algorithm for the Many Pattern/Many Object Pattern Match Problem,” *Artificial Intelligence* 1982](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(82)90020-0).
- **Historical bottleneck versus enduring limit.** Rete solved a real CPU bottleneck by exploiting that working memory often changes only slightly between cycles. Its enduring boundary is the time–memory tradeoff: saved partial matches accelerate sparse updates, but become costly or counterproductive when most data changes each cycle. That is an operating-regime condition rather than a failure that GPUs automatically erase.
- **Modern revival and verdict.** Rete remains part of rule-engine infrastructure. Drools’ current Phreak algorithm is an explicit descendant: it delays partial matching, uses node/segment/rule memories, pauses/resumes stack-based evaluation, and batches set-oriented propagation; official documentation describes it as more scalable than Rete in large systems. Therefore Rete is a useful inference substrate, not an AI architecture candidate. [Official Drools Phreak documentation](https://docs.jboss.org/drools/release/latest/drools-docs/drools/rule-engine/index.html).
- **Small falsifier only for a workload decision.** Generate production rules with shared prefixes and vary the fraction of working-memory facts changed each cycle. Compare naive rematching, Rete and Phreak at the same facts/rules; measure time and retained partial-match memory. The useful operating regime should show a clear update-fraction crossover; no architecture novelty is tested. No run.

#### AR-64 — Neural Network Pushdown Automaton (1992–1993): train a continuous stack, extract a discrete PDA

- **Original computation.** A finite recurrent controller reads the input symbol, hidden-state vector and current stack reading; it emits a new state plus a continuous push/pop/no-op action. The external analog stack stores discrete symbols with continuous lengths, and its new top is fed back to the controller. A joint endpoint/stack-length objective trains controller and stack behavior from positive and negative strings. After learning, states/actions are quantized and a discrete pushdown automaton is extracted. Sun et al. report experiments on balanced parentheses, (1^n0^n), and a deterministic palindrome language; the training sets were under 512 positive/negative strings for the reported grammars. [Sun et al., *The Neural Network Pushdown Automaton: Model, Stack and Learning Simulations*, U. Maryland TR 1993](https://api.drum.lib.umd.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/58808e6a-dddf-4ac5-9765-6c6206e64f6c/content).
- **Why it struggled / what changed.** Backpropagation through continuous stack actions and top-of-stack readings is difficult: tiny action changes can leave a tiny fraction of one symbol at the top and cause a discrete jump in the observed stack reading. The authors report numeric error accumulating on longer strings and difficulties learning palindrome stack actions without sufficient supervision/hints. Modern autodiff, GPUs, curriculum generation and larger synthetic grammars lower optimization and data costs; they do not remove discontinuous read semantics, controller ambiguity or extraction/verification needs.
- **Direct modern revival and exact residual.** Grefenstette et al. (NeurIPS 2015) reintroduce differentiable stacks, queues and deques for transduction; later stack-RNN analyses note that stacks can be harder to optimize than ordinary recurrent state and may be ignored in some settings. The old idea was partly early, but “RNN plus stack” is directly occupied. The most distinctive 1993 contribution is not external stack memory alone: it explicitly quantizes a trained continuous machine into a symbolic PDA, permitting formal verification and arbitrary-length operation if the extracted transition system is correct. [Grefenstette et al., NeurIPS 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02516); [Hao et al., CoNLL 2020 analysis](https://aclanthology.org/2020.conll-1.41/).
- **Disposition.** Keep as a strong historical bridge between neural learning and formal automata; do not promote NNPDA as new. A residual experiment could study whether extraction plus counterexample-guided repair makes the neural model a more data-efficient proposal generator than classical active grammar learning. This is a narrow training/inference pipeline and has substantial ILP, active automata learning and CEGIS prior art. Novelty confidence **0.5/5**.
- **Small falsifier.** Train on strings up to length 20 from held-out Dyck-(k)/visibly-pushdown grammars, extract and minimize a discrete PDA, then test exact recognition up to length 500 and on held-out grammar structures. Compare faithful NNPDA, modern neural stack, RNN/Transformer, and a symbolic active learner under equal oracle strings and total compute. Reject the revival claim if extraction fails, longer strings expose stack drift, it needs manually supplied hints, or it gives no data-efficiency advantage. No run.

#### HY-49 — Continuous neural stack × counterexample-guided automaton repair (demote; components are established)

- **Proposed coupling.** Let a differentiable recurrent stack model propose an approximate grammar controller; quantize it into a PDA, use a formal equivalence check or adversarial string search to find a counterexample, then feed the counterexample back as targeted training data and repeat extraction. The stack supplies a learnable structural prior; discrete checking converts approximate behavior into a falsifiable language-recognition claim.
- **Mechanistic change and potential benefit.** The extraction is not a post-hoc interpretability report: it controls the next training batch, making neural optimization and symbolic counterexample search alternate until the discrete machine passes a verification gate. This could use gradient learning to propose compact machines while exact automata provide a correctness boundary.
- **Prior-art collision and disposition.** NNPDA already quantizes the learned continuous controller/stack into a PDA; active automata learning, Angluin-style counterexample refinement and CEGIS already alternate hypotheses with counterexamples; neural-symbolic grammar learners already couple gradient models with symbolic constraints. The exact batch-selection policy may be a research question, but it is a hybrid training pipeline around an established language learner, not a new broad model class. Reject as an architecture claim; retain a small method comparison only if language generalization is a target. [NNPDA 1993](https://api.drum.lib.umd.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/58808e6a-dddf-4ac5-9765-6c6206e64f6c/content); [Angluin, “Learning regular sets from queries and counterexamples” (1987)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0890-5401(87)90052-6); [Jha & Seshia, “A Theory of Formal Synthesis via Inductive Learning” (2017)](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~sseshia/pubs/b2hd-jha-acta17.html).
- **Small disproof.** Compare the coupled loop against neural-stack training with random/hard-negative strings, Angluin-style active learning, and a neuro-symbolic grammar learner on Dyck-(k)/visibly-pushdown tasks. Charge every membership/equivalence query and training step; measure total queries to a correct extracted automaton, length generalization and verification cost. Drop it if the neural proposal does not reduce oracle queries or if approximate equivalence checking dominates. No run.

### Early associative and categorical architectures — 2026-09-27

#### AR-65 — Steinbuch’s Lernmatrix (1960–1961): one-shot relay associations

- **Original computation.** A binary feature pattern activates columns of a matrix; a supervised “learning step” latches selected input-to-meaning relay connections, and recall accumulates support for output rows. Steinbuch’s demonstration used 20 photocells and a 10-by-20 relay matrix. A person selected which meaning/output row to associate with the displayed pattern; it was not an autonomous feature learner. [KIT historical record and mechanism description](https://www.100objekte.kit.edu/en/object/056/); [Steinbuch, “Die Lernmatrix,” *Kybernetik* 1 (1961), 36–45](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00293853).
- **Was it bad or early?** Relay cost and hand-coded 20-bit visual features constrained the demonstration, so modern memory and learned visual encoders remove real engineering limits. But the core remains supervised associative storage plus row competition. The prototype’s small alphabet and manually selected label do not establish compositional recognition, invariance, or scalable representation learning. More compute cannot supply those missing mechanisms.
- **Modernization and closest prior art.** The association primitive was generalized by binary and graded associative memories, Willshaw-style clipped Hebbian storage, and modern high-capacity associative-memory models. An encoder in front can improve the codes, but does not make a relay/lookup matrix a new model class. A possible narrow revival is whether a quantized, write-once associative matrix gives a useful memory/energy/robustness tradeoff on-device; that is a memory implementation claim. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 as an architecture.**
- **Small falsifier.** On CPU, compare bit-packed Lernmatrix recall against nearest-neighbor storage and a tiny learned prototype table at the same bit budget. Sweep corrupted input bits, label imbalance, and number of stored patterns on both raw pixels and frozen learned features. Reject practical value if the matrix needs the feature encoder to approach the baselines or saturates sooner at matched memory. No run.

#### AR-66 — Willshaw associative memory (1969): clipped Hebbian writes and sparse one-step recall

- **Original computation.** A binary connection is switched on when a pre- and postsynaptic unit co-occur; the weight is clipped at one. At recall, a partial cue sends parallel input through this binary matrix and output thresholds retrieve the associated pattern, traditionally in one pass. It trades graded-weight accumulation for low-cost monotone writes; capacity depends strongly on sparse, low-overlap codes. [Willshaw, Buneman & Longuet-Higgins, *Nature* 222 (1969)](https://doi.org/10.1038/222960a0); [Sommer & Dayan’s technical account of the clipped rule and sparse-pattern regime](https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/papers/sd98p.pdf).
- **Was it bad or early?** Modern bit-parallel operations and larger memories make the matrix cheaper to simulate and store. They do not remove saturation/crosstalk: repeated OR-like writes erase which episode caused a connection, so dense or correlated codes become hard to distinguish. Capacity is a representational-load limit as well as a historical hardware limit. Later analyses quantify the sparse-activity dependence. [Sacramento & Wichert (2012)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.7196).
- **Modernization and verdict.** This is already modernized directly: a 2022 encoder–Willshaw-memory–decoder system evaluates completion, classification and generation on MNIST and missing-modality inference, with an iterative retrieval variant. This is useful evidence that old memory primitives can remain practical components, but the system combines established learned encoders with a known memory rule. Reject as a new model class; retain as a memory baseline. [Simas, Sa-Couto & Wichert (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.04827). **Novelty confidence: 0/5.**
- **Small falsifier for an application claim.** Sweep code density, association load, cue dropout and code correlation on CPU. Compare bit-budgeted Willshaw memory with exact lookup and a modern associative-memory baseline. Measure exact recall, false activations, bits per recovered association and update cost. Reject if useful recall requires manually orthogonal sparse codes or if performance loses to the matched memory baseline. No run.

#### AR-67 — Marr’s archicortex model (1971): sparse codon formation with recurrent completion

- **Original computation.** A three-layer circuit projects an event into a sparse middle “codon” representation and then to an output; modifiable recurrent collaterals among output units let a partial retrieval recruit missing components before a return path reconstructs the event. Marr framed the hippocampal formation as a temporary episodic store whose contents could later be recoded in neocortex. This is a concrete pattern-completion circuit proposal, not merely the broad idea of episodic memory. [Marr, “Simple memory: a theory for archicortex,” *Philosophical Transactions B* 262 (1971), original paper copy](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/academic/class/15883-f17/readings/marr-1971.pdf); [Morris & Willshaw’s technical commentary](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4360131/).
- **Was it bad or early?** Compute was a practical barrier to exploring the large capacity calculations, and later simulations could cheaply test much smaller versions. Yet a 1990 reassessment found the computational arguments underdetermined and the model insufficiently constrained; threshold setting, return-path details and memory-management choices were not fixed by the theory. Those are specification and identification problems, not GPU deficits. [Willshaw & Buckingham (1990)](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.1990.0165).
- **Modern descendants and disposition.** Sparse coding, hippocampal pattern completion, recurrent associative memory, and complementary-learning systems develop nearby pieces. Marr’s exact circuit remains historically important, but “sparse episodic memory plus completion/consolidation” is an occupied family, not a new general architecture. The defensible residual is a controlled test of whether its intermediate codon layer helps one-shot retrieval under matched capacity and interference. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 as a broad class; low as a biological model.**
- **Small falsifier.** Implement two- and three-layer binary sparse memories with the stated recurrent completion loop. Compare partial-cue recovery and interference under equal units, active connections and stored episodes; sweep thresholds without tuning on the test set. The codon layer earns further study only if it improves recovery/capacity robustly rather than shifting parameters. No run.

#### AR-68 — Brain-State-in-a-Box (BSB, 1977): clipped analog recurrent settling

- **Original computation.** A continuous state vector is repeatedly transformed by recurrent feedback and hard coordinate-wise saturation; Hebbian updates strengthen observed patterns. Inputs flow toward stable corners of a bounded state-space “box,” so the attractor reached acts as the category or completed pattern. The 1977 paper applies the same neural model to probability learning and categorical perception. [Anderson, Silverstein, Ritz & Jones, *Psychological Review* 84 (1977), original paper](https://www.dam.brown.edu/people/elie/am41%202012/BSB77.pdf).
- **Was it bad or early?** Modest computing made broad parameter sweeps expensive, but the original authors already listed structural weaknesses: hard saturation, oversimplified physiology, ignored operating details, and no specified mechanism to escape a stable corner. Hirsch later showed that under stated conditions BSB is constrained gradient descent on a quadratic cost, clarifying that it is a known optimization/attractor mechanism rather than a distinct unexplained computation. [Hirsch (1986)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-2496(86)90043-X).
- **Modernization and disposition.** GPUs can search larger correlated-pattern sets and learn front-end features; they do not by themselves solve pattern interference, reset or controllable retrieval. Hopfield and modern associative-memory work already occupy the central mechanism, and Hopfield/attention overlaps are documented earlier in this notebook. Retain BSB as an attractor-memory historical variant, not a candidate architecture. **Novelty confidence: 0/5.**
- **Small falsifier for a revival claim.** On CPU, compare BSB, a Hopfield-style attractor and nearest prototypes on noisy correlated patterns with a defined reset cue. Match state dimension and update count; measure exact completion, spurious attractors, interference and reset cost. Reject the claimed advantage if recall is no better or requires a separate reset circuit that erases any simplicity benefit. No run.

#### HY-50 — Growing state map × successor-feature error splitting (reject as a new hybrid)

- **Source mechanisms and exact proposed coupling.** A growing SOM/GNG contributes local prototypes and online topology edits; action-conditioned successor features contribute predictions about discounted future occupancy. Each prototype would accumulate successor vectors by action. Persistent, statistically significant multi-modality in a prototype’s successor predictions would trigger a split even when its observations are geometrically close; a merge would require both observation proximity and compatible future predictions. The interaction would make map granularity follow predicted control consequences rather than sensor-space distance alone.
- **Why it could help, and main failure modes.** A control map could spend states at decision-relevant transition boundaries, adapting after a door, actuator or route changes without uniformly refining the whole sensor space. However, successor features are policy-dependent; transition changes stale the cached predictions; weak observation cues can cause false splits; hidden-state aliases cannot be repaired by dividing identical current observations without adding history/belief state. Prototype count and successor-vector storage may grow rapidly.
- **Prior-art result.** The components and broad behavior are already close to published work. TD-AVQ incrementally partitions state space using signals generated by RL; a 2020 growing-SOM plus differential-learning system online-builds a state structure from input differences, reward and actions. DSAA learns discrete state-action abstractions by grouping states with similar successor representations. “MDP Abstraction with Successor Features” recursively clusters ambiguous states using option-termination distributions or achieved successor features; SNAC combines split successor-feature encoding with clustering for option learning. The exact proposed *online prototype split trigger* may be narrower than these methods, but it is an incremental state-abstraction rule inside established RL, not evidence of a new architecture. Reject the broad hybrid; keep only as a low-priority method comparison if adaptive abstraction becomes a concrete need. [TD-AVQ (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.engappai.2004.08.005); [growing SOM + differential learning (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asoc.2020.106723); [DSAA (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.03467); [MDP Abstraction with Successor Features (2022)](https://rlg.mlanctot.info/2022/papers/AAAI22-RLG_paper_6.pdf); [SNAC (ALA 2022)](https://ala2022.github.io/papers/ALA2022_paper_41.pdf).
- **Small falsifier if the method question is revisited.** In a CPU synthetic continuous MDP, create nearby observations whose action-conditioned futures diverge at a transition boundary, then switch transition dynamics and reward separately. Compare fixed-size SOM+Q, TD-AVQ, DSAA and successor-error-triggered growing prototypes at matched state and sample budgets. Record return, adaptation steps, false-split count and memory. Reject the trigger if it does not improve policy regret per stored state, or if its apparent gain disappears when context/history is represented fairly. No run; the strong prior-art collision makes this lower priority than the still-unresolved RAAM CPU redesign.

#### HY-51 — Cascade growth × Deep Feedback Control local signals (demote to a training-method test)

- **Source mechanisms and coupling.** Cascade-Correlation starts small, trains candidate units against residual output error, and installs a high-correlation unit; DFC uses a feedback controller to produce neuron-specific local learning signals and approximate Gauss–Newton updates. A narrow coupling would use DFC’s local update magnitude and held-out loss reduction to select *where* to grow capacity, then train/freeze the candidate using the local signal. This could make network growth follow a layer’s residual inability to fit rather than an externally fixed width.
- **Prior art and judgment.** Constructive learning already grows units to reduce residual errors: Cascade-Correlation and Upstart are direct precedents, and cascade families include several alternative candidate-training objectives. DFC’s local signal is an established credit-assignment rule. I found no primary-source exact match for the proposed DFC-driven placement rule, but merely combining local feedback with incremental unit insertion does not establish a new computational class; it is a possible optimization/control policy for structural growth. Demote from architecture candidacy. The closest sources establish the primitives, not novelty of this exact rule. [Fahlman & Lebiere, Cascade-Correlation (1989)](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/1989/hash/69adc1e107f7f7d035d7baf04342e1ca-Abstract.html); [Upstart (1990)](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1990.2.2.198); [Meulemans et al., DFC (NeurIPS 2021)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2021/hash/25048eb6a33209cb5a815bff0cf6887c-Paper.pdf); [constructive cascade comparison (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0925-2312(01)00630-0).
- **Possible advantage and failure modes.** Growth could allocate units to the part of a deep controller with persistent local error while avoiding full backpropagation and overwide layers. The DFC controller may itself be costly or unstable; local update magnitude may not measure irreducible capacity deficit; each added unit can overfit and candidate-search compute can exceed fixed-width training. The source methods have not established that local feedback identifies the best growth location.
- **Small falsifier.** On CPU, compare (a) fixed-width DFC, (b) Cascade-Correlation, and (c) DFC with one-unit growth at the layer whose local validation improvement is largest on staged parity and compositional rule tasks. Match parameter count and total candidate evaluations; report held-out accuracy, wall-clock, growth count and seed variance. Stop if the coupling fails to beat the better source method at equal budget, or if the placement signal does not predict held-out gains. No run; method-level priority only.

#### HY-52 — Prediction-error-gated heteroclinic state growth (reject as a new architecture)

- **Source mechanisms and proposed interaction.** Winnerless-competition/heteroclinic networks encode a sequence as continuous motion through metastable saddle states. The proposed extension would keep an expected next-saddle distribution at the active saddle, update its outgoing couplings when transitions surprise it, and add a new saddle only after the same unexplained branch recurs. Unlike simply placing a Markov predictor beside a dynamical model, surprise would alter the dynamical topology that generates the sequence.
- **Prior-art result.** Learned sequence storage in WLC networks predates this proposal: Seliger et al. learn a competition matrix that retrieves prerecorded spatial-pattern sequences. Voit and Meyer-Ortmanns later dynamically infer heteroclinic topology and saddle eigenvalues from an input time series by coupling a template to the data and adapting its eigenvalues. These works occupy sequence learning and data-driven structural inference. The narrower residual—using a predictive surprise statistic to decide when to add an unmodeled saddle—is not yet fully specified, and looks like a growth criterion atop an established dynamical sequence learner rather than a new general architecture. Reject the broad claim; leave the mechanism at low priority until a stable update rule and use case are defined. [Seliger, Tsimring & Rabinovich, *Physical Review E* 67 (2003)](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.67.011905); [Voit & Meyer-Ortmanns (2019)](https://doi.org/10.3389/fams.2019.00063); [Rabinovich et al., winnerless competition sequence coding (2001)](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.068102).
- **Likely advantages and failures.** A stable event-driven rule might add capacity only for recurring new sequence branches and preserve continuous dwell-time dynamics. But noise or timing variation may create false saddle growth; the surprise residual may not identify which outgoing connection failed; additional saddles can destabilize the heteroclinic channel; and local online repair may forget old paths.
- **Small falsifier.** Use CPU-simulated sequences with a recurring rare branch, timing jitter, and one genuine topology change. Compare fixed WLC, the published sequence-learning rule, a Markov-context model and the proposed recurrence-gated saddle insertion at matched state and parameter budgets. Measure branch recall, false insertions, old-path retention and timing error. Reject if surprise-gated growth cannot separate structural changes from timing/noise, or if its added states do not improve recall per parameter. No run.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Uttley’s conditional-probability machine (AR-69)

- **Original computation.** Uttley’s 1956–59 conditional-probability computer represents binary active/inactive channels and maintains a count/probability unit for each observed conjunction or subset. Given a partial active pattern, ratios between subset counts yield conditional probabilities for other channels; those probabilities support pattern completion, prediction, and conditioning. Delayed copies of channels let the machine distinguish coarse “before / simultaneous / after” relations and use sequence completion to predict what follows. Uttley describes probability state on a logarithmic rarity scale in the 1956 chapter; the physical computer described in the 1959 proceedings uses analog capacitor charge to count activity. Its five-input demonstration has 31 units, matching the 2^n−1 nonempty input subsets. [Uttley, 1956, “Conditional Probability Machines and Conditioned Reflexes”](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400882618-013); [Uttley, 1959, “The Design of Conditional Probability Computers”](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(59)90058-0); [Uttley, 1959, “Learning Machines” proceedings record](https://aitopics.org/download/aiclassics%3A88C673EB).
- **What originally limited it.** A five-channel analog build could demonstrate the rule but left capacity tiny. Exact explicit support for all subsets grows exponentially: 31 pattern units at five channels, about one million at 20, and over one billion at 30, before delayed copies, counters, or routing. Counting is not the only constraint: unseen conjunctions have no reliable estimate, and multiplying the number of channels does not supply a useful sensory representation. The design can weight the past, but the choice of decay and temporal discretization is external.
- **Was it simply early?** Faster processors, cheap memory, vectorized bit operations, modern event simulation, and learned encoders remove the 1950s construction and arithmetic constraints. They do not remove the subset-count explosion or statistical sparsity. Sparse tables can avoid allocating never-seen subsets but change the operational regime and require smoothing/backoff; learned encoders reduce the number of channels but may do the hard recognition work themselves. Later direct descendants/components already cover conditional prediction: Buhr built a 1960 adaptive binary-pattern completion/control computer based on Uttley’s proposal but with materially different estimation; context-tree weighting and Bayesian variable-order Markov models perform online conditional sequence prediction with storage proportional to represented contexts; connectionist conditional-distribution networks were published by 1995. [Buhr, 1960 thesis record](https://harvest.usask.ca/items/4988fecb-b284-4ae3-b25f-28dc259f9840); [Willems et al., 1995, context-tree weighting](https://doi.org/10.1109/18.382012); [Dimitrakakis, 2010, Bayesian variable-order Markov models](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v9/dimitrakakis10a/dimitrakakis10a.pdf); [Weigend & Srivastava, 1995, conditional probability distributions](https://doi.org/10.1142/S0129065795000093).
- **What may remain novel / disposition.** Nothing in the all-subsets counter principle is plausibly a new architecture class. Retain as archaeology and as a possible bounded online-memory baseline. A useful revival claim would have to show that direct counts plus partial-pattern completion beat a context-tree or compact conditional model at equal memory, data, and adaptation rate on a workload where inputs are genuinely sparse and the encoder is held fixed. Novelty confidence **0/5**; implementation relevance is workload-dependent.
- **Small falsifier (not run).** On CPU, stream sparse binary events with 8–20 channels, known conjunctions, partial-observation queries, and one abrupt dependency change. Compare (a) exact subset counters where feasible, (b) sparse subset counters with a fixed smoothing rule, (c) context-tree weighting on event history, and (d) an online pairwise logistic/Bayesian conditional baseline. Match memory caps and update opportunities; report conditional log loss/Brier score on missing-channel queries, full-pattern completion, recovery after drift, and bytes per useful association. The count machine is not worth pursuing if gains vanish against the compact models or require exponential memory; the test would evaluate a memory primitive, not novelty.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Uttley’s informon (AR-70)

- **Original computation.** The 1970 informon is a one-output adaptive unit with binary input/output activity, variable-conductivity pathways, and a probabilistic output rule driven by total excitation. The 1970 abstract states that variable conductivity is proportional to the negative Shannon-information function between a pathway’s input and output; repeated activity makes the unit discriminate the most frequent pattern, statistically independent inputs lose their pathway, and output firing frequency on a new input measures similarity to the learned pattern. The paper explicitly says spontaneous output is required, short-lived patterns need preceding short-term storage, and sustained exposure can drive all pathway strengths back toward zero unless hysteresis-like persistence is added. In 1976, Uttley adds a fixed pathway indicating labeled class membership during learning; the informon then predicts the class of unlabelled examples. [Uttley, 1970, “The Informon: A Network for Adaptive Pattern Recognition”](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-5193(70)90128-1); [Uttley, 1976, “A Two-Pathway Informon Theory”](https://doi.org/10.1016/0006-8993(76)90573-4).
- **Why it fell away / what modern technology changes.** Modern data, compute and differentiable information estimators make it much easier to test larger networks and learned front ends than Uttley’s small simulations and binary hand-prepared patterns. But a GPU does not clarify the local update: the published abstracts specify the information-related conductivity law, not enough implementation detail to silently substitute a modern MI gradient estimator. The 1970 paper’s own hysteresis and short-term-buffer qualifications expose real memory-management requirements. One output is also a narrow discriminator; multiple informons introduce arbitration, class balance, and scaling questions. More decisively, Sutton and Barto’s 1981 primary analysis explicitly derives the informon update as closely related to the Rescorla–Wagner/Widrow–Hoff rule, with a fixed inhibitory teacher pathway making the update more Hebbian-compatible. Linsker’s later Infomax principle instead maximizes information preserved from input to output, illustrating that “information-based learning” already spans different objectives and does not make the informon rule generically new. [Sutton & Barto, 1981](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.88.2.135); [Linsker, 1988, “An Application of the Principle of Maximum Information Preservation to Linear Systems”](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/1988/hash/ec8956637a99787bd197eacd77acce5e-Abstract.html).
- **Closest prior art and verdict.** This is a distinct historical learning mechanism, but not an open architecture class: it is a local adaptive discriminator, with substantial overlap in function with supervised associative learning, delta/LMS rules, novelty/competitive learning, and current conditional classifiers. The 1976 paper already studies the labelled-class/unlabelled-test setup. Keep the informon as a historical, falsifiable local-learning baseline; reject it as a new general model class. Any revival must first reconstruct the published finite-sample update from the full paper instead of calling a convenient MI estimator “faithful.” Novelty confidence **0/5** as a new class; low but nonzero interest as a local-learning comparison.
- **Small falsifier (not run).** After recovering the exact 1970/1976 update equations, test a small CPU stream with sparse binary features, changing class prevalence, independent nuisance inputs, and one class-boundary drift. Compare one faithful informon per class against the closest published update, logistic/LMS, and a competitive/ART-style learner at equal examples and memory. Measure balanced accuracy, calibration, nuisance-path suppression, adaptation, forgetting, and total update work. Reject a practical revival if it only wins under hand-chosen binary features, if it tracks majority prevalence rather than class identity, or if its reported advantage requires replacing its rule with backpropagation or a different MI objective. The primary-source equations and no-GPU CPU protocol are a prerequisite; no run yet.

#### HY-53 — Conditional-pattern counter memory × context-tree weighting (reject as a new architecture)

- **Source mechanisms and exact coupling.** Uttley’s conditional-probability machine answers partial-pattern queries from joint counts over binary channel subsets and can add delayed channels for temporal completion. Context-tree weighting recursively mixes predictive models at multiple context depths, providing online sequence prediction without storing a dense table for every possible context. The proposed coupling uses the context-tree posterior to select/weight the temporal context for each new event, while each leaf keeps a sparse subset-count table for conditional completion of currently unobserved channels. A repeated conditional-surprise signal would both update the leaf’s count weights and trigger expansion/pruning of the context tree. Thus temporal context controls which spatial/event conjunction counts are trusted, and partial-pattern predictions affect context growth; this is deeper than wiring a predictor’s output to a second module.
- **Why it would behave differently / why that is not enough.** The combination could separate identical observations with different recent histories and still complete missing features within each history, which a single global subset table cannot do. However, it is essentially a context-dependent Bayesian conditional model with online structure selection, close to variable-order Markov models, Bayesian context trees, and conditional-distribution networks. I found no primary source for this exact composition in this bounded search, but the exact coupling is not enough to support architecture novelty: the context tree already allocates temporal memory, and subset counts supply a conditional table. Their cross-product can make the exponential input-subset burden worse.
- **Disposition and falsifier.** Reject as a new broad architecture; retain only as a candidate workload-specific memory design if multimodal sparse streams become a concrete target. On CPU, compare the coupled model to flat subset counts, CTW per binary channel, and a compact conditional model on sequences where the same partial event has different futures by context, including drift and missing channels. Match total bytes and updates. Reject utility if the coupling cannot improve conditional log score and completion at equal memory, or if context splits fragment the data before estimates stabilize. No run; no novelty claim.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Gamba’s PAPA random-criteria probability machine (AR-71; cross-reference AR-33)

- **Original computation.** PAPA (Programmatore e Analizzatore Probabilistico Automatico) uses randomly generated visual criteria rather than a learned multilayer feature extractor. An image is evaluated by many A-units: random lines/masks or related criteria yield binary “yes/no” features (for example, whether a line’s crossings exceed a threshold). During labeled training, it stores how each criterion responds by class; inference combines class-conditional criterion probabilities, selecting the class with strongest support. Criteria with little discriminative value can be removed or regenerated in some reported versions. This is adjacent to, but more specific than, the multilayer hard-threshold “Gamba perceptron” already recorded in AR-33: the distinctive PAPA mechanism is random criteria plus probabilistic class memory and physical/optical scanning. The 1968 primary article describes pseudorandom criteria and a 64,000-bit memory; a contemporary U.S. technical report describes a 4,096-cell demonstrator, so those hardware figures likely refer to different configurations and should not be collapsed. [Borsellino & Gamba, 1961, mathematical theory](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02822644); [Palmieri & Wanke, 1968, “A Pattern Recognition Machine”](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00288927); [NBS, *Research and Development in the Computer and Information Sciences*, vol. 1, PAPA field report](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-C13-0f697013fa03db15c353d8d29d8f73b3/pdf/GOVPUB-C13-0f697013fa03db15c353d8d29d8f73b3.pdf).
- **Applications and contemporary variants.** PAPA was tested for character/pattern classification, optical random-mask classification, molecular silhouettes, and meteorological pressure-map recognition. An optical implementation used coherent-light diffraction-grating masks. The 1969 molecular-shape paper reports using PAPA-processed silhouette photographs to compare a set of ketones and nonketones with ant alarm-pheromone activity. [Kato & Tanaka, 1970, optical PAPA classification](https://doi.org/10.1143/jjap.9.793); [Amoore, Palmieri & Wanke, 1967, *Nature*](https://doi.org/10.1038/2161084a0); [Amoore et al., 1969, ant-pheromone study](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.165.3899.1266).
- **Why it struggled / what has changed.** Dedicated scanners, random-mask generation, photographic media, ferrite memory, and slow optical/electronic readout constrained the 1960s implementations; contemporary reports explicitly frame high-speed PAPA as a hardware problem. Current RAM/GPUs can emulate and scale random projections cheaply, while modern cameras and learned front ends remove the weak hand-engineered input boundary. But the core limits remain: random features may be redundant or irrelevant, class-conditional counts need examples for each criterion/class, and fixed random projections do not learn hierarchical invariances. The front end can consume all the gains if a pretrained encoder supplies the useful features. Hardware was a real bottleneck for throughput and experiments, but missing adaptive representation remains a structural limit.
- **Modern revival and prior-art judgment.** The central mechanism is already modernized as random-feature/kernel methods and randomized hidden-layer networks: Rahimi–Recht features map inputs through random projections before a learned linear model; ELM/RVFL freeze random hidden features and learn an analytic readout. PAPA’s random criteria and per-class evidence therefore do not constitute a new architecture family. More directly, Gram–Schmidt incremental ELM already scores a random candidate pool and adds useful features; improved GSI-ELM can also remove the weakest unit. A 2026 preprint now proposes residual-guided feature-pool selection and closed-form readout refitting for RVFL, ELM, and Broad Learning Systems. [Rahimi & Recht, 2007](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2007/hash/013a006f03dbc5392effeb8f18fda755-Abstract.html); [Huang et al., 2006, ELM](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2005.12.126); [Gram–Schmidt incremental ELM (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2017.01.049); [Akhtar et al., 2026 preprint, *Residual-Guided Randomized Neural Networks*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28267).
- **What may remain / disposition.** There is no broad architecture novelty. A low-resource vision or scientific-imaging workload could still favor random local criteria plus probability memory for speed, incremental updates, or interpretability; that is a utility claim, not a new model class. Preserve PAPA as archaeology and an unusually early random-feature system. Novelty confidence **0/5**; revival worth testing only if the target workload cannot be handled adequately by ELM/RVFL/random-feature and local-feature baselines.
- **Small falsifier (not run).** On CPU, compare a faithful binary-criteria PAPA implementation (random line/mask features plus class-conditional frequency/log-likelihood readout, optionally criterion replacement) with random-feature ridge/logistic, ELM/RVFL, and a small learned MLP on low-resolution shape/image classification. Use matched feature count, bytes, and training examples; test clean data plus translation/rotation/noise shift and a midstream class-distribution change. Report accuracy, balanced accuracy, calibration, adaptation examples, training/inference time, and feature-memory size. Reject a practical revival if it loses at matched resources or if any gain comes from a separately learned encoder. No run.

#### HY-54 — PAPA criterion replacement × residual-guided ELM readout (reject; direct modern prior art)

- **Source mechanisms and exact proposed coupling.** PAPA provides a pool of random binary pattern criteria and can identify low-value criteria; ELM/RVFL provides randomized hidden features and a closed-form linear readout. The proposed interaction would let the current readout’s residual determine which PAPA criteria are replaced: sample a candidate pool, score each candidate by its reduction in the regularized residual objective, replace the least useful criteria, then refit the classifier. Labels therefore change the random feature generator’s accepted feature distribution, rather than a random-feature layer merely sitting beside an independent classifier.
- **Prior-art result.** This interaction is directly occupied. The 2017 GSI-ELM selects high-quality candidates from a random pool using an orthogonalization criterion, while IGSI-ELM additionally removes a weak unit. The August 2026 *Residual-Guided Randomized Neural Networks* preprint implements a near-exact residual-scored candidate-pool/add-feature/closed-form-refit loop for ELM, RVFL, and BLS. The proposal’s class-conditional PAPA scoring/replacement detail is narrower but does not change the basic computational behavior; do not promote it. [GSI-ELM/IGSI-ELM](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2017.01.049); [Akhtar et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28267).
- **Possible advantages and failures.** Residual-guided candidates can avoid wasting units on duplicate random projections; PAPA’s class-specific probability memory may offer incremental updates and calibrated evidence. But repeated candidate generation and readout refits cost more than one-shot random features; optimizing the training residual guarantees only non-increasing regularized training objective, not better test performance; selection among many candidates may overfit. The 2026 preprint’s benchmark scope is UCI binary/multiclass classification; its abstract does not establish advantages for continual drift, calibration, regression, or broad perception.
- **Disposition and falsifier.** Reject as an architecture candidate; keep as a narrowly defined empirical comparison if feature-replacement behavior becomes relevant. Test on CPU against the published RG-ELM/GSI-ELM family, one-shot PAPA and standard ELM under matched candidate evaluations, feature count, and update/refit budget; evaluate held-out performance, drift recovery, and calibration. The proposed PAPA-specific addition is worthwhile only if it improves those metrics beyond the direct residual-guided baselines; training-objective descent alone is not evidence.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Petri nets as asynchronous event computation (AR-72)

- **Original computation.** Petri’s 1962 “Communication with Automata” represents a system as places, transitions, arcs, and a marking of tokens. A transition fires when its input conditions are met, atomically consuming and producing tokens; independent enabled transitions can proceed concurrently. Its state is an event/resource configuration rather than a fixed-step hidden vector. Petri argued that synchronous finite automata fail to model physical information flow in recursive problems and proposed local-time asynchronous structures extendable without stopping computation. The Hamburg archive hosts the dissertation record and English version. [Petri (1962; English translation/report 1966)](https://edoc.sub.uni-hamburg.de/informatik/frontdoor.php?la=en&source_opus=155); [dissertation bibliography](https://www.informatik.uni-hamburg.de/TGI/publikationen/public/1962/Petri62/Petri62_eng.html).
- **Input, output, and learning.** Inputs are events/resources or an initial token marking; execution produces legal event-firing orders, updated resource states, and enabled decisions. A plain Petri net does not learn: topology, guards, and transition effects are authored or discovered externally. Colored/timed nets attach values and durations to tokens/arcs. Process mining learns a model from traces, but total-order logs can hide true concurrency and alternatives. [Inductive Miner process discovery](https://pcoz.github.io/formally-verified-learnable-process-intelligence/api/discovery/).
- **Was it bad or early?** It was not a failed AI system; it became a durable formalism for concurrency, verification, manufacturing, process mining, and systems biology. Modern compute helps simulate, search, and fit large logs. Structural limits remain: reachable-marking state explosion, deadlock/liveness analysis cost, incomplete/noisy traces, and the need to specify semantics. GPUs do not make concurrent causal structure identifiable from ambiguous logs.
- **Modern descendants / prior art.** A 2020 Deep Petri Net uses hand-designed predicate logic and high-level fuzzy nets for task-specific supervised/unsupervised learning. A 2025 learnable timed-event net maps firing-time equations to max-plus operations and fits processing-time parameters. Action-Evolution Petri Nets (2023) embed executable nets in RL; PetriRL (2024) couples Petri process constraints with event-based deep RL and allows job operations to be added at inference without retraining. A 2026 Typed Petri Net paper formalizes neural-network layers and forward propagation compositionally; it is a model-description framework, not a new learning architecture. [Deep Petri Nets](https://doi.org/10.1177/0020294020923375); [learnable max-plus Petri net](https://doi.org/10.3390/make7030100); [Action-Evolution Petri Nets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02910); [PetriRL](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmsy.2024.04.028); [Typed Petri Nets for neural-network modeling](https://doi.org/10.1527/tjsai.41-2_FN26-I).
- **Possible utility and weaknesses.** Explicit token enabling exposes resource constraints and causal ordering, while event-driven execution avoids updating inactive subsystems on a global clock. This can suit concurrent robotics, workflow control, or manufacturing. It does not provide perception or broad generalization; hand-authoring the net can move the problem into the specification. Preserve Petri nets as archaeology and a systems substrate, not a new broad model class. Class novelty confidence **0/5**.
- **Small falsifier (planned, not run).** On a small asynchronous job shop with shared resources, noisy completion times, and new job templates arriving mid-run, compare an event-native net policy/simulator with an event-graph MDP/GNN and a time-stepped baseline. Match policy capacity and simulated-event budget; measure feasible schedules, makespan, transfer to unseen structures, simulation throughput, and state-space size. Reject a practical advantage if the net needs hand-built per-template wiring or loses at matched compute. CPU-only.

#### HY-55 — Petri token-lineage reward redistribution (reject; exact source-code prior art)

- **Coupling.** Record each action/event’s consumed and produced token IDs; trace backward from reward-producing tokens to their ancestor actions; redistribute delayed reward over the ancestors using temporal or depth-based weights; then train the policy/value system on the redistributed signal. This links execution provenance to credit assignment rather than merely placing Petri nets beside an RL policy.
- **Direct collision.** GymPN’s public Action-Evolution Petri Net repository documents and implements this exact loop: transition history stores consumed/produced tokens, token history stores parent IDs, causal-chain traversal finds ancestor actions, and reward is apportioned with exponential, linear, uniform, depth, or hybrid weighting before policy/value learning. It also implements postponement so process-evolution events can occur before a decision. This is an artifact-level prior-art result, not peer-reviewed evidence of effectiveness. [GymPN repository](https://github.com/bpogroup/gympn); [causal-RL documentation](https://github.com/bpogroup/gympn/blob/main/docs/postpone_causal.md); [source implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bpogroup/gympn/main/gympn/causal_traces.py); [A-E PN paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02910).
- **Adversarial caveat and verdict.** Provenance is not counterfactual contribution: a consumed token may enable but not be necessary for an outcome, and branches may be jointly necessary, redundant, or interacting. The source redistributes credit heuristically from lineage and delay/depth; it includes a code comment questioning its depth index. Reject as a new hybrid, while retaining a bounded utility benchmark. On generated concurrent nets compare lineage weighting, time-decayed eligibility/GAE, and exact simulator counterfactual contribution for necessary, irrelevant, jointly necessary, and alternate-cause events. Measure credit calibration, learning curve, response to irrelevant interleavings, and overhead. Falsify utility if lineage does not improve calibration/sample efficiency or disagrees with counterfactuals. CPU-only; not run.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Brooks subsumption and behavior-based robotics (AR-73; source-checked extension)

- **Original mechanism.** Brooks’s subsumption design uses asynchronous augmented finite-state machines organized into behavior layers. Modules communicate over low-bandwidth channels; a higher layer suppresses or inhibits a lower output while the lower behavior continues running. The 1985 MIT memo reports a detailed robot simulation; the 1986 journal paper reports a physical mobile robot in lab and machine-room areas. In 1989, an incrementally augmented AFSM network controlled the Genghis hexapod walking on rough terrain and following a person. [Brooks, MIT AI Memo 864 (1985)](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/362a32d0-a821-4a9d-a5ff-9e2b71c5539d); [1986 article](https://doi.org/10.1109/JRA.1986.1087032); [1989 robot paper](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1989.1.2.253).
- **Was it bad or early?** It was useful for reactive embodied control, so hardware was not the only obstacle; the original 1985 memo demonstrates a detailed simulation and the 1986 article reports a physical robot. Modern processors, sensors, GPU simulation, and learned perception reduce implementation limits. They do not solve designer-specified behavior decomposition, brittle priority conflicts, or missing long-horizon state/memory. Later analysis of subsumption visual programming notes a structural coupling cost: upper layers can inspect and interfere with lower-layer internals, so the layers are not clean black boxes and become harder to debug and maintain as the system grows. This is an architecture/interface limitation, not a compute shortfall. [Brooks, MIT AI Memo 864 (1985)](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/362a32d0-a821-4a9d-a5ff-9e2b71c5539d); [Banyasad & Cox (2008)](https://doi.org/10.5772/6226).
- **Modernization and verdict.** Behavior-based reinforcement learning already put distributed/asynchronous RL over a learned task-relevant topological map and showed real-robot puck foraging (Konidaris & Hayes, 2005). More decisively, Pore & Aragon-Camarasa (ICRA 2020) directly instantiate the obvious modern hybrid: behavior-cloned neural approach/grasp/retract modules plus a learned actor-critic/LSTM that chooses activation and inhibition in sequence. In simulated Fetch pick/place, their best modular/frozen-feature setup reached about 100% success by roughly 8,000 episodes, while their end-to-end comparator remained below 60% at 100,000; the modular-method comparison used three seeds, a short three-behavior task and privileged kinematic state, and authors left real-robot transfer for future work. This is a direct prior-art collision for learned subsumption arbitration, not broad evidence of generality. A 2024 preprint further explores safe arbitration graphs. Keep subsumption as a useful reactive-control pattern and baseline, not a new general AI architecture. [Konidaris & Hayes (2005)](https://doi.org/10.1177/105971230501300101); [Pore & Aragon-Camarasa (2020), full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2001.07973v2); [safe arbitration graphs (2024 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10170).
- **Small falsifier (planned, not run).** In a small simulated mobile robot, combine wander, obstacle avoidance, and target seeking; delay/drop target-behavior messages. Compare fixed priority with freshness- and safety-gated suppression. Measure collisions, goal completion, stalls, and interruptions. Reject practical value if gating fails to reduce unsafe stale proposals or rejects enough proposals to prevent progress. CPU-only.

#### HY-56 — Freshness/safety-gated learned suppression (reject; prior-art and HY-14 overlap)

- **Exact coupling considered.** A slow learned behavior may suppress lower-level behavior only when its proposal passes a safety check and freshness deadline; otherwise fast fallback control continues.
- **Prior-art judgment.** Existing HY-14 already couples predictive-state/risk/confidence arbitration to fast subsumption behaviors. Learned activation/inhibition is directly demonstrated by Pore & Aragon-Camarasa (2020), and safe fallback arbitration graphs are explored in a 2024 preprint. Freshness gating may be useful engineering, but does not change the representation or learning mechanism. Reject as a novel hybrid.
- **Small test.** Reuse AR-73’s delayed-proposal robot simulation to compare fixed priority, learned activation/inhibition, and freshness/safety gating at equal proposal/control rates. Test only the stale-message safety claim, not architectural novelty. Not run.

#### HY-55 CPU microexperiment — executed ancestry versus counterfactual allocation

- **Question and method.** Does the causal-token lineage rule identify only the action path that fired, or does it also estimate how much each available action changed the outcome? In a tiny deterministic toy, I reproduced uniform ancestry allocation from the GymPN method description and compared it with exact Shapley allocation over a known reward function. This is a logical microcase, not a run of GymPN and not an RL-performance benchmark.
- **Results.** A single necessary action received 1.0 from both methods. For an AND reward requiring A and B, both gave 0.5/0.5. With two interchangeable OR routes, the simulated reward fired along A’s token path: ancestry assigned A=1.0, B=0.0, while Shapley assigned A=0.5, B=0.5. With a causal A and unrelated interleaved C, both assigned A=1.0, C=0.0. Swapping the selected OR path would swap ancestry credit, while the Shapley split would remain symmetric.
- **Interpretation and limit.** This confirms the caveat: ancestry measures the realized provenance path, not counterfactual marginal contribution across alternate routes. It does not prove Shapley is the right RL target, and an on-policy learner may intentionally reward its selected successful path. It gives a minimal calibration task for later process-level evaluation; the broad hybrid remains rejected as existing prior art.
- **Resource record.** CPU-only Python 3.11.9 standard-library script piped through stdin; four deterministic cases with up to two actions; command wall time about 1.2 seconds including shell/interpreter startup. GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU process or device snapshot, as no GPU work was imminent. Live occupancy remains unknown. No script file was added.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Angluin-style active automata learning (AR-74; L*, 1987)

- **Original computation.** L* learns a finite-state acceptor from interaction with a teacher. It asks membership queries about strings, builds an observation table of prefixes and suffixes, proposes a DFA, and uses counterexamples to expose missing state distinctions. A state corresponds operationally to a class of histories that have the same residual future language. For a regular target with a finite alphabet, the original result gives polynomial learning time in the target's minimum DFA state count and the longest teacher counterexample. [Angluin, 1987, primary paper](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~lreyzin/papers/angluin87.pdf).
- **What it represents and repeats.** Its unit is a discrete automaton state representing a history-equivalence class, not a learned feature vector. It repeatedly queries the target, refines the table/hypothesis, and traverses the final DFA at inference. Input is a sequence over a known symbolic alphabet; output is acceptance or, for later transducer variants, a stateful output trace. Knowledge resides in the observation table and finite transition graph. The classic learning rule is query-and-counterexample refinement, not gradient descent; deployment-time change requires re-opening the query loop or retraining from new behavior.
- **Was it bad or early?** This was not mainly a compute-limited idea. The hard premise is the teacher: membership queries must be executable against the system, and exact equivalence queries are often unavailable. The original paper explicitly discusses replacing equivalence testing with random sampling in a stochastic setting, which weakens exact guarantees. Modern compute, parallel query caches, simulation, conformance testing, and model checking improve the tooling and approximate equivalence step. They do not make a huge or poorly abstracted event alphabet manageable, nor guarantee that a learned finite-state model captures a system with unbounded data/state.
- **Modern use and closest work.** Active automata learning is mature rather than abandoned: the official LearnLib framework provides active/passive algorithms, DFA/Mealy/Moore and other targets, query caching, parallel query infrastructure, counterexample analysis, and equivalence approximations. Aarts et al.'s Tomte work already uses counterexample-guided abstraction refinement to automatically refine event alphabets for extended finite-state systems and reports learning realistic components including biometric passports and SIP. The 2026 DeepDFA paper injects supplied DFA/Moore temporal rules into differentiable networks with learned grounding; a different 2024 paper called DeepDFA learns automata through neural probabilistic relaxations. These do not all reproduce L*'s exact oracle-learning mechanism, but jointly learning neural grounding and discrete temporal structure is already occupied territory. [LearnLib](https://learnlib.de/); [Aarts et al., FM 2012](https://sws.cs.ru.nl/publications/papers/fvaan/CEGAR12/); [DeepDFA: temporal logic in neural networks, 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03486); [DeepDFA: neural probabilistic automata learning, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08622).
- **Use, advantage, and failure modes.** Protocol conformance, stateful API testing, workflow discovery, and compact models of discrete control interfaces are good fits: explicit states can be inspected and counterexamples are actionable. It can outperform a generic sequence model when the true system is finite-state, exact symbolic transitions matter, and queries are cheap. It fails when the state/alphabet explodes, continuous parameters are essential, the interface cannot be reset or queried safely, or sampled equivalence tests miss rare behavior. It does not provide general perception or broad semantic learning by itself.
- **What could be new? Verdict.** Neither finite-state history quotienting nor active counterexample refinement is new. A possible narrow seam is a resource-bounded query policy that jointly chooses the next system experiment and the abstraction split under a fixed risk budget, with calibrated uncertainty about hidden transitions. That is not yet specified well enough to promote and likely intersects active conformance testing and alphabet-refinement research. Novelty confidence for a new architecture class **0/5**; retain L* as a strong formal baseline and possible component.
- **Small falsifier (planned, not run).** Generate deterministic stateful services with known hidden DFA/Mealy models, cost-skewed actions, noisy observations, and gradually refined event attributes. Compare standard L*/LearnLib with conformance testing, a passive learner, and a cost-aware joint query-plus-abstraction policy. Fix query and reset budgets; measure counterexamples found, state/transition recovery, cost to find rare faults, and abstraction size. Abandon the narrow policy claim if it does not improve fault discovery or model accuracy at equal query cost, or if it merely shifts cost to manual symbol design. CPU-only; no GPU work is warranted for this test.

#### HY-57 — Perception-symbol co-refinement with active automata learning (reject as broad hybrid)

- **Source mechanisms and proposed coupling.** A neural/perceptual front end maps continuous observations to event symbols; an active automata learner constructs a finite-state interaction model. The proposed deep coupling was to use a counterexample to decide both whether two automaton histories need distinct states and whether the perceptual event partition must split, then feed that revised partition back into new membership queries.
- **Why the coupling is attractive.** The perceptual mapper can compress an enormous raw observation space, while the automaton gives inspectable temporal state and counterexamples. If jointly refined, errors in grounding and errors in state abstraction could be separated rather than hidden inside a recurrent state.
- **Prior-art collision and limits.** Counterexample-guided alphabet abstraction for active automata learning already exists in Tomte (Aarts et al., 2012), including automatic refinement when an abstraction causes nondeterministic observations. Related state-local alphabet abstraction and later automated alphabet-refinement work extend that seam. Neural-network-to-automata extraction and DeepDFA's differentiable automata/learned-grounding work occupy nearby neural-symbolic territory. The proposed split rule has no precise objective or update proof yet; simply placing a neural symbolizer before L* would be a pipeline, not a new architecture. Reject the broad hybrid claim. A precise uncertainty-calibrated split objective could be studied as an algorithmic improvement, but it must be compared directly against alphabet refinement and automata extraction.
- **Small falsifier if revisited (planned, not run).** On a synthetic visual event stream with controlled symbol aliasing and a known Mealy machine, compare fixed learned symbols, Tomte-style refinement, and joint state/symbol counterexample refinement under equal labeling/query budgets. Measure exact transition recovery, split count, and held-out fault detection. Falsify the mechanism if it does not reduce queries or false state merges, or if its gains disappear when symbol labels are matched. CPU first; only use GPU for a separately justified perception encoder, after checking shared-device occupancy.

#### Ashby primary-source supplement (AR-08 / C031; no new candidate)

Ashby’s 1960 revised *Design for a Brain* makes the scale failure unusually explicit. After noting that the original Homeostat is fully cross-connected, he says this integration prevents it from accumulating partial adaptations and makes adaptation take an “un-brainlike” time; he argues that retaining partial successes requires some parts not to affect others. The relevant discussion is in sections 11/11–11/12 of the primary text. This refines the existing C031 note: the issue is not only random global search over too many parameter combinations, but also destructive interference between adaptations. [Ashby, *Design for a Brain*, revised 2nd ed., chapter 11 scan](https://www.ashby.info/Ashby%20-%20Design%20for%20a%20Brain%20-%20The%20Origin%20of%20Adaptive%20Behavior.pdf).

**Archaeology conclusion.** The Homeostat was both technologically early and algorithmically limited. A simulation can cheaply run more trials and modern learning can propose parameter changes, but neither automatically creates modular credit assignment or useful task objectives. The local-preservation remedy was already anticipated by Ashby, and later homeostatic robotics/adaptive-control work occupies generic implementations. Do not add an AR or candidate number for the same mechanism.

**Refined falsifier for the already-recorded C031 probe (still gated, not run).** Use a multi-loop plant across 4–8 recurring perturbation regimes, including return to previously seen regimes. Compare global random ultrastability, a local update that changes only a fault-attributed module, ordinary adaptive control, and a model-based fault-reconfiguration baseline at matched probing/interaction budgets. Measure time outside viability limits, recovery time, retention on returning regimes, and collateral parameter change in unaffected loops. The local-retention hypothesis fails if it does not reduce total recovery cost or viability violations, or if gains require a hand-coded fault-to-module map. This is a CPU utility experiment, not novelty evidence; the update/localization rule still needs an explicit specification before execution.

#### HY-57 prior-art follow-up — state-local abstraction and query-cost optimization

A targeted search found that the proposed residual seam is even more occupied than the first pass indicated. Isberner, Howar & Steffen (NFM 2013) automatically infer a separate input-alphabet abstraction for each automaton state, rather than only refining one global alphabet; counterexample handling is integrated with state and alphabet inference. Henry et al. (2025) extend automated alphabet refinement to compositional learning of synchronizing concurrent systems, with a LearnLib-based implementation and experiments on more than 630 subject systems. The separate idea of choosing queries under an experiment budget is also not a clean novelty seam: Aichernig & Tappler (2018/2019) use randomized, fault-based mutation testing to reduce the cost of approximate equivalence/conformance queries, reporting at least an order-of-magnitude reduction in several protocol experiments. These methods do not prove that every risk-aware joint policy is known, but they remove the claim that joint state/symbol refinement or cost-aware query selection is itself unexplored. [Isberner et al., NFM 2013](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-38088-4_9); [Henry et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16624); [Aichernig & Tappler, 2018/2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10817-018-9486-0).

**Revised disposition.** Keep the counterexample/query-budget idea only as an application-specific replication or comparison question; do not leave it on the active novelty shortlist without a sharply different objective, formal guarantee, and direct comparison against state-local alphabet abstraction, CoalA, and mutation-based conformance testing. No experiment was run.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Learning Classifier Systems and XCS (AR-75)

- **Original mechanism.** Holland’s classifier systems maintain a population of condition–action production rules. In CS-1, environmental inputs become messages, matching rules fire to produce new messages/actions, and credit can propagate through an internal message list via the bucket-brigade mechanism; a genetic algorithm discovers/modifies rules. Modern Michigan-style variants keep a population of rules active in one learner. XCS (Wilson, 1995) estimates payoff for each rule but assigns evolutionary fitness from prediction accuracy, runs genetic search within matching niches, and favors accurate general rules. [Sigaud & Wilson, 2007 historical survey](https://compbio.fmph.uniba.sk/vyuka/ml/old/2008/handouts/sigaud_wilson_lcs_survey.pdf); [Wilson, 1995 primary XCS paper](https://www.eskimo.com/~wilson/ps/xcs.pdf).
- **Information and repeated operation.** The represented knowledge is a finite population of local rules plus payoff/error/fitness statistics; some variants also store message state or action-effect predictions. Input is a feature/state description (or a message set); output is a selected action, payoff prediction, or class. Learning updates matched rules from reward/error, covers unrepresented situations, and occasionally evolves or deletes rules. At inference, matching rules vote or aggregate prediction. The system can learn online after deployment, but rule matching and discovery cost rise with population and feature count.
- **Was it merely too early?** Partly hardware, substantially algorithm. Vectorized match evaluation, larger simulation budgets, and replay make population sweeps cheaper today. The 2007 survey says research became less active in the 1980s because diverse early systems did not reliably achieve convincing performance; the move from strength-based search to XCS’s accuracy-based fitness was a methodological correction, not simply a hardware upgrade. Modern hardware does not solve representation bias, sparse reward/long-horizon credit, rule explosion, or feature drift. [Sigaud & Wilson, 2007](https://compbio.fmph.uniba.sk/vyuka/ml/old/2008/handouts/sigaud_wilson_lcs_survey.pdf).
- **Modernization and closest work.** LCS remains an active specialist area; a 2024 GECCO survey reviews work from 2022–2024, including architecture, explanation, applications, metaheuristics, and other contributions. XCSCF* uses code-fragment rules and layered transfer for harder Boolean problems. Neural hybrids are also direct prior art: deep-LCS classifiers contain a gate network and a per-instance prediction network; reproduction applies self-adaptive mutation while the prediction network learns by SGD during its lifetime. [Siddique et al., GECCO 2024 survey](https://doi.org/10.1145/3638530.3664165); [Alvarez et al., layered LCS](https://doi.org/10.1162/evco_a_00351); [Preen & Bull, Deep Learning with a Classifier System (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01118).
- **Potential use and verdict.** Rule populations may suit small or moderate state spaces where online updates, localized behavior, and inspectable conditions matter; XCS specifically can generalize without enumerating every state. It is not a broad alternative for raw perception, high-dimensional continuous input, or long-horizon reasoning without additional mechanisms. Existing XCS, ACS2+HER, deep-LCS, and other rule/evolution hybrids already appear in this notebook. Keep LCS as a comparison family and architecture archaeology, not a new candidate. Novelty confidence: **0/5 for the family or generic modernization**.
- **Small falsifier (planned, not run).** On CPU, use a 6-bit multiplexer target with additional irrelevant bits, then introduce a predeclared abrupt change in the address/data mapping. Compare a tuned XCS implementation with an online MLP under matched examples and wall-clock or operation budgets. Track test accuracy, post-change recovery samples, rule count/description size, parameter count, and runtime over independent seeds. The bounded rule-system advantage fails if XCS cannot retain a compact accurate mapping or recover at competitive sample/compute cost. This tests a useful niche, not general intelligence.

#### HY-58 — XCS rule gates selecting neural predictors (reject; direct prior art)

- **Components and coupling.** XCS contributes niche-conditioned condition–action rules and evolutionary population search. A learned predictor contributes a neural computation per selected rule. The proposed interaction is that a rule gate chooses which predictor runs for each input; genetic reproduction modifies both the gate and network architecture, while gradient descent updates each network’s weights during its lifetime. This would alter routing, computation cost, and the evolutionary unit rather than merely connect two models.
- **Prior-art result.** Preen & Bull’s 2021 deep-LCS paper implements this mechanism: each classifier contains a gating/guarding network and an associated deep prediction network, enabling per-instance conditional compute; it applies self-adaptive mutation during reproduction and SGD lifetime learning to predictors. Other LCS/neural work includes evolutionary autoencoder ensembles and neural prediction functions in XCSF. Therefore the generic XCS × neural conditional-computation hybrid is already instantiated. More recent conditional-computation policies and MoE routing are adjacent but not needed to establish this direct collision. Reject as a new hybrid. [Preen & Bull (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01118); [Preen et al., Autoencoding with a Classifier System](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10579); [XCSF representation survey, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1145/3638530.3664165).
- **Residual question, not a novelty claim.** Could an input encoder change online without invalidating the semantics of existing rule conditions? Possible mechanisms include versioned features or counterexample-triggered local rule split/merge, but no precise rule was found here and adaptive condition representations already have extensive LCS coverage. Do not promote until direct prior-art review and a distinct preservation invariant are specified.
