#### HY-58 prior-art follow-up — rule representation and feature co-learning

The possible encoder-drift residue is also too vague to retain as an implied novelty claim. A 2015 LCS representation review documents extensive alternatives for XCS rule conditions and local predictors, including real-valued geometric conditions, fuzzy rules, tree/code-fragment forms, and neural-network components; it emphasizes that representation choice determines how the input space is partitioned and generalized. A 2020 ACT-R cognitive classifier explicitly learns feature selection jointly with feature–class associations and feeds task/context information back into semantic perception. These are not all the exact proposed invariant-preserving rule-rewrite mechanism, but they show that adaptive representation and feature selection around rule learners are long-standing, occupied directions. [Shoeleh et al., *Knowledge Representation in Learning Classifier Systems* (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.04002); [Martin et al. (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10588-018-9279-3).

**Updated residue.** “Keep rule meaning stable while an encoder drifts” remains only a problem statement. Before considering even a methods prototype, define an invariant (for example, a bound on decision changes over a validated region), an update/rewrite algorithm, and a direct baseline against fixed-feature XCS, standard representation-adaptive LCS, and replay/retraining. Without those, any result would be an encoder-maintenance engineering choice, not evidence of a distinct architecture.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (AR-77)

- **Original computation.** Kosko’s 1986 fuzzy cognitive map is a signed, weighted directed graph whose nodes are named concepts with graded activation and whose edges express positive or negative influence. Each update propagates activation through the graph, commonly as a bounded transform of the weighted inputs, and repeats until a stable pattern or cycle appears. Users can run forward/backward what-if scenarios, add an intervention concept, or combine maps from multiple experts. The computation object is a recurrent causal-belief graph, not a fuzzy IF-THEN classifier and not a probabilistic Bayesian network. [Kosko, “Fuzzy Cognitive Maps” (1986)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0020-7373(86)80040-2); [Osoba & Kosko, “Beyond DAGs” (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.11247).
- **Input, output, learning, and memory.** Inputs are an initial concept-activation vector, an expert-specified or learned graph, and optionally a proposed intervention; output is a predicted activation trajectory/fixed point or qualitative scenario comparison. Knowledge is stored in graph topology and edge weights/functions. Classic maps often rely on expert elicitation; later learners fit edge weights with Hebbian/differential-Hebbian rules, least squares, evolutionary search, or swarm optimization. The system can update from new sequences if an online learning rule is chosen, but static inference itself does not imply continual learning.
- **Was it too early?** Modern RAM, GPUs, autodiff, and better optimization make larger maps and gradient-based fitting easier. That addresses computation and some parameter-search costs. It does not resolve the deeper problems: the concept vocabulary and candidate edges are often supplied by people; observational fit does not identify causal direction or remove confounding; learned dense graphs can fit spurious correlations; cycles may converge, oscillate, or diverge; fuzzy edge values are not calibrated causal probabilities. The 2023 systematic review of 2011–March 2023 found many extensions but few that address multiple shortcomings, and reported no released code among the reviewed extensions. [Schuerkamp & Giabbanelli, systematic review (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3610771); [Feng et al., robust FCM fitting under noisy data (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.08339).
- **Modernization and collision.** The 2026 KA-FCM paper replaces scalar edge weights with learned univariate B-spline functions, letting each edge model non-monotonic influence without adding hidden concept nodes. Its precise spline-edge parameterization is new relative to the checked older FCM mechanisms, but the broad goal of nonlinear causal edges is not: Hagiwara’s Extended FCM (1994) and Carvalho–Tomé rule-based FCMs (1999) already address nonlinear/non-monotonic relations; delay weights also appear in E-FCM. The 2026 paper reports toy non-monotonic inference, symbolic regression and Mackey–Glass forecasting; this does not establish calibrated causal discovery, high-dimensional scaling or broad model-class superiority. Earlier FCM learning algorithms and intervention scenario tools are also mature; distinguish prediction/what-if simulation from causal identification. The paper’s current bibliographic record is IEEE Transactions on Fuzzy Systems 34(6), 1884–1892 (2026). [Salmeron, KA-FCM (IEEE TFS 2026)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TFUZZ.2026.3680681); [arXiv version](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05136); [Hagiwara, E-FCM (1994)](https://doi.org/10.1541/ieejeiss1987.114.3_367); [FCMpy (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9575875/).
- **Potential utility, weaknesses, and novelty.** FCMs can make feedback assumptions inspectable and let domain experts run scenario changes in systems that do not fit a simple DAG; this remains useful in policy, engineering, or participatory modeling when the graph is explicitly understood as a model of stakeholder beliefs. The price is graph construction and uncertain edge semantics. The architecture family is established and actively extended, not an abandoned model waiting for GPUs. Novelty confidence for FCMs, learned FCMs, or spline-edge FCMs: **0/5**. Keep as a causal-feedback archaeology entry and possible interpretable baseline, not a new general AI class.
- **Small falsifier (CPU; initial slice executed below, broader test still pending).** Generate a 4-concept cyclic dynamical system with one monotonic edge, one inverted-U edge, and a return feedback edge. The initial slice compares known-graph scalar edges with spline edges under uniform state coverage and a held-out intervention sweep. The broader test should add a small MLP, observational trajectories with limited support, hidden confounding/misspecified topology, and matched parameter/update budgets. The “modern learning rescues FCM dynamics” utility claim fails if spline edges do not improve intervention prediction and edge-shape recovery at comparable capacity, or if gains disappear on realistic trajectories. This tests a known FCM modernization, not novelty.

#### HY-60 — Fuzzy feedback map × active causal intervention design (reject as a new architecture)

- **Source architectures and exact coupling.** FCM contributes a human-readable cyclic graph of fuzzy concept influences and an iterative scenario simulator. Active causal design contributes a posterior over candidate causal structures and chooses interventions that reduce uncertainty or distinguish hypotheses. A proposed coupling would retain several candidate cyclic FCMs, score candidate manipulations by expected disagreement in their predicted trajectories/equilibria, run the most informative intervention, and update local edge existence/function estimates from the observed response. The target is graph learning and computation scheduling: the model decides what system state to perturb, not only how to propagate a fixed graph.
- **Why it is complementary and how it might behave differently.** FCMs make loops and expert concepts easy to express but commonly learn from passive or elicited evidence; intervention design helps distinguish competing causal explanations with fewer experiments. A cycle-specific acquisition score could select interventions that separate long-run attractors or sign reversals that one-step edge scores miss. This is a coherent utility hypothesis for scientific system identification, but it remains a change to acquisition over causal-model hypotheses rather than a new model class.
- **Prior-art check and verdict.** Reject as architectural novelty. Active intervention choice for causal graphs has been studied since at least 2008, including sequential and batch designs; later methods optimize nonlinear Gaussian-process networks or target desired interventional outcomes. FCMs already model what-if interventions and have data-driven edge learning, while current FCM work already combines machine learning with scenario design. I found no source in this bounded search that exactly uses long-run attractor disagreement over candidate cyclic FCMs as the acquisition objective; that possible residual is a domain-specific acquisition rule, not evidence of a new architecture. [He & Geng, active causal network learning (JMLR 2008)](https://jmlr.org/papers/v9/he08a.html); [von Kügelgen et al., nonlinear active causal design (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.03962); [Zhang et al., optimal intervention design (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04744); [FCM scenario/ML intervention case study (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10714655/).
- **Small falsifier if pursued as a method.** In a synthetic 4–6 node feedback system, create a set of candidate FCMs with alternative cyclic edges and one possible non-monotonic influence. Compare random interventions, a standard active causal-design score, and long-run attractor-disagreement acquisition at equal intervention count and simulator budget. Measure graph/function recovery, counterfactual rollout error, attractor identification, and robustness to model misspecification. Reject the special acquisition rule if it does not reduce interventions needed or if improvements disappear against a matched general active-causal baseline. Not run; no architecture novelty claim.

#### AR-77 CPU prototype — scalar versus spline causal edges (executed; limited scope)

- **Protocol.** Pure NumPy on CPU. For five random seeds, fit a four-node cyclic update map from 2,048 uniformly sampled concept states and test on 4,096 held-out states. The known graph contains a 0→1→2→0 cycle, an inverted-U edge 1→2, and a 2/3→3 subgraph. Both models were given the true parent sets. The scalar FCM uses one logistic-link coefficient per known edge; the functional-edge variant uses nine piecewise-linear hat-basis values per edge and least squares in logit space. Evaluated held-out one-step prediction, 20-step rollout from shared random starts, and the target node’s response to setting concept 1 over a 101-point do-sweep while other concepts were fixed at 0.5. No neural encoder, graph learning, optimizer tuning, noise, or confounder was included.
- **Result.** Mean one-step RMSE was 0.035293 for the scalar-edge map and 0.000559 for the spline-edge map across seeds. On the do-sweep response curve for the inverted-U edge, RMSE was 0.071709 versus 0.001139. At rollout step 20, scalar-map RMSE ranged 0.04156–0.04473 while spline-map RMSE ranged 0.00068–0.00075. The direction is expected because the true nonlinear edge is in the spline model class and outside the scalar-edge model class. Parameter counts were 9 vs 49; this is not capacity-matched and does not reproduce the KA-FCM paper’s training setup. Because topology was supplied and training states broadly covered [0,1], this says nothing about discovering causal edges, recovering from passive data, or generalizing to out-of-support interventions.
- **Resources and decision.** Runtime was 0.112 s across all seeds; CPU only; peak VRAM 0 GB; memory use was small and not profiled. GPU-sharing status was not checked because no GPU was used; live GPU occupancy remains unknown. This confirms only the expected expressivity difference. It does not elevate FCMs or the spline-edge hybrid as a new class. Stronger next check: compare to a parameter-matched MLP and a misspecified/partially observed cyclic system, then test whether interventions improve graph/edge recovery beyond a general active-causal baseline.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Neural Turing Machines, DNCs, and differentiable external memory (AR-76)

- **Original computation.** The Neural Turing Machine (NTM, 2014) couples a recurrent controller to a differentiable external matrix. The controller emits soft content and location-addressing parameters; read heads form weighted sums and the write head erases/adds vectors. A DNC (2016) adds usage tracking and least-used-slot allocation plus a temporal-link matrix so read heads can follow write order in either direction. These systems represent explicit, mutable records and their relations in memory rather than relying only on a fixed hidden state or learned weights. A Memory Network (2014–15) is a related but distinct family: it stores facts/sentences and performs learned multi-hop retrieval, without being a general differentiable write-head machine. A 2016 memory-augmented net meta-learns to store new examples and retrieve them by content for one-shot learning. [Graves et al., NTM (2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.5401); [Graves et al., DNC (2016)](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20101); [Weston et al., Memory Networks (2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3916); [Sukhbaatar et al., End-to-End Memory Networks (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.08895); [Santoro et al., Memory-Augmented Neural Networks (2016)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v48/santoro16.html).
- **Input, output, learning, and memory.** Input is a sequence, query, or task state. Each step runs the controller, selects read/write distributions, mutates selected memory slots, and returns controller output combined with read values; a loss trains the controller and address behavior by backpropagation through time. Memory is a slot matrix plus, for DNC, usage and temporal-link state. The system can learn while deployed only in variants with test-time writes/updates; the classical NTM/DNC literature chiefly trains the addressing policy offline and uses learned policies during task execution. Inference is iterative and stateful, not an answer-decoder over one static representation.
- **What was hard: hardware and algorithm.** Hardware constrained memory size, long unrolled training, and parallel similarity scans. Sparse Access Memory (SAM, 2016) had already attacked dense reads/writes and BPTT storage, reporting large time/space reductions and adapting sparse access to DNCs; modern hardware did not first make the basic scaling issue visible. Yet several weaknesses are mechanism-level. NTM soft shifts and weighted reads can blur address mass over repeated operations. DNC de-allocation can lower a slot’s usage without erasing its old content, so content lookup can retrieve stale records; a later analysis also found that key/value entanglement harms lookup and repeated temporal-link traversal diffuses the address distribution. The full content scan is linear in slot count, while the DNC link matrix is quadratic in slot count. Planning budget also changes which algorithm the DNC learns and its generalization to larger inputs. Thus compute improves throughput, not address semantics, deletion guarantees, or the need for a valid multi-step algorithm. The 2016 NTM copy study calls long BPTT difficult and whole-memory linear access unscalable, but reports good extrapolation on its particular copy setup; failures should not be stated as universal. [Rae et al., SAM (NeurIPS 2016)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/by-source-2016-1803); [Csordás & Schmidhuber, DNC addressing analysis (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.10278); [Shamshoum et al., DNC planning budget (ICML 2024)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/shamshoum24a.html); [Aleš, NTM copy-task convergence study (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.02336).
- **Modernization and closest work.** Nearly every broad revival direction is occupied, across distinct memory mechanisms: SAM sparsifies differentiable reads/writes; Neural RAM gives learned pointer manipulation over variable-size random-access memory; lattice differentiable RAM uses constant-time local lookup under its storage assumptions; Memorizing Transformers keep a non-differentiable kNN key/value cache; Recurrent Memory Transformer carries learned memory tokens between segments; Infini-attention combines local attention with compressive long-term memory; TTT makes the recurrent state itself a model updated by a self-supervised learning step; Titans uses surprise/retention-shaped test-time neural memory alongside attention; MIRAS systematizes memory structure, retrieval objective, retention, and update rule. These are not all one architecture and do not solve the same tasks, but they directly occupy “persistent memory + learned controller,” “fast new facts,” “adaptive memory at test time,” and “structured memory-addressing hybrid” claims. [Neural RAM (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.06392); [Differentiable RAM using Lattices (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03474); [Memorizing Transformers (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.08913); [Recurrent Memory Transformer (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.06881); [Infini-attention (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07143); [TTT layers (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04620); [Titans (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00663); [MIRAS (2025 preprint; ICLR 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13173).
- **Potential value, weakness, and novelty.** Explicit writable memory can learn data-structure operations and retain exact episodes more directly than a fixed-size state, which was a meaningful advantage on graph, route, family-tree, and one-shot tasks. It may still serve as a useful specialist baseline where state is naturally relational and data can be written once and queried many times. It is not a new broad architecture class, and “modern hardware solves the old problem” is false: soft-address interference, memory management, slot scaling, write-policy learning, and computational planning remain. Novelty confidence for generic controller + differentiable memory or test-time associative memory: **0/5**. The historical verdict is “partly early, partly algorithmically flawed,” not “a good architecture that only needed GPUs.”
- **Small falsifiable experiment (CPU; partly executed below).** The first microexperiment isolates soft-address selectivity without training a controller. The broader planned check compares exact hash lookup, NTM-style cosine-softmax reads, sparse top-k reads, and DNC-style temporal-link traversal at 32–2,048 slots, then overwrites/deallocates records and queries after 1–12 link hops. It will report exact retrieval, address entropy, error by hop, runtime, and memory, including published controls for wiping deallocated slots and sharpening/renormalizing temporal links. Only the soft-read portion has run so far; the DNC link/overwrite controls remain unrun and are not represented by results below.

#### AR-76 CPU microexperiment — soft-address selectivity versus key ambiguity (executed)

- **Protocol.** CPU-only NumPy, three seeds at each of 32/128/512/2,048 slots, 32-dimensional unit-normalized Gaussian keys, scalar Gaussian values, query noise σ=0.15, cosine-softmax inverse temperature β=12. Tested independent keys and paired near-duplicates formed by perturbing a key by σ=0.05. Compared dense value retrieval, top-8 renormalized soft retrieval, and hard nearest-neighbor lookup. A second 2,048-slot sweep used five seeds and β ∈ {12, 24, 48, 96}. This is a mechanism probe, not an NTM/DNC training reproduction.
- **Result.** On independent keys, dense value MSE rose from 0.0067 at 32 slots to 0.4181 at 2,048 with β=12, as mean address entropy rose from 0.192 to 4.176. At 2,048 slots, increasing β reduced dense MSE to 0.0322 at β=24 and 0.0207 at β=48 (then 0.0222 at β=96): a controller that learns sharper selection can largely compensate in this easy random-key case. Under near-duplicate keys, exact nearest-address accuracy was only about 0.80 at all tested slot counts; at 2,048 slots, dense MSE was 0.5636, 0.3258, 0.2881, and 0.3063 for β 12/24/48/96. Sharpness improved average retrieval but could not separate noisy ambiguous keys and became slightly worse at the highest β. Top-8 soft reads improved over dense reads at high slot count but did not match hard nearest-neighbor retrieval. These results support a narrow selectivity/feature-collision issue, not a general failure of differentiable memory; the test uses a fixed similarity representation and does not learn the key encoder, temperature, memory writes, or link traversal.
- **Resources and decision.** Runtime was about 0.7 seconds for the size sweep and 4.4 seconds for the temperature sweep. The largest float64 similarity matrix was 2,048×2,048 (~32 MiB); peak process RSS was not profiled. GPU used: **no**; peak VRAM: **0 GB**; GPU-sharing status was not checked because this was CPU-only; live GPU occupancy remains unknown. This does not justify an architecture claim. It strengthens the proposed falsifier by showing that learned sharpening rescues clean random keys but not all near-duplicate/noisy cases. Next useful check: train or sweep a small key encoder/temperature and compare with top-k plus explicit disambiguation cues before drawing any system conclusion.

#### HY-59 — Episodic addressable memory × implicit fast-weight memory (reject as a new broad hybrid)

- **Source mechanisms and proposed coupling.** The explicit component writes records to addressable slots and supports exact or structured retrieval; the implicit component updates a small associative neural memory/fast-weight model from the same stream. A tentative interaction would use prediction surprise to decide which records are admitted to explicit storage, while a learned retention/update rule consolidates recurring regularities into the fast weights; retrieval disagreement would route a query to one store or the other. This changes write admission and retrieval arbitration, not merely the wiring of two independent memories.
- **Why the mechanisms complement each other.** Explicit slots can preserve isolated one-off facts and support exact lookup; parameter memory can compress repeated regularities and generalize between them. The desired new behavior would be a learned transition between exact episodic retention and lossy reusable structure, potentially making memory growth depend on recurring surprise rather than a fixed cache policy.
- **Prior-art result / disposition.** Reject as a broad hybrid. Complementary episodic/semantic learning and memory consolidation are longstanding; memory-augmented networks and neural Turing machines already combine neural controllers with explicit stores; Memorizing Transformers combine learned representations with a kNN store; test-time training, Titans, and MIRAS directly study learned fast-weight/associative memory and update/forget rules. The sketch does not yet specify a consolidation invariant or a distinct update objective that escapes these families. Adding surprise gating to explicit-vs-implicit routing would be a design choice, not architecture novelty. Keep only the application question of whether a particular workload benefits from exact-episode retention plus learned compression. [Santoro et al. (2016)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v48/santoro16.html); [Memorizing Transformers (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.08913); [TTT layers (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04620); [Titans (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00663); [MIRAS (2025/2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13173).
- **Falsifier if revisited as an application method.** On CPU, stream a controlled mixture of one-off facts and recurring rules with distribution shifts. Compare explicit-only, fast-weight-only, fixed hybrid, and surprise/retention-gated hybrid at equal bytes, update count, and query budget. Measure exact episodic recall, held-out rule generalization, forgetting of recurring facts, adaptation delay, and total memory. Reject the coupling’s practical value if it cannot improve the exact-recall/generalization tradeoff over these matched baselines, or if its gain comes from more storage or extra update compute. No run; this is not a novelty claim.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Predictive coding networks (AR-78)

- **Original computation and basic unit.** Rao and Ballard’s 1999 visual-cortex model is a hierarchical generative system: higher levels send predictions down, and lower levels send prediction errors up. In the later machine-learning PCN formulation, each level has state/representation activities and a generative map; some biological implementations use explicit error populations, while others encode errors through membrane or dendritic differences. At every settling step, activities move to reduce precision-weighted residual/free energy; after settling, synaptic weights update from local pre/post activity and errors (Hebbian-like outer products). A supervised network clamps input and target; prediction mode clamps the observed input and infers latent causes/output. Input is a sensory pattern or observation stream; output is a posterior-like latent estimate, reconstruction, classification, or next-state prediction. Long-term knowledge is in generative weights/precisions, and working memory is in the currently settling state/error populations; temporal variants retain prior state in recurrent connections or an explicit state buffer. [Rao & Ballard, 1999](https://www.nature.com/articles/nn0199_79); [Whittington & Bogacz, 2017](https://doi.org/10.1162/NECO_a_00949); [Millidge et al., temporal predictive coding, preprint 2023 / journal 2024](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011183).
- **What it was good for.** The architecture treats perception as revisable inference: latent states can change after top-down predictions and bottom-up evidence interact. That is a natural fit for denoising, inpainting, ambiguous or missing sensory features, associative recall, generative state estimation, and online perception/control where observations arrive continuously. Temporal PC has been derived as approximate Bayesian filtering and compared with a Kalman filter on tracking; its authors report similar observation prediction under learning, but also report that learned latent-state estimates were not better than their random-parameter model in that experiment. That distinction matters: good reconstruction/prediction does not establish that the inferred internal state is correct. The main proposed advantage is task-conditional belief revision and locally expressed updates, not generic classification speed or guaranteed biological fidelity.
- **Was it bad or early?** The idea was not simply defeated by slow 1990s hardware. Rao–Ballard was a neuroscience/perception theory, not a scaled trainable image model, and the later local-learning algorithm was articulated for machine learning in 2017. Then small datasets, missing autodiff/optimizer infrastructure, and eager software overhead made comparative work awkward. Current accelerators, large sensory datasets, modern optimizers, and compiled JAX implementations materially improve throughput and reproducibility: PCX reports up to 50× speedup from JIT versus its eager implementation. Yet the 2025 ICLR PCX benchmark shows that this is not a compute-only problem. In its A100 epoch comparison, PC took 1.94 s vs BP 1.82 s on FashionMNIST MLP, 3.86 vs 1.04 s on CIFAR-10 AlexNet, 5.33 vs 1.61 s on CIFAR-100 VGG-5, and 54.60 vs 7.59 s on Tiny-ImageNet VGG-7. Accuracy was comparable for small/medium models (up to about VGG-7 in their experiments), but deeper PC models lagged BP. The authors trace this to layerwise energy imbalance: forcing energy to propagate upward from the output can leave early-layer energy orders of magnitude smaller, with depth producing very small gradients. They also show weight/state-optimizer stability interactions and note that training time rises with both layer count and inference steps. Thus better hardware removes implementation overhead and permits larger experiments, but does not remove iterative settling, credit propagation, or the width/depth stability problem. These are partly algorithmic, not merely historical. [Pinchetti et al., ICLR 2025, PCX benchmark](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/581df42e8ebbeeac39aeda03519b7c0e-Paper-Conference.pdf).
- **Modernization already done / prior art.** Inference learning has been related to backpropagation, including limits under which local updates approach or equal BP. However, the exact-equivalence constructions impose assumptions and do not imply a cheaper practical algorithm. The 2023 critical evaluation proves that tested modified PC variants have time complexity no better than BP and discusses weight transport/symmetry and biological-plausibility caveats; PCNs also have formal (non-)convergence analysis. At the same time, the 2025 benchmark demonstrates competitive medium-scale performance and real reconstruction/associative-memory functions. Temporal PC already adapts the formulation for streams; Hybrid Predictive Coding (2023) already learns an amortized initialization for iterative settling and stops inference using prediction-error thresholds; Active Predictive Coding (2024) already couples state inference to actions, hierarchical prediction, SSL and RL; spiking formulations, including ICLR 2026 Difference Predictive Coding, already use sparse ternary error messages and adaptive event thresholds. Predictive coding therefore is an active research family, not an abandoned design waiting for its first modernization. [Frieder & Lukasiewicz, ICML 2022](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/frieder22a.html); [Zahid et al., 2023 critical evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.02658); [Millidge et al., Hybrid Predictive Coding, 2023](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011280); [Rao et al., Active Predictive Coding, 2024](https://direct.mit.edu/neco/article/36/1/1/118264/Active-Predictive-Coding-A-Unifying-Neural-Model); [Karlsson et al., DiffPC, ICLR 2026](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2026/hash/aa31dc84098add7dd2ffdd20646f2043-Abstract-Conference.html).
- **Scaling, hardware, and data.** Dense PCNs map to GPUs but can underuse them because many small iterative operations and recurrent dependencies replace one forward/backward pass. JIT compilation helps; the cited benchmark did not eliminate a several-fold epoch-time gap on its larger tasks. Neuromorphic/spiking versions may exploit sparse local communication on specialized devices, but claimed message sparsity should be validated as energy/latency on real hardware, not inferred from a low spike count. Training data is not categorically different from neural-network training: supervised pairs, unlabeled sensory streams, or simulation trajectories can be used, depending on whether weights, temporal dynamics, or active policies are learned. After deployment, local online weight updates and hidden-state inference are possible, but stability, forgetting, and calibration under nonstationarity need direct tests.
- **Novelty judgment and continue decision.** Generic hierarchical prediction/error units, local Hebbian inference learning, online temporal PC, adaptive settling, PC plus amortized inference, PC plus active sensing, and sparse event-driven PC are all occupied. Novelty confidence for a new broad model class: **0/5**. Keep PC as a serious archaeology/reference family and as a specialist baseline for iterative latent correction and continual state estimation. Do not promote a new candidate. A remaining empirical seam—not a novelty claim—is whether local temporal PC adapts to an abrupt change in a partially observed nonlinear system while preserving calibrated latent-state estimates better than standard online state-space/recurrent baselines at matched data and update budgets.
- **Small falsifiable prototype (planned, not run).** On CPU, generate short controlled sequences from a low-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system with noisy, partly masked observations and one unannounced switch in transition dynamics. Compare a faithfully implemented temporal PC filter with learned local updates against an EKF/linear-Kalman baseline where applicable and a small recurrent predictor with online updates; include an oracle-parameter PC upper bound and a frozen-PC control. Give each equal stream length and update opportunities. Report latent-state RMSE, next-observation NLL/RMSE, calibration, steps to recover after the switch, and wall-clock settling cost. The online-adaptation claim fails if learned PC predicts observations but cannot recover a useful latent state, if it loses to the matched recurrent/Kalman baselines on state and prediction metrics, or if the inference/update cost erases the adaptation benefit. This tests a narrow deployment niche, not architectural novelty.

#### HY-61 — Predictive coding × amortized inference for adaptive computation (reject as new hybrid)

- **Source architectures and coupling.** Predictive coding contributes a generative hierarchy whose latent activities iteratively settle by reducing prediction error. Amortized inference contributes a learned feed-forward initializer that maps an input directly to an approximate latent state. The proposed coupling is to train that initializer to predict the settled PC state, then use residual/error magnitude or uncertainty to allocate additional recurrent settling only to unfamiliar or difficult examples; a local update could adjust both the generative model and initializer from the same objective. Familiar inputs would use nearly one feed-forward sweep, while novel/ambiguous inputs would receive more iterative correction.
- **Why the interaction could matter.** A PCN’s context-sensitive correction is expensive, while a pure encoder can be fast but may fail under novelty or changed context. Training the encoder to initialize inference creates a shared objective and a variable transition between rapid guess and recurrent correction, changing inference scheduling rather than merely placing two models side-by-side. It could be useful when most observations are familiar but a small fraction require careful revision.
- **Prior-art result and verdict.** Reject as a new hybrid: this is already the central mechanism of Hybrid Predictive Coding (Millidge et al., 2023). Its published system uses a feed-forward network to predict iterative PC outcomes, combines amortized and iterative inference under one objective, adaptively spends more settling steps when needed, and reduces iterations as representations improve. General active-sensing PC is also covered by Active Predictive Coding. Rebranding error-based stopping, or adding a new confidence threshold, would be method tuning. No broad candidate promoted.
- **Small disproof test if useful for a particular workload.** Reproduce the published hybrid on a toy familiar/novel input stream and compare fixed-step PC, amortized-only, and error-triggered correction at matched accuracy and total multiply-adds. Add a distribution shift only as an external stress test. The adaptive rule has no practical value if it cannot preserve OOD correction while reducing average computation, or if it simply under-spends on hard but familiar examples. This is a replication/application study; no run.

#### HY-62 — Predictive coding × sparse event-driven message passing (reject as new hybrid)

- **Source architectures and coupling.** Dense PC inference sends continuous prediction/error signals repeatedly between levels. Event-driven/spiking computation communicates only when state changes cross a threshold, reducing dense message traffic. The proposed coupling would encode residual changes as sparse signed events, adapt thresholds to recent error scale, and update only populations downstream of changed messages; weight learning would remain local to active sender/receiver/error events.
- **Distinct behavior and likely value.** If exact enough, this could make recurrent settling asynchronous and reduce memory movement on neuromorphic hardware while retaining PC’s correction of inferred causes. Its failure modes are threshold-induced loss of small but cumulative evidence, oscillation/dead zones, threshold tuning that depends on input scale, and false energy claims when event sparsity is not measured on a device.
- **Prior-art result and verdict.** Reject generic novelty. ICLR 2026 Difference Predictive Coding already replaces dense floating-point PC messages with sparse ternary spikes, includes spike-compatible target/error updates, and uses adaptive threshold schedules for event-driven operation; its abstract reports more than 100× lower data movement than standard PC and competitive benchmark performance. The broader spiking-PC literature already covers explicit, membrane-potential, and implicit error codes; Predictive Coding Light and older sparse deep PCNs further occupy sparse/activity-gated inference. The remaining question is hardware/system validation or an exact robustness improvement, not a new architecture class. Do not claim the reported communication reduction is equivalent to end-to-end energy/latency savings. [Karlsson et al., ICLR 2026](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2026/hash/aa31dc84098add7dd2ffdd20646f2043-Abstract-Conference.html); [N’dri et al., spiking predictive coding survey, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2025.108371); [Predictive Coding Light, 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-64234-z).
- **Small disproof test if revisited.** On CPU first, stream a stationary and then shifted masked-sensor task through dense PC, thresholded PC, and sparse ternary-event PC at matched reconstruction/state error. Measure event count, fraction of missed low-amplitude changes, convergence/oscillation, and compute proxy. Then, only if communication reduction survives with no material error or adaptation penalty, consider device measurement. Reject if sparse traffic depends on loss of useful low-level evidence or if threshold recalibration cancels the savings. No run.
