#### GMDH evidence addendum — cross-reference the existing GMDH section (AR-79 addendum)

- **Original computation and unit.** Ivakhnenko introduced GMDH in 1968 as a computer-based method for inductive system modeling; the 1971 English-language *Polynomial Theory of Complex Systems* describes its construction procedure. A unit is a small “partial description,” classically a two-input quadratic polynomial such as `a0 + a1*x + a2*z + a3*x*z + a4*x^2 + a5*z^2`. Given input/output samples, the algorithm fits candidate units by least squares on a training subset, evaluates them on a checking subset, keeps the best candidate outputs, and forms a next generation by pairing survivors. It stops when adding another layer no longer improves the external criterion. This grows both the model’s equations and topology from examples, rather than optimizing a fixed network by global backprop. Input is usually a low-dimensional table or time-series lag vector; output is a fitted executable predictor/equation. The learned knowledge lies in the selected polynomial units, coefficients, and their directed composition. Inference is a feed-forward evaluation of the chosen polynomial graph; the original method has no persistent episodic memory or required online update state. [Ivakhnenko, 1968 bibliographic record](https://ndlsearch.ndl.go.jp/en/books/R100000136-I1574231875460562432); [Ivakhnenko, 1971 primary paper](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSMC.1971.4308320).
- **What information it represents / possible use.** Each active polynomial captures a low-order interaction among a small set of raw or previously computed variables. Layered products and sums can express higher-order relations while keeping each partial formula inspectable. Original uses include system identification, process forecasting, control modeling, and prediction from limited observations. Its plausible relative advantage is structural selection with compact algebra and less dependence on a human choosing layer count/width; its expected niche is small/medium tabular or scientific system identification where model form and latency matter. It does not provide the learned spatial hierarchies, translation tolerance, large-scale perception, or broad representation learning needed for general vision/language.
- **Why it did not dominate / was it early?** GMDH was not simply blocked by inadequate hardware: it was conceived as an algorithm that runs on a computer and was intended to work from relatively short data sequences. Early compute constrained the number of candidate polynomials and input variables that could be exhaustively considered, so parallel accelerators can now fit/evaluate independent candidates much faster. But modern hardware does not cure the quadratic pair enumeration at each layer, the combinatorial expansion under more variables or polynomial forms, validation-set selection bias, loss of useful weak interactions during greedy pruning, coefficient conditioning, or poor extrapolation by high-degree polynomials. Its reliance on held-out data is a principled defense against overfit but consumes scarce observations and can itself be overfit by trying many candidates. The 1971 paper already describes train/check splitting and selecting by check-set error; this is not a recent improvement. So GMDH appears more like a useful earlier niche method than a broadly useful architecture that disappeared only because computers were slow.
- **What changed and direct revivals.** The method has a long lineage rather than a dormant renaissance. Oh and Pedrycz’s 2002 self-organizing Polynomial Neural Networks (PNNs) retain GMDH’s validation-selected layer growth while allowing nodes to use different numbers of inputs and polynomial orders, explicitly addressing fixed two-variable quadratics and over-complex generated models. Later versions optimized polynomial-node weights using Levenberg–Marquardt or particle-swarm methods; a 2018 deep-polynomial time-series method uses a multi-layer GMDH stage to initialize structure/weights before gradient training; BP-GMDH variants are also published. Modern Π/P-nets use low-rank tensor factorization and hierarchical blocks to make high-order polynomial interactions trainable for vision, audio, graphs, and generation, but they generally do not reproduce GMDH’s greedy external-criterion growth rule. Current GPUs, autograd, and tensor factorization make polynomial representations more viable, but polynomial networks remain a model family with known coefficient/degree scaling and generalization issues. [Oh & Pedrycz, self-organizing PNNs (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0020-0255(02)00175-5); [PNN architecture analysis (2003)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0045-7906(02)00045-9); [optimization of SOPNN (2013)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0957417413000924); [deep polynomial neural networks (CVPR 2020)](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2020/papers/Chrysos_P-nets_Deep_Polynomial_Neural_Networks_CVPR_2020_paper.pdf); [GMDH-initialized deep polynomial forecasting (2018)](https://journals.vilniustech.lt/index.php/Aviation/article/download/2048/1649/4444).
- **Closest known work and novelty.** “A model that grows useful polynomial layers by score-and-prune,” GMDH-type neural networks, polynomial neural networks, and deep polynomial representations are all established. The original method can be read as structural model search over candidate executable equations; modern NAS and symbolic regression provide adjacent, broader structure-search traditions. Novelty confidence for GMDH or generic self-growing polynomial networks: **0/5**. Continue as an archaeology case and possible baseline for small-data, interpretable system identification, not as a candidate for a new general AI class. Strongest remaining practical question: whether this older selection rule offers a sample-efficiency/compactness trade-off on compositional interactions that a global low-order polynomial cannot represent, without losing to a compact modern regressor.
- **Small falsifiable prototype (CPU; executed; result below).** Generate a 10-feature low-dimensional regression problem with only four causal features: `a=x0*x1`, `b=x2*x3`, `y=a+b+0.5*a*b+noise`; train at several small sample sizes with separate fit, GMDH checking, and untouched test sets. Compare bounded pairwise-quadratic GMDH growth with a validation-tuned global degree-2 ridge model, and include an oracle-support polynomial baseline to show the benefit available if feature selection were known. Use multiple random seeds; report test RMSE, validation/test gap, selected graph size/depth, number of candidate fits, and CPU time. This is an intentionally favorable compositional target, not a general benchmark or novelty demonstration.

#### AR-79 CPU probe — bounded GMDH growth on compositional interaction (executed; limited scope)

- **Protocol.** NumPy only on CPU. For each of n={96, 192, 384} training examples and 12 independent seeds, inputs had 10 uniform features, only four of which affected the target: `a=x0*x1`, `b=x2*x3`, `y=a+b+0.5*a*b+GaussianNoise(σ=0.05)`. The sample was split into 60% coefficient-fit and 40% model-check subsets; a separate 3,000-example noisy test set was untouched. The bounded GMDH variant fit six-coefficient bivariate quadratics by least squares, evaluated candidates on the check set, retained the best six nodes per generation, grew at most three generations, and selected the best checking-set node across generations. It fit 75 candidate nodes per run (45 initial pairs then 15 pairs in each of two subsequent generations). Baselines were a 66-term global degree-2 polynomial ridge model whose penalty was selected on the same check set, and an oracle-support four-term regression over known `a`, `b`, `a*b` features. This is a controlled family-level probe, not a full reproduction of every historical GMDH selection heuristic. No GPU library was loaded or used.
- **Result.** Mean test RMSE (± sample SD across seeds) for GMDH / global degree-2 ridge / oracle support was: n=96, 0.1770±0.0994 / 0.2485±0.0318 / 0.0516±0.0009; n=192, 0.0994±0.0167 / 0.1139±0.0109 / 0.0513±0.0012; n=384, 0.0784±0.0128 / 0.0910±0.0057 / 0.0504±0.0005. GMDH beat ridge on 10/12, 9/12, and 10/12 seeds at those sample sizes. Relative mean RMSE reduction was about 29%, 13%, and 14%. Validation RMSE closely tracked test RMSE at n=192 and 384; at n=96 the mean validation/test gap was larger (0.155 vs 0.177), with high seed variability. The best output used about 5.8–6 unique polynomial units (roughly 35–36 active coefficients if counted as six per node), versus 66 coefficients in global degree-2 ridge, but GMDH evaluated 75 candidate nodes and is not compute-matched. The oracle residual is approximately the injected noise floor, so GMDH did not recover the true sparse support perfectly.
- **Interpretation and falsification.** On a target deliberately aligned with its compositional polynomial bias, bounded GMDH gave a modest but repeatable accuracy/active-parameter advantage over a global quadratic baseline. It did not reach the known-support solution, and at 96 samples it was unstable. This is evidence for a niche small-data system-identification baseline, not a new architecture and not proof that GMDH generally beats modern regressors. Its advantage may disappear when candidate evaluations are charged, topology selection is nested, support is less compositional, or data is shifted. Next fair check, if the niche remains useful: nested repeated model selection, a parameter- and compute-aware MLP/modern tabular baseline, noisy/misspecified interactions, and resampled topology stability. No broad claim is promoted.
- **Resources.** Runtime was 0.47 s for 36 runs; CPU only; Python 3.11.9 / NumPy 2.4.6; no scikit-learn installed, so no MLP baseline was run. Peak RAM/RSS was not profiled. GPU used: no; peak VRAM: 0 GB. No GPU snapshot was taken because no GPU run was imminent; current shared occupancy remains unknown. No other research process was inspected or affected.

#### HY-63 — GMDH external-criterion growth × low-rank deep polynomial blocks (demote; no broad novelty)

- **Source mechanisms and exact coupling.** GMDH contributes candidate generation by composing pairs of selected partial descriptions, least-squares local fits, and held-out model selection to choose which structures survive and when growth stops. Deep Π/P-nets contribute high-order multiplicative features represented with tensor-factorized neural blocks and trained by gradient descent. One possible coupling is to use an external check criterion to add/remove polynomial interaction blocks, while each block’s coefficients are low-rank factorized and updated by autodiff. The retained-block score would be recomputed after joint refitting; model growth is therefore coupled to representation learning instead of being a preprocessing step. This could let high-dimensional blocks express interactions compactly while the older criterion allocates topology.
- **Why they complement each other.** GMDH offers data-driven topology selection but uses a narrow family of local quadratic nodes and discrete greedy pruning. Factorized polynomial networks represent richer multiplicative functions and train efficiently but usually assume a chosen architecture and risk coefficient explosion/overfit. A tight feedback loop could make structural complexity depend on held-out utility while gradients refine local tensor factors. The possible benefit is compact compositional regression on small/medium data; failures include an expensive two-timescale structure/weight search, noisy validation-based birth/death decisions, polynomial conditioning, and losing differentiability at architecture changes.
- **Prior-art screen and disposition.** Demote rather than promote. Self-organizing PNNs from 2002 already generalize GMDH to selectable input arity and polynomial orders; optimized SOPNNs already refine weights after structure growth; 2018 work initializes deep polynomial network structure and weights using multilayer GMDH before gradient descent; genetic GMDH searches network structure; Π-nets already supply low-rank factorization for high-order polynomial neural networks. I did not verify one exact paper with the proposed repeated low-rank refit + held-out block birth/death loop. That absence is not a novelty claim: the ingredients and principal function (growing/selecting polynomial structure with learned coefficients) are directly occupied. A new result would need a distinct stability rule or a measurable search-efficiency/generalization property, not simply combining the familiar blocks.
- **Falsifier if revisited.** On CPU, compare fixed-width Π-net, conventional GMDH, and the coupled growth/refit model on synthetic sparse high-order systems and a small tabular dataset at matched data, compute, and prediction parameter counts. Keep a separate test set; use repeated nested validation so the growth criterion cannot see the final test. Measure predictive error, formula size, search cost, and topology stability across data resamples. Reject the coupling as practically useful if it fails to beat both baselines on the accuracy/compactness frontier, or if selected topology changes wildly across resamples. No run; not a promoted candidate.

#### ART modernization source audit — DeepART and Deep ARTMAP (AR-80; expansion of existing record)

- **What was already known in this notebook.** The earlier ART entry already records Fuzzy ART’s category-match/reset mechanism, the feature-geometry and vigilance limits, MPART/PAN, direct DeepART prior art, and a planned frozen-feature benchmark. This is a source-check and limitation update, not a new archaeology family or a claim that “deep ART” was previously unexplored.
- **DeepART, in the peer-reviewed 2025 paper.** Petrenko, Brito da Silva, and Wunsch derive local winner-take-all updates for fully connected and convolutional layers, interpret deep layers as modified complement-coded FuzzyART modules, and use a FuzzyARTMAP head for feature/category/label mapping. Its target is one-shot incremental lifelong vision learning. The publisher’s accessible method/evaluation description says the tested systems use selected MLP and CNN backbones and compares DeepART variants to FuzzyARTMAP; each DeepART variant beats that ART baseline on average in the reported benchmark/scenario combinations and reduces category growth. That is useful evidence that hierarchical features can mitigate ART’s high-dimensional/category-growth weakness. It does **not**, from the accessible comparison, establish parity with conventionally trained deep networks or strong replay/regularization continual-learning baselines. The claim is accordingly limited to improvement over ART-based comparators, not broad vision competitiveness. [Petrenko et al., Neural Networks 190 (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2025.107580); [publisher article preview](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0893608025004605).
- **Deep ARTMAP, in its March 2025 arXiv preprint.** This generalizes SMART/ARTMAP to multiple ART modules linked by one-to-many map fields. For each example, it first forms the top module’s category and trains lower modules backward through simplified ARTMAP links; each module can receive a different transform of the input. At inference, each transformed view is categorized and the hierarchy’s labels are aggregated. This makes it a real hierarchical online mechanism, but the transforms are functions supplied to the system, not a specified jointly learned representation mechanism. Crucially, the paper has no empirical results section: its stated limitation is that the order and quality of the transforms determine the resulting hierarchy, so useful settings may require experimentation and repeated simulations. An accompanying ART library makes implementation easier; it does not validate the claimed broad multimodal use. [Melton et al., Deep ARTMAP preprint, full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.07641v1).
- **Historical verdict.** ART was partly early: parallel hardware can accelerate category search; modern deep features reduce the poor raw-sensor geometry; scalable memory makes larger prototype banks practical; and one-pass/local updates still suit streaming novelty and open-set tasks. Yet vigilance, coordinate dependence, order/noise sensitivity, and the conflict between category granularity and prototype growth are mechanism-level tradeoffs. DeepART addresses representation depth and compares favorably to a shallow ART baseline, but its evidence boundary leaves the central question—whether those gains survive against strong deep continual learners under the same one-pass/task-access constraints—open. Deep ARTMAP adds a formal hierarchy but currently leaves transformation choice to the experimenter and lacks a benchmark demonstration. Verdict: modernized specialist, neither merely a bad idea nor a general model rescued by faster hardware.
- **Novelty disposition.** Do not promote a new ART class or hybrid. Deep local ART learning is occupied by DeepART; arbitrary-transform hierarchical ART mapping is now directly specified by Deep ARTMAP; modern feature + ART + graph/uncertainty/active sampling was already occupied by MPART; vigilance adjustment has a mature variant literature; and ART-match tracking × predictive error already intersects the notebook’s prior HY audit of ARTMAP as predictive ART. A DeepART-to-Deep-ARTMAP stack would be a natural modular composition, but absent a changed learning rule or inference behavior it is a component assembly, not a new architecture.
- **Small falsifiable experiment (planned, not run; updates earlier ART plan).** On a fixed, publicly available self-supervised feature stream with controlled class/domain shifts, compare raw-input FuzzyART, frozen-feature FuzzyARTMAP over a preregistered vigilance sweep, online nearest prototypes, an online linear head, and DeepART if its implementation/data protocol can be reproduced. Add a standard supervised deep baseline and continual-learning baselines only with matched access to labels, task boundaries, replay memory, and pass count; report both task-incremental and class-incremental results rather than pooling them. Measure accuracy/forgetting, category count and bytes, order/vigilance sensitivity, false novelty resets, wall-clock update and inference time, and feature-update cost separately. Falsify “modern features rescue ART” if frozen representations fail to lower category/memory cost at a matched retention/accuracy point, or if gains depend on task labels/boundaries absent from the online setting. CPU on cached features; no GPU is required for the first falsifier.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Cascade-Correlation (AR-81)

- **Original computation.** Fahlman and Lebiere’s 1989 Cascade-Correlation (CasCor) begins with input-to-output connections and no hidden layer. It trains the output map, then trains a pool of candidate units to maximize correlation with residual output errors. The winner is inserted permanently as a new feature detector; its input weights are frozen, and later units can connect to all earlier hidden units. Output weights continue adapting. Input is a labeled vector, repeated operation is residual-fit → candidate-unit competition → permanent feature birth, output is a class/value prediction, and knowledge is the growing cascade of frozen feature detectors plus trainable readout weights. Candidate units can be trained in parallel, which the original paper explicitly identified as hardware-friendly. On two-spirals, their reported 100 runs all solved the 194-point training set using an average of 15.2 units; their operation-count estimate was 19 million connection crossings on average versus reported 438 million for Quickprop on that benchmark. Treat this as a historical, task-specific comparison, not a modern matched benchmark. [Fahlman & Lebiere, NeurIPS 1989 primary paper](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1989/file/69adc1e107f7f7d035d7baf04342e1ca-Paper.pdf).
- **Why it attracted interest, and where it struggled.** It removes the moving-target problem for hidden features, avoids global backward credit through previously learned units, chooses topology as learning proceeds, and caches activations for the fixed part of the network. However, it buys this simplicity by greedily freezing candidate features. The original authors themselves note that repeated growth may create very deep, high-fan-in networks. A 42-dataset CasCor-family comparison found that flat rather than cascaded hidden units were slightly better on its tasks, with candidate-objective choice affecting regression/classification differently; this weakens a universal argument for cascaded growth. Later analyses cite poor generalization and overfitting under deep growth, while recurrent CasCor has a stronger representational limitation: Giles et al. show it cannot represent some finite-state automata with common monotone or threshold activations. These are not all the same algorithm, so do not transfer recurrent impossibility results to feedforward CasCor. [Prechelt, CasCor family on PROBEN1 (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0893-6080(96)00115-3); [Giles et al., recurrent CasCor limits (1995)](https://doi.org/10.1109/72.392247).
- **What modern technology changes.** Current CPUs/GPUs can evaluate candidate pools and cached feature banks more efficiently, and plentiful data supports honest validation-based stopping. Yet the architecture’s hard question is which greedy feature should become irreversible. Accelerators cannot repair a bad residual criterion, shift-sensitive feature, distribution change, or a cascade whose old units should be revised. The original paper already exploited parallel candidate evaluation and activation caching; therefore raw compute is not the whole explanation for its loss of prominence.
- **Modern descendants and prior art.** Constructive cascade variants remained an active research family through the 1990s/2000s and later deep-cascade variants retain node growth and frozen inputs. AdaNet (ICML 2017) adaptively selects network structure **and weights**, gives data-dependent generalization guarantees, and reports large-scale CIFAR-derived and Criteo experiments. It directly occupies broad claims that neural topology should grow automatically under data-driven structural selection. Modern network-growth, pruning, progressive networks, neural architecture search, and dynamic sparse training further make “add units when residual error remains” an occupied design space. The useful old feature is local candidate fitting with no credit propagation through frozen ancestors; no evidence here establishes that this is broadly better than modern alternatives. [Cortes et al., AdaNet (ICML 2017)](https://research.google/pubs/adanet-adaptive-structural-learning-of-artificial-neural-networks/); [Feng et al., Cascade-Correlation Growing Deep Network (2021)](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4893/14/5/158).
- **Possible niche and novelty.** CasCor may still be a clean baseline for low-data function approximation, cheap incremental feature construction, or settings where old features must remain fixed for auditability. Its limitations are growing inference depth, dense fan-in, candidate search cost, irreversible greedy choices, validation consumption, and weak guarantees under drift. No novel general architecture survives. The most plausible narrow experiment is not another growth rule; it is a fair test of when one-shot frozen feature construction reduces update cost without harming shift adaptation.
- **Small falsifiable prototype (planned, CPU; no run).** Reproduce the two-spirals mechanism first, then test a controlled sequence of low-dimensional nonlinear tasks with a boundary shift. Compare faithful CasCor, a shallow candidate-growth variant, a fixed-width MLP trained by Adam, and AdaNet or a reproducible structural-selection baseline. Match candidate evaluations, training examples, validation access, final parameter count, and total multiply-accumulates as closely as practical; use multiple seeds and untouched shifted test distributions. Report training and shifted-test error, growth depth/units, candidate-search operations, update latency, and retention of old regions. Falsify the proposed niche if the frozen cascade only wins by spending more candidate compute, overfits the validation stream, or recovers from shift materially worse than the matched baseline. Start CPU-only; a GPU is unnecessary for this scale.

#### HY-64 — Cascade-Correlation candidate growth triggered by ART resonance failure (demote; narrow method question only)

- **Source architectures and what they contribute.** Cascade-Correlation (AR-81) grows a feedforward representation by training candidate units against residual error, then freezes a winning unit. Fuzzy ART/ARTMAP (existing ART entry and AR-80) supplies local category competition, online category birth, and match tracking that can preserve established categories. The potential complement is specific: ART can indicate which incoming cases are not represented at the current granularity; candidate-unit correlation can search for a feature transformation that reduces the mismatch rather than immediately storing another high-dimensional prototype.
- **Proposed coupling.** Keep a FuzzyARTMAP category/map field as the streaming controller. When repeated, labeled resonance failures in one category or a stable subset cross a threshold, use those cases plus a bounded replay set of adjacent resonant examples as the candidate pool. Train CasCor units to correlate with the map-field residuals for that subset; install a candidate only if it reduces held-out map errors without creating more cross-category confusion. Recompute only affected category prototypes in the new feature coordinate system, preserve the old-space fallback, and let future samples route between old and refined feature views by resonance. This is more than placing an ART head after a network: category mismatch determines where representation capacity is allocated, while the new representation changes future category matches.
- **Why it might behave differently / potential advantage.** Plain CasCor grows against output residuals globally and can waste units on already-easy regions; plain ART responds to a mismatch by searching or creating another prototype, which can inflate memory when the feature geometry is poor. Localized mismatch-triggered feature growth could trade a small number of shared learned units for many redundant prototypes, while retaining one-pass category updates in stable regions. Plausible applications are nonstationary streams with recurring subtypes, where old categories must remain inspectable and a small novelty rate can trigger representation refinement.
- **Prior art and adversarial verdict.** The broad ingredients are occupied. GFTART replaces FuzzyART’s F2 categories with growing-cell-structure modules, changes its winner/vigilance comparison, and explicitly aims to reduce category proliferation while preserving input topology; it is direct ART plus structural growth, though not CasCor residual-correlated hidden-unit birth. Fuzzy ARTMAP with temporary nodes already adds online pruning during supervised ART growth. DeepART learns local feature representations through modified ART-like dense/conv layers and reports reduced category growth relative to FuzzyARTMAP. Separately, CasCor, AdaNet, and the constructive-network literature already cover residual-driven unit/subnetwork selection. I did not locate this exact conditional coupling in the targeted search, but that is not evidence of novelty: the desired effect, “grow representation to reduce category proliferation,” is already directly pursued by DeepART and GFTART. Demote the architecture claim; at most this is a niche allocation policy to compare against them. [GFTART, Kim et al. (2011)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0925231210003711); [online pruning for FAM/FAMDDA (2009)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00521-008-0191-5); [DeepART (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2025.107580); [AdaNet (2017)](https://research.google/pubs/adanet-adaptive-structural-learning-of-artificial-neural-networks/).
- **Weaknesses and novelty.** Candidate training may spend more work than creating a prototype; a FuzzyART map mismatch is partly determined by hand-set vigilance; replay examples may bias the residual; feature growth can shift every dependent prototype and break the stability that ART was meant to provide; conditional old/new feature routing can itself become another classifier. Recomputing affected categories may also violate strict one-pass learning. Novelty confidence for a broad architecture class: **0/5**. Confidence that the exact gate is absent from the bounded search: **1/5**.
- **Small falsifier if a domain-specific study justifies it (planned, not run).** Use a CPU synthetic stream with two recurring nonlinear classes, a controlled representation change, noisy nuisance dimensions, and one rare subtype that becomes separable only after a nonlinear feature. Compare FuzzyARTMAP, CasCor alone, a simple ART→CasCor serial pipeline, DeepART if its code/data can be reproduced, and the proposed mismatch-gated coupling. Match examples, replay bytes, number of candidate evaluations, validation access, and final feature/prototype memory. Measure old-class retention, accuracy, category count, false resonance resets, new-unit count, update operations, and recovery time after the shift. Reject the coupling if it does not improve the accuracy–memory–update-cost frontier over the best standalone or serial baseline, if it needs more replay or labels, or if remapping harms previously stable categories.

#### Continuation/resource update — ART and constructive growth (2026-09-27)

- AR-80 distinguishes the peer-reviewed DeepART result from the still-unvalidated Deep ARTMAP preprint and narrows their demonstrated scope. AR-81 records Cascade-Correlation as a valuable constructive learning mechanism whose historic speed claim was tied to small tasks and whose irreversible growth brings representation/generalization costs. HY-64 tests the complementary ART/CasCor rationale against GFTART, temporary-node FAM, DeepART, and AdaNet; the general architecture claim is demoted, with only a tightly budgeted category-triggered allocation comparison retained as an optional methods experiment. No candidate was promoted.
- This continuation used primary-paper/publisher review and notebook synthesis only. CPU use: none; GPU use and peak VRAM: 0 GB. No live GPU snapshot was taken because no GPU experiment was imminent, so shared-device occupancy remains unknown. No Claude process or file was inspected or affected. Only Codex_Research.md was edited.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Reservoir Computing, Echo State Networks, and Liquid State Machines (AR-82)

**Status:** established architecture family, partly modernized and still useful in temporal/specialized settings; not a new candidate. This entry expands the one-line reservoir item already in the archaeology index. Do not count ESN, LSM, SORN, or NG-RC as separate new architecture candidates merely because their names differ.

- **What the original families computed.** Jaeger’s 2001 Echo State Network (ESN) and Maass, Natschläger, and Markram’s 2002 Liquid State Machine (LSM) independently made recurrent dynamics useful without training every recurrent connection end-to-end. An ESN repeatedly updates a vector of nonlinear unit states from the current input and previous reservoir state, typically with a fixed, randomly drawn recurrent matrix; a linear readout maps those states to predictions. An LSM uses spiking/recurrent “liquid” dynamics and a filtered state/readout, emphasizing real-time processing of continuously varying inputs. A stream of inputs is transformed into trajectories; the supervised output weights are fitted separately. The common primitive is **input-driven transient dynamics as a temporal feature map**, not next-token prediction or an attractor memory. In standard RC training, the reservoir is fixed or separately adapted and the readout is trained, often by regularized linear regression. [Jaeger’s ESN report, GMD 148 (2001)](https://doi.org/10.24406/publica-fhg-291111), [Maass et al., *Real-Time Computing Without Stable States*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12433288/), and the survey by [Lukoševičius & Jaeger (2009)](https://www.ai.rug.nl/minds/uploads/2261_LukoseviciusJaeger09.pdf).
- **Information, input/output, and memory.** Inputs may be real-valued signals or spike trains. Reservoir units represent recent input history in their transient state; memory is distributed in recurrent dynamics, not principally stored in trainable weights. Repeated operation is state update → collect states → readout. Output may be a class, control signal, or next sample. The memory is generally *fading*: old input influence decays according to the selected dynamics. ESN states are typically analog-valued; LSM states are spike timings or filtered spike activity. Learning may be batch ridge regression or online readout adaptation; later variants adapt reservoir weights, topology, leak/time constants, or node excitability. Inference is naturally streaming and can be causal with low latency.
- **Why it attracted interest.** It avoids the hardest recurrent credit-assignment problem, gives a cheap linear fit, can work with modest training sequences on dynamical-system tasks, and can use a physical medium’s native dynamics. LSM’s perturbation-centered view also rejects the assumption that useful computation needs discrete stable attractor states. This remains a real alternative for low-power temporal processing and some dynamical-system identification tasks.
- **Why it struggled / “born too early?” verdict.** Historical compute limits did restrict node count and simulation speed, especially for dense recurrent state updates and realistic spiking models. Modern GPUs, simulation libraries, accelerators, and specialized analog/photonic devices help run larger or faster reservoirs. Yet scale was never the only obstacle: the random state map may be irrelevant to the task; spectral radius, leak, input scaling, sparsity, and sampling time interact; the echo-state/fading-memory regime can be fragile; and a linear readout cannot repair information that the reservoir failed to preserve. Bigger random reservoirs multiply compute and tuning burden, and do not ensure a useful representation. Fixed dynamics also struggle when the task regime changes or useful memory should be selectively retained. These are design and statistical limitations, not just 1990s hardware constraints.
- **What technology has changed.** Cheap parallel state updates, stable linear solvers, GPUs, larger data streams, and optimization/search make reservoir design easier. Modern encoders can supply much better features than raw sensory inputs; differentiable or locally plastic updates can adapt dynamics; simulation supports controlled task distributions; physical neuromorphic, photonic, and electronic implementations offer new latency/energy tradeoffs. However, GPU parallelism does not automatically make sparse recurrent updates efficient, and using global autodiff through all recurrent weights gives up part of the original training-cost advantage. Physical reservoirs add input/output transduction, calibration, noise, reset, and reproducibility constraints. Thus hardware helps the implementation and search problem, but does not settle the representational question.
- **Evidence the idea was not merely abandoned.** SORN (2009) combines local STDP, synaptic normalization, and intrinsic plasticity so that unsupervised temporal sequence learning does not simply destabilize network activity. Its own authors explain why isolated STDP updates are difficult: changing connections changes activity, which in turn drives more plasticity; homeostasis is part of the solution, not an optional cosmetic add-on. [Lazar, Pipa & Triesch (2009)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2773171/). NG-RC (2021) establishes that, for important dynamical-system settings, a recurrent reservoir can be replaced by explicit delay coordinates and nonlinear features: it is mathematically connected to nonlinear vector autoregression and avoids a random recurrent matrix. In their Lorenz-63 setup, the published model uses 28 features from a two-step embedding and reports under 10 ms training on a single-core desktop for its specified short training sequence. This is strong evidence that a large random reservoir is unnecessary for some smooth low-dimensional dynamics, not a claim that recurrence is universally unnecessary. [Gauthier et al. (2021)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-25801-2), [authors’ code](https://github.com/quantinfo/ng-rc-paper-code).
- **A modern hybrid that already occupies a tempting idea.** The 2022 **SO-ConvESN / SORN-E** paper first clusters action-sequence inputs using an ART/Instantaneous Topological Mapping mechanism, then uses the learned centroids and interconnectivity map to deterministically initialize ESN input and recurrent weights; a convolutional stage extracts multiscale temporal features. It directly occupies “input-shaped or ART-organized reservoir + convolutional sequence readout.” Its RQA analysis reports more stable activation dynamics than random reservoirs under its tested configurations, and the authors report competitive skeleton-action results on MSRA3D and Florence3D. The paper also identifies noise sensitivity: corrupted MSRA3D joints can form or update ART nodes. Its own outlook calls for incremental learning, node pruning, and better hyperparameter selection. The evaluations are task-specific and do not establish general-purpose online learning. [SORN-E primary paper PDF (2022)](https://jier.um.edu.my/index.php/MJCS/article/download/34808/14848).
- **Terminology collision to avoid.** “SORN” refers to two different mechanisms in this literature. The 2009 *Self-Organizing Recurrent Neural Network* uses recurrent excitatory/inhibitory cells with STDP, synaptic normalization, and intrinsic plasticity. The 2022 *Self-Organizing Reservoir Network* in the SO-ConvESN paper uses ART + ITM clustering to initialize an ESN. Do not treat the latter as a direct later implementation of the former without evidence; the shared acronym obscures distinct learning and state-generation mechanisms. [2009 SORN](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2773171/), [2022 SO-ConvESN](https://jier.um.edu.my/index.php/MJCS/article/download/34808/14848).
- **Other modern revivals and prior art.** A 2024 physical-reservoir tutorial and emerging-electronics review document ongoing physical implementations rather than a dead historical branch. An adaptive-oscillator paper demonstrates a *self-learning physical reservoir computer*: plastic oscillator states are used as physical nodes and can tune reservoir parameters. This occupies a broad claim that physical reservoirs could learn their own useful dynamics after deployment. [Stepney, *Physical reservoir computing: a tutorial* (2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11047-024-09997-y), [Liang et al., emerging electronics review (2024)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41928-024-01133-z), [Shougat, Li & Perkins, PRE (2024)](https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.109.064205). A recent optical NG-RC experiment shows the physical-computing branch is also being extended to explicit nonlinear feature maps, with measured task and device-specific scope. [Optical NG-RC (2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12280216/).
- **New 2026 literature check: “evolving” need not mean online rewiring.** Tolle et al. optimize reservoir prediction and an emergence score over human-connectome or random recurrent graphs using evolutionary search over hyperparameters (including spectral radius, density, readout regularization, input strength and bias). Each task is one of six 3-D chaotic flows, with a 100-node reservoir and an analytical readout; the paper reports bidirectional correlation between predictive performance and its emergence measure. The trained recurrent system is still a fixed reservoir for inference: the evolutionary process tunes configurations offline rather than learning a continually rewired network on each new input. This is a useful modern experiment on structure–function analysis, but not evidence that online network evolution has become a general learning architecture. Caveats: synthetic low-dimensional dynamics, a defined information-theoretic emergence metric, and evolutionary hyperparameter optimization mean correlation between emergence and prediction should not be read as proof that emergence causally improves task generalization. [Tolle et al., *Patterns* (2026)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13100675/), [code/data](https://github.com/Imperial-MIND-lab/emergentReservoirs).
- **Falsifiable CPU prototype — quadratic NG-RC versus a small ESN on Lorenz-63 (run).** This is a narrow task-class probe, not an architecture benchmark. I generated 8,500 Lorenz-63 points by RK4 at `dt=0.01`, standardized from the first 5,000 points, trained chronologically on those 5,000, used points 5,000–6,499 to approach/inspect the forecast region, and scored the final 2,000 one-step targets using true preceding states. NG-RC used current plus one lag (6 scalar coordinates), constant/linear/all quadratic products (28 total features), ridge `1e-6`. ESN used 100 simulated nodes with 10% recurrent sparsity, spectral radius 0.9, input scale 0.5, direct input skip, 104-dimensional readout, ridge `1e-4`; I ran three reservoir seeds. One-step standardized RMSE: NG-RC `6.45e-6`; ESN seeds `0.00151`, `0.00325`, `0.00144` (median `0.00151`). With a common autonomous rollout start 50 points into the test segment, and a normalized state-error cutoff of 0.5, NG-RC lasted 747 steps; ESN lasted 73, 18, and 31 steps. Fit/runtime was about 0.0006 s for the NG-RC readout and 0.08–0.10 s for each ESN seed including state generation/eigendecomposition, on CPU with Python 3.11.9 / NumPy 2.4.6. An initial script had a one-row target alignment error and was corrected before recording any scores.
- **Interpretation and caveats.** This is an intentionally favorable case for a quadratic delay model: Lorenz-63 has a smooth low-dimensional polynomial vector field, and the step is small. The readout parameter counts differ (84 NG-RC versus 312 ESN readout coefficients, plus a 100×100 recurrent matrix with about 1,000 active entries), the ESN was not extensively tuned, this is one trajectory and one regime, and the closed-loop cutoff/horizon is only a tiny synthetic proxy for task utility. In particular the huge horizon gap must not be attributed to architecture class alone. The result verifies the implementation and illustrates a real decision point: on this class, explicit nonlinear delay coordinates capture the relation with very few fitted coefficients and a random reservoir adds unnecessary variability. It does not refute ESN/LSM on high-dimensional, non-polynomial, noisy, event-driven, or sensor-specific tasks. Published NG-RC already reports much the same task-class outcome, so the experiment adds a local reproducibility datapoint, not novelty.
- **Potential use and remaining research value.** Reservoir methods remain worth treating as baselines/components for streaming control, embedded sensing, spiking/neuromorphic processing, rapid readout fitting, and domains where a physical substrate naturally supplies nonlinear temporal state. The worthwhile research seam is not “a reservoir with learning,” “a better random reservoir,” “more reservoir nodes,” or “ART plus reservoir”: those are established families. A possible unsolved *evaluation* question is when explicit finite-history features, local plastic recurrent state, or a physical substrate wins under matched energy, latency, drift, and sensor-noise constraints. No broad architecture candidate survives this audit. **Novelty confidence for the reservoir family: 0/5; practical value as a specialized computational mechanism: moderate.**
- **Small next falsifier.** If revisited, compare fixed ESN, an online/local-plastic reservoir (SORN/e-prop-adjacent implementation), quadratic NG-RC, and a properly tuned gated RNN on (a) low-dimensional smooth dynamics, (b) a delayed non-polynomial process, and (c) noisy regime switches. Match input features, training stream, readout/update compute, memory, and tune budget. Measure one-step error, autonomous prediction horizon, online recovery, operations/energy, and seed variation. The audit’s broad claim that reservoirs are broadly better is falsified if explicit delay models or gated RNNs match task quality and adaptation at lower matched resource cost across the target classes; any hardware claim additionally needs device-level I/O/reset/calibration accounting.

#### HY-65 — Error-triggered allocation between NG-RC and recurrent reservoir (reject as architecture claim; optional scheduling study)

- **Source mechanisms.** NG-RC/NVAR turns explicit recent samples into a compact nonlinear basis with a cheap ridge readout. An ESN/LSM turns ongoing history into learned or fixed transient recurrent state and can represent dynamics not captured by a short explicit lag basis. The proposed coupling targets complementary limits: NG-RC can be compact and interpretable for smooth, sampled dynamics but is sensitive to lag/sampling/nonlinearity choices; a reservoir can create richer temporal features but may be unnecessarily expensive or random for easy intervals.
- **Exact coupling considered.** Run NG-RC as a low-cost predictor. Track calibrated residuals over time and by input/regime. Only when repeated residuals exceed a threshold would the system instantiate or activate a small recurrent reservoir to predict the unresolved residual; reservoir state would then update online while NG-RC continues to carry the base prediction. When residual confidence recovers, decay the recurrent correction and stop spending the recurrent update budget. Thus the error history controls a persistent change in computation schedule/model state, rather than concatenating features and training one readout.
- **Why behavior could differ.** It would use explicit polynomial history as a cheap default computation and dynamically allocate recurrence only to contexts where fixed-lag features fail. The hypothesis is lower average update cost than a full hybrid while retaining the hybrid’s ability to model hidden memory or unusual nonlinearities. Potential use is sensor/control time series with mostly predictable dynamics and occasional regime transitions.
- **Prior-art attack.** This generic source pairing is directly occupied: Chepuri et al. (2024) introduce a traditional RC–NGRC hybrid and report that a small reservoir can recover performance when NG-RC/RC alone are limited by sampling, nonlinearity, sparse training, or hyperparameter choices. It combines complementary features but does not, from the accessible abstract, establish the proposed error-triggered persistent activation rule. Beyond the direct hybrid, 2026 work adds a reference-state library as a dynamic reservoir update bias; 2026 NG-RC work enforces an echo-state-like stability condition; and adaptive reservoir readout compression makes effective state capacity expand/shrink with prediction error/complexity. Adaptive models, gated mixtures, structural plasticity, and evolving reservoirs make a broad “turn on capacity on residual” novelty claim weak even if the exact trigger schedule was not located. [RC-NGRC hybrid, Chepuri et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0206232); [dynamic structural bias, Liu et al. 2026](https://journals.aps.org/prresearch/abstract/10.1103/5nbr-bqxb); [NG-RC echo-state stability constraint, Pyragas & Pyragas 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physleta.2026.131939); [adaptive-compression ESN (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2026.116495).
- **Advantages if it works:** avoid paying for recurrent updates on simple predictable intervals; retain a compact interpretable baseline; perhaps react to change without always deploying the full hybrid.
- **Failure modes:** residual thresholds can fire late under chaos, noise, or unobserved shifts; residuals can also be small while the internal state is wrong; activation can create latency spikes; repeatedly switching modes can destabilize readout calibration; it may need replay or labels to train the recurrent correction; the full hybrid may already be cheaper; simpler adaptive NG-RC, a standard online state-space model, or a small always-on reservoir may dominate.
- **Novelty/decision.** No distinct general architecture is promoted. Exact error-triggered persistence is a bounded search gap, not demonstrated novelty. Confidence that the broad idea is new: **0/5**; confidence that this exact scheduler was absent from the small targeted query set: **1/5**. Demote to a task-specific scheduling hypothesis only.
- **Small falsifiable experiment (planned, CPU; not run).** Construct a switching stream that alternates between a low-dimensional quadratic system and a delayed nonlinear regime, with controlled observation noise and abrupt/gradual changes. Compare a tuned ESN, NG-RC, the published-style always-on concatenated RC–NGRC hybrid, and residual-triggered reservoir allocation. Equalize total update/multiply budget and online tuning access. Measure average and 95th-percentile compute, detection/recovery delay, prediction error during and after switch, mode-switch count, and long-run stability. Reject the scheduler if it fails to beat the always-on hybrid’s quality–compute frontier or if threshold tuning/mode-chatter costs consume the saved updates.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Predictive State Representations and Observable Operator Models (AR-83)

**Status:** established model family; earlier candidate seed retained only as a baseline/evaluation direction. This entry expands the notebook’s original PSR/OOM idea rather than creating a new class.

- **Original computation.** Jaeger’s Observable Operator Models (OOM, 1997/2000) represent a stochastic sequence process by a finite-dimensional real vector and observation-conditioned linear operators. Littman, Sutton, and Singh’s Predictive State Representation (PSR, 2001) makes the state of a controlled system a vector of conditional probabilities for selected future action-observation “tests” (core tests). After a new action-observation pair, recursively update those predictions using probabilities of extended tests; every future test prediction can be reconstructed from the core-test state if the chosen basis is sufficient. This is a state representation grounded in observable futures, instead of a posterior over hidden physical states. The repeated primitive is **maintain and linearly update a compact bank of future-event predictions**. Input: action-observation history. Output: future test probabilities, filtering state, and an object for model-based planning. Knowledge is stored in selected tests and their extension/projection operators. The 2001 paper proves that any finite POMDP can be represented by a linear PSR with no more core tests than states in a minimal POMDP; the PSR may be smaller. [Jaeger, OOMs (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1162/089976600300015411), [Littman, Sutton & Singh, PSR (NeurIPS 2001)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2001/file/1e4d36177d71bbb3558e43af9577d70e-Paper.pdf), [Singh et al., learning PSRs (ICML 2003)](https://cdn.aaai.org/ICML/2003/ICML03-093.pdf).
- **Learning and inference.** Linear PSRs can be fitted by moment/spectral/two-stage-regression methods or online supervised updates to predictions of extension tests. Inference is an explicit operator update conditioned on the observed action and outcome. Planning can simulate future observations/actions in the learned state. No external memory is required if the prediction vector is sufficient, but selecting and storing enough core tests can itself become the memory cost. The PSR is not a classifier, generic RNN, or mere auxiliary next-token head.
- **Why the family mattered.** Latent-state representations are often unidentifiable up to coordinate changes and may require solving a hard inference problem inside a learned generative model. PSRs use statistics of observable events as the state and can learn directly from action-observation traces. This can yield compact representations, interpretable test predictions, and direct compatibility with filtering/planning. Predictive state can encode regularities a POMDP posterior would store only through a potentially larger hidden-state distribution.
- **Why broad adoption struggled; was it too early?** Hardware shortage is not the main explanation. The original papers explicitly leave core-test discovery/model learning as hard problems. A useful test basis must be found from trajectories generated by a sufficiently exploratory policy; rare action-observation tests have noisy estimates, and update denominators can be close to zero. In finite data, estimated linear operators can produce negative or invalid probabilities, especially under rank/model mismatch. The 2003 learning paper notes negative projection entries and that generate-and-test discovery of core tests may be difficult. Spectral methods can be consistent under assumptions yet give negative probabilities empirically when sample size or rank choice is poor. [Zhao & Poupart, *A Sober Look at Spectral Learning* (2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.4631). Continuous sensory inputs require a feature/test embedding, and nonlinear/high-dimensional settings raise kernel and sample complexity. Larger datasets and GPUs help estimate moments and fit kernel maps but do not guarantee an adequate test basis, good exploration coverage, calibrated probabilities, or robust model selection. Thus the family was partly early for modern perception and data scale, but it was not merely waiting for fast hardware.
- **Modernization already performed.** Several lines directly address old constraints. Hilbert-space embeddings of PSRs extend state/prediction updates to continuous-valued actions and observations with conditional operators in an RKHS; this helps raw robotics signals but can add kernel storage and compute. [Boots, Gordon & Gretton (2013)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.6819). Predictive State Inference Machines (PSIM, 2016) directly learn a composition of predictors for the filtering update and optimize closed-loop inference quality rather than first fitting a generative latent model; the paper gives realizable and agnostic guarantees and robotics/simulation tests. [Sun et al. (2016)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v48/sun16.html). The 2015 unified treatment shows the close relation among OOMs, PSRs, and stochastic multiplicity automata, so weighted automata are not an unexplored alternative name. [Thon & Jaeger (2015)](https://jmlr.org/papers/v16/thon15a.html).
- **Direct modern hybrid collisions.** Predictive-State Recurrent Neural Networks (PSRNN, 2017) are a genuine deep coupling: a 3-mode weight tensor applies a bilinear state-observation update, observation gates the predictive state, a normalized state is iterated, two-stage regression initializes parameters, and BPTT refines them; tensor factorization reduces parameter count. The paper reports experiments on four datasets and explicitly notes that consistency guarantees are retained in the discrete realizable setting but not in the full continuous setting. This already occupies “PSR operator state + expressive recurrent neural update.” [Downey et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.09353). Predictive-State Decoders (2017) use a different, lighter coupling: an auxiliary decoder/loss trains an ordinary RNN hidden state to predict statistics of future observations; this occupies the broad claim “make recurrent states explicitly predictive.” [Venkatraman et al., NeurIPS 2017](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/file/61b4a64be663682e8cb037d9719ad8cd-Paper.pdf). Spectral initialization plus gradient refinement and predictive-state policy networks are additional direct lineages; generic PSR+RNN, PSR+deep encoder, PSR+planning, or predictive-state auxiliary supervision must not be promoted as new.
- **Current best assessment.** The central idea “represent state as predictions of future observations” is already a coherent theory, with theory, learning algorithms, continuous extensions, nonlinear inference predictors, planning, and RNN hybrids. Remaining value is a careful engineering/application question: can a calibrated predictive state be discovered and maintained online from high-dimensional, shifting sensorimotor streams without either oracle core tests or an overlarge kernel basis? That is useful research but does not establish a new class. **Novelty confidence for PSR/OOM itself: 0/5; confidence that a broad PSR-neural hybrid is new: 0/5.**
- **Small falsifiable revival experiment (planned, CPU; not run).** Use the small Tiger POMDP or a three-state controlled POMDP with aliased observations and a hidden state that must be remembered through uninformative steps. Generate action-balanced trajectories at several data budgets. Compare a linear PSR with manually chosen core tests, an automatically discovered core-test PSR, a PSRNN initialized by two-stage regression and refined by BPTT, a matched GRU, and an exact Bayesian filter oracle. Evaluate held-out multi-step action-conditioned Brier/calibration error, invalid-probability rate, sample count and closed-loop reward under the same small planner. The specialist-revival claim is falsified if the PSR variants fail to improve calibration or reward per data/parameter budget over the GRU, or if apparent gains require oracle tests that discovery cannot recover. This is a replication/utility test, not a novelty prototype.

#### HY-66 — Predictive-state operators × recurrent neural updates (reject as new hybrid)

- **Source architectures.** OOM/PSR contributes a state with explicit future-test semantics and statistically structured updates. A recurrent neural model contributes flexible nonlinear state transitions and gradient-based fitting.
- **Exact coupling.** PSRNN uses bilinear tensor contractions over the current predictive state and observation to implement an observation-conditioned update; principled two-stage-regression initialization is refined by BPTT, with optional tensor factorization. Predictive-State Decoders instead attach a learned auxiliary future-statistic decoder to a regular RNN objective. These are two materially different couplings, and both have primary-paper precedents.
- **Why the interaction can matter.** In PSRNN, future-observation semantics shape the state, while learned multiplicative updates give nonlinear expressivity. In PSD, predictive supervision pressures an otherwise opaque hidden state to preserve future-relevant information. The interaction changes the update/objective, rather than merely placing a PSR beside a GRU.
- **Prior-art verdict.** Reject the general hybrid claim: the exact bilinear PSRNN mechanism and the recurrent predictive-state auxiliary-loss mechanism are published and source-checked. Continuous-kernel PSRs and PSIM also occupy nonlinear-observation and direct-inference-learning directions. A remaining paper could compare reliability/calibration under distribution shift, but adding attention, a vision encoder, extra future horizons, or uncertainty gating does not by itself make a new architecture. [PSRNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.09353), [Predictive-State Decoders](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/file/61b4a64be663682e8cb037d9719ad8cd-Paper.pdf), [PSIM](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v48/sun16.html).
- **Weaknesses and falsifier.** PSRNN’s continuous-case consistency caveat, sensitivity to test/state dimension and scarce event coverage, and the cost of BPTT remain; PSD can become ordinary auxiliary prediction if test horizons provide weak evidence about useful hidden state. A fair replication on controlled POMDPs should compare the direct hybrid, an auxiliary-loss GRU, a standard GRU, linear PSR, and exact filtering; match parameters/data/optimizer steps and report calibration and reward. Reject the mechanism-specific advantage if predictive-state grounding does not improve calibration or control at equal resources, or if the gains disappear when test selection is learned rather than supplied.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Error-correcting neural computation (AR-84; C007 follow-up)

**Status:** the broad Error-Correcting Belief Code candidate is rejected as an architecture claim. Coding-theoretic protection is established at the representation, network-training, and hardware-dataflow levels. The proposed use of codewords for belief states is also underspecified: a syndrome can detect departures from a codebook, but does not establish whether a codeword is semantically true or whether the represented belief is calibrated.

- **Original computation and historical limits.** Judd and Munro (NeurIPS 1992) showed that injecting random hidden-unit errors during backpropagation can spread internal representations apart and improve resistance to misfiring or permanently failed nodes. This directly precedes the proposal to make intermediate representations redundant and fault tolerant. The likely cost was representation capacity/accuracy under reliable hardware, not just weak compute; their result is about robustness to unreliable units, not general uncertainty reasoning. [Judd & Munro (1992)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/1992/hash/c361bc7b2c033a83d663b8d9fb4be56e-Abstract.html)
- **Direct modernizations and prior art.** Later work is not limited to output labels: coded DNN approaches protect intermediate activations from erasures, while COLA combines ECOC with separated output paths and orthogonalized internal features to reduce correlated hardware errors. Zlokapa et al. construct a universal fault-tolerant neural network from biological grid-cell error-correcting codes, with a reliability threshold under neuron faults. Analog DNN work applies redundant residue number systems in the dataflow and trains in that coded arithmetic, including forward and backward operations. FPGA work combines SECDED and learned fault tolerance. These results occupy fault correction inside neural computation and show that modern accelerator/noisy-device constraints have already revived the subject. [Coded DNNs for Robust Neural Computation (NVMW 2020)](https://nvmw.ucsd.edu/nvmw2020-program/unzip/current3/nvmw2020-final23.pdf); [Zlokapa et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12887); [COLA (ICML 2023)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/yu23a.html); [fault-tolerant analog neural networks (2024)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-49324-8); [SECDED-protected FPGA MLP (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2012.07.001).
- **What could still be distinct, and why it currently fails.** A precise code-preserving algebra for multi-step relational belief operations could in principle go beyond ECOC labels or noisy arithmetic. But the candidate gives no operation family, code construction, or proof that learned updates preserve distance/correction radius. General nonlinear transformations do not preserve a codebook; re-encoding after each transformation adds compute and can hide rather than correct semantic error. Existing error-correcting neural representations and intermediate activation coding make “apply syndrome checks at every composed step” too broad to claim as new. No source checked here establishes the exact relational-algebra variant as a standardized class, but absence in this bounded search is not positive novelty evidence. **Novelty confidence: 0/5 for broad C007; 1/5 for an unformalized operation-preserving relational-code seam.**
- **Decision and falsifier.** Do not run or promote the previous C007 prototype as a novel architecture: a fair comparison would have to specify the algebra and coding theorem first. If that specification is later produced, the smallest useful test is a multistep relational-query toy under injected bit flips/erasures, comparing an operation-closed code, ordinary redundant activations, HDC/VSA, and noise-trained MLP at equal redundancy and compute. Falsify the proposed advantage if the code’s correction radius is lost after one operation, if re-encoding cost erases the gain, or if it does not improve exact answer recovery over these baselines. This is a gate for a future method study, not an experiment run now.

#### HY-67 — Error-correcting state code × compositional belief operations (reject as new hybrid)

- **Source mechanisms and proposed coupling.** The candidate combined error-correcting representations with iterative relational or belief updates. The interesting coupling would require operations to act on encoded states while producing locally checkable syndromes, with a demonstrated guarantee that each operation preserves or predictably changes the code distance. Merely encoding activations and decoding after a layer is already represented by fault-tolerant DNN and hardware-dataflow work.
- **Prior-art and mechanism audit.** Direct prior art spans noise-trained distributed codes in hidden layers (1992), coded intermediate activations (2020), neural computation from biological codes with a fault threshold (2022), and learning/error coding for accelerator defects (COLA 2023 and RNS-coded analog DNNs 2024). The 2013 FPGA MLP adds SECDED. The proposed relational operation closure is the only plausible residue, but C007 did not supply a closed operation set, a code family, or a new learning rule. Therefore this is not promoted. A new name for “coded states plus operations” would be terminology, not a distinct hybrid.
- **Smallest disproof experiment if formalized later.** Measure end-to-end exact recovery through 1, 2, 4, and 8 relational operations with calibrated flips/erasures; report code rate, syndrome/decode operations, latency, and error propagation against equal-rate repetition, HDC, and noise-trained MLP. Drop the mechanism if protection collapses with depth, if the decode overhead dominates, or if equal-rate baselines match it.

#### AR-84 correction — encoded computations already preserve checks through operations

A further source check sharpened the C007 verdict. Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (Huang & Abraham, IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1984) explicitly encodes matrix-level data, redesigns algorithms to operate on encoded inputs and produce encoded outputs, and demonstrates checksum preservation for addition, multiplication, scalar products, LU decomposition, and transpose. Its full checksum matrices have distance four and permit single-element error correction. This is a direct predecessor to “operations act on coded intermediate states while checks diagnose faults”; the claim that code-preserving operation is a novel ingredient is therefore false in the arithmetic domain. The remaining distinction would have to be semantically learned operators over belief/relation states with guarantees stronger than algorithm-specific checksum closure. [Huang & Abraham, Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance for Matrix Operations (1984)](https://people.bordeaux.inria.fr/gaupy/ressources/teachings/2019/algo_hpc/articles-2019/abft.pdf).

The agent audit also verified that Zlokapa et al. do more than store a redundant state: their construction interleaves decoder/error-correction and encoder/logical activations to implement universal Boolean computation below a neuron-noise threshold. This is still a designed fault-tolerant gate construction, not learned belief semantics, but it narrows the gap further. A neural associative-memory plus expander-code decoder provides another direct noisy-recall baseline. [Zlokapa et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12887); [Mazumdar & Rawat (AAAI 2017)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/download/10515/10374). The cheap toy should not be run until a learned semantic algebra is specified; a toy where XOR preserves a linear code would only demonstrate a known closure fact.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — incremental consequences and learned communication budgets (AR-85)

**Status:** C020 and C014 remain useful engineering questions, not new architecture classes. This follow-up compares their computational primitives against older symbolic/control work and modern learned descendants.

- **C020 / Predictive Delta Ledger.** Doyle’s Truth Maintenance System (TMS) (IJCAI 1977; expanded 1979) records justifications for beliefs and incrementally changes supported conclusions when assumptions are retracted or contradictions discovered. This is close historical prior art for a persistent consequence ledger. [Doyle (1977), IJCAI](https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/77-1/Papers/035.pdf); [Doyle (1979), TMS](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(79)90008-0). Modern self-adjusting computation gives a formal semantics integrating memoized reuse and change propagation, and Differential Dataflow extends incremental computation to nested iteration while retaining update histories and reusing unaffected regions. [Acar et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.0478); [McSherry et al. (CIDR 2013)](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2013/Papers/CIDR13_Paper111.pdf).
- **Neural reuse directly occupies the broad hybrid.** Incrementally-Computable Neural Networks discretize intermediate values with vector quantization so edits do not unnecessarily invalidate unchanged hidden computations; the paper reports OPT-125M document classification with comparable accuracy and 12.1× fewer median operations on atomic edits. Thus the generic hybrid “persistent neural conclusions + delta-only recomputation” already has a close modern architecture. [Sharir & Anandkumar (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.14988). A 2014 incremental causal-network construction also learns causal event links online, though causal edges are not justification-validity edges. [Acharya & Lee (2014)](https://bslee.w3.uvm.edu/papers/ICNC_published.pdf).
- **Historical explanation.** Memory capacity and compute were real costs for early truth maintenance and production-rule systems, and modern storage/incremental dataflow improve throughput. But the core difficulties are semantic and algorithmic: alternative justifications, cycles, negation, unseen conditional branches, and correctness under retraction. Hardware cannot make a learned correlation edge a sound dependency. GPU/AD acceleration may help learn update hints; it cannot replace a conservative validity proof. The exact learned-edge plus audited invalidation conjunction remains only an integration hypothesis, very low novelty, and must beat both a TMS-style explicit graph and modern incremental neural baselines.
- **C014 / Communication-Budget Machine.** Communication complexity and rate-distortion already define the bit-versus-task-quality problem. Learned message content, recipients, timing, and bandwidth constraints are also directly established: TarMAC learns message contents and recipients with multi-round communication; ETCNet translates limited bandwidth into a penalty threshold and learns event-triggered send decisions under a constrained MDP. Communication-limited control predates deep learning, while modern RL/AD makes protocol and scheduler learning practical. These sources close the broad architecture/hybrid claim. [Yao, communication complexity (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1145/800135.804414); [TarMAC (ICML 2019)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/das19a/das19a.pdf); [ETCNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.04978); [Kesper et al., learned event-triggered communication/control (2023)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v211/kesper23a/kesper23a.pdf).
- **Potential residue for C014.** A shared scheduler could price bits by calibrated counterfactual downstream value while tracking receiver-side cached-message age and learning when stale state remains valid under topology shift. This is narrower than rate-distortion, learned message gating, or learned scheduling, all of which already exist. Do not call it new unless a targeted search finds no such value-of-information/cached-state combination and a controlled experiment shows transfer to unseen team sizes and network failures at exactly matched realized bit/latency budgets.

#### HY-68 — learned semantic dependency graph × truth-maintenance / incremental neural computation (demote)

- **Sources and coupling.** The proposed system learns dependency links among opaque model-derived claims, then uses edits and corrections to invalidate only a dependent slice, with a conservative audit before reusing cached answers. TMS provides explicit justifications and assumption retraction; self-adjusting computation and Differential Dataflow provide dependency-aware incremental propagation; Incrementally-Computable Neural Networks reuse neural work after atomic input edits.
- **Decision.** The broad combination is occupied. The narrow residual is learning the *validity* of semantic dependencies between opaque conclusions from counterfactual corrections, then selectively invalidating neural-derived claims while proving stale answers cannot pass. No exact direct paper was confirmed for this full conjunction, but the novelty confidence is very low because its pieces and neighboring combinations are established. Keep as a correctness/economics question only.
- **Small falsifier if revisited.** Reuse C020’s mutable-world protocol but include full recomputation, oracle graph, TMS, Differential Dataflow/DRed, and Incrementally-Computable Neural Networks as baselines. Include unseen branches, negation, alternate supports, and cycles; require zero unflagged stale outputs. Reject if audit/fallback cost removes speedup or if explicit incremental baselines dominate at equal correctness.

#### HY-69 — event-triggered control × learned bandwidth-limited message protocols (reject as broad hybrid)

- **Sources and coupling.** Event-triggered control schedules communication/computation when state changes justify it. Multi-agent learned protocols already train message content, addressing, and send gates; ETCNet directly learns when to send under bandwidth limits, and later work learns communication options jointly with distributed control.
- **Decision.** The proposed generic pairing is not new: the interaction changes message timing and control, but that is precisely the established problem setting. A possible value-of-information scheduler that accounts for cached receiver state, counterfactual action value, delayed/drop messages, and transfer to unseen network topologies is only a specification gap, not a novelty claim.
