#### CAA archival follow-up — primary record still missing, Q-table lineage is clear (AR-65 supplement)

The independent source hunt found bibliographic confirmation of Bozinovski's 1981 UMass internal report, *A self-learning system using secondary reinforcement*, and the 1982 chapter of the same title, but did not recover either full original. The UMass Autonomous Learning Lab archive lists the 1982 chapter; the author's official bibliography independently lists it. Later accounts reconstruct CAA as a state-by-action crossbar: select from action preferences at the current state, evaluate the successor state using shared matrix values, and use that value as secondary reinforcement for the preceding state-action choice. The initial state-valence associations come from a “genetic environment,” so the reward-free label must not be read as absence of an inherited evaluative prior. The same author describes the later Q-method as a variant of the CAA procedure. This makes the useful historical point a precursor tabular value-learning lineage, not a new model class. Exact original rules remain unverified until the 1981/82 primary text is recovered. [UMass historical bibliography](https://all.cs.umass.edu/legacy/comp.html), [author bibliography](https://www.scsu.edu/faculty/stevo_bozinovski.php), [later technical retrospective](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2018.11.017).

#### CPN archaeology follow-up — Grossberg's earlier instar–outstar map is the nearest origin (AR-92 supplement)

The exact CPN rule is prototype competition plus supervised associative output learning: normalize input/prototype vectors, select the most similar Kohonen unit, move its vector toward the input, and move the corresponding Grossberg outstar weights toward the simultaneously presented target. At inference the winner selects a prototype output; allowing several winners yields a weighted smoother estimate. A primary-lineage check finds that Grossberg had already combined instar recognition and outstar output learning in a three-layer input-to-output mapping network in 1976; Hecht-Nielsen's 1987 contribution named and popularized the counterpropagation family. Thus novelty is even lower than a simple SOM-plus-readout formulation suggests. Later work includes CPN applications and modified variants; a 2007 open account calls it a stochastic estimator and documents its normalized, sequential update procedure. Modern prototype/RBF/local models subsume the useful function. [Grossberg's instar/outstar lineage](https://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Recurrent_neural_networks), [Hecht-Nielsen 1987 record](https://opg.optica.org/ao/abstract.cfm?uri=ao-26-23-4979), [detailed 2007 algorithm exposition](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2006WR005509).

#### Old-architecture archaeology — MOSAIC paired predictors/controllers (AR-93)

- **Original computation.** MOSAIC (Modular Selection and Identification for Control) keeps multiple modules, each pairing a forward model with an inverse controller. A forward unit predicts the next state from current state and motor command. The paired inverse unit proposes a command for the desired next state. A module responsibility combines a prior learned from contextual sensory cues with a likelihood from forward prediction error. That same responsibility weights controller outputs and gates learning in both members of the pair. Thus prediction errors partition experience, select policies, and assign credit to module-local learning; this is more specific than merely routing among independent experts. [Wolpert & Kawato (1998), primary paper](https://bicr.atr.jp/~kawato/Ppdf/1217.pdf), [Haruno, Wolpert & Kawato (2001)](https://wolpertlab.neuroscience.columbia.edu/sites/default/files/content/papers/HarWolKaw01.pdf).
- **Unit, information, inputs, and output.** The unit is a predictor-controller pair specialized to some region of contextual dynamics. It represents a local action-to-state model and its inverse policy. It receives state, efference copy/action, desired state, and contextual sensors; outputs are predicted state, responsibility, and a responsibility-weighted motor command. Knowledge lives in forward/inverse parameters and a responsibility predictor. Learning is online from action outcomes: forward models learn prediction, inverse models receive gated motor-learning signals, and the context predictor learns to anticipate posterior responsibility.
- **Why it struggled and what changed.** A single controller must fit many context-dependent dynamics; modularity protects old skills and lets multiple skills combine. The hard parts were discovering the right module count and partition, learning inverse models, and handling noisy or partially observed sensors. These were not only compute limitations. eMOSAIC directly added module-specific state estimators for noisy/partially observed settings and demonstrated squatting and object-carrying on a real humanoid in 2012. Modern GPUs, simulators, learned vision encoders, and robot logs improve scale and sensory inputs, but the core predictor-conditioned controller mixture is already a mature control architecture; mixture-of-experts, adaptive multiple-model control, hierarchical MOSAIC, and reinforcement-learning MOSAIC cover close variants. [Sugimoto et al. (2012), eMOSAIC](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2012.01.002).
- **Verdict and smallest falsifier.** Worth retaining as a specialist old architecture and a strong controller baseline; broad model-class novelty 0/5. It may outperform an uncoupled gate when feedback reveals a context that was misleading before action, because its prediction likelihood can revise the context prior and direct credit to the responsible module. Falsify that specific utility if a matched predictive mixture-of-experts or shared contextual controller matches switching regret, few-shot recovery, prior-skill retention, and OOD composition at equal parameters and rollout budget. A cheap CPU test uses a two-link reaching plant with abrupt friction/object-mass switches, deceptive visual context, and delayed/noisy feedback; compare faithful MOSAIC, predictive MoE without paired inverse learning, shared controller, and MPC. No experiment run.

#### CAA mechanism clarification — one shared crossbar carries both action preference and consequence valence

The author's 2014 reconstruction supplies more precise rules than the earlier short note. Given a one-hot current state, action selection scores each action from the corresponding crossbar row plus exploration noise. After the transition, the successor state's “emotion” is thresholded from its weighted action values, with its initial valence/thresholds inherited from the genetic environment. The selected weight connecting the previous state to the chosen action is then updated by this successor emotion; in the author's notation, the single crossbar rule is w[a,j](t) = w[a,j](t-1) + x[j](t-1)y[a](t-1)v(t). There is no separate critic table in the described CAA procedure: the action-preference matrix is also reused to compute consequence-state valence. Memory can be exported as a chromosome after learning, a Lamarckian inheritance proposal. This is a more distinctive compact RL implementation than generic “emotion gating,” but it remains a tabular action/state controller whose initial valence is provided externally by an evolved prior; the paper is a retrospective, not the missing 1981 memo. The author's 2014 account reports maze and simplified cart-pole demonstrations, but its cart-pole representation uses ten CAA states and a ternary force set, versus 162 states in the compared ASE/ACE setup, so do not infer matched general control superiority. [Bozinovski, “Modeling Mechanisms of Cognition-Emotion Interaction in Artificial Neural Networks, since 1981” (2014 retrospective)](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/275541379_Modeling_Mechanisms_of_Cognition-emotion_Interaction_in_Artificial_Neural_Networks_since_1981).



#### AR-24 primary-source and prior-art follow-up — feature growth was proposed, not demonstrated (2026-09-27)

The full 1959 Selfridge paper confirms several boundaries worth keeping explicit. The hierarchy's cognitive and data levels are specified by the task; designers choose a vocabulary of plausible computational subdemons and then hill-climb class-specific evidence weights. Mutated fission and conjugation are proposed mechanisms for generating replacement subdemons, but the paper does not report a completed evaluation of that full growth loop: Selfridge says he could not be sure how much of the Morse program would have been run, and only fair tests of the hill-climbing procedures had taken place at the time of writing. His tentative self-monitoring signal is a strong winning margin after prior supervised training, not an autonomous validation mechanism. The system ran on an IBM 704. Modern compute can cheapen parallel scoring but cannot be credited with reviving an experimentally validated open-ended feature learner. [Selfridge, primary 1959 text](https://gwern.net/doc/ai/nn/1959-selfridge.pdf).

The residual is already occupied at several useful levels. Uhr and Vossler's 1961 pattern recognizer explicitly starts without a fixed operator set, generates and refines operators based on problem-space behavior and success/failure, and constructs a secondary code; that predates the proposed “new operators from residuals” seam. Smieja's 1996 reflective MINOS implementation directly modernizes Pandemonium with neural workers/monitors, backpropagation and automatic input-space modularization; it reports gains on discontinuous functions and two spirals, but limited advantage for parity and OCR, demonstrating that modularity's payoff is task-dependent. AKIRA later combines a Pandemonium daemon kernel, limited shared energy, a blackboard and BDI-style mechanisms, so “add shared-workspace coordination/resources” is also established. These papers do not prove every possible feature-growth rule, but they reject the broad architecture and hybrid claims. [Uhr & Vossler (1961)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1460690.1460751), [Smieja (1996)](https://doi.org/10.1109/72.478395), [Calvi & Pezzulo, Designing Modular Architectures in AKIRA](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=622f08d2626ca985c230b68d0dedcbabfcc6bfc7&repid=rep1&type=pdf).

**Decision:** keep AR-24 and HY-27 as archaeology/method comparisons only. There is no new model-class candidate. Any future CPU revival should compare a faithful task-defined Pandemonium, including its bounded growth operations, against Smieja-style learned modularization and a modern fixed-feature control at matched feature-evaluation, memory and label budgets. A win would be a narrow continual-feature-construction result, not evidence that the broad Pandemonium architecture is novel. Confidence in broad novelty remains **0/5**.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — morphological neural computation (AR-94)

- **Name and computational primitive.** “Morphological network” refers to related but distinct models, so do not collapse them into one algorithm. One line learns image structuring elements with hit/miss-style operations; another replaces ordinary weighted-sum aggregation by lattice operations, chiefly dilation/max-plus or erosion/min-plus. A representative morphological neuron computes a maximum or minimum of input-plus-weight terms, followed by any threshold/activation; morphological associative memories use max/min algebra to store or complete patterns. [Ritter & Sussner, An Introduction to Morphological Neural Networks (1996)](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/3660348_An_introduction_to_morphological_neural_networks), [Ritter, Sussner & Díaz-de-León, Morphological Associative Memories (1998)](https://doi.org/10.1109/72.661123), [Wilson, Training Structuring Elements in Morphological Networks](https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781482277234_A35619877/preview-9781482277234_A35619877.pdf).
- **Represented information, repeated operation, input and output.** Weights or structuring elements encode order-sensitive shape templates or extrema over feature values. For dilation, a unit can be written y_i = max_j(x_j + w_ij); erosion uses a corresponding min-plus form. Repeating layers composes these extrema maps; a memory version retrieves a stored pattern by a max/min projection. Input can be a binary/grayscale image or an ordered feature vector; output is a transformed feature map, label score or recalled pattern. The basic operation is a parallel reduction, but only winning term(s) dominate each local gradient.
- **Learning, inference and memory.** Historical variants use constructive or heuristic structuring-element learning and one-shot memory construction; modern discriminative versions use subgradients or smooth approximations to fit layers end to end. Inference is a feed-forward sequence of max/min reductions. Knowledge resides in weights, structuring elements and (for associative memory) stored templates. Modern GPU reductions, automatic differentiation and larger data make implementations and deeper compositions easier. Max/min kinks are not a fatal differentiability barrier: the operations are differentiable almost everywhere, with standard subgradient handling.
- **Was it bad, early, or both?** This was not primarily a promising general intelligence design defeated by 1980s compute. The primitive can be a good fit for geometric/shape structure and offers simple lattice-algebraic behavior, but its inductive bias depends on a useful ordering of features; extrema aggregate information very differently from averaging dot products, and gradients can be sparse when only a few extrema win. Increased compute does not fix a poor order structure or guarantee broad sample efficiency. Original memory-capacity results concern exact recall under stated assumptions, not unlimited robustness to arbitrary corruption or a universal long-term memory.
- **Modernization and closest prior art.** The family is already directly modernized: Deep Morphological Neural Networks train exact morphological operators in a deep-learning setting; the 2019 Morphological Network: How Far Can We Go with Morphological Neurons? studies representational and evaluation properties; later smooth morphological layers, binary morphology networks and min-max-plus networks address optimization or broader approximation. The last family stacks linear, min-plus and max-plus layers and supplies trainable parameters plus a universal-approximation result. That establishes capacity, not practical superiority. A Google system also called “MorphNet” is a separate resource-constrained channel-pruning method and should not be confused with morphological neural networks. [Deep Morphological Neural Networks (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.01532), [Charisopoulos & Maragos (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.00109), [Min-Max-Plus Neural Networks (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.06358).
- **Use cases, possible advantage and failure modes.** Plausible uses include shape-sensitive vision, binary morphology, template completion, monotone/extrema-structured signals and max-plus timing/path computations. At matched parameter or label budget it might outperform a conventional convolutional feature learner where the target is explicitly compositional in erosions/dilations, or when a small structured memory is preferable to retraining a deep feature bank. Likely failures are extrema sensitivity to outliers, dead/sparse gradients, poor performance when no meaningful feature order exists, and comparisons that accidentally favor it with task-matched templates. It is a specialized primitive, not a new general model class.
- **Novelty judgment.** Reject a broad morphological neural architecture candidate and any generic morphology-plus-CNN or max-plus timed-event hybrid. The operators, end-to-end training, hybrid convolution layers, associative memories and trainable max-plus networks all have direct prior work. What remains potentially useful is only a domain-specific matched-budget evaluation, not an identified novel coupling. Novelty confidence: **0/5**.
- **Small falsifier if the utility question is pursued.** CPU-only synthetic 32×32 binary shapes composed from branches, holes, erosion/dilation, occlusion and texture distractors; hold out combinations rather than random instances. Compare an exact morphological network, mixed morphology/convolution model and compact CNN at matched training examples, parameters and inference-operation budget. Measure held-out-composition accuracy, corruption robustness, label efficiency, inference cost and performance across multiple seeds. The structural-bias claim fails if morphology helps only on nearly duplicated templates or does not beat the matched CNN on held-out combinations. This tests a narrow use case, not novelty; no experiment run.

#### Associative-memory archaeology supplement — Kosko’s bidirectional associative memory (no new AR number)

The source check confirms a small descriptive gap, not a candidate gap. Kosko’s 1987 adaptive BAM has two neuron fields A and B connected by one n-by-p matrix M. A state in field A activates B through M; B feeds back to A through the transpose Mᵀ. The fields alternately update until the pair reaches a stable energy minimum. Stored long-term memory is the cross-field matrix, and paired patterns (Aᵢ,Bᵢ) can be queried from either side. The adaptive version uses correlation/Hebbian-style local updates; the paper also proposes “sampling adaptive” learning in which many examples are shown briefly without waiting for full convergence, allowing a noisy association or simple continuous mapping to emerge from the sample stream. This is hetero-associative recurrent completion, distinct from a single-field Hopfield autoassociator in its paired-state semantics, but closely related to the notebook's Hopfield/associative-memory coverage and modern key-value retrieval. [Kosko, Adaptive Bidirectional Associative Memories (1987), primary paper](https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.26.004947); [Kosko, Bidirectional Associative Memories (1988)](https://sipi.usc.edu/~kosko/BAM.pdf).

**Disposition:** keep as a brief historical cross-reference only. Paired associative recall, iterative settling, and correlation-based learning are established; the main unresolved questions are crosstalk, spurious stable pairs, correlated-pattern capacity, and settling cost, none of which is removed merely by more compute. A potential utility comparison would test two-way retrieval from partial/noisy cues against a modern explicit key-value memory under matched storage and update budgets, measuring completion, false pairings and latency. That is a reproduction/application study, not architecture novelty; no experiment run.


#### Old-architecture archaeology — Associative Search Network (AR-95)

- **Original computation.** Barto, Sutton, and Brouwer's 1981 Associative Search Network (ASN) is a connectionist memory whose job is to discover which output pattern should be associated with each input key. The environment supplies a real-valued context vector, the network emits a binary action/output vector, and an external scalar payoff evaluates it. Stochastic associative-search elements adjust their input-output associations so that repeated contexts increasingly elicit high-payoff outputs. The paper combines pattern recognition (associate keys with outputs) and stochastic function optimization (search for rewarding outputs); its stated problem gives payoff after an action, rather than a transition-value bootstrapping rule. The companion Landmark Learning paper instantiates this as spatial movement along odor gradients. [Barto, Sutton & Brouwer (1981), primary paper and UMass-hosted PDF](https://all.cs.umass.edu/pubs/before_94/BiolCyb40-1981.pdf); [Barto & Sutton (1981), primary companion paper](https://all.cs.umass.edu/pubs/before_94/barto_81.pdf); [UMass publication record](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~barto/pubs-Barto.html).
- **Unit, information, input/output, and learning.** A unit is a stochastic associative-search element with context-conditioned weights and stochastic output. The network represents context-to-action associations, with action patterns distributed over adaptive elements rather than stored as an explicit table of optimal responses. At each interaction it receives the context, samples an output pattern, acts, and receives scalar feedback; learning changes the association so that better-scoring outputs become more likely on recurrence. The inference mechanism is one forward policy response under stochastic exploration. There is no separate successor-state value model in the original associative-search formulation. The memory is the learned associative weights; learning and inference are interleaved.
- **Was it bad or early?** It was neither a failed general architecture nor simply a technology waiting for GPUs. ASN defined a useful contextual search problem, and the family was developed into associative stochastic learning automata, multilayer reinforcement-trained feature mappings, actor-critic, and policy-gradient methods. The 1982 layered associative-search network already used a first layer to adaptively construct a representation and a second layer to solve the task linearly. Williams's 1992 REINFORCE paper gives a general gradient-following class for stochastic connectionist units and explicitly integrates it with backpropagation. These sources close generic claims that scalar-reward associative search, neural policy perturbation, or reinforcement-trained feature construction would now be a new architecture. [Barto, Anderson & Sutton (1982), publisher/PubMed record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7093360/); [Williams (1992), author-hosted paper](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~barto/courses/cs687/williams92simple.pdf); [Williams (1992), Springer record](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00992696).
- **What changed, and what did not.** GPUs, automatic differentiation, modern perception encoders, and simulators can make the context space richer, reduce hand-built features, and provide many cheap trials. They do not remove the estimator variance of reward-only search, the need to explore informative alternatives, or the need for temporal credit assignment on long-horizon tasks. Those changes yield modern neural contextual-bandit/policy-gradient systems rather than a distinct revival of the original ASN. The historical weak point is task scope and learning signal structure, not just slow 1981 hardware.
- **Closest work, possible use, and novelty.** The nearest lineage is associative stochastic learning automata / ASE, associative reward-penalty networks, REINFORCE, and current policy-gradient/contextual-bandit learning. A compact local associative policy might still be a useful baseline for sparse-action robotics or low-data per-context adaptation, but its mechanism is not broadly new. **Disposition: archaeology and baseline only; no candidate promotion; novelty confidence 0/5.** The original paper claims solvability under specified conditions, not a universally scaling intelligent system. No claim of influence from ASN to CAA is supported by the checked sources.
- **CAA comparison and priority boundary.** ASN is firm 1981 primary-source evidence that connectionist action associations could be optimized from scalar payoff without a teacher specifying the correct action pattern. It therefore makes an unqualified claim that the CAA was “the first connectionist reinforcement learner” unsafe. The mechanisms are not identical: later author descriptions of CAA give a state-by-action crossbar whose shared entries select actions and estimate successor-state desirability, then feed that valence back as secondary reinforcement; ASN's published formulation performs stochastic payoff search for a context-to-output association and does not describe that shared bootstrapped successor-state computation. Both are dated 1981 and the CAA original memo/chapter remains unavailable, so chronology, priority, and independence cannot be resolved from the inspected records. Treat the claimed delayed-credit mechanism as retrospectively described, not verified against the original CAA. [Bozinovski et al. (1996), author follow-up describing the four-step CAA rule](https://www.ed.aaai.org/Papers/Symposia/Fall/1996/FS-96-02/FS96-02-003.pdf); [UMass bibliography for the 1982 chapter](https://all.cs.umass.edu/legacy/comp.html); [Finnish National Library physical catalog record](https://kansalliskirjasto.finna.fi/Record/fikka.20355); [Indiana University physical catalog record](https://iucat.iu.edu/iub/1673049).
- **Small falsifiable reproduction.** On CPU, implement the faithful stochastic associative-search element on a contextual bandit with repeated contexts and scalar payoff, then add a compositional context split and a held-out context combination. Compare the original element, an equal-parameter softmax REINFORCE policy, and a simple value-based contextual-bandit baseline under identical feedback and trial budgets. Measure regret, reward-estimate variance, generalization to held-out combinations, and sensitivity to rare contexts over at least 20 seeds. The claim that the original mechanism offers a useful low-data/generalization advantage fails if it does not improve regret or held-out context performance at equal parameters and interactions. This is a replication/benchmark, not a novelty experiment; it is low priority.
- **Potential ASN × CAA hybrid audit (HY-91; reject).** One could let ASN provide stochastic context-conditioned action proposals while reusing the CAA crossbar's successor-state value as a baseline/secondary reinforcement signal for those proposals. The units contribute policy exploration; the crossbar contributes bootstrapped consequence evaluation. But this is the standard actor-plus-critic division: Barto, Sutton & Anderson's 1983 adaptive search element/adaptive critic work already couples a stochastic policy with a learned reward evaluator, while Williams's REINFORCE paper establishes the broader gradient-following family for stochastic connectionist policies. The coupling does not create a new computation schedule or memory semantics, and the two source mechanisms are already close relatives rather than complementary architecture classes. Reject as a new hybrid (novelty 0/5); only compare as an actor-critic reproduction if useful. [Barto, Sutton & Anderson (1983), journal record](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSMC.1983.6313077); [Williams (1992)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00992696).

#### Old-architecture archaeology — connectionist internal models and latent learning (AR-96)

- **Original computation.** Sutton and Barto's 1981 paper presents an adaptive network that learns an internal model in a simplified analogue of a latent-learning maze task. An agent can explore a maze before reward is available, then use acquired structure when a goal is introduced. The authors explicitly position it as a simulated proof of principle for model-dependent behavior such as latent learning and novel associative chains, not as a demonstrated general planner. [Sutton & Barto (1981), primary UMass-hosted paper](https://all.cs.umass.edu/pubs/before_94/CognitionBT-1981.pdf); [author publication page and abstract](https://incompleteideas.net/publications.html).
- **More explicit mechanism.** Sutton and Pinette's 1985 follow-up describes a recurrent network of simple neuron-like processing elements that learns observed stimulus-to-stimulus relationships. Its units predict future stimuli through multi-step chains of predictions. In a stochastic maze, the network learns the maze by wandering before reinforcement is introduced; later reward learning reaches a solution faster than without the exploration period. This makes the old mechanism more precise: predictive transition structure is acquired from observation, then re-used when reward makes a route valuable. [Sutton & Pinette (1985), primary archive copy and abstract](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/7j2202xq).
- **Unit, representation, learning and inference.** The computational units are recurrently connected adaptive predictors over stimulus features. Persistent knowledge is a learned predictive transition structure. During exploration, transitions are learned from stimulus succession without needing immediate external reward for each transition; at inference, the network composes learned transitions to anticipate outcomes and support choice. The early paper does not report a scalable general-purpose search algorithm or modern high-dimensional sensory encoder. The 1985 paper specifies a stochastic maze simulation and multiple-step stimulus prediction, not an explicit arbitrary continuous-state planner.
- **Was it bad or early?** Simulation cost and weak sensing limited the scale and realism of the tests; current compute, differentiable recurrent models, large-scale video/self-supervised prediction, and accurate simulators can train far richer predictive state models. But the basic coupling of learned dynamics with simulated planning is not waiting for modern compute: Sutton's Dyna architecture integrated real experience, an incrementally learned possibly incorrect world model, planning on that model, and reactive execution in 1990/91. Modern learned-model planning is also established: MuZero learns latent dynamics, reward, value, and policy quantities useful for search and combines that model with tree planning. Better hardware expands capacity; it does not make the broad mechanism new, and model error under imagined rollouts remains a central risk. [Sutton (1990), Dyna integrated architecture, ML Anthology/primary paper](https://mlanthology.org/icml/1990/sutton1990icml-integrated/); [Sutton (1991), Dyna DOI record](https://doi.org/10.1145/122344.122377); [Schrittwieser et al. (2020), MuZero, Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-03051-4).
- **Closest prior art and remaining distinction.** The 1985 multi-step recurrent stimulus predictor is a clear direct continuation of the 1981 paper; Dyna and later model-based RL occupy the interaction between learning from real data and planning on an internal model. MuZero demonstrates that modern systems may predict planning-relevant latent quantities rather than reconstruct every sensory detail. No distinct new architecture class remains in the broad internal-model claim. A narrower possible question is whether reward-free predictive exploration yields better revaluation after goal relocation under a matched transition-data budget; this is a cognitive/model-based RL utility question, not a novel class.
- **Small falsifiable reproduction.** On CPU, use a small stochastic maze with a reward-free exploration phase followed by goal placement or relocation. Compare a reactive stimulus-action association, a recurrent multi-step stimulus predictor inspired by Sutton–Pinette, and tabular Dyna-Q with the same exploratory transitions and state access. Measure model error, steps to goal after reward appears, transfer after goal relocation, and performance under blocked/changed corridors across 20 seeds. The proposed latent-learning utility fails if predictive pre-exposure gives no post-reward sample-efficiency gain over the reactive learner at equal exploration data, or if it loses to the Dyna baseline without a distinct compute or transfer advantage. No experiment run; this is a replication-quality falsifier, not a novelty test.
- **Disposition:** retain as an important early world-model/predictive-learning antecedent; broad candidate rejected (novelty 0/5). The idea was partly early in its sensory and simulation tools, but its computational premise has already been modernized. No exact 1981 implementation claim beyond what the accessible article/abstract supports.

#### Hybrid collision check — recurrent predictive model × modern planning (HY-92; reject as broad novelty)

A recurrent predictor that learns stimulus transitions from reward-free experience could be coupled to a planner that rolls the model forward when a goal or reward changes. The predictor supplies latent transitions; planning converts them into prospective action values and reuses exploration. This is a meaningful mechanism interaction, but the same core is already expressed by Sutton–Pinette's predictive chains, Dyna's alternating real/model experience and planning, and modern model-based RL including MuZero's learned model plus tree search. The older network may be a useful historical baseline for measuring latent-state/model quality, but replacing its units with modern encoders or adding a learned planner does not create a novel coupling. Reject the broad hybrid claim (novelty 0/5). A narrow test is the AR-96 goal-relocation experiment with model-based and reactive ablations; falsify utility if pretraining transitions does not improve rapid reward revaluation at matched transition data and planning budget.

#### C002/AR-97 prior-art follow-up — online and compositional Koopman models already occupy the open mechanism

C002's provisional remaining question was whether a learned observable dictionary could add, retire, and compose operators online as interventions exposed new dynamics. A current source pass materially narrows that gap:

- **Variable-object composition is already direct prior art.** Li et al.'s 2020 compositional Koopman model uses a graph encoder for object-centric embeddings and a block-wise linear transition operator shared across objects. The stated purpose is to generalize to variable object counts and adapt to new environments/unknown physical parameters; demonstrations include rope manipulation and soft robots. This directly occupies the idea of compositionally reusable operators for new physical arrangements. [Li et al., ICLR 2020 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08264); [authors' project page](https://koopman.csail.mit.edu/).
- **Parameter-conditioned operator families also exist.** Guo et al. jointly learn an invariant dictionary and a parametric family of projected Koopman operators for static or time-varying system parameters; the paper includes prediction and optimal-control results. Earlier parameter-varying Koopman work interpolates local lifted linear models as system parameters change. [Guo et al. (2023), primary preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01124); [Lee et al. (2023), Parameter-Varying Koopman Operator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10278).
- **Novelty-triggered streaming adaptation directly occupies online basis growth.** Loya and Tallapragada (2024) use a Grassmannian distance between observability subspaces to identify novel trajectory segments; novel segments enter an archive and trigger operator/basis updates, while redundant segments are discarded. This does not literally implement arbitrary symbolic birth/death of operator modules, but it closes the broad proposed mechanism of surprise/novelty-triggered online adaptation of Koopman basis capacity. [Loya & Tallapragada (2024), primary IFAC paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ifacol.2024.12.016); [open author-hosted copy at NSF PAR](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10621673).
- **Distribution-shift adaptation has become a strong contemporary baseline.** NeurIPS 2025 MetaKoopman learns a matrix-normal/inverse-Wishart prior over the operator and updates its posterior in closed form from recent trajectories, reporting calibration and adaptation results including a full-scale truck/trailer field evaluation. [MetaKoopman, NeurIPS 2025 proceedings](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/2a5dd6bad2d10966a8bfa254dfb7dc76-Abstract-Conference.html).
- **2026 work further closes generic online adaptation.** AdaKoop (submitted June 2026; arXiv lists KDD'26 acceptance) detects abrupt pattern switches by statistical tests, updates parameters incrementally for gradual change, and reports evaluation across 71 benchmark datasets. Meta-Adaptive Koopman Operators (MAKO, Automatica 2026) meta-learns an operator model across nonlinear parameter settings and adapts online to unseen settings; a separate 2026 deep time-varying Koopman paper explicitly incorporates iterative online model updates and forgetting of outdated data. [AdaKoop, arXiv:2606.04930](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04930); [MAKO, Automatica 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.automatica.2026.112827); [Deep Koopman iterative learning for time-varying systems, Automatica 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.automatica.2026.113054).

**Verdict.** C002 is a recognized operator-learning family, and its suggested additions—online adaptation, novelty-triggered archive updates, parameterized dynamics, composition across objects, and mode switching—are now represented directly. Modern compute was useful for higher-dimensional observation maps and broader evaluation, but it did not reveal a missing architecture class. Keep Koopman methods as structured-dynamics baselines; do not promote online dictionary growth as new.

**Narrow unresolved test, not a new class.** A small CPU study could ask whether an explicitly factorized operator predicts *unseen combinations of independently varied physical factors* (for example, mass and damping) better than monolithic parameter-conditioned models. Train only on single-factor changes and a subset of interactions; compare fixed EDMD, parameter-varying Koopman, compositional Koopman, and a learned parameter-conditioned operator at equal transition data and rollout budget. Measure multi-step error, calibration, closed-loop constraint violations, and recovery after a held-out combination appears online. Reject utility if factorized composition does not improve held-out combinations or if it gains only by storing a separate operator per combination. Existing compositional/parametric Koopman papers make this a low-priority replication/evaluation question, not an architecture novelty experiment. No experiment run.

#### C004/AR-98 prior-art follow-up — geodesic atlas is an established method family, not a new model class

C004 proposed a memory made of local charts, landmarks and tangent maps; repeated inference would route between charts and compose geodesic steps to produce a path, interpolation or local prediction. Its broad motivation was transfer over curved sensor, motion, chemistry or control spaces. A fuller prior-art search finds direct precedents at each central level, including chart construction, neural representations, downstream geometry, dynamics and control.

- **Adaptive chart construction predates the candidate.** Pitelis et al.'s *Learning a Manifold as an Atlas* (CVPR 2013) jointly optimizes continuous chart parameters and discrete data assignments. The method adjusts chart regions in response to local noise, curvature and sample sparsity; it is already more specific than “Isomap plus local patches.” [CVPR primary paper](https://www.cv-foundation.org/openaccess/content_cvpr_2013/papers/Pitelis_Learning_a_Manifold_2013_CVPR_paper.pdf).
- **Topology-aware chart growth and merge have been demonstrated.** Cohn, Devraj and Jenkins' *Topologically-Informed Atlas Learning* begins with small charts and merges them bottom-up only when doing so preserves topology. It was demonstrated on synthetic manifolds, motion-capture human motion and articulated-object kinematics. [ICRA author page and paper link](https://tommycohn.com/projects/tial.html); [arXiv preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00429).
- **Neural representation learning on atlases is known.** Korman's 2021 work adapts encoder output to chart-valued manifold representations and adds an MMD regularizer; it tests SimCLR and triplet metric learning, including low-dimensional embeddings. [Primary preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07062).
- **The 2026 direct differentiable-atlas proposal closes C004's downstream-operation gap.** Robinett et al.'s AISTATS 2026 paper supplies a data structure for a differentiable atlas, an unsupervised point-cloud atlas learner, and Riemannian optimization primitives. Its reported studies include a Klein-bottle classification problem and RNA-velocity analysis. This closely matches C004's chart memory plus geometric routing/operation concept, although it is a proof of concept in selected settings rather than a universal architecture. [AISTATS/PMLR primary paper](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v300/robinett26a.html); [full text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17772).
- **Chart-local learned dynamics are also direct precedent for an atlas/predictor hybrid.** Floryan and Graham's *Data-driven discovery of intrinsic dynamics* (Nature Machine Intelligence, 2022) learns an atlas autoencoder, models dynamics within each chart and switches chart coordinates through overlaps. It demonstrated low-dimensional models of high-dimensional nonlinear systems, including a reaction-diffusion system and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky dynamics. [Nature Machine Intelligence paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-022-00575-4). The 2020 *Neural Manifold Ordinary Differential Equations* paper separately integrates manifold geometry and continuous-time neural dynamics. [NeurIPS primary paper](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2020/hash/cbf8710b43df3f2c1553e649403426df-Abstract.html).
- **The “few-shot transfer” use case needs tighter accounting.** Geodesic shortest-path routing, manifold representation learning, metric learning, chart-transition computation and manifold planning each have established methods. A persistent landmark graph or a learned perception front end can be useful implementation choices, but neither changes the computation enough to support novelty. The most defensible surviving question would have to demonstrate a particular decision or intervention signal changing chart allocation in a way not reducible to known adaptive charts or transition-based state abstraction.

A recent arXiv proposal, *The Neural Differential Manifold* (submitted 2025), describes layers as charts, a learned local metric, and curvature/volume penalties. It does not report experiments in its nine-page text, labels its own curvature/volume terms heuristics, and leaves chart birth/merge or topology change for future work. Its proposed natural-gradient step also needs a clear mathematical map from the representation-space metric to the parameter-space Fisher matrix; the text states this relationship but does not establish it. Treat this as a public conceptual proposal, not as a validated empirical architecture or proof of novelty. Its existence further argues against novelty based on the phrase “neural manifold.” [arXiv record and text](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.25113v1).

**Decision:** reject C004 as a new architecture class. Its basic primitive is a recognized geometric representation and inference family; nearly every proposed sub-mechanism already has direct antecedents. A useful domain application may remain, but broad claims of few-shot generalization, topology preservation, persistent charts or geodesic reasoning are unsupported as novelty claims. Confidence that C004's broad mechanism is new: **0/5**. No experiment was run.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — explicit manifold representations for reinforcement learning (AR-99; 2004–2005)

This is an important older intersection of topology, local function approximation and reinforcement learning. It must be distinguished from later “latent manifold” methods: the 2004 system explicitly models the *task state's reachable topology* using chart domains, rather than discovering only a low-dimensional latent manifold from sensory samples.

1. **What it originally did.** Glaubius and Smart's 2004 method covers reachable state space with overlapping charts. Each chart has a local approximator; smooth blend functions combine them into a global action-value function. The paper updates chart-local functions with Q-learning and connects the representation to CMAC/tile coding. It emphasizes avoiding Euclidean generalization through an obstacle: states close in coordinates but separated by walls should not be treated as behaviorally close. Its chart-allocation strategies include random coverage, random-walk neighborhoods and a growth procedure based on transition-distance statistics. The 2005 follow-up reuses experience between regions judged similar from observed transition behavior. [Glaubius & Smart, AI&M 2004 primary paper](https://cdn.aaai.org/Workshops/2004/WS-04-08/WS04-08-003.pdf); [Glaubius, Namihira & Smart, 2005 author-uploaded workshop paper](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/247619823_Speeding_up_Reinforcement_Learning_using_Manifold_Representations_Preliminary_Results).
2. **Historical limitations.** The 2004 evaluation used simple WallWorld and Mountain Car tasks, constant or linear local approximators, and one million randomly selected state-action training pairs. The authors themselves restricted the formulation to off-policy value learning, arbitrary state/action sampling and one nonzero reward; policy quality was mainly illustrated rather than summarized by a robust aggregate score. Axis-aligned chart construction and hand-visible low-dimensional coordinates limit its reach. These are serious evaluation and representation constraints, not merely lack of GPU throughput.
3. **What changed technologically.** Modern simulators can cheaply provide transition samples and counterfactual action probes; neural encoders can handle visual state; differentiable chart maps and modern optimizers can train local models; replay and distributed data generation can improve coverage. These reduce perception, data collection and implementation costs. They do not guarantee that learned charts preserve the task's transition topology, that local value functions blend stably, or that experience sharing is safe under reward changes and partial observability.
4. **Has it already been modernized?** Several relevant branches exist: Cohn et al.'s topology-aware atlas learning (AR-98); learned manifold representations on neural encoders; Floryan–Graham chart-local learned dynamics; manifold-based RL by locally linear reconstruction (2016); and task-relevant RL representations using rewards and actions. The 2005 manifold-RL follow-up already couples chart similarity to transition outcomes for reuse, so a modern encoder plus transition-sensitive chart merging is an occupied baseline, not a new hybrid. [Xu et al., TNNLS](https://doi.org/10.1109/TNNLS.2015.2505084); [Yuan et al., task-relevant RL representations](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2024.111788).
5. **Why it struggled / born too early?** The underlying insight was sound and narrowly useful: the state-space metric used for generalization should respect reachable paths and local transition behavior. It was not an abandoned general architecture waiting for hardware alone. Its main boundaries are chart quality, coverage, nonstationary reward/policy, curse of dimensionality, and how to blend local approximators. More compute helps sample and fit richer charts but can also hide a hand-built chart bias if baselines receive less domain structure.
6. **Modernization worth testing, not promoting.** A small CPU simulator test could recreate WallWorld with a hidden or moved obstacle and later relocate the goal. Compare (a) a global Euclidean linear/MLP value model, (b) the 2004 chart-local model with its original growth rule, (c) charts learned from transition-neighborhood data, and (d) a topology-aware atlas baseline. Hold state-action samples and parameter/update budgets equal. Measure success, steps to reward, cross-obstacle value leakage, chart count, and adaptation after the obstacle or reward moves. Falsify practical utility if charts do not improve success or sample efficiency at matched budgets, if they share values across behaviorally distinct regions, or if rebuilding/chart inference costs erase the learning gain. This would establish whether modern methods make an old domain-specific technique practically stronger; it would not establish a novel architecture.
7. **Disposition.** Keep as a valuable pre-deep-learning architecture antecedent and a candidate for a bounded reproduction. Do not promote as new. Its hybrid connection to learned geometric encoders, local dynamics or replay is already occupied at the broad mechanism level.

#### HY-93 — learned atlas × chart-local controller/value learner (reject as a broad new hybrid)

- **Sources and contribution.** The older source contributes task-state topology, chart-local value approximation, smooth overlap blending, and transition-statistic-based chart growth or reuse. A modern atlas learner contributes chart construction from point clouds; a local dynamics/controller module could add action prediction and planning inside charts.
- **Coupling tested for novelty.** A plausible deep coupling is to split, merge or preserve a chart according to action-conditioned transition disagreement, then update all overlapping local value models with shared transition/reward evidence. The intended behavior is that chart boundaries follow decision-relevant changes (walls, controls, dynamics), rather than only ambient geometric curvature. That is a real interaction between representation growth, control and credit assignment.
- **Prior-art collision.** The 2004 method already grows chart regions using transition-distance statistics; the 2005 follow-up already defines transition-similar chart groups and shares experience; later manifold RL learns local value features; Floryan–Graham and CANDyMan learn local dynamics in atlas charts; adaptive atlas algorithms already change chart size or merge charts. Therefore, “atlas + controller,” “transition-triggered chart growth,” or “learned chart + replay” alone is not new.
- **Narrow remainder and failure modes.** A possible empirical seam is a statistically calibrated *action-and-reward equivalence test* for experience transfer under goal relocation or partially observed dynamics, with explicit false-sharing control and bounded chart growth. This could still be just a better criterion for an established architecture. It may fail through noisy transition estimates, overly fine charts, slow coverage, reward dependence, discontinuity at chart boundaries, or expense exceeding a global function approximator. No precise unoccupied model class is identified.
- **Small disproof test.** Use the AR-99 WallWorld test and then relocate a goal without changing dynamics. Compare transition-only chart equivalence against action-and-reward predictive equivalence and a global neural/linear value baseline, matching transitions, replay, parameter count and planning budget. Reject the coupling's utility if the richer equivalence test does not reduce cross-wall value leakage or speed reward revaluation, or if it fragments charts enough to reduce coverage and increase cost. If it wins, classify as an improved abstraction/experience-reuse method unless a distinct reusable learning law emerges.
- **Verdict:** reject broad hybrid novelty (confidence **0/5**); retain the small experiment as a low-priority architecture-revival/evaluation test.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — computational autopoiesis and second-order cybernetics (AR-100)

**Question:** did autopoietic computation fail because 1970s hardware was too weak, or is it an artificial-life organization principle rather than a general learning architecture?

- **Original mechanism (1974).** Varela, Maturana and Uribe formalized autopoiesis as a network of production processes that continually produces components and relations that regenerate the network's own boundary and operating conditions. Their computational minimal model used a two-dimensional discrete space populated by substrate, catalyst and link particles. Local reactions make links; links bind into chains and membranes; an enclosing membrane makes a self-maintaining bounded chemical system possible. The repeated operation is local reaction, movement and bonding. The represented “knowledge” is physical state in particle types, concentrations, spatial arrangement and bond topology; it has no general task symbols or external answer decoder. [Varela, Maturana & Uribe, *Autopoiesis* (1974)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0303-2647(74)90031-8); [accessible paper scan](https://repositorio.uchile.cl/bitstream/2250/160309/1/item_34548860810.pdf).
- **Learning and inference boundary.** The 1974 model is a self-producing dynamic system, not a supervised or reinforcement learner. Its continuing state evolution is not itself evidence of inference, and stable boundary maintenance is not the same as acquiring task knowledge. Memory can be embodied in persistent structure or concentration, but the original paper does not define a reusable learning rule, objective, symbol system or broad application task. Later evolving artificial-chemistry systems can add selection and adaptation; those are extensions with their own explicit mechanisms.
- **Historical failure was not just low compute.** McMullin's reconstruction of the original algorithm found ambiguities and inconsistencies between the prose algorithm and reported behavior. The key reproduction problem was premature bonding of link particles, which undermined formation of the intended membrane/self-maintaining behavior. This is a model-specification and mechanistic problem; faster hardware would run the same unclear or mistuned dynamics faster. Larger simulations and modern tooling help systematic parameter sweeps but do not establish that the system has an AI learning capability. [McMullin, *Computational Autopoiesis: The Original Algorithm* (1997)](https://www.eeng.dcu.ie/~alife/bmcm9701/); [McMullin's 30-year review (2004)](https://www.eeng.dcu.ie/~alife/bmcm-alj-2004/html-single/).
- **What has changed / modern descendants.** GPUs can parallelize local reaction, CA or agent-based simulation; differentiable chemistry relaxations can help tune continuous reaction rates; modern evolutionary search and synthetic data can test robustness under many disturbance regimes. These techniques make experiments cheaper. They do not solve the hard question of what would count as cognition beyond survival/maintenance, how a self-produced boundary supports compositional task learning, or how to preserve individuality under noisy dynamics. Adjoint methods or gradient tuning of reaction parameters may also optimize away the autonomy being claimed if the desired behavior is encoded externally.
- **Direct modernizations and nearby work.** A 2020 digital-organism study analyzes creation and persistence of Conway gliders as minimal persistent individuals; it expressly separates persistence from the added complications of reproduction. Bartlett and Louapre's *Provenance of Lyfe* (2022) embeds short/long chemical memory and associative learning in Gray–Scott reaction-diffusion spots that exhibit self-replication and homeostasis; this is direct prior art for autopoietic chemistry plus associative learning. A 2024 Boids-based simulation combines aggregate behavior with artificial self-production and active assimilation of external components. [Beer, *An Investigation into the Origin of Autopoiesis* (2020)](https://direct.mit.edu/artl/article/26/1/5/93263/An-Investigation-into-the-Origin-of-Autopoiesis); [Bartlett & Louapre (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.106.034401); [Lawrence et al., Boids and artificial autopoietic organization (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0303264724001308).
- **Recent uses of the word need mechanism-level reading.** A 2026 software-lifecycle position paper proposes “autopoietic architectures” for self-construction and foundation-model reasoning units, but states challenges and does not present a definitive implemented architecture. A separate 2026 “Autopoiesis” LLM-serving system continuously synthesizes and rewrites serving-policy code against runtime measurements; that is online controller/program adaptation with an explicit objective, not a demonstrated system that physically or computationally produces and maintains its own organization in the 1974 sense. These are useful adjacent prior art for self-modifying systems, but the shared term should not be treated as evidence of shared architecture. [Software lifecycle position paper (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13934); [LLM-serving policy evolution (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07144).
- **Second-order cybernetics audit.** Including the observer inside the observed system is a modeling constraint, not yet a distinct computational primitive. To make it executable, specify a state representing the agent's sensor/actuator/measurement process, a repeated update, and a measurable benefit from the agent adapting that process. Once those are specified, nearby methods include active perception, dual control, online system identification, learned observation models and metacognition. No new model class follows from the observer label alone. I found no operational mechanism in the broad “second-order cybernetics” phrase that merits a standalone candidate.
- **Potential use and failure.** Autopoietic processes may be useful in artificial life, fault-tolerant distributed materials, self-repairing robotics or simulations of minimal agency where continued existence depends on local resource exchange. Likely failures include ambiguous criteria for identity and self-production, sensitivity to reaction-rate or initialization choices, destruction of boundaries by disturbances, and a gap between viability behavior and general learning. It is not broadly useful AI merely because it persists.
- **Small falsifiable experiment if pursued.** Reproduce the minimal particle chemistry with perturbations to link-bonding rates and boundary damage. Compare original rules, corrected/reparameterized rules, and an explicit non-autopoietic membrane controller at matched particle and energy budgets. Measure persistence, repair after damage, component turnover, robustness across random seeds and sensitivity to the premature-bonding rate. Falsify the “too-early implementation” claim if behavior disappears under modest parameter variation, or if persistence requires hand-set geometry/initial conditions that encode the outcome. For a learning claim, add a switched two-cue temporal association only after the maintenance behavior replicates; require performance beyond a no-memory chemistry and matched finite-state baseline while maintaining the boundary. The 2022 chemical associative-learning paper already covers the broad latter combination, so any additional result is likely a new replication or robustness study.
- **Disposition.** Keep autopoiesis as an important cybernetics/artificial-life architecture tradition and a useful conceptual lens for self-maintenance. Reject it as a new broadly useful AI architecture class on current evidence. The early work was partly constrained by simulation/model-specification technology, but the central unsolved boundary between self-maintenance and general learning is conceptual and experimental, not solved by modern GPUs.

#### HY-94 — autopoietic chemistry × associative learning (occupied; useful ALife study only)

- **Source mechanisms.** The autopoietic model contributes a boundary-producing chemical network whose persistence depends on component production and local resource exchange. The associative-learning mechanism contributes chemical species acting as short- and long-term memory for temporal cue correlation.
- **Exact coupling and resulting behavior.** In *Provenance of Lyfe*, chemical memory is embedded in Gray–Scott reaction-diffusion spots that also self-replicate and maintain homeostatic patterns. A temporal association becomes useful to an autonomous dissipative structure, rather than an external digital learner. This is a meaningful material-level interaction between persistence and adaptation.
- **Prior art and novelty.** The direct combination is already published in 2022. Adding modern simulation throughput, another cue schedule, or stronger reaction-rate tuning does not make the hybrid new. The 2024 Boids-based autopoiesis paper separately occupies aggregate coordination plus self-production. Treat both as artificial-life work, not general AI architecture proposals.
- **Potential advantage and failure.** The coupling could test how much memory can emerge within a self-maintaining material substrate and whether an agent trades resources between repair and prediction. It may fail to generalize beyond trained temporal schedules, lose its learned chemical state during turnover, or need externally tuned reaction rates and boundary initialization.
- **Small utility test, not novelty test.** Under matched total substrate/energy flux, switch the cue contingency after chemical spots have learned the first association and perturb the membrane. Compare chemical-memory agents, ablations without long-term memory, and digital finite-state controllers. Measure post-switch reacquisition, repair success, false cue responses and lifetime. Reject utility if apparent learning is explained by static reaction-rate differences, if the learning state is destroyed by repair, or if resource cost makes a digital controller uniformly better. Do not run unless the notebook later prioritizes artificial-life utility over architecture novelty.
- **Verdict:** reject as new hybrid (novelty **0/5**); retain as a prior-art and experimental-design reference.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — VSM, operational cybernetics, and second-order learners (AR-101)

**Question:** was the Viable System Model (VSM) an executable AI architecture that lacked modern implementation technology, or an organizational control model whose computation must be supplied by other methods?

- **Original computational picture.** Stafford Beer’s VSM recursively organizes a viable system through five interacting functions: S1 performs autonomous operations in the environment; S2 coordinates operational units and damps oscillation; S3 regulates current internal operations and resources, with S3* providing direct audit; S4 models and scans the environment for future change; S5 establishes policy/identity and resolves the S3-now/S4-future balance. Information and control move between these functions, and each S1 may itself be modeled as a viable system. The represented state is organizational/environmental state, resource use, plans, and policies; the repeated operation is communication and feedback control across time scales. These are functional roles, not specified neural or symbolic units.
- **What the source leaves open.** VSM does not prescribe a general state representation, objective function, forecasting procedure, policy-update rule, learning signal, inference algorithm, or implementation-level computation schedule. A system can be “VSM-shaped” while importing nearly all its actual intelligence from separately designed controllers, planners, forecasters, or humans. Thus its main historical limitation was not weak hardware; it is a normative/structural model that does not settle the computational details needed for a reusable learner.
- **Was it modernized already?** Yes, at the software-architecture level. Herring and Kaplan’s 2001 *Viable System Architecture* turns VSM principles into recursive viable components, special interfaces, and dynamic subsystem assembly. It describes a high-level reference architecture and an illustrative e-commerce application; the paper says the prototype was under construction, so this is a design/implementation program rather than evidence for a learned AI architecture. [Herring & Kaplan, primary DOI record](https://doi.org/10.1109/HICSS.2001.927249); [accessible VSA paper](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1058b698ab4a9158ac8e0473b20c31cb6041d0da&repid=rep1&type=pdf).
- **Runnable feedback machinery already existed nearby.** IBM’s Autonomic Management Engine documented a functional MAPE-K loop: Monitor, Analyze, Plan, and Execute share Knowledge; the engine reads resource models, sensors and event buses and invokes effectors at a configured cycle time. This supplies concrete monitoring, decision algorithms, corrective plans and actuation—functions that a VSM software mapping would otherwise need to implement. IBM also describes both flat and hierarchical autonomic managers for complex multi-tier applications. It is an operational self-management architecture, not by itself a general machine-learning architecture. [IBM Autonomic Computing Toolkit / Autonomic Management Engine manual](https://www.redbooks.ibm.com/redbooks/pdfs/sg246665.pdf); [IBM architectural approach to autonomic computing](https://research.ibm.com/publications/an-architectural-approach-to-autonomic-computing).
- **Second-order cybernetics has more specific computational descendants than the label suggests.** Bhalwankar and Treur’s 2021 three-level adaptive network explicitly represents (i) a mental model, (ii) first-order network adaptation that changes that model, and (iii) second-order adaptation that controls when observational and instructional learning occur. It demonstrates a learner requesting instruction after observing a car-driving relation; this is a concrete computational mechanism, but a narrow educational case study, not evidence that the whole second-order-cybernetics tradition defines a broad model class. [PLOS ONE primary article](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0255503).
- **Ashby-box continuation.** Cretu’s 2020 *Learning the Ashby Box* synthesizes an observer/controller for variable-structure black-box systems and describes autonomous construction, deconstruction and reconstruction of its own function. This is a much more executable observer-inclusive cybernetic mechanism than second-order cybernetics as an abstract slogan. Its closest general families remain online system identification, adaptive/dual control and self-modeling networks; the cited case does not establish broad transfer or outperform those baselines. Treat it as a specific algorithm to audit against AR-08/C031, not as confirmation of a new general architecture. [Publisher abstract and paper metadata](https://www.sciencedirect.com/org/science/article/pii/S0368492X20000882); [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1108/K-06-2019-0439).
- **What current technology changes.** Simulation, event buses, cheap telemetry, distributed control and automatic parameter search make it easier to instantiate and stress-test recursive controllers. Modern learned predictors can fill an S4-like forecasting role. These are enabling components, not a recovered VSM learning law; they also introduce new issues such as delayed messages, interacting control loops, inconsistent local objectives and coordination cost. The absence of a universal S4/S5 algorithm is conceptual rather than a GPU bottleneck.
- **Disposition.** Keep VSM as an architecture-design and control lens. Do not promote it as a new general AI computation. Second-order adaptive networks and Ashby-box observers provide more concrete mechanisms worth comparing, but each needs a sharply defined task and baseline. The “born too early” hypothesis is weak for VSM itself: software implementations and autonomic control preceded current deep-learning hardware, while its key missing ingredient is algorithmic specification.
- **Small CPU falsifier for practical utility, not novelty.** Implement a discrete-event plant with 4–8 autonomous operators sharing limited resources, conflicts between their actions, telemetry delays, and an unseen dependency/regime shift after warm-up. Compare (1) a flat MAPE-K controller, (2) hierarchical MAPE-K with one manager per operator and a coordinator, and (3) the same hierarchical system with explicit VSM-like recursive boundaries, independent S3*-style audit/exception messages, and a separate S4-style future-change model. Give every controller identical observations, action primitives, forecasts, policy constraints, total update budget and message budget. Measure viability-constraint violations, recovery time, oscillation/conflicting-action count, task throughput, and communication/control overhead over held-out perturbations. Falsify the VSM-structure utility claim if recursion/audit does not improve recovery or constraint satisfaction once compute and messages are matched, or if gains are offset by instability and overhead. No experiment is scheduled yet.

#### HY-95 — recursive VSM roles × MAPE-K control loops (reject as a new architecture)

- **Source mechanisms.** VSM contributes recursive operational autonomy, coordination to reduce oscillation, current-resource control, future-environment modeling, policy resolution, and an audit/exception path. MAPE-K contributes an executable monitor–analyze–plan–execute loop sharing a knowledge store, with sensors, effectors, resource models and asynchronous events.
- **Exact coupling considered.** Instantiate a MAPE-K controller inside each autonomous S1 unit, connect sibling controllers through an S2-like coordination channel, use an S3-like layer for resource bargaining and audit, assign environmental forecasting to S4, and let S5 maintain explicit viability constraints/policy. The interaction changes controller topology and scheduling across local and system-wide time scales; it is more precise than merely naming a multi-agent system after VSM.
- **Why it still does not establish novelty.** VSA already translates VSM into recursive software components and interfaces. IBM MAPE-K and hierarchical autonomic managers already implement local feedback controllers with higher-level coordination. Nesting one known feedback loop inside another and assigning Beer’s role labels leaves the underlying update laws imported from MAPE-K and task-specific planners. I found no validated result showing that the combined structure yields a distinct learning mechanism. Novelty as a general AI architecture: **0/5**; possible value as a control-organization ablation: **2/5**.
- **Failure modes and possible niche advantage.** Explicit local autonomy plus audit may improve recovery when cross-unit dependencies change and telemetry is incomplete. It can also multiply nested control loops, create stale/delayed knowledge, oscillate between local and global policies, or consume more communication/control effort than it saves. “Viability” must be operationalized as constraints or service-level measures, not treated as an objective by itself.
- **Smallest useful test.** Use the AR-101 discrete-event plant and compare flat MAPE-K, hierarchical MAPE-K, and hierarchical VSM-mapped MAPE-K with audit. Hold all policies, predictors, compute and communication budgets fixed. If explicit recursion/audit does not reduce violations or recovery time under unseen dependency shifts at matched budgets, reject the utility claim. Even a win would support a control architecture organization result, not a new general learning architecture.

#### ACS2HER primary-source verification addendum (no duplicate candidate)

The existing ACS2HER hybrid entry is confirmed by the full January 2026 preprint. ACS2 represents condition–action–effect rules and learns them with anticipatory learning, reinforcement updates and genetic generalization. ACS2HER stores goal-conditioned transitions after failed episodes, relabels visited states as virtual goals, and re-runs the same rule-learning machinery on replayed/relabelled transitions. This is a genuine change to learning data and classifier-population growth, but the specific ACS2 × HER method is already published; the broad classifier-system architecture is older ACS2. [ACS2HER full paper and pseudocode](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.09400v1).

The closer matched baseline sharpens the earlier notebook summary: in deterministic Maze 6, ACS2HER learned reliable transitions faster than plain ACS2 but *more slowly than ACS2ER at the same replay intensity*. At M=8, ACS2ER reached 95% transition knowledge at 239 trials; ACS2HER K=2/M=8 needed 381 trials. ACS2HER populations exceeded 3,000 classifiers versus about 474 for ACS2. Reported exploration time reached 3,746 seconds for K=4/M=8 versus 36 seconds for ACS2. In stochastic FrozenLake, ACS2HER goal success was below ACS2 and ACS2ER in the reported configurations; the largest configuration took 22,491 seconds versus 13 seconds for ACS2. The authors call the study preliminary, limit it to two small grids, and note weak statistical testing and sensitivity to stochastic outcomes. These are paper-reported results, not a reproduction. They demote the hybrid on matched efficiency; they do not imply that HER is generally harmful. [Maze 6 result tables](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.09400v1#S3.T1); [FrozenLake result tables](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.09400v1#S3.T5); [limitations](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.09400v1#S6).

**Follow-up gate:** if reproducing it, compare ACS2, ACS2ER, ACS2HER and a modern goal-conditioned replay baseline under equal interaction count, total learning updates, wall-clock, and rule/memory budget; report success, transition-model accuracy, classifier count and confidence intervals on deterministic and stochastic tasks. The claim worth testing is whether interpretable rule induction benefits from hindsight relabeling *per unit total cost*. Falsify it if ACS2HER has no matched-budget success or sample-efficiency benefit, or if apparent model coverage comes from large unreliable rule growth. This remains a CPU-only reproduction proposal, not a novelty candidate.

The finding also corrects the broad cybernetics table: specific computational descendants exist even though “second-order cybernetics” alone is not an algorithm.

#### CAA archaeology update — 1996 report clarifies the alleged “self-reinforcement” (AR-65 supplement)

A targeted source search did **not** recover Bozinovski’s 25 November 1981 CAA report or the 1982 Trappl-volume chapter. It did recover the full 1996 AAAI Fall Symposium paper *Emotion, Embodiment, and Consequence Driven Systems*, which states that it reports early 1981 CAA experiments and supplies an algorithm. This is a useful author/coauthor retrospective and implementation description, **not** the missing 1981/82 original. [1996 AAAI report PDF](https://www.aaai.org/Papers/Symposia/Fall/1996/FS-96-02/FS96-02-003.pdf); [full-text mirror with searchable method/results](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/253997680_Emotion_Embodiment_and_Consequence_Driven_Systems).

- **Algorithm recovered from the retrospective.** A crossbar weight `w(a,s)` for each action and situation is used both to bias action choice and to calculate the successor situation’s internal desirability/value. The stated loop is: in state `s`, bias/perform action `a`; arrive at successor `s'`; compute `V(s')` from the weights associated with `s'`; increment the prior `w(a,s)` using that successor value; then make `s'` the current state and continue. The simplest rule is desirability-only (`w'(a,s) = w(a,s) + V(s')`); cost- and discount-sensitive variants and a reinforcement-style update are also given. The authors say an emotional-value selector might be a maximum or a thresholded neural sum and warn that this choice affects convergence. This specification remains retrospective evidence; do not cite it as text recovered from the 1981 memo.
- **The “no external reinforcement” qualification matters.** The report says the agent’s “genetic environment” supplies a species/genome vector that initializes emotion/desirability for situations before learning. The internal valence is then used as secondary reinforcement. Thus this is not learning values from nothing: a task-relevant evaluation prior is externally specified through an inherited initialization. Calling that “self-reinforcement” describes where the *step-by-step* teaching signal is computed, not where its goals or initial value labels came from.
- **What was actually shown.** The report describes a 22-situation, 3-action maze with one positively evaluated terminal situation and states that a path was learned in about 11 iterations, with values propagating backward from the goal. The authors explicitly say that the sensor-to-situation classifier is external to the delayed-reinforcement CAA task, assumes a suitable learned situation partition, and is not solved by the experiment. It is a small discrete demonstration, not a scale or robustness result; there are no modern matched baselines or broad perception results.
- **Relation to later value learning.** The report itself calls the crossbar entries later “Q-values” and states that the Q-method is a variant of the CAA procedure. With `V(s') = max_a Q(s',a)`, the reported update is a simple bootstrapped action-value backup, with initial valence acting as a terminal-value prior. This is a useful historical antecedent for internal successor-state valuation and credit propagation, but not an unoccupied general learning primitive. It also means earlier statements about CAA being a different broad architecture from actor–critic/Q-learning should be read narrowly: the shared table/use of successor desirability is a real representational detail, while the broad bootstrapped value-learning computation is familiar.
- **Was it merely too early?** The tiny tabular simulation could have run on 1981 hardware; the reported experiment proves no GPU-scale bottleneck. What the older setup did not supply was robust high-dimensional situation discovery, learned perception coupled to the value updates, or generalization beyond a hand-sized state graph. Modern encoders and GPUs can help with perception, but then the value-learning core is still compared against DQN, actor–critic, successor features and model-based RL. The unresolved issue is whether the initial desirability prior and on-route update give any *measurable* sample-efficiency, safety or interpretability benefit, not whether the table can be made larger.
- **Disposition and smallest fair reproduction.** Keep CAA as historically meaningful tabular credit assignment / internally generated secondary reinforcement, not as a new model class. If it is ever reproduced, use the 22-node maze only as a fidelity check; then compare original desirability-only and discounted variants against tabular Q-learning, reward shaping with the same initial values, and an actor–critic baseline over held-out maze topologies, equal transition counts and identical state/action encodings. Measure goal success, steps to goal, sensitivity to initial valence, recovery when the goal moves, and compute. Falsify utility if its gains vanish when baselines receive the same value prior, or depend on the hand-built state classifier. Do not implement an approximate “1981 CAA” while the original text and exact initialization remain unavailable.
