#### Old-architecture archaeology — Adaptive Logic Networks (AR-102; 1970s–1990s)

**What the architecture computes.** An Adaptive Logic Network (ALN) is an adaptive binary tree that builds Boolean decision structure out of thresholded linear tests and logical compositions. In the Atree variants used for real-valued approximation, linear-threshold units form piecewise-linear regions, and AND/OR (equivalently, MIN/MAX views of the composed function) combine them. The network consumes fixed-width Boolean or numeric feature vectors plus a target/class during supervised adaptation; it returns a class or a scalar function value. Its repeated computation is (a) evaluate the active tree/linear pieces, and (b) pass responsibility for error to selected active elements so their local parameters/logic can specialize. Knowledge is explicit in threshold coefficients, tree structure, and MIN/MAX or Boolean operators; the model does not require a learned dense latent space. The small number of required comparisons and the ability to omit irrelevant subtrees were intended to make evaluation fast.

The historical primary-source trail begins with Armstrong's adaptive Boolean element patent and Armstrong & Gecsei's 1979 paper, *Adaptation Algorithms for Binary Tree Networks*. The 1979 abstract says heuristic responsibility specializes portions of the tree to subsets of input vectors and reports pattern-recognition/OCR applications. The CMU AI repository preserves the Atree simulation package record and a substantial application bibliography. A 1998 SPIE paper gives a concrete FPGA implementation: nine FLEX8K devices and 512 KB RAM, conversion from Atree-trained models to hardware, and on-board learning; it also says board resources kept network sizes in the small-to-medium range. [1979 paper record and abstract](https://dblp.org/rec/journals/tsmc/ArmstrongG79), [CMU Atree/ALN archive](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/project/ai-repository/ai/areas/neural/systems/atree/0.html), [1998 FPGA implementation and full text](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235864864_Implementation_of_Adaptive_Logic_Networks_on_an_FPGA_board), [Armstrong patent](https://patents.justia.com/patent/3934231).

- **What it represents / unit / learning / inference.** A node is a simple threshold or logic element; the overall object is a tree of local piecewise-linear regions. Supervised examples choose which regions/elements are responsible and update the active element(s), instead of globally adjusting every network weight. Inference follows the resulting tree, evaluates a limited set of linear pieces, and composes them to return a prediction. Long-term memory is the expanded tree plus element parameters. There is no external episodic-memory mechanism.
- **Use cases and plausible advantage.** Potentially useful for low-latency tabular/control prediction where monotone or piecewise-linear behavior is appropriate, the feature vector already exists, and a compact auditable model matters. The plausible advantage is a favorable inference/update-cost versus accuracy frontier for that niche, plus explicit piecewise structure. The old literature reports OCR, feature detection, movement/FES, machine-failure and control applications; these reports establish that ALNs were used, not that they outperform present baselines.
- **Why revival is not automatically justified.** The “too early” story is weak for core compute: by the late 1990s, software kits and small FPGA implementations existed, and papers reported real-time control. Modern memory/compute could support larger trees and richer input encoders, but that would not remove tree growth, piece proliferation, data-coverage requirements, sensitivity to user-set training parameters, or poor fit to raw high-dimensional perception. The ALN representation’s readability does not guarantee a short or stable model. A contemporaneous thesis on magnetic-material modeling explicitly reports that generated trees could become large, defeating a compact-parameter objective and making knowledge extraction slow; this is a structural risk rather than an old GPU shortage. [Example discussion of ALN model-size limits](https://central.bac-lac.gc.ca/.item?app=Library&id=NQ64660&oclc_number=1006726983&op=pdf).
- **Closest work and novelty judgment.** Adaptive piecewise-linear fitting, model/oblique trees, MARS, min-max networks, and differentiable decision forests all occupy substantial parts of this computation. MARS uses hinge-basis terms and greedy fitting rather than ALN responsibility on a logic tree; the implementations are not identical, but the predictive function class and compact local partitioning goal collide directly. [MARS paper](https://www.stat.yale.edu/~lc436/08Spring665/Mars_Friedman_91.pdf), [Deep Neural Decision Forests](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_iccv_2015/html/Kontschieder_Deep_Neural_Decision_ICCV_2015_paper.html). Novelty as a broad architecture class: **0/5**. Possible remaining contribution is an evidence-based niche efficiency claim or a modern training/regularization study, not the tree-with-local-responsibility mechanism itself. Confidence in non-novelty: **high**.
- **Small falsifiable experiment (CPU only).** Implement or use a faithful Atree-compatible learner and compare ALN against MARS, an oblique/model tree, and a small MLP on (1) noisy piecewise-linear control surfaces and (2) smooth/non-piecewise tabular tasks, with held-out regions and a modest covariate shift. Match training data, total tuning budget, prediction latency target, and model-memory budget; report error, calibration, tree/piece count, update/evaluation time, and memory. The revival/utility claim fails if the ALN does not improve the accuracy–memory–latency frontier on the intended piecewise-linear niche, or if any gain depends on substantially more tuning or uncharged feature engineering. A win would justify a specialized learner study, not a general AI architecture claim. No implementation or experiment has run.
- **Hybrid audit.** ALN × modern vision/language encoder would feed learned features to an existing supervised tree model; ALN × Koopman/control would couple a fitted piecewise model to control planning. Neither has a distinctive coupling yet, and both resemble feature-extractor-plus-model composition. Do not promote a hybrid without a changed learning or inference law and a direct comparison to adaptive trees, differentiable forests, and piecewise-linear system identification.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Adaptive Self-Organizing Concurrent Systems, AA2 (AR-103; 1988–1990s)

**Original mechanism and bounded claim.** ASOCS is a network of many simple computing elements that operate in parallel and asynchronously. The system is programmed incrementally with if–then rules expressed as Boolean conjunctions; learning changes network connectivity/topology in a distributed way. AA2 (Adaptive Algorithm 2) is a particular revision intended to improve memory and knowledge maintenance over earlier ASOCS models. The 1991 paper says that insertion of a new rule takes O(log n) parallel adaptation time, where n is node count, and that data processing acts as a parallel hardware circuit with O(max(d, log n)) latency for maximum path depth d. It also claims support for learning from examples and handling contradictory rules/examples. The 1988 article abstract specifies latest-input precedence when conflicts occur. Treat contradiction handling as explicit conflict-policy support, not as discovery of a semantically coherent resolution. [1991 primary paper, *A Self-Adjusting Dynamic Logic Module*](https://axon.cs.byu.edu/papers/martinez_91a.pdf), [indexed full-text copy with abstract and complexity statements](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/074373159190037A), [NASA record and 1988 abstract](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19880039023).

- **Input, output and repeated operation.** The data path consumes Boolean assignments for a predefined variable set and returns the circuit response/classification implied by the incrementally supplied rule base. The repeated operations are distributed local topology updates when a new conjunction arrives, and asynchronous circuit evaluation afterward. The knowledge store is the reconfigured network itself rather than a conventional explicit rule database. The rule vocabulary and Booleanization of the task remain external.
- **What it does well / what it cannot establish.** The interesting primitive is online, topology-changing compilation of logical constraints into a parallel circuit, with a claimed logarithmic update depth and circuit-like inference. It may suit machine protection, fault recovery, rule-based control, or logic systems where the propositions and conflict policy are already supplied. It does not learn raw perception, construct useful variables from sensory streams, or acquire an open-ended world model. “Generalization” over large input spaces is within the Boolean rule setting, not evidence for broad concept learning.
- **Was it simply too early?** Fine-grain asynchronous hardware and a clean mapping from the theoretical distributed update to an economical physical fabric could have been limiting; modern FPGAs, programmable logic, and event-driven simulators make re-evaluation easier. Yet the paper already targets parallel hardware and provides asymptotic update/inference arguments, so GPU scarcity is not the central missing ingredient. A GPU also does not naturally reproduce asynchronous local topology rewrites; CPU simulation can check structure/logic counts, while an FPGA experiment would be needed to validate wall-clock and energy advantages. The separate learning and processing modes mean the model is not automatically an interleaved modern online learner.
- **Prior art / novelty.** ASOCS/AA2 is itself a named historical architecture, not a newly identified candidate. Modern Tsetlin Machines learn Boolean clauses through finite-state automata and have online FPGA realizations; they provide an important comparator for rule learning at the hardware edge, though their clause-learning rule and representation are not AA2's dynamic reconfiguration. BDD/trie-based incremental rule compilers and SAT/logic synthesis are additional engineering comparisons, not identical learners. [FPGA architecture for online Tsetlin Machine learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01027), [1996 location-independent ASOCS transform for parallel dynamic insertion/deletion](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9040065/). Novelty as a broad AI class: **0/5**. Potential remaining value: a reproducible, cost-accounted benchmark of dynamic circuit learning under rule updates, if its costs are favorable. Confidence in this assessment: **high**.
- **Small falsifiable experiment (CPU structural test first).** Recover the AA2 update pseudocode from the 1991 paper and build a deterministic event-driven simulator. Generate streams of overlapping, redundant, and contradictory conjunction rules at increasing rule/variable counts. Compare AA2 with an incremental BDD/trie rule base and an online Tsetlin Machine on exact agreement with the declared recency/conflict semantics, update work, allocated nodes/bits, query work, and memory after every prefix. Count communication/scheduling events rather than claiming theoretical parallel time from a sequential CPU. Falsify a useful revival if measured total work or storage grows poorly, consistency depends on hidden rule-order assumptions, or the claimed update advantage vanishes when node allocation, conflict maintenance and inference are charged. If that structural test is promising, a modest FPGA run could measure latency/energy against a clause-based FPGA baseline. No GPU or CPU experiment has run yet.
- **Hybridization screen.** ASOCS × a modern encoder could translate detected concepts into propositions and insert learned rules, but without a new encoder-to-rule learning law this is a familiar perception-plus-symbolic-rule pipeline. ASOCS × Tsetlin is also not novel merely because both use Boolean clauses; a potentially testable interaction would need one system to alter the other’s update/credit-allocation policy or dynamically decide which clauses/circuit regions to allocate. No such specific mechanism has been verified. Do not advance HY-96 yet.

#### AR-102 primary-source mechanism and hardware correction

The ALN family needs a chronological distinction. Armstrong’s 1974-filed / 1976-published patent describes an adaptive **Boolean** network element with two inputs and one output. Each element can implement AND, OR, LEFT or RIGHT; two bounded counters record target-output evidence for the unequal input pairs. A responsibility signal decides which elements can update, and its suggested variants include hill-climbing, latest-error and global-search responsibility. The inventor explicitly notes that a universal learner for every Boolean function would need an impractically large state/part count; the patent’s stated generality is not a polynomial-size guarantee. [Armstrong, US Patent 3,934,231, description and claims](https://patents.google.com/patent/US3934231A/en).

Later Atree ALNs extend this family to real-valued approximation with threshold units and MIN/MAX combinations. Do not imply that every Atree unit or training version is identical to every patented two-input Boolean element: the 1998 FPGA paper reports Atree 2.7 and a related tree implementation, not which responsibility variant it uses. Its historical hardware record is more specific than the earlier summary: the Altera RIPP10 had nine FLEX8K devices in total (eight array devices plus an interface), with 512 KB RAM. A pre-trained inverted-pendulum controller used 18 trees with 2,048 leaves each and 60 input bits; 4,096 pattern evaluations reportedly took 27 ms with the board versus 10,934 ms in standard Atree software and 3,626 ms in the software fast variant. On-board learning was demonstrated on a much smaller seven-layer, 128-leaf pattern task, and the authors explicitly say the available logic restricted learning networks to small/simple tasks; host ISA throughput limited the large evaluation run. This is evidence of a real specialized hardware advantage on those 1990s workloads, not evidence of modern broad usefulness or scalable model growth. [Oliver et al., 1998, full paper](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235864864_Implementation_of_Adaptive_Logic_Networks_on_an_FPGA_board); [CMU Atree archive and references](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/project/ai-repository/ai/areas/neural/systems/atree/0.html).

**Implication for AR-102:** classify ALN as an established tree/logic learner with demonstrable fast hardware evaluation and limited on-board learning, not as a general architecture that merely lacked GPUs. Preserve the CPU niche falsifier, but a later deployment claim must compare against compiled decision trees, FPGA logic, and contemporary tree/forest implementations on the same workload and include host-transfer and update costs.

#### AR-103 source correction — rule coverage, generalization, conflict cost, and hardware

The meaning of “generalization” in the AA2/AA3 literature must be qualified. In AA2, the input is a **partial Boolean rule**: omitted variables are explicit don’t-cares, so one input rule can cover a region of Boolean input space. The 1991 paper’s statements about discovering critical variables and generalizing describe execution over that supplied partial-rule region. A fully specified labeled pattern with every variable asserted is different: it covers one atomic cell. A later BYU dissertation says AA2 may answer “don’t know” for uncovered regions, AA3 uses a default/no-match response, and AA1 is the variant that attempts to generalize. A later 2006 paper explicitly reports that AA1, AA2 and AA3 converge on arbitrary Boolean pattern sets, but only AA1 shows meaningful out-of-sample generalization. This reconciles the claim conflict without dismissing the earlier AA2 description: supplied don’t-care structure already carries generality; AA2 is not thereby shown to infer labels reliably for unobserved points from ordinary fully specified examples. [Martinez & Campbell, AA2, §1–2](https://axon.cs.byu.edu/papers/martinez_91a.pdf); [Wilson, *Prototype Styles of Generalization*, §§2.1, 2.3](https://axon.cs.byu.edu/papers/wilson.thesis94.pdf); [Giraud-Carrier & Martinez, i-AA1*, §I](https://axon.cs.byu.edu/papers/cgc_smc2006.pdf).

- **AA2 computation.** Positive/negative partial-rule instances are built from shared two-input AND nodes (PNodes) and are read through positive/negative OR collectors. AA2 can report “don’t know” if no instance matches. The parallel-time claims concern this distributed hardware model: rule insertion is stated as O(log n), with data evaluation O(max(d, log n)) for maximum depth d and n nodes. They do not establish serial CPU speed or total work/storage bounds.
- **AA3 is distinct.** AA3 uses a binary-tree-style organization of PNodes and positive/negative DNodes, with a different no-match/error behavior and an architecture designed to simplify physical interconnect compared with AA2. Its paper also makes bounded parallel-time claims. AA3’s own analysis concedes that some Boolean functions (its example is white-noise recognition on a raster) can still require exponential resources; dynamic growth avoids wasting a fixed universal tree on compressible functions, not worst-case complexity for every function. A reported average near two nodes per instance in one single-output simulation is a workload-specific average, not a worst-case guarantee. [Martinez & Campbell, AA3, §§VII–IX](https://axon.cs.byu.edu/papers/martinez_91b.pdf).
- **Contradiction policy is not semantic conflict resolution.** AA2/AA3 give newer rules priority and use discriminant-variable adaptation (DVA) to split/repair partially conflicting old instances. A later ASOCS dissertation bounds instance-set size increase by `m*n - m + 1` for an incoming rule of n variables conflicting with m stored instances, and describes DVA fragmentation as a growth problem. Thus “handles contradiction” means rule-order-sensitive overwrite/refinement with a potentially growing representation, not principled belief revision. AA3’s parallel bound must be kept separate from this state-growth cost. [Rudolph, *A Location-Independent ASOCS Model*, DVA section](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=ea53ba3fe77d2f23f9993c75aad89aec02d3f504&repid=rep1&type=pdf).
- **Historical hardware status.** These were not GPU-dependent sketches: AA2 authors describe an initial VLSI design/fabrication, AA3 reports proof-of-concept VLSI fabrication, and PASOCS (a priority ASOCS variant) was later reported on a multi-chip-module substrate. The enduring bottleneck was efficient dynamic interconnect, rule maintenance and growth as much as raw compute. [Stout et al., PASOCS VLSI, 1994](https://scholarsarchive.byu.edu/facpub/1167).
- **Revised experiment contract.** Do not compare AA2 directly with Tsetlin as if their supervision were identical. First, an explicit-rule lane should stream partial rules, including contradictions, and compare AA2 against an exact priority-rule interpreter/compiled BDD; match semantics and charge DVA/node growth, update work and queries. Second, a labeled-example lane should compare a generalizing ASOCS variant (AA1/i-AA1*) against Tsetlin/online rule learners under equal examples and memory. CPU event simulation can check exact outputs, growth and operation counts; only a subsequent FPGA experiment can validate parallel latency/energy. Reject practical revival if rule fragmentation dominates, an exact interpreter/BDD is smaller and as fast, or claimed generalization disappears outside explicitly supplied don’t-care regions.

#### HY-59 historical coupling follow-up — sequence chunking × fast-weight memory (low-priority method test)

Schmidhuber’s 1992 **sequence chunker** is an under-recorded time-scale architecture: recurrent predictors form a self-organizing hierarchy; only unexpected inputs (plus timing signals) are passed upward, and lower levels may be frozen once they stop improving. It was motivated by long time lags, reduced sequence descriptions and fewer training examples, with the required hierarchy depth unknown. [Schmidhuber, *Learning Complex, Extended Sequences Using the Principle of History Compression* (1992)](https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/chunker/).

A concrete hybrid hypothesis would let each predictor level emit a surprise/boundary signal that controls *which key-value associations a delta-rule fast-weight memory writes, how long the write remains active, and at which temporal scale it is indexed*. The chunker contributes slow-to-fast temporal abstraction; fast weights contribute rapid online associative storage. This would change the memory-write schedule and index representation, not merely concatenate two modules. It could help recurring sequences plus rare delayed bindings by avoiding writes for predictable routine events while retaining event boundaries and their aftermath.

The broad coupling is nevertheless occupied. Hierarchical Multiscale RNNs learn latent temporal boundaries, neural event-segmentation models learn sparse latent events and higher-level predictions, and Titans directly uses a neural associative memory updated at test time by momentary and past surprise with data-dependent surprise decay and forgetting. Gated DeltaNet couples adaptive gating to a delta rule for targeted memory modification; fast-weight programmers are themselves a mature line. These methods cover the core proposal that temporal surprise/context should shape online memory updates. A chunker-level variable-length memory lifetime may be a narrower unverified combination, but no distinct learning law or broad class has been established. [HM-RNN (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.01704); [hierarchical event anticipation (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.02042); [Titans, NeurIPS 2025, surprise and test-time memory update](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/a4ca07aa108036f80cbb5b82285fd4b1-Paper-Conference.pdf); [Gated DeltaNet, ICLR 2025](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/4904fad153f6434a7bcf04465d4be2cc-Paper-Conference.pdf); [Schlag et al., recurrent fast-weight programmers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.06295).

**Disposition.** Do not add a new architecture candidate. If revisited, the cheapest CPU test is a semi-Markov sequence task with recurring motifs, a rare delayed key-value dependency and a context switch. Compare a GRU, delta fast-weight memory, a modern hierarchical/event-segmentation predictor, Titans-style surprise memory, and the exact hierarchical-boundary-gated write rule. Match parameters, memory bytes, update count and sequence data; measure delayed-binding accuracy, post-switch adaptation samples, writes per correct binding, retention of routine associations and operation count. Falsify utility if hierarchical surprise gating does not improve accuracy/write efficiency over Titans-style surprise memory or improves only by retaining more memory. No new run was launched; no GPU work was planned.

#### HY-59 prior-art correction — hierarchical surprise-gated event compression (2020) and MIRAS design space (2025)

The sequence-chunker × fast-weight follow-up had omitted a direct event-compression predecessor. Humaidan, Otte & Butz's *Fostering Event Compression using Gated Surprise* already couples a deep contextual LSTM that forms compressed event/context codes to a surprise-driven GRU-like switch that selectively routes those codes down to a recurrent function predictor. Its update gate is explicitly fed surprise, and the lower predictor's unexpected error can trigger a context transition. Context codes stay fixed while the gate is closed. This is a close prior for surprise-contingent hierarchical memory/context scheduling, published in 2020; it is not merely a broad similarity to HM-RNN. [Humaidan et al., arXiv:2005.05704, architecture §§3.1–3.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.05704).

The scope limit matters. The evaluation uses four synthetic function regimes, only a 10-hidden-unit LSTM, and a context layer that receives supplied context/event information in advance of the switch. Surprise and gate opening are therefore not evidence that the system discovers boundaries from unconstrained sensory streams. The authors describe integration of surprise estimated directly by the lower predictor and prediction of future event boundaries as future work. The reported effect—good prediction when a prepared context code is passed at a boundary—is evidence for selective top-down context routing, not for general event abstraction or broad autonomous learning. Modern compute would permit larger stress tests, but it does not remove the privileged-context/evaluation-design limitation. [paper, §§4–5](https://arxiv.org/html/2005.05704v1).

A second collision further narrows the proposed fast-memory write/retention mechanism. The 2025 MIRAS framework describes sequence memory models through four design choices: associative-memory architecture, attentional-bias objective, retention gate, and memory learning algorithm. Surprise-triggered retention or delta-rule writes are thus within a formalized modern memory-design space, even if a particular hierarchical-event-timescale policy has not been located. [Behrouz et al., *It's All Connected* / MIRAS (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13173). Titans is a concrete surprise-dependent test-time associative memory descendant; Gated DeltaNet supplies a gated delta-rule update. These sources make a generic "surprise gates long-term fast-memory writes" novelty claim untenable.

**Remaining narrow question.** I have not found, in this pass, a paper that explicitly lets *different learned chunker levels* assign independently persistent key-value writes to event-indexed fast memory, then lets later event-scale predictions retrieve/override those writes under a regime switch. This is only a search residue, not a novelty claim: event compression, test-time associative memory, surprise-conditioned retention, and delta updates are each established and their composition is a conspicuous next experiment. Keep it at novelty confidence 0.5/5 and do not create a new model class. A cheap utility probe, if ever prioritized, should compare (a) surprise-write delta memory, (b) hierarchical event compression alone, (c) a fixed-lifetime chunk-addressed table, and (d) event-level timescale-indexed writes on a semi-Markov task with recurring motifs, a delayed key-value binding, and context reversal. Match memory bytes, update count and access budget; track binding accuracy after boundary and context switch, writes per retained correct binding, interference, and memory expiry. Falsify the mechanism if scale-specific expiry/indexing gives no advantage over surprise-gated memory at matched resource cost or only wins because it receives boundary labels.

- **Disposition update:** HY-59 remains a low-priority comparison. Gated-surprise event compression (2020) is direct hierarchical-routing prior art; Titans plus the broader MIRAS design space occupy surprise-conditioned online-memory update/retention. Any residual coupling is a narrow event-scale memory policy to test against those methods, not an architecture candidate.

#### HY-88 prior-art correction — Sifter makes representation revision an explicit baseline

The independent symbolic-architecture audit identified a closer Copycat descendant than the previous HY-88 entry recorded. Sotoudeh & Thakur's Sifter (Onward! 2020) is explicitly derived from Copycat, but encodes arbitrary relational structures as triplet facts and performs analogy as a search over workspace-update-rule applications. Its rules can infer new relations, refine the represented inputs, and add analogy structures; later analogy steps can use earlier ones. This is direct prior art for a revisable relational workspace and analogy-guided program reasoning, not just a related program-synthesis system. The paper says Copycat's own implementation is letter-domain-specific and Sifter is designed for arbitrary relations. [Sotoudeh & Thakur, primary paper (2020)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.06592), especially §§4.1–4.5.

Important limitation: Sifter's current update rules encode domain knowledge (the authors describe some as hard-coded); its structural analogy machinery is largely oblivious to relation semantics. Its own future-work section calls out dynamic representation granularity, heuristics for choosing when to expand files/structures, a shared workspace for multiple reasoning engines, and meta-reasoning about recurring search snags. Therefore the proposed learned representation-edit policy is narrowed but not demonstrated by Sifter. This is a plausible methods question only: learn when to apply a reusable edit inventory across task families while holding the available operations and relational facts constant. Do not claim new analogy/workspace architecture. [paper, §§4.3, 5.1–5.3 and future-work discussion](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.06592).

**Experiment correction.** If the existing HY-88/LCRR probe is ever run, add Sifter's authored update rules and a Sifter-like deterministic search as direct controls alongside Copycat-style stochastic codelets, Metacat's learned snag-based meta-control, and fixed-structure SME/ACME or rule search. Use ambiguous-grouping relational analogies with held-out transformations. Charge representation size, rule-application count, backtracking/search time and transferred edits. The narrow claim is falsified if learned edit/control policies do not transfer beyond the training grammar, or if a fixed Sifter rule set or deterministic rule search matches accuracy/cost. Sifter makes the experiment more concrete but lowers architecture novelty; keep HY-88 demoted.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — homeokinesis and time-loop sensorimotor control (AR-104; 2001–2020)

**Question:** did intrinsic sensorimotor control disappear because it lacked modern compute, or because a self-organizing drive does not by itself guarantee useful task behavior?

- **Original mechanism and unit.** Der's homeokinetic principle closes an adaptive loop between a robot controller and an internal sensorimotor model. The model learns next-state prediction from prediction error. The controller is updated from a time-loop / postdiction error: after observing the next sensory state, the system asks whether the preceding sensory state can be reconstructed through the inverse learned dynamics. The controller adapts toward a balance between predictable effects and sensitivity of actions to sensory inputs. In the author's account, a forward-predictive model alone required an externally supplied activity drive; a retrospective model could develop activity through symmetry breaking and fluctuation amplification. The state is continuous sensor and motor history, controller/model parameters and body-environment dynamics, not symbols or facts. Repeated computation is closed-loop action, prediction, postdiction and local parameter adaptation. [Der, author description of homeokinesis](https://www.informatik.uni-leipzig.de/~der/Forschung/homeoki.html); [Der & Martius, *Self-organized control for musculoskeletal robots* (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.02990).
- **Input, output and learning/inference.** Input is a live sensor stream and the robot's own recent actions; output is motor commands that generate coherent, changing sensorimotor behavior. There is no external answer-decoding stage or task label in the basic rule. Model parameters minimize ordinary sensory prediction error; controller parameters descend the time-loop objective, using the learned local dynamics/Jacobian. A 2016 musculoskeletal-arm paper reports spontaneous object-affordance behavior: shaking a half-filled bottle to excite water motion and driving an attached pendulum into circular motion. Memory resides in the controller and predictor parameters plus the robot's physical dynamics. Learning continues online after deployment.
- **Historical bottleneck and what changed.** This was not simply born before usable robotics: a 2001 paper demonstrated a situated behavior measure and learning dynamics on Khepera robots; the 2016 work shows simulated musculoskeletal interaction. The core online matrix updates are lightweight and do not require large datasets or GPUs. Modern simulators, tactile/proprioceptive sensing, differentiable/system-identification tools and pretrained perception can broaden the available sensory state, and deeper recurrence can increase behavioral repertoire. They do not solve the objective mismatch between internal predictability/sensitivity and an externally useful goal, nor the need to stabilize a controller that changes its own training distribution. [Der (2001), primary publisher record](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1431761304700385).
- **Modernization already exists.** DIAMOND (2020) directly stacks homeokinetic controller/model loops into deep recurrent layers; neighboring layers adapt together and spontaneous activity in higher levels can drive lower layers. Its evaluations are simple simulated wheeled/spherical robots: coverage of a 10×10 arena stays below 50%; inner activity decays on flat terrain, and the authors state that the task set is too simple to generalize conclusions to complex environments. Thus a proposed “homeokinesis but deeper” revival is occupied and existing evidence is narrow. A 2011 open paper on guided self-organization already biases behavior using rewards, teaching signals or motor symmetries while retaining the intrinsic exploration process; an actor-critic/homeokinetic exploration combination is also published. [Smith et al., *The DIAMOND Model* (2020)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurorobotics/articles/10.3389/fnbot.2020.00062/full); [Martius & Herrmann, guided self-organization (2011)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1471-2202-12-S1-P149); [Smith & Herrmann, *Homeokinetic Reinforcement Learning* (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-28258-4_9).
- **Strength, failure and applicability.** A plausible niche is unsupervised sensorimotor bootstrapping for robots whose body/object dynamics are informative, especially compliant or redundant bodies where action reveals affordances. It can generate exploratory actions without a hand-authored reward. But an internally coherent trajectory can be irrelevant to the task, unstable, repetitive or chaotic; it may continue exploring after the task is solved. Performance depends on model/controller learning-rate ratio and body feedback; the prediction/postdiction gradients can be sensitive to imperfect local inverses and sensor delay. Exploration is not equivalent to coverage of task-relevant states. Hardware offers a natural prior and an operational objective; the same mechanism on an abstract digital agent may not have meaningful embodiment.
- **Closest work and novelty.** Homeokinesis is an established named learning/control architecture, and its deep hierarchy, reward/teacher guidance and RL exploration integrations are direct prior art. Novelty as a new broad model class: **0/5**. Historical hardware was sufficient for basic physical experiments; richer modern sensing/simulation is an extension opportunity rather than an explanation for why the architecture was not broadly adopted. The enduring question is usefulness and stability under task constraints, not raw scalability.
- **Small falsifiable CPU experiment (utility, not novelty).** Simulate a continuous differential-drive robot with range/proprioceptive input. After intrinsic warm-up, change one wheel's gain and surface friction; then give all methods the same short-horizon goal-reaching tasks and interaction budget. Compare time-loop homeokinetic exploration, action-energy-matched temporally correlated noise, forward-model learning-progress/RND exploration, and a simple homeostatic prediction-error controller. Measure controllable-state coverage, held-out goal success per interaction, recovery after the dynamics shift, action energy, unstable/oscillatory time and sensitivity over learning-rate seeds. Falsify the useful-exploration claim if homeokinesis fails to improve reusable state coverage or goal acquisition at matched action/interactions, or works only in a narrow hand-tuned rate range. CPU-only small simulation is appropriate; no GPU was used or experiment run.

#### HY-97 — homeokinesis × deep hierarchy/reward learning (reject as a new hybrid)

- **Source mechanisms and exact coupling.** Basic homeokinesis co-adapts a sensorimotor controller and predictor so time-loop postdiction error shapes the controller's exploration. DIAMOND couples such units recursively: each layer's controller treats lower-layer states as its sensor stream, predicts their consequences, and can generate spontaneous activity that drives the layer beneath it. Guided self-organization separately adds reward/teaching/symmetry signals that bias rather than replace the self-organized behavior manifold; homeokinetic reinforcement learning adds an exploration controller to an actor-critic learning path.
- **Why this is a real interaction but not novel.** The deep loops alter the source of activity across temporal/representational levels, while weak reward/teaching can constrain intrinsic behavior. This is more than a frozen front end attached to an unrelated policy. However, DIAMOND and the 2011 guided/RL papers already publish these couplings. “Homeokinesis + deep model,” “homeokinesis + goal reward,” and “homeokinesis + actor-critic exploration” are all occupied at the broad mechanism level.
- **Likely advantages and failure modes.** The coupled controller may generate coherent body-dependent exploration and let a task objective bias it into a useful region. It may instead wander, become unstable, spend motor energy without task-relevant coverage, or require carefully hand-tuned intrinsic/extrinsic learning-rate balance. Deeper activity can vanish where lower levels already predict sensory input, as DIAMOND reports.
- **Cheap disproof.** Use the same actuator-shift robot task as AR-104 and compare DIAMOND-style hierarchy, guided homeokinesis, ordinary homeokinesis and actor-critic/random exploration at matched interactions, action energy and tuning budget. Falsify a claimed synergy if the combination cannot improve held-out goal acquisition or shift recovery over whichever component is strongest, or if gains disappear after tuning costs and energy are charged.
- **Disposition:** reject broad hybrid novelty; keep the homeokinesis utility study only as an embodied-control benchmark.

The finding is a useful correction to “born too early”: the mechanism reached physical robots quickly; general utility, not compute, is the enduring problem.

#### HY-59 correction — interactive dual-reservoir chunking (2018) is another direct neighbor

AR-82 already records Asabuki, Hiratani & Fukai's *Interactive Reservoir Computing for Chunking Information Streams*; this is now cross-referenced here because it directly narrows the sequence-chunker × fast-weight hybrid. Their “dual RC” has two non-identical, fixed recurrent reservoirs receiving the same sequence. Each reservoir's FORCE-trained readout teaches the other; the pair's mutual prediction synchronizes selectively to recurring temporal chunks without an external chunk label. It explicitly handles streams where ordinary transition-probability segmentation fails, with letter and visual sequences. [Asabuki et al., primary open paper (2018)](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006400).

This is not a key-value memory: the learned readout/feedback dynamics become chunk-selective, while the reservoir wiring is fixed. Its source also documents constraints that compute alone may not remove: chunk learning needs a modest amount of input noise (none can leave the system at an arbitrary-feature solution; too much destroys chunk response); beyond a chunk size around 10 the measured correlation declined in the tested configuration, and increasing reservoir size beyond roughly 200 did not reliably improve the chunk signal. Therefore the sequence-chunking part is not an unexplored primitive waiting to be paired with memory. Any further event-scale addressable-storage claim should include dual-RC chunking, Humaidan's surprise-gated context router, Titans/MIRAS and Gated DeltaNet as distinct baselines; exact API semantics and memory budget must be matched. Keep HY-59 as a low-priority methods comparison, novelty confidence below 0.5/5, and do not add a candidate.

#### HY-98 — XCS rules over learned predictive tests for aliased control (demote; memory-XCS and PSR mechanisms are close)

**Complementary source mechanisms.** XCS supplies a population of condition–action classifiers with payoff predictions, accuracy-based fitness and genetic rule discovery. A predictive-state representation (PSR) describes hidden state by predictions of future action–observation tests. A tentative coupling would let rules condition on a compact predictive vector; when distinct histories matched by one rule lead to different futures/actions, an active distinguishing test could be added and only affected rule conditions split/refined. This could let a rule population add exactly the future experiment needed to separate an aliased situation instead of appending the same fixed-width observation/action history everywhere.

**Closest prior art closes the broad seam.** XCS with memory conditions adds a message list recording sensory history, attaches memory conditions to some classifiers, and detects non-Markov states; recursive PSXCS spawns subordinate XCS systems with history windows only where more history is needed. Earlier GLS treats classifier systems as model-free POMDP learners; ACSM and ACSMr add internal memory and aliased-state detection to anticipatory rule systems. Separately, PSR learning/planning already learns an action-conditioned predictive model directly from action–observation sequences and plans in it; spectral PSR models can be gradient-refined under model mismatch. These methods occupy classifier rules plus selective history/state memory and PSR state plus control. They do not establish the exact per-rule dynamically grown test bank proposed here, but the remaining idea may simply be an explicit-state feature representation fed into a rule learner. [Zang et al., memory-condition XCS (2012)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.0424); [Hamzeh et al., recursive PSXCS (2009)](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3233/FI-2009-191); [Boots et al., PSR learning and planning (2009)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.2385); [Jiang et al., PSR gradient refinement (AAAI 2016)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/10270).

**How behavior might change, and why it may fail.** Per-rule tests could provide interpretable, local state discrimination and avoid giving all classifiers the same long history. But test discovery requires interventions; uninformative actions leave hidden states indistinguishable. A shared predictive vector may be simpler and already sufficient. Rule/test cross-products can explode, multiple valid PSR bases may be poorly conditioned, and evolutionary generalization may undo condition refinement. No broad AI architecture novelty follows.

**Small falsifiable experiment.** Use a symbolic key-door maze with visually identical locations whose correct action depends on a hidden switch and one mid-run transition reversal. Compare ordinary XCS, memory-condition XCS, RPSXCS, a fixed PSR plus planner, and the per-rule adaptive-test version. Match population size, experience, memory bytes, action/measurement budget and planning work; expose all systems to the same possible probe actions. Measure success, environment steps, test/rule counts, memory growth, held-out transfer and samples to recover after reversal. Falsify any utility claim if local test growth does not reduce experience or rule count versus RPSXCS / fixed PSR at the same budget, or if gains disappear under informative but cost-matched probes. This is CPU-only and currently not run.

**Disposition:** reject the generic XCS × PSR hybrid as novel (class novelty **0/5**). Preserve per-rule predictive-test discovery only as a low-priority comparison, confidence **1/5**; its further work is justified only if the costed maze experiment can be implemented using a source-grounded PSR learner and exact memory-XCS baselines.

#### HY-59 prior-art correction — HAT (2020) and HARN (2026) close the broad event-memory seam

A direct reread of Chien & Honey's HAT paper narrows the event-scale chunker proposal further. HAT stacks local “autoencoder-in-time” units. Each compresses current input together with its local context, reconstructs that pair, and uses local reconstruction error/surprise to gate both context integration and the information passed upward. Levels have different intrinsic time constants; the stack is feed-forward between levels with recurrent local context. HAT was developed to account for neural temporal-context construction/forgetting data and gives surprise-sensitive temporal grouping, though it is not an external key-value store, and the paper does not demonstrate a broad task-learning architecture. This is a direct computational predecessor for surprise-gated hierarchical context construction, not just a conceptual neighbor. [Chien & Honey, *Neuron* (2020), full author manuscript](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7244383/).

The 20 September 2026 arXiv preprint HARN makes the remaining generic coupling even less distinct. HARN keeps a persistent state and gated matrix-valued associative memory per time scale; a level's persistent state/memory is overwritten only when that level's completed-bar event fires. A key/value retrieval residual called “surprise” scales a bounded outer-product memory write. States then interact through same-event cross-scale resonance and a directional lower-to-higher evidence path. This occupies the combination of asynchronous per-level persistent memory, residual/surprise-dependent associative writes, and cross-scale temporal communication in a concrete domain. Its authors explicitly frame the contribution as an event-driven state-transition protocol with one neural parameterization, rather than universal superiority or novelty of each component. [Saidd, *HARN* (arXiv:2609.26822v1, 20 Sep 2026)](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.26822v1).

There is a domain distinction: HARN's update events are supplied completed-bar timestamps, not boundaries learned from unconstrained sensory sequences. But HAT already has locally surprise-gated hierarchical temporal context, while Titans/MIRAS/Gated DeltaNet cover surprise-sensitive test-time associative memory, and the 2018 dual-reservoir model directly learns unsupervised sequence chunks. The proposed sequence-chunker × fast-weight idea therefore does not currently support a distinct broad mechanism. The only remaining testable residue is whether *learned* boundary lifetimes provide better delayed-binding retrieval across a context reversal than established surprise-memory or chunking baselines; call this a narrow methods hypothesis, not an architecture candidate, and set novelty confidence effectively to 0/5.

HARN's empirical comparison is not a utility result for this hypothesis: its PatchTST/TimeXer baselines see only the anchor-timeframe inputs and use different targets and training protocols, whereas HARN sees all timeframes. The paper labels that comparison descriptive. A zero-change persistence baseline is listed as required but unreported; its ablation variants are single-run observations with configuration/provenance caveats; and inactive levels' candidate encoders are still computed, so masking preserves state but does not establish computation savings. A static source audit is not an experimental leakage test. These caveats do not undermine HARN as a protocol specification; they limit performance/speed claims. [HARN, §§1, 3–6, 8–10](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.26822v1).

**Disposition / minimum useful test.** Preserve the semi-Markov recurring-motif + rare delayed key/value binding + abrupt context-reversal test only as a low-priority controlled comparison. Match memory bytes, reads, writes, and update FLOPs across (i) fixed-lifetime chunk table, (ii) a chunker-only learner, (iii) surprise-gated associative memory in the Titans/MIRAS family, and (iv) event-lifetime-gated delta writes. Include dual-RC and HAT-inspired hierarchical context baselines. Reject utility if event-lifetime writes do not improve delayed binding after reversal at equal resources, or if any gain comes from extra retained bytes/writes. No experiment was run.

#### Exploratory primitive scan — continuation paths, topological defects, and renormalization (negative results)

A fresh invention scan tested three mechanisms against primary literature and the existing candidate ledger. None survives as a new broad architecture class; the ideas remain valid specialist methods and may be useful as component-level research.

- **Solution-path continuation as state.** The imagined unit was a point/tangent on a branch of solutions indexed by a task parameter; inference for a nearby task would continue the branch, with explicit branch-point handling. Homotopy continuation has long been used to optimize neural networks, the 2019 Homotopy Training Algorithm grows a neural network along a continuous path, and the 2023 Continuation Path Learning paper trains a model to represent the whole path of intermediate solutions. The broad computational primitive is therefore established as an optimization/training procedure, not a distinct deployed model class. A possible narrow CPU probe is smooth parameter drift plus an intentional bifurcation, comparing pseudo-arclength continuation with warm-start gradient descent, online Newton and MAML at equal derivative/function evaluations; do not pursue unless branch memory adds value beyond standard continuation cost. [Chen & Hao, HTA (2019)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6894535/); [Lin et al., Continuation Path Learning (ICML 2023)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/lin23n.html).
- **Topological-defect/event processor.** The proposed primitive was an incrementally updated cycle/cavity, with birth/death scale retained as a bounded event summary. Differentiable persistent-homology layers, topology-aware objectives, topological graph/cell-complex networks, streaming persistence and online topology-inference methods already cover the core operations. The notebook's Topological Workspace candidate is also an internal collision. Modern hardware may lower throughput cost but does not create the missing general task representation or establish a novel learning law. Only consider the point-stream shape-change probe as a domain-specific comparison of early detection/storage against static persistent homology and adaptive-map baselines. [Gabrielsson et al., *A Topology Layer for Machine Learning* (AISTATS 2020)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v108/gabrielsson20a.html); [streaming persistent homology](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00454-018-0030-0); [online graph-topology inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.03653).
- **Task-preserving renormalization machine.** The proposed unit was a learned coarse-graining map plus its induced effective dynamics; inference would move across scales while task predictions or actions remained invariant. This is a real and growing scientific-model family, but direct modern precedents include the variational-RG/deep-learning mapping, neural Monte Carlo RG, and a 2026 scale-shared neural RG flow for percolation that extrapolates from small lattices. This makes it an excellent physics-specialist architecture direction, but not a general-class novelty claim. A CPU falsifier could test crossing-probability and spanning-cluster transfer from small to larger percolation lattices against fixed block averaging, CNN pooling and graph coarsening at matched compute; no such experiment ran. [Mehta & Schwab, variational RG and deep learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3831); [Chung & Kao, neural Monte Carlo RG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.05703); [Alvez et al., *Neural Renormalization Group Flow for Percolation* (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26764).

#### HY-98 prior-art closure update — rule-local adaptive history and online PSR test discovery

A closer historical hit substantially closes the remaining “grow a discriminator only where a rule needs it” idea. In **XCS-SL** (2014), each classifier carries a variable-length condition over past time steps; evolutionary mutation can grow or shrink its own history length, and fitness-based selection favors useful history sizes. The authors demonstrate a layered multiplexer benchmark and activity-of-daily-living sequence labeling. This is a direct predecessor for rule-local, adaptive temporal context allocation, although its memory entries are past input conditions rather than PSR probabilities for future action–observation tests. [XCS-SL, *Classifier Systems for Sequence Labeling* (GECCO 2014 paper)](https://www.cmap.polytechnique.fr/~nikolaus.hansen/proceedings/2014/GECCO/proceedings/p565.pdf).

The earlier TCS (2002) also addresses perceptual aliasing with time-dependent classifier conditions and temporal tags: the current perception can be linked to preceding information, and conditions can use variable temporal length; its reported demonstrations are POMDP maze tasks. AXCSM (2005) is another named adaptive XCSM extension proposing variable-length memory, but the accessible abstract is thin; retain it as a bibliographic lead rather than overstate its exact update law. [Fukuyori, Hara & Nagao, TCS (2002), DOI 10.1541/ieejeiss1987.122.7_1218](https://doi.org/10.1541/ieejeiss1987.122.7_1218); [Liu & Nagao, AXCSM (2005), DOI 10.1007/11539902_69](https://doi.org/10.1007/11539902_69).

On the PSR side, McCracken & Bowling's NeurIPS 2005 constrained-gradient learner already discovers core tests online from a stream and updates PSR predictions. Its own limitations are relevant: a poorly conditioned prediction matrix or bad core-test additions can prevent new tests from being selected, and authors identify removal of dependent tests and schedule changes as future work. This leaves a specific *coupling implementation*—which local test to activate for which classifier—and possible efficiency gains, not an unoccupied broad adaptive-test mechanism. [McCracken & Bowling, *Online Discovery and Learning of Predictive State Representations* (NeurIPS 2005)](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2005/file/c3008b2c6f5370b744850a98a95b73ad-Paper.pdf).

**Revised disposition.** HY-98 remains rejected as a new hybrid. Novelty confidence for the class is **0/5**; method-level residue is now **0–0.5/5** and means only an explicit local allocation rule layered over established adaptive-history classifiers and global PSR test discovery. The exact PSR/per-classifier construction remains unverified, but exact-PSR sufficiency makes a local test bank redundant for predictive correctness; its only credible value is compute/storage allocation or rule interpretability. A test is worthwhile only if it can beat XCS-SL/AXCSM/TCS, memory-XCS, RPSXCS and fixed/global online PSR on aliasing while matching probe actions, experience, memory bytes and rule count. Falsify if the adaptive local bank buys accuracy only with more observations, rules, or stored tests. No experiment ran.

Cross-reference for HY-59: **Worth Remembering** (June 2026 arXiv) adds a separate direct application of Bayesian-surprise-gated episodic writes in a V-JEPA-2 latent space, coupled to 4D scene-graph memory for robot QA and event segmentation. It is external episodic storage, not a fast-weight delta-rule memory; it strengthens the claim that surprise-selective memory formation is broadly occupied without erasing that implementation distinction. This paper is already in the memory/robotics hybrid scan, so no candidate is added. [Gorlo et al., *Worth Remembering* (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03787).

#### Archaeology correction — Truth Maintenance Systems already encode control in assumptions; repair hybrid folds into PDL/CEGIS

The symbolic-architecture audit sharpens the historical interpretation of Doyle's 1979 TMS. The primary abstract explicitly includes dependency-directed backtracking, revising models of other reasoners' belief systems, and embedding control structures in patterns of assumptions. The TMS was presented as a problem-solver subsystem for a reasoner that must act on limited information and later revise assumptions after contradiction; it was not merely a passive explanation log. This closes the temptation to describe assumption-conditioned reasoning control as a new primitive. [Doyle, *A Truth Maintenance System*, MIT AI Memo 521 (1979), primary archive](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/5377b306-4ecc-4687-b1f5-78cbb4a0543a).

HEARSAY-II likewise had distributed independent knowledge sources, a hierarchical shared hypothesis blackboard, and a scheduler that prioritized pending knowledge-source activities by estimated usefulness. This further closes generic “learned blackboard focus of control” hybrids already rejected in HY-04/HY-37/HY-38. [Erman et al., *The Hearsay-II Speech-Understanding System* (1980), primary paper](https://mas.cs.umass.edu/Documents/Erman_Hearsay80.pdf). General-purpose belief maintenance also already extends TMS dependency updates from true/false/unknown to graded, infinite-valued beliefs. Worst-case nonmonotonic TMS inference is NP-complete; more hardware helps typical bookkeeping but cannot remove the combinatorics of alternative belief supports. [Chesñevar et al., *Towards a General-Purpose Belief Maintenance System* (2013)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.3084); [Elkan, *A Rational Reconstruction of Nonmonotonic Truth Maintenance Systems* (1990)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(90)90086-F).

The proposed patch-proposer × TMS coupling—each repair hypothesis as an assumption, counterexamples as nogoods, retract only dependent edits while caching unaffected subproofs—has useful systems semantics but is already subsumed by notebook HY-13's dependency/provenance maintenance and the established CEGIS/verifier loop. No new candidate is added. If ever evaluated, compare against chronological restart and incremental SMT/CEGIS on interacting patches at equal proposal and verifier budgets; measure verified fixes, repeated subproofs, verifier calls, support-graph growth, and runtime. Reject if localized rollback does not reduce repeated work or if dependency labels cost more than recomputation. This is a low-priority software-engineering comparison, not an architecture class.

#### HY-98 / HY-59 wording correction — canonical mechanism for AXCSM and *Worth Remembering*

Springer's 2005 AXCSM abstract provides the exact canonical mechanism: a first XCS tier learns a suitable history-register length for a position, and a second XCSM tier chooses an action using that memory. Describe it as per-position adaptive memory selection, not confidently as per-rule PSR-test adaptation; a related JSAI domestic abstract uses the more rule-focused wording, but the Springer paper is the precise source for this version. [Liu & Nagao, Springer ICNC 2005 chapter](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/11539902_69). XCS-SL (GECCO 2014) separately evolves variable-length temporal conditions per classifier. Together with TCS and online global PSR core-test discovery, these are strong occupation of the generic local-history allocation idea while leaving the exact PSR-feature graft unverified.

The v3 (6 June 2026) *Worth Remembering* paper specifically computes causal overlapping V-JEPA-2 latent windows, fits a local diagonal-Gaussian prediction model, gates writes using a robust median/MAD threshold on surprise, and stores sparse event records (including temporal/pose context) in a 4D scene graph for downstream retrieval. It is an external episodic record system; it is not a learned associative fast-weight write or delta-rule consolidation mechanism. Its authors report robot QA and event-boundary results but list the Gaussian surrogate for causality and temporal retrieval as limitations. Preserve this distinction when listing it as surprise-gated memory prior art. [Gorlo et al., v3 full paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.03787v3).
