#### Old-architecture archaeology — reward-modulated eligibility plasticity / three-factor learning (AR-105; 1982–2026)

**Original computation.** In a three-factor rule, a synapse's pre/post activity leaves a temporary local eligibility trace; a third signal arriving later (reward, prediction error, or teaching signal) decides whether and in which direction that eligible change becomes a weight update. Florian's 2007 modulated-STDP paper explicitly stores a decaying trace of recent pre/post spike pairings at each synapse so delayed reward can still modify the associated connection. It demonstrates rate- and temporal-code XOR plus target-firing-pattern learning in small integrate-and-fire simulations. The unit is a synapse with local trace state; the repeated operation is spike-pair trace update followed by modulator-gated weight change; persistent knowledge is in weights, transient credit is in traces. [Florian, *Neural Computation* (2007)](https://direct.mit.edu/neco/article/19/6/1468/7190/Reinforcement-Learning-Through-Modulation-of-Spike); [author PDF](https://www.florian.io/papers/2007_Florian_Modulated_STDP.pdf).

**Born too early?** Only partly. The core hypothesis and toy demonstrations did not require GPU-scale training, so lack of modern compute does not explain the absence of broad deployment. Modern accelerators, autodiff, meta-learning, event simulators and neuromorphic chips reduce engineering and online trace-computation costs. But the difficult issues are structural: a single global reward/modulator is a weak credit signal in a large network; trace state/update traffic scales with plastic synapses; long delays require slowly decaying traces that interfere across episodes; and strong performance often reintroduces nonlocal error information or expensive outer-loop training. Technology has softened the cost, not removed the credit and trace-interference limits.

**Modern revivals and collisions.** E-prop factorizes recurrent-network gradients into forward-computed local eligibility traces and neuron-specific learning signals, approximating the learning signal to obtain online updates; it is a direct modern treatment of three-factor credit, evaluated on tasks including TIMIT. Differentiable plasticity meta-trains Hebbian plasticity coefficients in networks with millions of parameters and supports rapid post-training adaptation, but its plasticity rule is optimized using gradient descent. Meta-SpikePropamine jointly optimizes a plastic SNN and modulatory SNN with an outer BPTT loop for delayed-reward cue association, making a learned modulatory controller × eligibility trace hybrid prior art. Synaptic tagging-and-capture models extend the time scale from seconds-long credit to hours-long consolidation in recurrent spiking networks. In 2026, Vassallo & Taherinejad add online synaptic- and axonal-delay parameters to e-prop-like three-factor rules; this directly occupies learning temporal delays alongside weights. NeuMoSync (2026 preprint) further occupies input-conditioned neuron-specific modulation of effective weights/activations for continual learning, though it is a conventional backprop-trained deep network rather than a classical trace-based SNN. [e-prop](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=SkxJ4QKIIS); [differentiable plasticity](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/miconi18a.html); [Meta-SpikePropamine](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2023.1183321/full); [synaptic tagging/capture model](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7977149/); [online three-factor delay learning (2026)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1814505/full); [NeuMoSync (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04358).

**Hybridization verdict.** “Reward-modulated STDP × eligibility,” “local trace × learned global modulator,” “eligibility × backpropagation/error,” and “eligibility × learnable temporal delay” are all already represented by the papers above, plus error-triggered three-factor updates/ETLP elsewhere in this notebook. No new hybrid survives from combining old plasticity with modern optimization or hardware. Modernization helps execution but does not make the rule family a new architecture class.

**Possible narrow utility question and falsifier (not novelty).** On CPU, use a small recurrent rate/spiking network on a delayed cue-integration stream with distractors and episode remapping. Compare terminal reward without traces, fixed-decay three-factor eligibility, e-prop-style local trace + teaching signal, and a small BPTT recurrent baseline; optionally add the 2026 learnable-delay update only after reproducing its published mechanism. Match parameter count, stream exposure, reward timing, update FLOPs and memory bytes, and report prequential reward, adaptation time, trace/weight storage, forgetting and sensitivity to delay/decay. Falsify practical value if traces do not outperform no-trace learning at long delays, or if any gain over BPTT fails to compensate for its update/trace cost, weak credit assignment or tuning sensitivity. This is a bounded utility replication only; no experiment was run.

**Disposition:** established local-learning mechanism with active modern descendants; partly enabled by current tooling, but not merely a pre-GPU idea. Novelty confidence **0/5** for a model class and **0/5** for generic three-factor hybrids. Keep as archaeology and as an optional neuromorphic/online-learning baseline. No GPU experiment was planned or run; browser/CPU literature only, attributable GPU use and peak VRAM 0 GB, occupancy and Claude sharing unknown. Only `Codex_Research.md` was edited.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — artificial neuron–astrocyte networks / slow contextual switchboard (AR-106; 2011–2026)

**Old mechanism and history.** Artificial neuron–glia networks date back at least to Porto-Pazos et al. (2011): artificial astrocytes sense patterns of neuronal connection activity and adjust synaptic connections, and evolutionary experiments compare neuron-only vs neuron-glia multilayer classifiers on four classification problems. The reported gain was problem- and network-dependent, particularly for test accuracy; this early work did not establish a general replacement for neural networks. Computational astrocyte models already covered calcium dynamics, tripartite synapses, network signaling and plasticity, so the idea was being modeled before large modern accelerators. [Porto-Pazos et al. (2011), primary full text](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0019109); [Manninen et al. review of calcium-mediated astrocyte models (2018)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/computational-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fncom.2018.00014/full).

**Mechanism revisited.** The most specific architecture is Vedovati et al.'s 14 September 2026 preprint. A slow astrocyte-like recurrent module updates once per trial from the previous context/action and reward; its output selects a low-rank, spatially tiled modulation of the effective recurrent weights in a fast neuron-like RNN. The fast network performs an inner delayed-match-to-sample task; its reward also informs the slow module. Both are trained offline (low-level supervised learning and high-level A2C/GAE), but at deployment the learned parameters are fixed. Under latent changes among four stimulus-response contexts, the slow dynamics accumulate reward prediction errors. Reward-conditioned bifurcations move attractors, and stochastic reward omission plus attractor shallowness produces entropy-dependent “stickiness” before switching. This gives a concrete hybrid automaton: continuous slow-state motion, then a discrete context/action change that retunes fast dynamics. [Vedovati et al., *A neural-astrocyte architecture implements a hybrid automaton for evidence accumulation* (arXiv:2609.16217v1)](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.16217).

**Was it too early?** Better simulation, differentiable training, multi-timescale sequence models and modern RL make it easier to study such coupled dynamics. But raw compute is not the main missing capability. The old design was already feasible on small multilayer problems; lingering limits are the uncertain abstraction of astrocyte signaling, task-specific controller/reward wiring, slow integration and context-switch lag, and difficulty proving a useful capability beyond an RNN with explicit hidden state. The 2026 model itself evaluates only instances drawn from one parameterized hierarchical task family and points to cross-family transfer/meta-learning as future work. Its monolithic policy-gradient RNN control struggles in that exact setup, but a Bayesian change-point detector, explicit context posterior, recurrent meta-RL, or matched hypernetwork controller would be stronger tests of whether the biological partition is necessary. The 2026 authors explicitly say their deployed learned policy does not adapt its parameters per se; it embeds fixed parameters that respond to inputs. [Vedovati et al., §§II–IV](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.16217).

**Modernization and nearest architecture collisions.** AstroNet (CVPR 2023) already uses a learned astrocyte network to adaptively reweight neuron connections for network-structure learning and classification; it is a structure-learning analogue, not the same RL context-switching mechanism. A 2022 Physical Review Research paper studies a neuron–astrocyte associative-memory model in which multiplicative noise and astrocytic coupling induce pattern loading/storage/retrieval. A 2023 contextually guided/meta-plasticity model from the 2026 authors and earlier work precede the specific slow-fast design. Thus “add astrocytes to a neural network,” “astrocytes choose/sparsify connections,” “astrocytes store associative memories,” and “slow glial state guides neural context” are all directly occupied. [Han et al., *AstroNet* (CVPR 2023)](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2023/papers/Han_AstroNet_When_Astrocyte_Meets_Artificial_Neural_Network_CVPR_2023_paper.pdf); [Ermolaeva et al., *Noise-induced artificial intelligence* (Phys. Rev. Research 2022)](https://journals.aps.org/prresearch/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevResearch.4.043069); [Gong et al., *Astrocytes as a mechanism for contextually-guided network dynamics and function* (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012186).

**Strongest useful advantage / failure modes.** A slow, spatially tiled control network may protect long-timescale task evidence from being overwritten by fast task execution, and sparse local glial communication might coordinate distributed modules. But hysteresis can become stubborn perseveration; noisy reward omissions can cause false context switching; a low-rank discrete switch may fail when contexts overlap or blend continuously; fast/slow credit assignment can be difficult; and performance may come from added parameters or task-informed modularization rather than astrocytic dynamics. Biological plausibility is not itself utility for artificial tasks. Current evidence does not show generally better continual learning, sample efficiency, or inference cost.

**Hybrid disposition.** The old neuron–glia mechanism coupled with modern A2C, low-rank hypernetwork modulation, and timescale-separated recurrence is now explicitly instantiated in the 2026 preprint. This is a real interaction, but not an open generic hybrid. Novelty confidence: **0/5 for a broad model class; 0/5 for the generic slow-modulator × fast-network mechanism**. Retain AR-106 as useful specialist-model archaeology and a candidate baseline for latent-context control.

**Small falsifiable CPU utility experiment (not run).** Reconstruct a compact four-context bandit/task with stochastic feedback and variable context dwell times. Compare slow-astrocyte low-rank modulation against (1) parameter-matched monolithic RNN, (2) explicit Bayesian/change-point context inference plus the same fast controller, (3) GRU/meta-RL with an equivalent hidden-state budget, and (4) a low-rank hypernetwork without slow/astrocyte-specific dynamics. Match experience, hidden-state/parameter count where possible, reward, optimizer/tuning budget and inference operations. Sweep unseen dwell-time distributions, overlapping contexts, false reward omission rate and local-network connection loss. Measure cumulative reward/regret, context posterior accuracy, delay/false-switch rate, forgetting and wall-clock/update work. Falsify a useful astrocyte-specific claim if the explicit Bayesian or hypernetwork baseline matches switching and transfer at equal budget, or if the slow module gains only on the training volatility distribution. A biology claim additionally needs experimentally grounded signaling and timescale constraints; a task simulation cannot establish that biology.

Resource: browser and notebook analysis only; no code or experiment ran. GPU use and attributable peak VRAM 0 GB; no GPU snapshot was taken because a GPU run was not imminent, so current occupancy/Claude usage remain unknown. Only `Codex_Research.md` was edited.

#### AR-106 addendum — astrocyte-gated eligibility is now directly occupied (2026)

**Direct prior art.** Dong & He’s *Astrocyte-Gated Multi-Timescale Plasticity* (AGMP), published 27 January 2026, closes the generic slow-astrocyte × eligibility-trace × teaching-signal combination more directly than the earlier three-factor and neuron–astrocyte papers did. In a deep SNN, a synapse-local eligibility trace is multiplied by a broadcast error signal and a postsynaptic-neuron astrocyte-like slow activity state. The activity state is normalized within its layer and passed through a sigmoid to gate updates; a homeostatic bias update is an additional mechanism. The implementation uses LIF/ALIF units and fixed random feedback matrices for hidden-layer errors, with surrogate-gradient-derived eligibility. This is a learned online plasticity rule inside an SNN, not a distinct general model class. [Dong & He (2026), full article](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2025.1768235/full), especially §§3–4.

**What “born too early?” resolves to.** Modern tools help with direct training, event-stream benchmarks, recurrent SNNs and efficiency reporting, but AGMP does not establish that the underlying idea was blocked only by old hardware. It uses a broadcast teaching/error signal and surrogate-gradient machinery; its full update is not purely local. The stated constant temporal-memory property means memory does not grow with sequence length: state still scales with synapses for eligibility and neurons for astrocyte variables, in addition to parameters. Its own analysis says the gate is driven by local activity/load, while the task error is broadcast. Thus this is a practical metaplasticity rule, not a new autonomous learning substrate.

**Evidence and limits.** The paper reports 80.1% on SHD and 31.4% average accuracy on 10-task Split CIFAR-100 (with 55.7% forgetting), versus GEM’s reported 45.2% CIFAR-100 average accuracy; the no-gate ablation drops Split N-MNIST from 82.6% to 51.3%, while changing SHD only from 80.1% to 79.5%. That task-specific ablation is evidence that the gate matters more for the reported continual-learning setting than for static temporal recognition. But the cross-paper benchmark table alone is not enough to establish matched protocols or reproducibility: architecture/data-processing and training budgets for each imported baseline are not fully enumerated next to results, no public implementation link was found in the article, and reported memory is not independent of synapse count. Treat the gains as a published result to reproduce, not settled proof of a general advantage. The authors themselves leave global error broadcast as a limitation/future direction. [AGMP results and ablation tables](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2025.1768235/full#h4).

**Related 2026 convergence.** A separate April 2026 arXiv preprint combines STDP route reinforcement with astrocytic calcium transients that suppress recently visited states for partially observed grid navigation; it calls the short-term effect “Topological-Context Memory.” It occupies the broad old-STDP × slow astrocyte-memory × exploration hybrid, although results are limited to grid-world and a subset mapped to a simulated memristive crossbar. A separate April 2026 *Neurocomputing* liquid-state-machine study uses artificial astrocyte-like units for chaotic time-series prediction and reports that neuron-plus-astrocyte networks learn where either alone does not. Together with AstroNet (2023) and the slow-context A-RNN above, this makes “add slow astrocytes to modern networks” a crowded mechanism family. [Tsybina et al. (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15391); [Yang et al., *Neurocomputing* (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S092523122600202X); [AstroNet (CVPR 2023)](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2023/papers/Han_AstroNet_When_Astrocyte_Meets_Artificial_Neural_Network_CVPR_2023_paper.pdf).

**Disposition and remaining test.** Reject slow astrocyte-gated eligibility as a new model class or broad new hybrid (class novelty **0/5**; generic hybrid novelty **0/5**). Keep AGMP as a modern baseline for online continual SNN work. The smallest informative replication is CPU-first on a small event-SNN/continual task: full AGMP versus the same eligibility/error/homeostasis rule with gate removed, with matched initialization, stream order, per-synapse trace state and tuning budget; report per-task accuracy/forgetting and memory as bytes versus both sequence length and synapse count. If the gate’s advantage disappears under matched tuning or does not persist across task order/shift schedules, reject its practical value. The agent report was read, but no code or experiment was run. Browser/notebook only, attributable GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB; live occupancy and Claude sharing were not checked because GPU work was not imminent.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — dendritic computation (AR-107; 2003–2024 revivals)

**Original computation.** The two-layer pyramidal-cell hypothesis models terminal dendritic branches as nonlinear subunits whose activity combines at the trunk/soma, giving one cell more expressive computations than a point neuron. The related dendritic neuron model (DNM) is a simplified nonspiking artificial unit: nonlinear synaptic transforms feed multiplicative branch interactions, with structural pruning and a generalized delta-rule. These are not interchangeable: DNM is an engineered nonlinear unit, while multicompartment neuron models simulate constrained electrical compartments. “Hierarchical dendritic network” is not a single canonical architecture name in the audited literature. [Poirazi, Brannon & Mel (2003)](https://www.cs.jhu.edu/~ayuille1/courses/Stat271-Fall13/Poirazi_etal03b.pdf); [Todo et al. (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2014.07.011).

**Why it struggled historically and what changed.** Detailed compartmental simulation was expensive; differentiable tooling and event-driven neuromorphic hardware were immature, while local dendritic plasticity lacked a broadly useful credit signal. Modern GPU simulation, automatic differentiation, surrogate gradients and specialized simulators reduce these engineering barriers. Yet dense tensor models are highly optimized, so explicit branches can remain slower and larger; biologically constrained branch interactions limit how freely subunits can combine; and dendritic local learning still needs useful error/teaching feedback. These are not all solved by more compute.

**Modern revival and prior-art check.** Differentiable Dendritic Neural Networks (DENNs) use learned branch-local nonlinearities; basal/apical segregated compartments have been used for local deep credit assignment; detailed-neuron learning rules estimate synaptic influence from dendritic voltage/timing; DEP combines two-compartment LIF neurons with event-based learning; Dendrify makes multicompartment network simulation easier; DendSN explores deep spiking networks with nonlinear branches; and predictive coding has been implemented in dendritic compartments. These directly occupy dendrites × learned deep networks, dendrites × local credit, dendrites × event-driven SNNs and dendrites × predictive coding as general hybrid claims. They mostly show feasible mechanisms or restricted tasks, not a uniform win over parameter-matched conventional networks. [DENNs (NeurIPS 2018)](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2018/hash/e32c51ad39723ee92b285b362c916ca7-Abstract.html); [Guerguiev, Lillicrap & Richards (2017)](https://elifesciences.org/articles/22901); [local dendritic learning rule (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8691952/); [DEP (2021)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2021.601109/full); [Dendrify (2023)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-35747-8); [DendSN (2024 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06355); [dendritic predictive coding (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05303).

**What may remain, and experiment.** No new class or unoccupied generic hybrid remains. The best residue is an engineering hypothesis: under strict event sparsity and local online remapping, branch-local plasticity might improve adaptation per spike or joule enough to offset its compartment state and communication. Falsify this cheaply on CPU with a small dendritic SNN and parameter-matched point-neuron SNN on delayed temporal XOR, then remap cue-to-label associations midstream. Match the learning signal/update budget; record recovery examples, old-task retention, spike count, state bytes and runtime. If dendrites do not improve adaptation at comparable spike count and runtime, drop the branch-specific utility claim. This tests utility, not novelty. The old idea was partly early as an engineering target, but its main architectural descendants are already modernized. Worth retaining as a specialized baseline; not worth advancing as a new broad model class. No prototype/GPU experiment ran; attributable GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB and live occupancy/Claude sharing unknown.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — adaptive critic designs / approximate dynamic programming (AR-108; 1977–present)

**Original computation.** Werbos’s Heuristic Dynamic Programming (HDP) estimate of 1977 predates the modern naming of temporal-difference learning. Adaptive Critic Designs later distinguished: HDP learns a scalar cost/value critic; Dual Heuristic Programming (DHP) learns the derivative of the cost-to-go with respect to plant state; Globalized DHP (GDHP) learns both. Action-dependent versions include control action in the critic input. Common implementations add an action network and sometimes a learned plant model, so the system can update a value or value-gradient estimate from online transitions and improve a continuous controller. This is not an alternative broad model class to modern RL: it is a control-oriented approximate-dynamic-programming/actor-critic family with special critic targets and stability concerns. [Werbos (1977/1990) HDP account](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0893608090900883); [Prokhorov & Wunsch (1997), adaptive critic design families](https://doi.org/10.1109/72.623201); [ADP book chapter, critic variants](https://lisc.mae.cornell.edu/LISCpapers/ADP_Book_Chapter_03.pdf).

**Why it struggled; born too early?** Exact dynamic programming scales exponentially with state dimension, and learned critics can be inconsistent, unstable, or biased under stochastic dynamics; a differentiable/learned model can add another source of error. The 1997 review describes HDP, DHP and GDHP as distinct practical designs rather than one settled algorithm, and the 1998 stability critique documents that then-current ADP variants could lack unconditional stability or produce wrong stochastic results. Modern GPUs, autodiff, replay, simulation, safety filters and learned dynamics ease approximation and experiment costs. They do not remove the Bellman curse of dimensionality, closed-loop instability from critic/model error, or the difficulty of safe exploration in real plants. [Werbos (1998) stability critique](https://arxiv.org/abs/adap-org/9810001); [2024 ADP/RL review](https://doi.org/10.1109/JAS.2023.123843).

**Modernization and collision audit.** Adaptive critics remain active in control research, including event-triggered and continuous-time variants, neural and spline critics, and combinations with modern data-driven/RL methods. A 2024 paper, for example, already couples incremental adaptive critics with tensor-product B-spline value approximation and recursive-least-squares temporal-difference updates. Therefore “GPU-scale actor/critic,” “critic value gradients,” and “event-triggered critic updates” are occupied broad directions. A deep neural controller with a differentiable physics engine is also functionally overlapping model-based policy optimization/control rather than an unexplored architecture. The narrow distinction between value-critic and derivative-critic targets can still matter in a specific plant, but it is algorithm selection, not new class. [Feng et al. (2024), online spline adaptive critic](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0016003224007786); [Wang et al. (2024), ADP/RL review](https://doi.org/10.1109/JAS.2023.123843).

**Hybrid analysis.** ADP × neural system identification is structurally complementary: the identifier estimates plant transitions while the critic approximates future cost and the actor chooses controls. However, model-based adaptive critics and learned-dynamics control predate deep learning; adding modern neural dynamics/autodiff alone does not create a new coupling. The useful question is whether state-derivative critics provide better sample efficiency or stability margins than scalar value critics when the model is only partially learned and dynamics drift. A minimum CPU falsifier is a low-dimensional nonlinear plant with an unannounced friction/damping shift: compare HDP scalar critic, DHP derivative critic, model-based adaptive critic, and a tuned MPC or contemporary actor-critic under matched simulation interactions. Record cumulative cost, constraint violations, recovery time, critic/model error and wall-clock work. Drop the derivative-critic advantage if it does not improve the cost/stability frontier, or if its gradient estimates amplify model error after the shift.

**Disposition.** Retain as old-RL/control archaeology and a specialized baseline; reject as a genuinely new architecture class (novelty **0/5**). The family was not simply killed by weak hardware: its descendants are still used, and its hard problems are approximation and closed-loop guarantees. CPU/browser review only; no prototype ran, GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB, current occupancy and Claude share unknown because no GPU work was imminent.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — model-reference adaptation and self-tuning regulators (AR-109; 1958–1973)

**Original mechanisms.** Model-reference adaptive control (MRAC) compares a plant’s output with a desired reference-model response and updates controller parameters online to reduce tracking error. The 1961 MIT rule approximates gradient descent on squared tracking error through parameter-sensitivity signals. Self-tuning regulators (STR) instead repeatedly estimate a plant model, originally with least squares, then recompute a minimum-variance controller from the current estimate. These are feedback-control learning loops over controller/plant parameters, not general representation-learning architectures. [Whitaker, Yamron & Kezer (1958), MIT Instrumentation Laboratory report](https://books.google.com/books?id=3V-jtgAACAAJ); [MIT-rule 1961 law reanalyzed for stability](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-08-034085-2.50031-6); [Åström & Wittenmark, *On Self-Tuning Regulators* (1973), primary full text](https://lup.lub.lu.se/search/files/8888379/7017.pdf).

**Was the old idea bad or too early?** The STR paper explicitly discusses implementation on a small process computer, so the core estimate-and-retune cycle was not waiting for GPUs. Its theorem is conditional on parameter estimates converging and focuses on discrete-time SISO linear plants with fixed unknown parameters. Real impediments include persistent excitation, biased/mismatched plant models, changing delays or parameters, actuator limits and safe exploration. The MIT rule’s instability is also not simply a compute issue: the 1987 analysis shows stability depends on adaptation gain, reference-input magnitude/frequency and the plant/transfer function; the rule is not globally convergent, motivating Lyapunov redesign. Modern autodiff, fast estimation and simulation make extensions easier to test, but do not remove these system-identification and closed-loop-stability constraints. [MIT rule reanalysis](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-08-034085-2.50031-6); [2019 STR-to-RL tutorial](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.11392).

**Modern collisions and verdict.** Adaptive/MRAC systems, self-tuning and adaptive MPC, and actor-critic control are active descendants; an online identifier feeding a controller is the settled core of adaptive control. These ideas have broad practical usefulness in plants with unknown dynamics but are not new AI model classes. A CPU falsifier for claims that current methods remove old limits would use a switched second-order plant with an unmodeled pole, delay and saturation. Compare MIT-rule MRAC, Lyapunov-bounded MRAC, STR, and a safe adaptive-MPC baseline at matched actuator/risk limits; record tracking error, overshoot, constraint violations and recovery after shifts. If the simple MIT rule only works in a narrow hand-tuned regime, its historical failure was algorithmic robustness rather than insufficient compute; if STR needs unsafe excitation or a stationary plant, its favorable identification-controller coupling does not generalize. **Disposition: 0/5 novelty; retain as control-learning antecedent, no candidate.** No code/GPU experiment ran; GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB and current occupancy/Claude share unknown.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — symbiotic neuroevolution and H-ESP (AR-110; 1995–2005)

**Original computation.** SANE evolves neuron genotypes rather than only complete networks. It repeatedly samples a team from the neuron population, instantiates a network, evaluates task fitness, credits each participating neuron, and recombines the higher-ranked individuals. ESP separates roles into neuron subpopulations, improving specialist retention and enabling recurrent networks. H-ESP (2005) deeply couples two evolutionary levels: component subpopulations assemble/evolve neurons, while a level of complete networks preserves and recombines successful combinations; a better whole network can migrate its components down to the subpopulations, and improved component assemblies can enter the whole-network population. This is more than using evolution to tune one fixed network: it explicitly searches both modules and compositions. [Moriarty & Miikkulainen, primary SANE report](https://nn.cs.utexas.edu/downloads/papers/moriarty.learning-sequential.pdf); [1996 SANE journal article](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1018004120707); [Gomez & Schmidhuber, H-ESP primary paper (GECCO 2005)](https://people.idsia.ch/~tino/papers/gomez.gecco05.pdf).

**Historical bottleneck and modern change.** Evaluation throughput was a real constraint: the SANE car-sequencing experiment used 800 linear-threshold neurons, assembled 40 teams per generation and took about 40 minutes for 100 generations on an IBM RS6000 25T; its held-out 50-problem set averaged 26 search backtracks versus 85 for a domain heuristic and 781 for random ordering. The same report notes 11 hours of CPU time for a 200-generation Othello-search experiment. Modern vectorization, GPU population evaluation and cheap simulation can speed candidate evaluation. They do not solve expensive or sequential environment episodes, collaborator-dependent credit (the same component’s fitness changes with teammates), destructive competition between complementary specialists, or overfitting to the evaluation task. In two-mode pole balancing H-ESP solved 8/10 runs, ESP 6/10 and the cited RL-LSTM baseline 2/10, but this was a small old comparison and not a matched modern algorithm study. [Moriarty & Miikkulainen SANE report, pp. 6–10](https://nn.cs.utexas.edu/downloads/papers/moriarty.learning-sequential.pdf); [H-ESP, §3 and results](https://people.idsia.ch/~tino/papers/gomez.gecco05.pdf).

**Nearest prior art and hybrid judgment.** Cooperative coevolution, ESP, whole-network evolution and H-ESP already occupy component-level × whole-network-level evolution, so reimplementing this in modern simulators or adding gradient fine-tuning does not create a new hybrid. Lifetime learning smoothing fitness (the Baldwin effect) is also established; Hinton & Nowlan’s 1987 demonstration already combines lifetime plasticity with genetic search, and Ackley & Littman (1990) studied gradient learning plus evolution. New mixed population/gradient methods have extensive later descendants. [Hinton & Nowlan (1987)](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/evolution.htm); [Ackley & Littman (1990)](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/1990/file/b6f0479ae87d244975439c6124592772-Paper.pdf). **Novelty: 0/5** for SANE/ESP/H-ESP or generic module-plus-network evolution. There is a revival question, not a new architecture question.

**Small falsifier / disposition.** CPU-only delayed-cue T-mazes with 10/30/100/300-step lags and held-out maze layouts can compare ESP, H-ESP, whole-network evolution and a small recurrent actor-critic at equal environment calls, tuning budget and evaluation episodes. Measure success per episode, wall-clock, held-out transfer and whether H-ESP’s upper population helps over ESP. Falsify a modern utility claim if the advantage disappears under equal simulator calls or does not transfer to layouts/delays absent from evolution. The primitive was partly too early because repeated assembly/evaluation was slow, but modern compute does not fix noisy collaborator credit or data hunger. Worth a small revival benchmark; not worth promoting as a new broad class. No prototype/GPU experiment ran; GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB, live occupancy and Claude sharing unknown.

#### Hybrid prior-art closure — adaptive computational meshes and learned hierarchies (HY-99; 2019–2025)

**Graph Element Networks (GENs): finite-element substrate × message-passing graph.** GENs already instantiate a strong version of learnable computational geometry: a GNN’s nodes are placed in a continuous metric space; input samples are interpolated onto node states; repeated message passing propagates local information; query points read out by interpolation and decoding. Training can move node locations and recompute local edges to allocate representation/computation to spatially difficult regions. The same weights are run at different mesh sizes/precision, and the paper tests PDEs, object pushing, and novel-view scenes. This is a real substrate-level coupling, but “learnable mesh as spatial memory/computation” is published prior art. Importantly, the authors only suggest node add/remove search as a possible extension and say it was not yet experimentally explored; their experiments tune positions/connectivity with fixed node count. Do not overstate GEN as solving open-ended architecture growth. [Alet et al., ICML 2019, primary full text](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.09019), §§3–4.

**Other close hybrids, audited directly.** Active Predictive Coding generates lower-level state-transition and action-policy RNN parameters from higher-level state/action embeddings using hypernetworks; each micro-step predicts sensory input and uses prediction error to update the latent state, then returns a summary to the higher level. It trains world dynamics self-supervised and policy through RL/planning. The paper uses only two levels and a fixed number of micro-steps, and identifies scaling/deeper planning as future work. This directly closes generic predictive-coding × hypernetwork-generated subprogram × active-perception/hierarchical-RL proposals; exact coupling is known, even if broad utility remains unproven. [Rao, Gklezakos & Sathish, Active Predictive Coding (2024 journal; arXiv 2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.13461), §§4–7.

Liang & Boularias (L4DC 2021) already train a high-level finite-state task machine together with a low-level manipulation policy under sparse terminal success/failure feedback; the machine tracks task progress and guides action, using observed 6D object poses/semantic labels plus relevant action history. This closes a broad FSM × learned controller × sparse self-supervision hybrid. Keep in mind it is a structured manipulation solution with semantic inputs, not autonomous discovery of arbitrary state variables from raw perception. [PMLR 2021 primary page](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v144/liang21a.html).

Huang et al. (NeurSys 2025) propose differentiable synthesis of both behavior-tree architecture and execution nodes: a grammar-defined discrete structure is relaxed to optimize with environment reward, then a valid discrete BT is extracted and its leaves fine-tuned. This is deeper than simply placing a learned policy inside a hand-written BT, but it is already published prior art for continuous architecture search × symbolic/reactive execution. [PMLR 2025 primary page](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v288/huang25a.html).

**Disposition and cheap falsifiers.** Reject the generic combinations as newly discovered hybrids (novelty 0/5). For a computational-mesh proposal, test a learned-coordinate GEN against uniform/adaptively refined finite elements and fixed-node GEN on heterogeneous Poisson fields with sharp, randomly located discontinuities, equalizing node count and message FLOPs; fail if compute does not concentrate where error is high or held-out discontinuity locations lose the accuracy/compute gain. For generated hierarchical programs, test APC against embedding-conditioned RNN and option-critic baselines on procedurally varied rooms, ablating generated weights versus concatenated embeddings; fail if transfer is no better or relies on hand-coded abstractions. For BT synthesis, compare relaxed/extracted BT, fixed-grammar BT and MLP under equal environment steps on randomized layouts; fail if discrete extraction loses reward or held-out generalization disappears. These are low-cost utility replications, not novelty demonstrations. No code/GPU experiments ran; attributable GPU use and peak VRAM 0 GB; occupancy and Claude share unknown because GPU work was not imminent.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — Markov Brains and evolving feedback-gate plasticity (AR-111; 2010s)

**Architecture and primitive.** Markov Brains use a recurrent state buffer of input, hidden and output bits/values, updated in parallel by heterogeneous deterministic or probabilistic logic gates. A genome encodes each gate’s arity, wiring, and truth/probability table; unlike a uniform layer of shared-form neurons, different gates can compute distinct local functions and can write to several buffer states. Gate structure and behavior evolve through mutation/selection. The technical report explicitly describes the system as a probabilistic finite-state machine, and acknowledges that the category boundaries with finite-state and hidden Markov systems are not crisp. [Hintze et al., *Markov Brains: A Technical Introduction* (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.05601).

**Lifetime learning mechanism.** Sheneman & Hintze (2017) added feedback gates to probabilistic logic gates. A feedback gate remembers recent input-output pairs; genetically selected internal positive/negative feedback lines cause the probability assigned to a chosen output for that input pattern to increase/decrease, with renormalization of the other outcomes. A short history queue (up to four updates in the described implementation) allows delayed internal evaluation. Evolution selects the gate wiring and the circuits that generate these internal feedback signals, while lifetime learning changes probability tables. This couples genome-scale structure search with online local parameter adaptation. The authors report 300 evolutionary runs in a variable-mapping grid-navigation task; agents evolved to use the feedback gates performed better on average, and silencing the gates degraded adapted behavior. The environment supplies sensory information but not an objective reward label—the internal feedback-evaluation machinery is itself evolved. [Sheneman & Hintze, *Evolving autonomous learning in cognitive networks* (2017), primary article record/full-text index](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29196623/); [open full-text mirror](https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2%3A1557899/FULLTEXT01.pdf); [code repository](https://github.com/LSheneman/autonomous-learning).

**Was it bad or too early?** The discrete gates are easy to simulate and could be batched on current hardware; hardware was not the main obstacle to the original small-to-moderate experiments. Large-scale evolutionary sweeps are expensive, so GPUs/simulators may improve search throughput, but the architecture still needs many behavior evaluations and the internal evaluation signal can be wrong. More severe limitations are binary/discrete inputs (in some implementations), finite hand-bounded gate arities/genome size, context-specific feedback credit, serial environment rollouts, and difficulty proving useful learning outside the crafted artificial-life task. Modern encoders, differentiable gate relaxations or richer sensor representations may help, but each moves away from the original evolvable-logic mechanism and does not solve fitness attribution or safety.

**Nearest prior art and novelty.** Evolvable deterministic/probabilistic circuits overlap Cartesian Genetic Programming, genetic programming, circuit evolution and stochastic finite-state controllers. Genome-selected gates plus state-buffer recurrence are an existing named architecture, not a new candidate. More importantly, evolution × lifetime learning is an established hybrid: Baldwin-effect search (Hinton & Nowlan, 1987), gradient learning plus genetic search (Ackley & Littman, 1990), SANE/H-ESP, and later plastic neuroevolution are close precedents. The narrower “internal evaluator is evolved alongside feedback-gated gate probabilities” is the particular Markov Brain mechanism and is already published in 2017. [Hinton & Nowlan (1987)](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/evolution.htm); [Ackley & Littman (1990)](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/1990/file/b6f0479ae87d244975439c6124592772-Paper.pdf); [SANE/H-ESP, AR-110 above]. No class-level novelty remains (0/5); keep as a distinct low-level comparator for evolvable plastic computation.

**Small CPU falsifier and value.** On a tiny contextual T-maze where an unannounced sensor-to-action mapping changes, compare fixed Markov Brains, feedback-gate brains, externally rewarded feedback-gate brains, and a similarly sized recurrent policy with a local plastic trace. Match genome/evaluation budgets and stream exposure; measure adaptation episodes, old-context interference, evolved gate count, persistent probability-table bytes, and performance when internal evaluator lines are ablated or corrupted. Reject the practical claim if internally evolved feedback does not reduce remapping interactions over fixed gates, if it exploits environmental side information, or if it works only for the trained mapping transition schedule. This separates architecture utility from evolutionary search cost; it is a proposed test, not a new-class demonstration. No code/experiment ran; CPU/browser research only, GPU use/peak VRAM 0 GB and live GPU/Claude use unknown because no GPU run was imminent.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — fuzzy relational systems and sup-T compositional neurons (AR-112; 1976–2000)

**Original computation.** A fuzzy relational system represents a graded mapping between concepts as a relation matrix `R ∈ [0,1]^(n×m)`. Given an input membership vector `x`, max–min inference computes `y_j = max_i min(x_i, R_ij)`; more generally, sup–T composition replaces min with a triangular norm. Relational equations ask which input, output, or relation values satisfy such a composition. Sanchez formalized composite fuzzy-relation equation solving in 1976. Blanco, Delgado & Requena then used a max–min neural network to identify a relation from examples and adapted backpropagation with a smoothed derivative (1994/1995). Stamou & Tzafestas (2000) made the compositional operation itself a one-layer neural primitive: each generalized neuron performs sup–T composition; its connection weights are relation entries; an online rule updates them using the relation’s topology. They claim perfect recall when the induced relation equation has a solution. This is a more specific architecture than a standard ANFIS controller or a fuzzy cognitive map: its core unit computes an algebraic relation composition. [Sanchez (1976), primary paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(76)90446-0); [Blanco et al. (1995), publisher record](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0165011494002512); [Stamou & Tzafestas (2000), article record and abstract](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/matcom/v51y2000i3p301-314.html); [Stamou & Tzafestas (1999), fuzzy relation equations](https://doi.org/10.1109/3477.809025).

**Was it bad or too early?** The max/min or sup–T operations are easy to parallelize and already ran at modest scale on 1990s hardware; lack of GPUs was not the central obstacle. GPUs/autodiff make larger batches and smooth relaxations easier, but do not supply a trustworthy concept vocabulary or identify a unique relation from underdetermined examples. Solution sets may be empty or nonunique; dense relations grow quadratically with concept count; small training sets can fit seen pairs without supporting unseen compositions. These are identifiability and representation problems, not simply throughput limits. The relation-equation solver literature continues, but solving these equations does not make them a general learned architecture; ANFIS and neuro-fuzzy systems already occupy broad learnable fuzzy inference. No general architecture novelty is identified (0/5); the family is worth retaining as a narrow relational-induction baseline.

**Prototype that could change the revival verdict.** On CPU, generate sparse hidden max–min / product-T relation graphs with 8–32 graded concepts, noisy membership observations and held-out multi-hop compositions. Compare an exact solver when feasible, the 1995-style smooth max–min learner, the 2000 compositional online learner, matched ANFIS, and a parameter/edge-matched relational GNN. Score relation recovery, held-out compositional inference, calibration, sensitivity to empty/multiple solution sets, memory and runtime as concept count grows. Falsify a revival claim if it memorizes seen pairs, relation recovery is unstable under mild noise, or ANFIS/GNN matches accuracy and calibration at lower cost. This is a utility benchmark only. No experiment ran.

#### AR-83 addendum — causal-state machines already have neural, kernel, active, and quantum variants

Computational mechanics defines two observed pasts as the same causal state when they imply the same conditional distribution over futures. The resulting epsilon-machine is a minimal predictive unifilar automaton for a stationary process; it is a theory of process representation and reconstruction, not an unoccupied general-purpose AI architecture. [Shalizi & Crutchfield, *Computational Mechanics: Pattern and Prediction, Structure and Simplicity*](https://csc.ucdavis.edu/~cmg/compmech/pubs/cmppss.htm).

Several apparent “modern revival” gaps are already occupied. Zhang et al. train an RNN to predict future observations, then extract continuous/discrete causal-state representations for POMDP policy learning. Brodu & Crutchfield infer kernel epsilon-machines in RKHS for continuous-valued and continuous-time observations, including chaotic flows; this softens the finite-alphabet/front-end limitation but leaves kernel coverage and state-identification issues. Local causal states extend the method to spatiotemporal fields. Collins & Shen's surprise-driven architecture actively experiments and splits/refines/merges internal states, while Bayesian Structural Inference samples candidate unifilar topologies. Thus “neural encoder + causal-state discretization,” “continuous RKHS causal states,” and “surprise-triggered causal-state growth” are existing mechanisms, not open classes. [Zhang et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.10437); [Brodu & Crutchfield (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.14821); [local causal states](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.00515); [Collins & Shen, SDE](https://robots.isi.edu/prl/collins2017-a-robust-cognitive-architecture-for-learning-from-surprises.pdf); [Strelioff & Crutchfield, Bayesian structural inference](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.89.042119).

Quantum epsilon-machines encode classical causal states as nonorthogonal quantum memory states and can reduce memory required to reproduce some stochastic processes relative to a minimal classical machine; small quantum-processor demonstrations exist. This is a real, unusual memory mechanism, but it addresses stochastic-process generation/prediction and needs quantum state preparation/control. It does not yet support a general-purpose AI claim. [Gu et al. (2012)](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms1761); [experimental implementation (2017)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5291701/). The old obstacle was partly finite-alphabet and data/estimation cost; modern kernels and encoders address that, but cannot resolve non-identifiability, nonstationarity, or informative-data requirements. **Disposition:** keep causal states as an interpretable model and adversarial benchmark; no new candidate. A CPU benchmark can compare oracle-topology epsilon-machines, CSSR/BSI, neural causal-state models, PSRs, and GRUs on increasing state-count/noisy renewal and Even processes, matching trajectories and memory; drop the modernization claim if state recovery or calibrated multi-step forecasts collapse before the GRU/PSR baselines do.

#### AR-73 source-depth supplement — subsumption was not waiting for faster hardware; learned arbitration predates deep RL

Brooks's layered controller uses parallel finite-state transducers coupled by side-tapped message wires. Higher layers interfere with lower layers through **suppression** (replace or block an input message for a set interval) or **inhibition** (block an output); there is no centralized global controller. The design's intended primitive is incremental, fast sensor-to-action behavior, not a trainable general representation. Its real-time behavior was practical on early mobile robots, so the architecture was not blocked primarily by slow hardware. Lack of a world model and long-horizon state is a deliberate scope/representation tradeoff; faster GPUs do not remove it. [Brooks, *Intelligence Without Representation* (1991), original architectural account](https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse599j/12sp/papers/BrooksIntelligenceWithoutRepresentation.pdf); the earlier [1986 layered-control paper](https://people.csail.mit.edu/brooks/papers/representation.pdf).

The often-claimed “learning revival” is also established: Shewchuk & Viola's 1989 subsumption learner embeds utility-guided action learning in the layers and attaches a certainty factor to learned responses; a 1991 robot-learning paper gives modules separate simple rewards and encodes history in module applicability. Togelius (2004) evolves a layered subsumption neurocontroller. Pore & Aragon-Camarasa (2020) train simple behavior networks from demonstrations and use actor–critic arbitration to activate/inhibit them; their evidence is a three-seed MuJoCo pick-and-place simulation with privileged state and hand-decomposed skills, not physical or task-general proof. That last paper is a direct close collision for “learn layer arbitration,” already partly noted in AR-73; this supplement closes the broader deep-RL hybrid claim. [Shewchuk & Viola (1989), Brown primary archive](https://cs.brown.edu/research/pubs/techreports/reports/CS-89-17.html); [1991 subsumption/RL robot report](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/chapter/edited-volume/abs/pii/B9781558602007500684); [Togelius (2004)](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0405027); [Pore & Aragon-Camarasa (2020), primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.07973).

**Disposition and revival test.** Retain as a bounded low-latency robotics control baseline, not a broad AI class; class-level novelty 0/5. A CPU simulation with randomized obstacles, variable sensor latency/dropout and a narrow passage could compare fixed subsumption, learned suppression/inhibition, recurrent policy, and a modern behavior-arbitration baseline under matched action latency and controller bytes. Measure success, collisions, worst-case response delay, failure recovery and sensitivity to unmodeled objects. A revival claim fails if layered arbitration does not improve the safety/latency frontier at equal control capacity, or if gains depend on hand-labeled behaviors unavailable in new layouts. The probe tests practical niche, not novelty. No experiment ran.

#### HY-100 — actively selecting predictive-state tests is occupied (reject the broad hybrid)

The original hybrid sketch conflated two distinct operations. A PSR test is a predicted future action–observation sequence used as a model coordinate; selecting or discovering such tests is not the same as issuing a physical sensor query. McCracken & Bowling's online method discovers candidate/core predictive tests from observed data and monitors conditioning of the core-test matrix; Liu & Zhu select a finite spectral test/history basis using model entropy. Neither source demonstrates that its basis selector schedules physical sensor reads. Active sensing is a neighboring, independently established control problem (for example, jointly learned sensing and recognition), but that does not turn PSR basis selection into sensor-call reduction. [McCracken & Bowling (2005), abstract and full paper](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2005/file/c3008b2c6f5370b744850a98a95b73ad-Paper.pdf); [Liu & Zhu (2016), PSR model-entropy basis selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.09076); [Shibata et al. (1996), active sensing and recognition learned jointly](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jnns/3/4/3_4_126/_article/-char/en).

Broad novelty remains closed: online core-test discovery, entropy-based basis choice and active sensing each have prior art. A narrower unverified method question is whether a resource-aware scheduler can maintain or switch among predictive basis tests per action while preserving multi-step forecasts and control value at equal data and memory. This concerns basis maintenance and numerical conditioning, not fewer physical sensor calls. A suitable matched benchmark would compare fixed tests, entropy-selected tests, online discovery, and the local scheduler on identical trajectories; score forecast log loss/calibration, policy value, model bytes, conditioning and basis-switch churn. It is a low-priority efficiency study (novelty 0–0.5/5), not a new hybrid. No experiment ran.

Three independent no-edit research scans were synthesized and source-checked by the lead. AR-112 adds max–min/sup–T fuzzy relational computation as a distinct historical mechanism underneath the notebook's existing fuzzy-system coverage; it is a useful CPU benchmark but not a new class. AR-83 now records causal-state minimality and existing neural, kernel, active, local-spatiotemporal, and quantum variants. #### AR-112 CPU smoke experiment — operator-matched compositional generalization (executed; limited positive)

**Question.** Does an explicit max–min relation layer help predict combinations of familiar concept activations that were excluded from training, when the data were generated by that same relation operator? This is a narrow architecture-bias check, not a novelty test or a reproduction of Stamou & Tzafestas's 2000 online learning rule.

**Setup.** CPU-only PyTorch with CUDA visibility disabled; 8 input concepts and 8 outputs. Each output used two nonzero max–min relation entries. Training inputs activated one feature or an allowed pair; four fixed feature pairs were excluded from training and used for held-out composition tests. Compared a trainable 64-parameter max–min relation matrix against ReLU MLPs with widths 4 (76 parameters) and 16 (280 parameters). Used 64, 256, or 1,024 examples, 300 Adam steps, and three generator/initialization seeds per setting (27 fits total). Metric: MSE on the unseen paired inputs.

| Training examples | Max–min relation, 64 params | MLP width 4, 76 params | MLP width 16, 280 params |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 | 0.037883 (range 0.033741–0.055943) | 0.033973 (0.024432–0.047638) | 0.029646 (0.027095–0.056455) |
| 256 | 0.000001 (0–0.014062) | 0.028459 (0.025494–0.035647) | 0.019075 (0.018497–0.022923) |
| 1,024 | 0.000000 (0–0.011956) | 0.019801 (0.014465–0.042156) | 0.013370 (0.010420–0.016083) |

**Interpretation / limits.** At low data, the relational model did not win; its median training MSE was 0.0279 versus 0.0076 for the width-4 MLP, indicating harder fitting/optimization. At 256+ examples, the median held-out error was nearly zero, but one of three seeds retained about 0.012–0.014 MSE, so optimization is not robust in this tiny run. The task gives the relational model its exact inductive bias and excludes only selected two-feature combinations, so this demonstrates neither broad generalization nor superiority under noisy, dense, misspecified or changing relations. It is a limited positive for the narrow, old model family: exact operator structure can improve composition generalization after enough observations, while the learned dense relation may be harder to fit than an unconstrained approximator at very low sample counts. No class novelty follows.

**Resource record.** Runtime 13.46 s; 8×8 models; 27 CPU fits; peak VRAM 0 GB and no GPU initialized (`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` empty). Live GPU occupancy/Claude sharing were not checked because the experiment could not access the GPU. No experiment files were created; only this notebook was edited. **Next falsifier:** repeat with noisy membership inputs, relation sparsity shifts, and targets generated by a smooth nonlinear function that is not max–min; drop the revival claim if the held-out advantage vanishes under mild noise/misspecification or depends on the exact target generator.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — KBANN and theory-refining neural networks (AR-113; 1989–1994)

**Original architecture.** KBANN maps a domain theory written as propositional/Horn rules into a feed-forward neural net. Rule antecedents/consequents become input, hidden and output units; dependencies become weighted links; weights/biases are set so the untrained network reproduces the supplied theory. Extra low-weight connections provide degrees of freedom for changing the rule theory, then ordinary backpropagation refines it on labeled examples. The knowledge is therefore present in topology and initial parameter values; example-driven correction is encoded in subsequent weight changes. Towell & Shavlik explicitly frame it as using incomplete or even incorrect rules plus examples to fill one another's gaps; their molecular-biology experiments report better generalization than several learning and biology baselines. Later work extracts revised symbolic rules from the trained network, closing an insertion→refinement→extraction loop. [Towell & Shavlik (1994), primary full text](https://ftp.cs.wisc.edu/machine-learning/shavlik-group/towell.aij94.pdf); [Towell & Shavlik (1991), rule extraction primary paper](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/1991/file/ed265bc903a5a097f61d3ec064d96d2e-Paper.pdf).

**Was it bad or too early?** Not mainly hardware-limited: the original method already ran meaningful biological datasets on 1990s systems. GPUs and modern encoders can increase scale and supply perceptual features that propositional inputs lacked, but they do not make it easy to obtain a correct vocabulary or domain theory. The original syntax is restrictive (propositional/Horn-like rules and a chosen feature set); bad rules can bias or slow fitting, and a learned net may cease to correspond cleanly to its seed rules. Neural-to-rule extraction can itself require combinatorial search: the primary paper notes its exhaustive subset method is impossible to implement and needs heuristics that trade accuracy for compactness. Modern differentiable logic, probabilistic programming, rule losses and knowledge-constrained networks are extensive descendants, so “inject rules into a neural net and learn” is not a new hybrid. [Towell & Shavlik (1994), §§2–5](https://ftp.cs.wisc.edu/machine-learning/shavlik-group/towell.aij94.pdf); [informed-machine-learning survey](https://doi.org/10.1109/TKDE.2021.3079836); [neural-symbolic survey (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2023.06.028).

**Use and falsifiable revival probe.** KBANN is plausible when approximate expert rules exist and examples are scarce, especially where rule refinement/extraction matters. On CPU, synthesize a small relational/biomedical-style task with controlled fractions of correct, missing and wrong rules; compare rule-only inference, KBANN, equal-size random-initialized MLP, and a modern differentiable-rule-loss baseline at equal examples and parameter budget. Measure sample-efficiency, held-out combinations, false-rule correction, rule fidelity after training and extraction cost. The revival claim fails if wrong rules create persistent negative transfer, or if KBANN only wins when its supplied rules already encode most of the answer. It remains established hybrid archaeology, not a new architecture (novelty 0/5). No experiment ran.

#### HY-101 — deep perception plus rule-seeded neural topology is not a new hybrid

A plausible modern coupling would let a self-supervised visual or language encoder ground predicates, use those predicates to initialize a KBANN-like rule topology, then use task examples/counterexamples to revise the neural parameters and extract updated rules. The intended complement is clear: encoders supply learned grounding, rules supply sparse relational structure, and examples repair missing or wrong rules. But KBANN already couples rule-derived topology/weights with neural refinement and rule extraction; modern knowledge injection and neuro-symbolic methods already connect learned representations to logic, including first-order extensions, probabilistic rule evaluation and neural constraint correction. Merely replacing KBANN's hand-engineered input features with an encoder is a front end plus established rule/logic model, not a different computational class. [Towell & Shavlik (1994)](https://ftp.cs.wisc.edu/machine-learning/shavlik-group/towell.aij94.pdf); [survey of prior-knowledge integration](https://doi.org/10.1109/TKDE.2021.3079836); [KENN, neural networks enhanced with logical knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.06087); [statistical-relational/neuro-symbolic survey](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.artint.2023.104062).

**Disposition and small disproof test.** Reject generic encoder × KBANN or KBANN × modern differentiable logic as new hybrids (0/5). If a practical evaluation is justified, vary rule correctness and data scarcity on synthetic visual-relation scenes; compare frozen encoder + KBANN, end-to-end perception-classifier, and encoder + differentiable-rule baseline at matched labeled scenes and compute. Falsify the practical complementarity claim if encoder grounding still needs hand-labeled predicates, wrong rules are not corrected more efficiently than the other baselines, or rule extraction cannot preserve held-out accuracy. This checks whether old topology seeding has a modern niche, not novelty.

#### Candidate sweep C034–C038 — diverse computational primitives screened and rejected (2026-09-27)

These are five distinct primitives from the architecture-inventor scan. They are recorded as rejected ideas rather than renamed “survivors”; the nearest literature closes each broad mechanism. Sources were checked against primary proceedings/papers or the originating project. No class-level novelty remains in this batch.

**C034 — Reversible trace recurrence (reject as broad novelty).** A recurrent state is updated by bijections, with an explicit short trace recording the few overwritten bits when an input event requires forgetting. It represents state and reversible transformations; each step consumes input plus prior state and emits updated state/output; inference runs the inverse-compatible transition and optionally consults the trace; training could use ordinary sequence loss or local prediction error. Persistent memory is the recurrent state and trace. It could reduce activation storage during long sequence training, while trace events might make forgetting inspectable. But reversible recurrent neural networks already reconstruct hidden activations for backward passes, and the original paper explicitly identifies inability to forget as the price of perfect reversibility, adding auxiliary bits to address it. Modern compute improves throughput but cannot remove the information-theoretic need to retain what was erased; the trace risks becoming ordinary state storage. [MacKay et al., Reversible RNNs (NeurIPS 2018)](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2018/hash/4ff6fa96179cdc2838e8d8ce64cd10a7-Abstract.html). Possible residual: a principled, task-adaptive trace budget with explicit bounded-memory guarantees, but this is an algorithmic refinement, not a new class (novelty 0.5/5). Falsifier: compare bijective recurrence with learned trace allocation against GRU and reversible-RNN baselines at matched state bytes; drop the mechanism if sequence accuracy or adaptation does not improve at equal memory.

**C035 — Sheaf constraint weaver (reject; only a narrow diagnostic residue).** Each local predictor stores a value/section on a graph patch; restriction maps align overlapping patches, while repeated local updates attempt to reach a globally compatible section. The represented information is local beliefs plus how neighboring coordinate systems agree; input is overlapping local evidence, output is a coherent global estimate or a conflict score. Learning fits local functions and restriction maps; inference alternates local message/consistency updates. Memory lives in patch states, maps and optional cohomological residuals. Potential use: distributed sensor fusion or graph reasoning with explicit localization of contradictions. Sheaf neural networks and sheaf diffusion already learn cellular sheaves and propagate graph signals; Seely (2026) applies sheaf cohomology to linear predictive-coding networks and studies irreducible prediction-error patterns, closing the broad “topological contradiction score for neural inference” claim. [Barbero et al., Neural Sheaf Diffusion (NeurIPS 2022)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/file/75c45fca2aa416ada062b26cc4fb7641-Paper-Conference.pdf); [Seely, Sheaf Cohomology of Linear Predictive Coding Networks (PMLR 2026)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v282/seely26a.html). Hardware does not resolve the core issue: useful patch definitions and restriction maps must be learned, and nonzero cohomology need not identify which local evidence is wrong. At most, calibrated conflict localization/abstention under distribution shift remains a domain-specific utility question (novelty 0.5–1/5, low confidence). Falsifier: on synthetic graphs with controlled contradictory regions, compare the sheaf residual to calibrated uncertainty, graph residual networks and predictive-coding errors; reject if it cannot localize contradictions under unseen topology or simply tracks degree/noise.

**C036 — Argument graph dynamics engine (reject; direct architecture collision).** Arguments/claims are nodes with support and attack edges; repeated learned message passing updates acceptance scores or candidate extensions. The input is a directed argument graph, output is node acceptance or a set of extensions, and state memory is the current score vector. Supervision can use labels generated by argumentation semantics; inference iterates the graph update. It may exploit local structure where symbolic solvers face large graphs, but the core primitive is already an argumentation graph neural network: IJCAI 2020's AGNN learns recurrent message passing for Dung semantics and can guide search over extensions. [Craandijk & Birkemeyer (IJCAI 2020)](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2020/231). More compute improves graph throughput but does not create a different update rule, and semantics-specific labels remain necessary. No broad novelty (0/5). Falsifier for utility only: evaluate calibration and exact semantic accuracy on larger unseen graph structures against the AGNN and exact solver; reject if it fails out-of-size generalization or gives no runtime/accuracy tradeoff.

**C037 — Equivalence-space learner (reject; equality saturation already combines search and learned guidance).** Store many equivalent program/expression forms in an e-graph; learn which rewrite transformations are useful and when to extract a low-cost representative. It represents equivalence classes rather than one current program; input is a program plus a cost/task objective, output is a transformed candidate; learning may rank rewrites/extraction decisions from solved tasks; inference adds equivalent forms, merges congruent nodes and extracts. Memory is the e-graph and rewrite library. This could preserve alternatives until downstream evidence chooses among them, but Ruler learns rewrite rules using e-graphs, Guided Equality Saturation learns which rewrite rule to apply, and later ML-guided equality saturation learns search/extraction guidance. [Ruler (OOPSLA 2021 project and paper links)](https://github.com/uwplse/ruler); [Guided Equality Saturation (POPL 2024)](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/308331/); [Machine Learning Guided Equality Saturation (2025)](https://thok.eu/publications/2025/egraphs-mlges.pdf). The mechanism is compelling for program optimization but bounded by domain-specific equational theories, e-graph explosion and reward/cost correctness; generalizing from code search to a general cognition architecture is unsupported. Novelty 0/5. Falsifier for an application claim: under equal node/time budgets compare learned rewrite scheduling with best-first and ML-guided EqSat on held-out rewrite systems; reject if gains vanish out-of-domain or cost models choose semantically invalid results.

**C038 — Stochastic bitstream computer (reject as a general architecture; retain as hardware substrate).** Encode a scalar by the proportion of ones in a random bitstream and compute approximate arithmetic with simple logic gates; neural layers can learn weights/activations in this representation. Inputs and outputs are probabilities/numeric values, repeated operation is bitwise stochastic arithmetic, and memory is stream generators/registers. Potential advantage is low-area hardware tolerant of some faults. But stochastic-computing neural networks and stochastic CNNs already implement and train these models; a 2024 FPGA study also identifies the precision–latency tradeoff, random-number-generation overhead and weaker regression behavior. [Hirose (1996), stochastic neural network learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0893608096000251); [stochastic CNN review/implementation (2020)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33424530/); [FPGA stochastic-compute CNN study (2024)](https://doi.org/10.34133/research.0307). Faster GPUs do not fix a substrate designed for area/energy tradeoffs; stream length can make latency grow while sampling noise limits precision. Keep as a hardware-aware representation for specialized inference, not a new model class (novelty 0/5). Falsifier: on regression and classification at a fixed energy/area budget, compare bitstream length schedules with fixed-point/INT8; reject if accuracy-adjusted latency/energy does not improve, especially on regression.

**Cross-domain negative sweep.** Constraint-programming plus learned branching is mature in Lazy Clause Generation solvers; reversible RNNs were already closed above; learned dependency maintenance overlaps truth-maintenance/self-adjusting computation and Differential Dataflow already recorded under C029/HY-68; learned database query optimizers (for example Bao/Neo) remain workload-specific rather than a general computational class. These do not merit duplicate candidate IDs. Recurrent lesson: modern hardware can lower search and communication costs, but it does not by itself resolve explicit knowledge representation, correct dependency tracking, objective specification or domain shift.

#### AR-112 robustness experiment protocol — CPU-only (executed below)

The earlier three-seed result used an exactly max–min-generated sparse relation and therefore gives the model its preferred operator. To test whether that narrow gain survives modest departures, run 15 seeds at 8 inputs/8 outputs and 256 training examples, comparing the 64-parameter max–min relation layer, MLP width 4 (76 parameters) and width 16 (280 parameters). Conditions: (1) sparse max–min relation with noisy memberships/targets and held-out input pairs, (2) denser max–min relation with the same held-out-pair protocol, and (3) a smooth non-max–min target on continuous inputs. Select learning rate on a validation split from the same three-value grid for every model and seed; report median and spread of clean held-out MSE, fit failures, and runtime. No ANFIS/neuro-fuzzy baseline was included, so this is not a complete specialist-baseline comparison. The practical-revival claim should be dropped if the relation layer loses its advantage under mild observation noise or only wins on its exact operator, even though the broader literature novelty verdict is already 0/5.

#### AR-112 robustness experiment — relation bias survives noise but fails under operator mismatch (executed; 2026-09-27)

**Setup.** CPU-only PyTorch, 8 inputs/8 outputs, 256 training examples and 15 generator seeds per condition. Models: 64-parameter trainable max–min relation layer; ReLU MLP width 4 (76 parameters); ReLU MLP width 16 (280 parameters). For each seed/model, learning rate was selected on validation data from {0.005, 0.02, 0.05}; each candidate ran 200 full-batch Adam steps. Conditions: sparse relation (two nonzero entries/output) with Gaussian membership noise σ=0.035 and target noise σ=0.01; denser four-entry/output exact max–min relation; and a continuous-input smooth sigmoid target with dense affine and pairwise-interaction terms. The first two conditions train on singleton/allowed-pair patterns and test on held-out feature pairs; the smooth condition uses random continuous inputs and an independent test set. Metric is clean held-out MSE.

| Target condition | Max–min relation, 64 params | MLP width 4, 76 params | MLP width 16, 280 params |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sparse max–min, noisy observations | 0.00164 (q10–q90: 0.00148–0.00174) | 0.02872 (0.01873–0.04212) | 0.01314 (0.01109–0.01904) |
| Dense max–min, clean observations | 0.000716 (0.000613–0.000908) | 0.03050 (0.02217–0.03539) | 0.01550 (0.00722–0.01920) |
| Smooth target outside max–min family | 0.01277 (0.01026–0.01573) | 0.00523 (0.00210–0.00767) | 0.000238 (0.000198–0.000335) |

**Interpretation.** The matched relation primitive generalized to excluded input pairs with low error despite mild membership/target noise, and the result was consistent across these 15 small synthetic seeds. Dense max–min structure also favored its matched model. On the smooth misspecified target the relation model lost to both MLPs, with the wider MLP about 54× lower median MSE. This is evidence that the structural bias, rather than a universal capacity advantage, drove the two wins. However, the exact operator still generated the two favorable tasks, the MLP width-16 comparator had over 4× the parameters, all three models used the same limited 200-step budget, and the learning-rate grid's median winner was its upper endpoint for most model/condition pairs. This does not establish superiority to ANFIS, neuro-fuzzy systems or relational GNNs, and it does not change the 0/5 broad novelty assessment. Preserve AR-112 as a useful specialized relational-induction baseline; pursue only if a real domain supplies graded relations and composition structure.

**Resource record.** Runtime 105.05 s; 405 CPU fits (15 seeds × 3 conditions × 3 models × 3 learning rates), 200 steps/fit. CUDA visibility was empty; CPU only, peak VRAM 0 GB, no GPU initialized and no GPU process started. Live GPU occupancy/Claude sharing were not inspected because this was a CPU run; no process was touched. No result files were created; only `Codex_Research.md` was edited. The protocol above is now complete; next utility check, if pursued, needs an ANFIS or relational-GNN baseline and a task whose relation operator is not revealed to the learner.
