#### Old-architecture archaeology — frames, scripts, and procedural knowledge structures (AR-126; established representation systems)

**Original mechanism.** Minsky's frame is a structured memory record for a stereotyped object or situation. Slots hold expected properties, relations, values, and procedural knowledge about how a frame is used or revised; a partially matching situation selects a remembered frame and adapts details to fit current evidence. FRL (1977) implements defaults, constraints, inheritance, procedural attachment, and annotations over related frame records. KRL (1977) explicitly tries to integrate procedural knowledge with declarative forms and controls how facts/descriptions are accessed. GUS (1977) puts frame-driven understanding into a cooperative, restricted English-dialog domain. Schank and Abelson's scripts represent conventional event sequences with roles, scenes, entry conditions, expected actions, and outcomes; plans and goals support causal/intentional interpretations beyond a static slot record. [Minsky, *A Framework for Representing Knowledge*, MIT AI Memo 306 (1974)](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/0eca0164-cb5f-42de-8c86-43f54b23306d); [Roberts & Goldstein, *The FRL Manual*, MIT AI Memo 409 (1977)](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/ddd83d5b-940b-4d55-9319-844ccb972075); [Bobrow & Winograd, KRL (1977)](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog0101_2); [Bobrow et al., GUS (1977)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(77)90018-2); [Schank, scripts (IJCAI 1975)](https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/75/Papers/021.pdf); [Schank & Abelson, *Scripts, Plans, Goals, and Understanding* (1977)](https://www.routledge.com/Scripts-Plans-Goals-and-Understanding-An-Inquiry-Into-Human-Knowledge/Schank-Abelson/p/book/9780898591385).

**Repeated operation and represented information.** The system stores frames, instances, slot values/defaults, inheritance links, attached procedures, and sometimes a script/event graph. Input is a perceived or stated situation; the system cues a frame/script, matches current facts to slots or roles, inherits compatible defaults, runs procedural checks/fillers, and updates the representation or invokes a plan when evidence conflicts. Output is a structured situation model, inferred unstated facts/events, or a goal-directed continuation. In the original systems, most frame/script libraries and their grounding were hand-authored; the representations supplied a reasoning/data structure, not a general learning mechanism that discovers correct frames from raw experience.

**Was it bad or early?** The 1970s systems were executable on available hardware and demonstrated useful narrow-domain behavior. Current vision/language encoders, larger corpora, and simulators substantially improve the input evidence and permit wider frame inventories. They do not remove the costly parts: deciding which frame applies, defining the slot/event vocabulary, resolving exceptions and conflicting defaults, learning causal/temporal structure from reporting-biased narratives, and checking whether a filled slot is grounded in the world. In other words, weak perception was partly a historical limit; knowledge authoring, schema selection, open-world exceptions, and semantics were not simply compute bottlenecks. GUS's cooperative travel-booking domain is evidence for a constrained frame-driven interface, not general language understanding.

**Modernization and direct prior art.** Neural frame-semantic parsers use contextual representations to identify FrameNet frames and fill role arguments; transformer-based open-domain parsers make this a direct learned-perception-plus-frame-structure coupling. For scripts, a 2022 ACL study found that zero-shot pretrained language models produce event sequences with omissions, irrelevant/repeated events, and temporal misordering; its script-induction pipeline fine-tunes on sequence examples and adds learned filtering/reordering stages. ACL 2023 work induces hierarchical event schemas from LLM knowledge with incremental prompting and verification, and NutFrame (LREC 2024) benchmarks LLM-based conceptual-structure induction over FrameNet. These modern systems improve proposal/grounding, but they do not turn the frame record, role-filling, or script sequence into a new computation. [Open-Domain Frame Semantic Parsing Using Transformers (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.10998); [Sancheti & Rudinger, *What do Large Language Models Learn about Scripts?* (ACL 2022)](https://aclanthology.org/2022.starsem-1.1/); [Open-Domain Hierarchical Event Schema Induction (ACL 2023)](https://aclanthology.org/2023.acl-long.312/); [NutFrame (LREC-COLING 2024)](https://aclanthology.org/2024.lrec-main.1079/).

**Use, weaknesses, and verdict.** Frames remain useful when a task has a stable vocabulary, missing facts can be inferred from domain regularities, and explanations need explicit slots and provenance. Scripts help with conventional event ordering and narrative gaps. Main failures are incomplete or stale schemas, wrong defaults, frame-selection errors, and brittle behavior on novel combinations or atypical events. The old representation is neither a general learner nor a new architecture class; generic modern neural grounding into frames/scripts is already direct prior art. `USE THE CLASSICAL MACHINE — NOT A NEW ARCHITECTURE` for the proposed slot/default/script operations; use a learned encoder/parser only as a component. Novelty confidence **0/5**. No candidate is promoted and no experiment is run or scheduled.

#### Hybrid collision — learned frame/script grounding × explicit frame and event memory (HY-111; established coupling)

The frame/script side contributes typed situation slots, defaults, role relations, and conventional event transitions; the learned parser contributes contextual frame selection and argument filling from language. This can convert text or perception into an explicit frame and then use defaults/causal scripts to infer missing roles or plausible events. Transformer FrameNet parsers already perform contextual frame and role prediction, while modern script-induction pipelines and open-domain event-schema work couple language models to explicit event structures and verification. The interaction changes the inference representation and can improve inspectability, but the broad mechanism is already occupied. Advantages are structured outputs and explicit assumptions; failures are wrong frame selection, false default completion, event-order errors, and distribution shifts outside the frame inventory. Reject as a new hybrid (**0/5**); a new language model or hand-built schema does not add a new architecture primitive. No experiment was run.

#### Old-architecture archaeology — KL-ONE classification and the subsumption operation (AR-127; 1982–1985)

**Question.** Does a learned, typed concept hierarchy require a new operation beyond frame inheritance and semantic networks, or did an early formal knowledge-representation system already perform the same computation?

**Exact operation found.** KL-ONE concepts denote sets. A concept description includes primitive superconcepts and role sets with number restrictions and value descriptions. The classifier tests whether concept A subsumes concept B by comparing their primitive subsumers and matching role sets; for each role it checks that A's cardinality constraint includes B's and that A's value description subsumes B's. Inherited components are included. It then locates the new concept in the taxonomy ordered by subsumption and records the entailed parent/child links. The 1983 paper's example derives `PARENT ⊒ GRANDPARENT` even though that parent link is not stated in the grandparent definition. This is the same computation as “infer a type hierarchy from structured concept definitions,” not merely the same goal. [Schmolze & Lipkis, *Classification in the KL-ONE* (IJCAI 1983)](https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/83-1/Papers/072.pdf); [Brachman & Schmolze, *An Overview of the KL-ONE Knowledge Representation System* (1985)](https://cse.buffalo.edu/~rapaport/Papers/Papers.by.Others/brachman.schmolze.85.pdf).

**Guarantee and limitation.** The 1983 authors describe the classifier as informally sound and terminating, but explicitly say completeness was not established; a `FAIL` result therefore did not prove non-subsumption. This is a historical implementation limitation, not evidence that the operation was absent. Description logics made the concept/role semantics explicit and studied classification within language fragments selected for decidability and tractable reasoning. The broader transition from semantic networks and frames to formally interpreted description logics is already established history; AR-126 separately covers frames, defaults, and scripts. [Schmolze & Lipkis (1983), classifier guarantees](https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/83-1/Papers/072.pdf); [Ozaki (2020), survey of DL ontology learning and formal semantics](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13218-020-00656-9).

**Hardware and missing-information check.** KL-ONE classification was a rule over supplied concept/role descriptions and a supplied vocabulary. Modern compute can speed classification or handle larger ontologies, but it does not choose a correct domain vocabulary, infer intended meanings from ambiguous evidence, or erase the formal fragment's reasoning costs. The classifier's exact operation existed; what was difficult was authoring and validating its input knowledge, plus ensuring the procedure was complete for the chosen language.

**Verdict.** `USE THE CLASSICAL MACHINE — NOT A NEW ARCHITECTURE` for concept subsumption, insertion into a formal taxonomy, and inferred class membership. No candidate is promoted.

#### Hybrid collision — learned type/concept induction × subsumption classification (HY-112; occupied)

The concrete proposal is: take a vocabulary, a DL or typed-relation language, labeled instances or text, and an existing knowledge base; propose/refine a class expression; ask a reasoner for subsumption, consistency, or instance checks; then write the accepted definition into the TBox and update its taxonomy. In the required form:

`STATE = TBox vocabulary and concept descriptions + ABox instances/labels + inferred taxonomy`

`OPERATION = search or propose a class expression, then classify it by subsumption/consistency/instance reasoning`

`WRITE = add or refine the TBox definition and place it in the entailed subsumption hierarchy`

`GUARANTEE = logical guarantees are bounded by the selected DL fragment/reasoner; learned coverage or semantic correctness comes from examples, a teacher, or review, not from classification alone`

This full learning-plus-classifier operation is occupied at several levels. DL-Learner (2009) explicitly learns description-logic/OWL concepts from examples for ontology construction and maintenance, using established inductive-learning methods and reasoner interfaces. A 2020 survey catalogs ontology-learning approaches based on association-rule mining, formal concept analysis, ILP, computational learning theory, and neural networks; it also states the common assumption that the target vocabulary and DL language are already known. [Lehmann, *DL-Learner: Learning Concepts in Description Logics* (JMLR 2009)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v10/lehmann09a.html); [Ozaki (2020)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13218-020-00656-9).

The recent collisions are direct, not just adjacent. Barua & Hitzler (PMLR 2025) generate DL class expressions from instance examples and background knowledge with LLMs, then use Pellet to check outputs and feed reasoner feedback into the hybrid. Magnini et al. (first published online 25 August 2026) adapt ExactLearner/Angluin-style membership and simulated equivalence queries to use LLMs as teachers for learning EL terminologies. Their results vary by domain; the reported mean F1 for the technical Cell ontology is 0.284, so this establishes the operation and exposes reliability limits, not a robust universal learner. Mohamed et al.'s DistTDT (published 23 September 2026) uses DL concept refinements and the subsumption hierarchy to induce terminological decision trees, with a distributed reasoner for instance and entailment checks. Its own description frames the method as extending established top-down tree induction, refinement operators, and DL reasoning. [Barua & Hitzler (2025)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v284/barua25a.html); [Magnini et al., *Actively Learning EL Terminologies from Large Language Models* (ECAI 2025 proceedings, online 2026)](https://doi.org/10.3233/FAIA251009); [Mohamed et al., *DistTDT* (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10115-026-02891-2).

Replacing symbolic search with a language-model proposal policy changes how candidates are generated; it does not supply a different classification or write operation. Runtime invention of the vocabulary is separately covered by AR-125/HY-110 (predicate invention, program-library learning, schema induction, and the 2026 dynamic-schema registry). Knowledge acquisition, open-world evidence, ontology quality, and choice of language remain real costs, but they are not an uncovered computation.

**Disposition.** Reject learned concept induction × formal classifier as a new hybrid (**0/5**). It reduces to concept/ontology learning or ILP/refinement search + a description-logic reasoner/classifier, optionally with a neural/LLM proposal component. No experiment run.

#### Model revision for description-logic concepts (AR-128; exact 2026 operation, not an architecture candidate)

A stronger type-learning proposal might require a concept to be revised as new positive and negative evidence arrives, rather than merely classified once. The operation can be made precise as:

`STATE = a finite DL concept C and a set of positive/negative pointed interpretations`

`OPERATION = minimally change C so that a designated set of models is added, removed, or both`

`WRITE = a new finite DL concept C′ in the same description language`

`GUARANTEE = satisfy rationality/minimal-change conditions when a suitable finite representation exists`

Ozaki & Ribeiro's AAAI 2026 paper formalizes exactly this model-change problem for DL concepts. It distinguishes eviction (remove models), reception (add models), and revision (remove and add models together), and demonstrates that revision is not generally reducible to a simple serial composition of eviction and reception. That caveat is real: this is a distinct formal logical operator, not just a renamed update. But it is now an existing symbolic operation that directly occupies any candidate whose exact transition is concept revision from pointed-model evidence. The paper also proves compatibility/non-compatibility results for EL-bottom and ALC; the DL language may be unable to express the exact desired model set, so a universally exact, minimally changing revision guarantee is impossible in some cases. [Ozaki & Ribeiro, *Model Change for Description Logic Concepts* (AAAI 2026)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/39008).

**Disposition.** No architecture candidate survives. A neural/LLM evidence proposer plus a DL model-revision operator remains a proposal/search component connected to a known formal state-update operation. Do not claim a universal preservation guarantee beyond the representability conditions proved for a selected logic.

#### Incremental ontology reclassification and stream maintenance (AR-129; exact update machinery)

The adjacent candidate operation is “edit learned type definitions or receive/delete new facts, then update only affected hierarchy/conclusions while keeping the result equivalent to full reasoning.” It already has both TBox- and ABox-level machines, with distinct scopes:

- For **TBox edits**, Parsia, Halaschek-Wiener & Sirin (WWW 2006) present incremental OWL-DL classification under axiom additions and removals, implemented in Pellet. They explicitly describe classification as view maintenance and truth maintenance over selected ontology entailments. Cuenca Grau et al. (2010) reuse results across ontology versions, and Kazakov & Klinov (2013) demonstrate incremental OWL EL classification without bookkeeping. [Parsia et al. (2006)](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=028fbbe44131e76889dc2304d5abda2c92f0aede&repid=rep1&type=pdf); [Cuenca Grau et al. (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10817-009-9159-0); [Kazakov & Klinov (2013), ISWC demo](https://files.ifi.uzh.ch/ddis/iswc_archive/iswc/ab/2013/iswc2013-Nov13/iswc2013.semanticweb.org/content/demos/15.html).
- For **ABox streams under a fixed TBox**, Proost & Bonte's March 2026 preprint defines incremental semantics for sliding DL windows, preferred repairs when assertions conflict, and semi-naive OWL 2 RL materialization maintenance. Its related-work section directly discusses counting, DRed, FBF, and earlier incremental stream materialization. It also draws a scope boundary: stream ABoxes share a fixed TBox; its current algorithms cover OWL 2 RL and non-recursive inconsistencies, and the authors list background knowledge/recursive inconsistency handling as limitations. This is useful current work, but the update decomposes into windowed stream processing + preferred-repair semantics + incremental materialization/provenance. [Proost & Bonte, *Incremental, Inconsistency-Resilient Reasoning over Description Logic ABox Streams* (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.01799).

**Reduction result.**

`STATE = classified TBox + ABox facts + derived consequences/supports`

`OPERATION = add/remove axioms or time-windowed assertions; invalidate and rederive affected entailments; optionally select a consistent repair`

`WRITE = updated ontology version, taxonomy/materialization, and any retained provenance`

`GUARANTEE = equivalence to full classification/materialization or specified repair semantics, within the supported DL/update regime`

The exact work is divided between incremental DL classification, model revision, TMS/DRed-style invalidation, and incremental databases/stream reasoners already in the known-machine library. A learned proposal step that decides which axiom to add is not a new update primitive. No architecture candidate is promoted.

#### Hybrid collision — structure growth with a conservative-extension guarantee (HY-113; exact logic check)

A particularly plausible demand on a learned ontology builder is: “add a new type/module, but guarantee that no old-vocabulary conclusions change except where explicitly allowed.” This is not a new write rule. It is a conservative-extension condition: T₁ ∪ T₂ must entail exactly the same axioms/subsumptions over the old signature as T₁. The condition has been used directly for ontology refinement, merging, modularity, and identifying whether edits affect unrelated ontology sections. [Lutz et al., *Conservative Extensions in Expressive Description Logics* (IJCAI 2007)](https://www.csc.liv.ac.uk/~frank/publ/ijcai07.pdf).

The guarantee is expensive and language-dependent, not free. In the cited paper, deciding conservative extension is 2-EXPTIME-complete for ALCQI; stronger model-conservativity is Π₁₁-hard already for ALC. Thus a practical architecture must pick a DL fragment and exact checker, restrict the preservation question, or accept approximation. Adding a learned proposer in front of that checker does not create the guarantee; it delegates it to a known logic problem. This overlaps AR-125/HY-110 on runtime vocabulary growth and AR-128 on concept revision.

**Verdict.** Reject “learned schema growth with no unintended old consequences” as a broad new primitive (**0/5**). A candidate must state a preservation property different from deductive/model conservativity and not reducible to proof search or an existing ontology checker. No experiment run.

#### Proof-carrying commits for structural updates (AR-130; occupied by PCC and verified systems)

**Candidate attack in exact form.** A learner proposes a new executable component, topology, or internal rule; it must attach a proof that the change satisfies a safety or semantic-preservation policy; a small trusted checker accepts the state transition only if the proof verifies.

`STATE = current executable/model state + proposed delta + formal policy/specification + certificate`

`OPERATION = check the certificate against the policy and the proposed state; accept or reject the commit`

`WRITE = atomically install the proposed state only when the checker accepts`

`GUARANTEE = the installed program satisfies the stated policy, assuming a sound checker and an adequate policy`

This producer-proof / consumer-check / accept-on-success mechanism is the central operation of **proof-carrying code** (PCC), not a new architecture primitive. Necula (POPL 1997) specifies that the untrusted code producer supplies a machine-checkable proof of compliance with a consumer-defined safety policy; the consumer validates the proof and then executes the code. Necula & Schneck (2002) explicitly extend PCC to untrusted high-level proof rules: the producer can supply those rules with a proof that their invariant entails the trusted low-level memory-safety policy. This closes the variant in which the changing system also invents the proof vocabulary or intermediate safety rules. [Necula, *Proof-Carrying Code* (POPL 1997)](https://doi.org/10.1145/263699.263712); [Necula & Schneck, *Proof-Carrying Code with Untrusted Proof Rules* (2002)](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~necula/ISSS02/).

There are clear modern ML components, but they stay within this verifier pattern. Desmartin et al. (2024) build a formally certified checker for proof objects emitted by the Marabou neural-network verifier; it independently checks the solver's UNSAT proof and formally verifies the checker core. Henzinger, Kueffner & Yu (2025) monitor learned neural control-barrier certificates during deployment over a finite lookahead region, detecting incorrect certificates at runtime. The latter checks whether a neural certificate's stated safety condition holds in a bounded operating region; it does not prove arbitrary semantic equivalence of network edits. [Desmartin et al., *A Certified Proof Checker for Deep Neural Network Verification* (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10611); [Henzinger et al., *Formal Verification of Neural Certificates Done Dynamically* (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11987).

**Reduction boundary.** The exact computation divides into (a) a user/system policy, (b) candidate transformation or code generation, (c) proof production by search/theorem proving, (d) proof checking, and (e) transactional commit. If the intended policy is “no old-signature consequences change,” HY-113's conservative-extension checker supplies that property. If the policy is runtime safety, PCC, typed assembly, or verified contracts supply the producer/checker protocol. If the state is neural, a neural-network verifier/certificate checker can establish only the properties encoded by its formal query. In every case, a language model may propose a delta or proof, but it cannot turn a missing or incorrect specification into a sound guarantee. Proof production may be costly; verifying a certificate does not by itself establish usefulness, task correctness, or that the policy captures owner intent.

**Disposition.** Reject proof-carrying structural edits as a new architecture (**0/5**). The proof-gated commit is exact established PCC/certified-verification machinery composed with an existing structural editor. No experiment run.

#### Hybrid collision — learned update proposal × proof-carrying commit (HY-114; direct pattern match)

This is the neural/LLM form of the same protocol: learned proposer emits an update and possibly a certificate; a trusted proof checker tests it; a transaction layer commits or rejects. PCC already defines the same producer/consumer operation for untrusted code and supports proof rules supplied by the producer when accompanied by a proof of their soundness relative to a lower-level policy. Certified DNN verification already attaches independently checkable proof objects to neural properties. The remaining learning problem is proposing useful updates and choosing an adequate formal contract. Proposal search, proof search, contract inference, and transactional commit are known machines; a verifier's acceptance is a guarantee only relative to that contract. Reject the generic hybrid (**0/5**). No experiment run.

#### Specification induction for self-edits (AR-131; known inference-and-verification pipeline)

The next possible primitive is not merely proving a proposed update safe, but inducing the safety contract that should govern the update. To test whether this is a distinct operation, separate candidate generation from the source of normative information:

`STATE = current program/model, edit proposal, execution traces or examples, a formal specification language, and verifier feedback`

`OPERATION = generate a candidate invariant/contract; check it for consistency and proof utility; refine it using counterexamples or semantic mutations`

`WRITE = attach a selected specification to the edit and pass it to a conventional verifier before commit`

`GUARANTEE = the candidate passes specified legality/proof checks; any semantic-safety guarantee is relative to the inferred contract, not automatically to the designer's intent`

Historical and current systems already occupy the operation. Daikon dynamically mines **likely** invariants from execution traces to support program evolution; its guarantees are bounded by observed executions and the chosen invariant templates, so a property unviolated by the traces is not thereby proven universally. [Ernst et al., *Dynamically Discovering Likely Program Invariants to Support Program Evolution* (TSE 2001)](https://plse.cs.washington.edu/daikon/pubs/invariants-tse2001-abstract.html). The formal CEGIS/SyGuS pattern starts with a logical correctness specification and grammar, proposes candidate programs, and uses a verifier to return counterexamples until a candidate satisfies that supplied specification. It solves search and proof relative to the stated spec; it does not infer whether the spec captures the desired policy. [Alur et al., *Syntax-Guided Synthesis*](https://sygus-org.github.io/assets/pdf/Journal_SyGuS.pdf).

Recent systems make the learned-spec variant explicit. AutoSpec+ (ACL 2026) has LLMs generate proof-relevant candidate specs for program components and uses a symbolic verifier to check legality, satisfiability, and proof adequacy, rejecting or repairing candidates iteratively. SpecSyn (arXiv preprint, April 2026) segments programs and refines generated specifications using semantically non-equivalent program mutations and variant discrimination. These are direct instances of candidate-specification generation + machine-checkable refinement. They improve formalization, but the cited descriptions do not establish that the selected contract represents an external designer's complete intent. [Wen et al., *Formally Specifying the Intended Behavior of the Program* (ACL 2026)](https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-demo.66/); [Ma et al., *SpecSyn* (arXiv:2604.21570, preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.21570).

The decisive boundary is information, not architecture: traces and finite examples are compatible with multiple non-equivalent policies. A verifier can prove a candidate contract true of a program or adequate for a formal proof obligation, but the truth of that contract does not show it is the policy a designer intended. If the system gains an oracle that answers policy-membership or hypothesis-equivalence questions, that is the next exact-machine comparison: query learning and active concept/automata learning. If no such oracle or normative input exists, policy adequacy is underdetermined; no amount of certificate checking repairs the missing target.

**Disposition.** Reject generic learned specification induction as an uncovered architecture operation (**0/5**). It reduces to dynamic invariant mining, constrained specification synthesis, and verifier-guided refinement. Keep the distinction between proving a supplied/inferred spec and identifying the intended spec explicit. No experiment run.

They occupy candidate generation and proof-guided refinement. They do not eliminate the information gap between a contract that passes checks and the owner's intended policy. #### Interactive identification of intended update policies (AR-132; occupied by query learning)

An apparent escape from the specification-information gap is to let the learner ask the owner questions about proposed states or behavior traces and update its policy hypothesis from answers. State the mechanism as:

`STATE = a target policy in a fixed hypothesis class + a finite query/answer table + a current policy hypothesis`

`OPERATION = choose membership queries and equivalence/conjecture queries; revise the hypothesis from answers and counterexamples`

`WRITE = the currently identified policy automaton or concept`

`GUARANTEE = recover the target in the supported concept class under the specified oracle contract and complexity assumptions`

This is the classical query-learning model. Angluin's 1988 treatment enumerates membership, equivalence, subset, superset, disjointness, and exhaustiveness queries, and gives efficient query-learning methods for formal language/concept classes. Her L* algorithm learns an unknown regular set from a teacher answering membership queries and equivalence queries with counterexamples; its guarantee depends on the teacher representing the target exactly, and on the unknown policy being a regular language over a fixed alphabet. The 1987 paper explicitly notes the oracle burden: an equivalence teacher must have a precise target representation and decide equality against conjectures. [Angluin, *Queries and Concept Learning* (1988)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00116828); [Angluin, *Learning Regular Sets from Queries and Counterexamples* (1987)](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~lreyzin/papers/angluin87.pdf).

Applied to edit policies, a membership oracle can say whether a proposed trace/edit is acceptable; an equivalence oracle can say whether a candidate formal policy is exactly the intended one and return a discriminating counterexample. These answers supply the missing normative information. Adaptive selection of informative examples is part of the known query-learning operation, not a new internal computation. When the owner cannot answer the membership question consistently or the hypothesis class cannot express the policy, the exact-learning guarantee does not apply. Asking questions does not autonomously discover unarticulated intent; it makes the source of that intent explicit.

**Disposition.** Reject interactive policy identification as a new primitive (**0/5**). It reduces to active concept/automata learning plus an explicit target oracle. The oracle may be valuable in a system, but its normative answers are external input, and the update rule is established query learning. No experiment run.

#### Per-edit semantic validation for self-modifying systems (AR-133; translation validation)

Proof-carrying updates are one way to verify a structural edit. A more direct variant omits trust in the proposer and asks a checker to compare the actual before/after states after every edit:

`STATE = source executable/model + proposed transformed executable/model + formal semantics and a refinement/equivalence relation`

`OPERATION = decide or prove whether the transformed state refines or preserves the source semantics; otherwise return a counterexample or unknown`

`WRITE = commit only an update that passes the relation checker`

`GUARANTEE = each committed transformation satisfies the stated relation, subject to the checker’s semantic model and completeness/scope`

Compiler theory already names this exact pattern **translation validation**. Pnueli, Siegel & Singerman (1998) propose validating each individual translation after it is produced rather than proving the translator correct once for all inputs. Necula's 2000 GCC infrastructure compares intermediate programs before and after each optimization pass and checks semantic preservation. This is directly the per-edit check a self-modifying program or neural code generator might request. [Pnueli et al., *Translation Validation* (TACAS 1998)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0054170); [Necula, *Translation Validation for an Optimizing Compiler* (PLDI 2000)](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~necula/Papers/tv_pldi00.pdf).

Modern scope is concrete but limited. Alive2 validates LLVM IR transformations using an SMT-based refinement check; it is bounded to control resource use, and its authors state there are circumstances in which it can miss bugs, including loop behaviors beyond its bound. LLM-generated rewrite work has already been coupled to this validator pattern: a 2024 preprint plugs an LLM into Alive2-guided transformation feedback, and a September 2026 preprint reports a learned LLVM optimizer with Alive2 enforcing semantic preservation for generated rewrites. The proposals differ; the verifier/gate operation is the same. [Lopes et al., *Alive2: Bounded Translation Validation for LLVM* (PLDI 2021)](https://web.ist.utl.pt/nuno.lopes/pubs.php?id=alive2-pldi21); [LLM-assisted translation validation (2024 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16797); [Verified Learning for Compiler Optimization (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27214).

**Reduction boundary.** This closes update correctness when the candidate edit is an executable transformation and the desired relation can be stated over a shared semantics. It does not make arbitrary neural-state equivalence decidable, ensure that refinement captures task value, or guarantee a complete answer for bounded/incomplete validators. Those limitations constrain the promised guarantee; they do not create a new primitive. A learned edit proposer followed by relational verification and commit is synthesis/proposal + translation validation + a transaction.

**Disposition.** Reject per-edit semantic validation as a new architecture operation (**0/5**). It is established translation validation/relational program verification, with exactness bounded by language semantics and checker capability. No experiment run.

#### Live code and state replacement (AR-134; occupied by dynamic software updating)

The next variant is an update applied while the system is already running, with persistent state migrated into a changed code or representation schema. This is more than a static code rewrite because live control state, stacks, heaps, and object representations may straddle the version boundary:

`STATE = (running code P, live execution/state s, replacement code P′, state transformer τ, allowed update points)`

`OPERATION = reach a safe update point; install P′; transform or lazily migrate s with τ; redirect control/state accesses to the new version`

`WRITE/TRANSITION = (P,s) → (P′, τ(s))`, possibly with a runtime that keeps multiple versions or migrates state lazily

`GUARANTEE = type/representation safety or specified behavioral correctness across the transition, subject to update-point, transformer, and semantic checks`

Dynamic software updating (DSU) already formalizes this exact transition. Kitsune updates an entire running C program and allows programmer-specified transformations from old-version state to the representation expected by new code. Ginseng inserts indirections and wrappers, checks safe update points, and supports eager or lazy state/type transformation; it combines patch generation, state migration, and a runtime installation protocol. These are direct prior-art machines for persistent in-process structural changes. [Hayden et al., *Kitsune: Efficient, General-purpose Dynamic Software Updating for C* (OOPSLA 2012)](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~mwh/papers/hayden12kitsune.html); [Neamtiu et al., *Practical Dynamic Software Updating for C*](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~mwh/papers/ginseng.pdf).

The formal boundary is established too. Gupta, Jalote & Barua define online version-change validity and show that the general validity problem is undecidable, then give sufficient conditions for a procedural language. Later DSU verification work models old and new program versions plus a state transformer and checks code-level or behavioral properties with theorem proving/model checking. Therefore a generic architecture cannot promise safe arbitrary self-edits merely by adding a runtime update protocol; it must restrict the update regime, supply the migration transformation, and specify the preserved behavior. [Gupta et al., *A Formal Framework for On-line Software Version Change* (IEEE TSE 1996)](https://doi.org/10.1109/32.485222); [*Formalization and Verification of Behavioral Correctness of Dynamic Software Updates* (ENTCS 2013)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.entcs.2013.02.013).

**Reduction result.** Persistent execution-state preservation across self-edits decomposes into dynamic linking/version replacement + an explicit state transformer or migration strategy + update-point safety analysis + semantic validation. New labels, learned migration policies, or neural patch generation may improve the proposal step, but they do not supply a novel transition operation. DSU itself has tradeoffs the candidate must state: programmer-directed transforms are not automatically inferred from intent, safety is update-regime dependent, and validity in the general model is undecidable.

**Disposition.** Reject live self-modifying code/state migration as a new primitive (**0/5**). It reduces to DSU, state transformation, dynamic linking, and update verification. No experiment run.

#### Reflective interpreters and executable forms as data (AR-135; occupied by metacircular interpretation/reflection)

The remaining “self-aware computation” proposal might require a running system to expose and alter the machinery that evaluates its own code, not merely edit a source tree or hot-swap a module. This has a precise historical form:

`STATE = object-level program + the active evaluator state (environment, continuation/control state, and semantic rules)`

`OPERATION = reify selected evaluator state as program-accessible data; compute a meta-level transformation; resume object-level execution under the resulting reflective semantics`

`WRITE/TRANSITION = modify or replace control/evaluation structures, then reflect the changed interpreter behavior into the running computation`

`GUARANTEE = behavior follows the explicitly defined object/meta-level semantics; reflection itself does not ensure that a change is safe or improves task performance`

This is computational reflection, not a missing primitive. LISP 1.5's manual gives executable symbolic expressions and the `eval`/`apply` interpreter as programs, with definitions installed into the active system; its compiler is itself written in Lisp and bootstrapped by compiling itself. That is code-as-data plus interpretation and ordinary mutable definitions. Smith's 3-Lisp goes further: a procedural-reflection architecture represents the running process's environments and continuations in program-accessible structures, organized as an infinite but finitely implementable tower of interpreters. A program can make previously implicit evaluator state explicit and define constructs by manipulating it. Maes's 1987 work also surveys and builds reflective language architectures. These sources directly occupy runtime inspection and modification of one's own computational process. [McCarthy et al., *LISP 1.5 Programmer's Manual* (1962)](https://www.softwarepreservation.org/projects/LISP/book/LISP%201.5%20Programmers%20Manual-1961.07.14.pdf); [Smith, *Reflection and Semantics in Lisp* (POPL 1984)](https://doi.org/10.1145/800017.800513); [Maes, *Concepts and Experiments in Computational Reflection* (1987)](https://doi.org/10.1145/38807.38821).

**Reduction boundary.** Merely making internal computation inspectable is reflective reification; changing its rules is meta-level programming; constructing a new expression or rule is program synthesis; safely applying an update is DSU/PCC/translation validation. A neural proposer can choose the meta-level edit, but that does not change these operations. A candidate would need to specify a state/update guarantee unavailable to the language's reflection semantics, and then survive the known verification/update checks.

**Disposition.** Reject generic runtime self-inspection and self-redefinition as a new architecture operation (**0/5**). Lisp's interpreter, code-data representation, and 3-Lisp's explicit evaluator-state tower already provide the strongest direct historical collision. No experiment run.

#### Runtime creation/revision of executable rules and programs (AR-136; occupied by learned rules and program search)

A reflective runtime may change its rules as experience accumulates. The relevant operation must be distinguished from generic code mutability:

`STATE = executable rule/program library + current problem-solving trace/examples + task objective or evaluator`

`OPERATION = infer or generate a candidate procedure from traces/examples, revise it from outcomes, and insert it into persistent executable memory`

`WRITE = add, replace, or select productions/program trees that will participate in future inference/execution`

`GUARANTEE = task improvement, faster repeated problem solving, or empirical fit to the supplied domain evidence; absent a formal proof, no universal correctness guarantee`

This is a classic AI operation, with materially different mechanisms but no single missing primitive. **Soar chunking** backtraces from a result created in a subgoal to the working-memory conditions that supported it, forms a production, and inserts that production immediately into long-term procedural memory. The chunk replaces repeated subgoal search in later matching situations; Soar's newer explanation-based behavior summarization explicitly addresses generality/correctness problems in earlier chunks. [Official Soar manual, “Procedural Knowledge Learning”](https://soar.eecs.umich.edu/soar_manual/04_ProceduralKnowledgeLearning/); [Laird, Rosenbloom & Newell, *Towards Chunking as a General Learning Mechanism* (AAAI 1984)](https://cdn.aaai.org/AAAI/1984/AAAI84-049.pdf).

**Meta-DENDRAL** operates one level higher: given mass spectra/structure examples and domain constraints, RULEGEN proposes candidate fragmentation rules, and rule modification/evaluation seeks a set that explains the data. The result is new domain knowledge for Heuristic DENDRAL, acquired through constrained hypothesis generation and empirical evaluation. **Genetic programming** makes whole program trees the population subject to variation and fitness selection. Both already span rule invention and executable-structure search. [Buchanan et al., *Automatic Rule Formation in Mass Spectrometry by Means of the Meta-DENDRAL Program* (JACS 1976)](https://doi.org/10.1021/ja00436a017); [Cohen & Feigenbaum, *Program Synthesis by Meta-DENDRAL* (IJCAI 1979)](https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/79-1/Papers/004.pdf); [Koza, *Genetic Programming* (MIT Press 1992)](https://gpbib.pmacs.upenn.edu/gp-html/Koza_1992_GPdgc.html).

Current learned-code systems preserve the same operation-level decomposition. AlphaEvolve directly changes program code, evaluates candidates with task-specific automatic evaluators, and uses evolutionary selection to continue search; its authors describe the search/evaluator coupling as the system. [Novikov et al., *AlphaEvolve: A Coding Agent for Scientific and Algorithmic Discovery* (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13131); [Google DeepMind overview](https://deepmind.google/blog/alphaevolve-a-gemini-powered-coding-agent-for-designing-advanced-algorithms/). A novelty claim cannot be founded on self-generated edits, persistent insertion into an executable library, or outcome-driven selection alone.

**Reduction result.**

`learned executable structure = trace/result explanation or program-tree proposal + generalization/search + fixed or externally assessed objective + insertion/selection`

The exact generative operation varies: explanation-based generalization, scientific rule formation, or evolutionary code search. This diversity does not establish an uncovered general primitive; each is covered by rule learning/program synthesis methods, and applying the result is runtime mutability or DSU. An actual survivor would require a precise `WRITE/TRANSITION + GUARANTEE` beyond these mechanisms—for example, a new correctness guarantee or a way to obtain normative value without a supplied task objective, verifier, or teacher.

**Disposition.** Reject generic experience-driven creation of executable rules/programs as a new architecture (**0/5**). Soar, Meta-DENDRAL, genetic programming, and 2025 AlphaEvolve occupy the main exact variants. No experiment run.

#### Continuation/resource update — learned executable structure (2026-09-27)

AR-136 closes automatic rule/program creation and revision against Soar's explanation-based chunking, Meta-DENDRAL rule discovery, genetic programming, and LLM-guided evolutionary program search. The exact write operation—derive a procedure/rule/program candidate from evidence, evaluate/generalize/select it, then insert it into future execution—is established. Remaining open issue is evaluator/objective invention: systems so far rely on domain data, a task fitness function, verifier, or teacher. No candidate survives. Literature and formal reduction only; no experiment, benchmark, test, code, or background job; GPU action/use 0 GB. Next: audit self-generated evaluators/objectives against reward learning, preference learning/inverse reinforcement learning, scientific discovery systems, and verification-guided synthesis. Only `Codex_Research.md` was edited locally.

#### Evaluator/objective induction for self-modifying computation (AR-137; occupied by reward learning and intrinsic objectives)

The strongest remaining version asks the system to invent the criterion that decides whether a new rule, module, or program is an improvement. Separate three meanings that are often blurred:

`STATE = candidate behaviors/edits + observations, demonstrations, preference labels, or domain data`

`OPERATION = infer a reward/preference model or define an intrinsic progress objective; use it to rank candidates or generate further tasks`

`WRITE = select executable structure and possibly update the learned evaluator`

`GUARANTEE = optimize the modeled objective or increase a pre-specified intrinsic measure; no guarantee that the measure captures an unobserved designer goal`

There is established machinery for each source of the criterion. **Learning from human preferences** trains a reward model from pairwise judgments of trajectory segments and then applies RL. **Inverse reward design** treats a hand-designed proxy reward, interpreted in its training context, as evidence about a latent intended reward and performs risk-aware planning under posterior uncertainty. Both address the fact that a supplied or inferred score may fail to express intent; neither obtains normative information without the human preferences, proxy-design assumptions, or prior. [Christiano et al., *Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences* (NeurIPS 2017)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/7017-deep-reinforcement-learning-from-human-preferences); [Hadfield-Menell et al., *Inverse Reward Design* (NeurIPS 2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.02827).

If “self-generated” means an intrinsic objective, that operation is also explicit prior art: Schmidhuber's formal creativity theory rewards learning progress/compression improvement, while POET co-generates environments and their solutions using specified novelty/competence criteria. These mechanisms generate goals or learning challenges according to a chosen internal heuristic; they do not prove that the internally chosen measure equals an external normative objective. [Schmidhuber, *Formal Theory of Creativity, Fun, and Intrinsic Motivation* (IEEE TEC 2010)](https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/creativitybook.pdf); [Wang et al., *Enhanced POET* (ICML 2020)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/wang20l.html).

**Reduction boundary.** Selecting better structure requires some ordering signal. If it is a task score, this is optimization/search. If it is inferred from demonstrations or pairwise judgments, this is preference learning/IRL. If it is intrinsic compression or learning progress, the criterion is pre-specified by the designer. If it is a verifier, PCC/synthesis uses a formal specification. If the architecture invents a new score, the score's own quality needs an objective or external evidence, returning to the same problem one level up. This is a regress of normative grounding, not an uncovered computation.

**Disposition.** Reject generic self-generated evaluation/objective induction as a new architecture primitive (**0/5**). Reward learning, inverse reward design, and intrinsic-motivation/open-ended challenge generation occupy the main machine classes; none establishes normative correctness without external preferences, a prior, or a chosen intrinsic proxy. No experiment run.

#### Continuation/resource update — objective and evaluator induction (2026-09-27)

AR-137 closes self-evaluator/objective generation against preference-based reward modeling, inverse reward design, compression-progress intrinsic reward, and POET-style co-generation of tasks and agents. These provide optimization criteria from labels, proxy/prior assumptions, or designer-chosen intrinsic measures. They do not derive external normative intent from behavior-free computation. The adversarial pass still has no surviving architecture candidate. Literature and formal reasoning only; no experiment, benchmark, test, code, or background job; GPU action/use 0 GB. Next: restart diverse primitive exploration from the shared research map, selecting a bottleneck that does not collapse to learned executable structure/evaluation, and reduce it before designing any experiment. Only `Codex_Research.md` was edited locally.

#### Calibration audit — primitive, architecture, and pipeline (AR-138; 2026-09-27)

**Scope and authority.** Read the owner-updated `AGENTS.md` and `SHARED_RESEARCH_MAP.md` from fetched `origin/main`, the current Codex resume/rolling state, and the bounded Claude-to-Codex calibration handoff found in commit `382bb2b`. Did not read either other lane's research notebook. Local `main` is nine commits behind and contains pre-existing tracked edits plus staged local `AGENTS.md`/`SHARED_RESEARCH_MAP.md` additions, so it was not fast-forwarded; remote governance was treated as authoritative. Neither governance file nor the shared map was edited. This is literature/formal work only; no experiment or benchmark ran.

The audit applies the updated test: component decomposability kills a **primitive** claim only when the component performs the same operation; it does not settle an **architecture** claim. For architecture, the comparison must preserve important state transitions, guarantees, learning behavior, information flow, and relevant scaling/resource behavior. Turing-machine simulation and mere ability to write an interpreter are not equivalence tests.

All five required controls are simulable by a general-purpose machine. This is true by ordinary algorithmic encoding and is not evidence for or against architectural novelty; the question below is which specialized transitions and properties the relevant replacement preserves.

| Historical mechanism | Exact operation and closest prior | What a naive replacement loses | Calibration result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attention / Transformer (2014–17) | A single softmax attention read is a normalized similarity-weighted value sum: with an exponential dot-product kernel it is a Nadaraya–Watson-style kernel read over key/value memory. Bahdanau et al. learned query-dependent alignment; Vaswani et al. stack all-position self-attention and position-wise networks without recurrence. [Bahdanau et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473); [Vaswani et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762); [Nadaraya (1964)](https://doi.org/10.1137/1109020) | A recurrent encoder/decoder retains sequence-dependent computation and a long path between positions. The Transformer paper gives self-attention O(1) sequential operations and O(1) position-to-position path length per layer, at O(n²d) work; an ordinary RNN or local convolution does not preserve that information flow/resource tradeoff. An explicitly batched QK-score/softmax/value-read decomposition does preserve it, because it is the same attention layer. | **Primitive:** direct operation collision; do not call weighted content retrieval new. **Architecture:** the attention-only, globally mixing stack merits its own architecture review; kernel regression alone does not kill it. This is a sensible distinction only if earlier self-attention architectures are checked too; it does not establish a fresh candidate now. |
| Residual connections (2015) | A residual block writes `x' = x + F(x)`; its Jacobian gives the backward signal a direct identity term in addition to `J_F`. Skip/addition and gated carry paths predate ResNet; Highway Networks are a close same-era architecture. [He et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385); [Srivastava et al., Highway Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.00387) | A plain serial stack can approximate an identity mapping in its forward function, but it has no guaranteed identity gradient path; every layer would have to learn a pass-through. A parallel branch plus addition preserves the residual transition and gradient route—it is already the residual architecture, not an equivalent plain stack. | **Primitive:** identity and addition are known. **Architecture:** the update rule has a material optimization/gradient-flow property, so the old “known addition means no architecture novelty” rule is too strong. Highway Networks narrow the claim; the fixed ungated additive route must be compared directly rather than equated with generic gating. |
| Backpropagation (reverse-mode AD) (1970–86) | Reverse-mode automatic differentiation applies the chain rule backward over a computation graph to return exact parameter gradients. Linnainmaa's 1970 thesis predates neural-network popularization; Werbos described neural/control applications and Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams demonstrated useful learned representations. [Linnainmaa (1976 article referencing 1970 thesis)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01931367); [Werbos (1974 thesis)](https://gwern.net/doc/ai/nn/1974-werbos.pdf); [Rumelhart et al. (1986)](https://doi.org/10.1038/323533a0) | Replacing the algorithm with the same forward graph plus a reverse adjoint sweep does not change gradients, parameter updates, learning behavior, or asymptotic graph cost. Local learning rules would lose exact global gradients, but that is not the replacement under comparison. | **Primitive:** `KILLED — EXISTING MECHANISM`. This does not imply backprop is a new neural architecture. The historical achievement was applying and demonstrating a known differentiation mechanism for useful multilayer learning; a new standard should not mistake impact for an uncovered operation. |
| Diffusion models/processes (2015–21) | The 2015 model defines a forward Markov noising chain and learns reverse transitions; DDPM makes this a tractable variational model. Score-based models already estimated noise-conditioned scores and sampled with annealed Langevin dynamics. The later reverse-SDE treatment relates/encapsulates score-based and diffusion probabilistic approaches. [Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03585); [Ho et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239); [Song & Ermon (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.05600); [Song et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456) | A one-shot generator loses the explicit sequence of noisy states, reverse transitions, and associated variational likelihood bound. Score estimation plus a reverse-SDE solver can preserve the continuous-time marginal process; it does not literally reproduce every finite-step DDPM transition or its discrete training objective. | “Score matching + Langevin” is too coarse to prove exact equivalence. **Architecture/process:** at introduction the learned reverse Markov chain was a meaningful generative organization; subsequent score-SDE work established a unifying neighboring architecture. The updated standard avoids both extremes: neither component names alone kill it nor does a new objective label rescue a claim already covered by the same reverse process. |
| CDCL SAT solving (1996 onward) | State is a clause database, assignment trail, implication graph, and search heuristic state. A conflict is resolved against implication reasons to derive an asserting clause; the solver backjumps, adds the clause permanently, and propagates it in future branches. GRASP introduced conflict analysis, nonchronological backtracking, and stored conflict causes. [Marques-Silva & Sakallah (1996)](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/262031/) | “DPLL, then run resolution” does not preserve the mechanism unless learned clauses enter the active database, change future propagation, and drive backjumping. DPLL without learning corresponds to tree-like resolution; asserting-clause CDCL with restarts p-simulates general resolution. A 2026 result proves polynomial-time solving of Ordering Principle formulas by a deterministic CDCL configuration against an exponential tree-like/DPLL lower bound. [Pipatsrisawat & Darwiche (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.artint.2010.10.002); [Samar et al. (SAT 2026)](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.SAT.2026.30) | **Architecture/solver positive control:** the integrated learned-clause state transition has proof-system power and worst-case scaling properties absent from the no-learning decomposition. This is a real architecture/system distinction, not a new primitive for resolution or backtracking. The p-simulation result is about proof size/capability, not a promise that every CDCL run is fast. |

**Historical calibration decision.** The updated rule is more sensible than the old pipeline rule: it rejects backpropagation as a new operation, does not call Transformer/ResNet/CDCL mere sums of known components, and forces an explicit property comparison. It also blocks false positives: direct same-operation prior art still kills attention-read, reverse-mode differentiation, and generic monoid folding. A system may still be a pipeline when its parts, wired in an ordinary decomposition, preserve the transition and the property being claimed.

**Handoff claim audit and positive counterexamples.** The handoff's claim that almost every important ML mechanism collapses to its named predecessor is overbroad. The first counterexample is **Strassen matrix multiplication (1969)**: it computes the same matrix-product function from the same additions and multiplications, but a new arithmetic circuit uses seven recursive subproducts rather than eight and gives O(n^log₂7) < O(n³) arithmetic operations. This is an algorithmic efficiency mechanism, not a new specification; the direct predecessor (classical multiplication) does not reproduce the cost bound. It demonstrates why “built from known low-level operations” is not a kill by itself. [Strassen, *Gaussian elimination is not optimal*](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02165411). CDCL is a second, architecture/system-level counterexample with a formal proof-system separation above. The SAT 2026 separation is a new deterministic-CDCL-vs-DPLL result, while p-simulation of resolution is an earlier general proof-system result; these are distinct claims and should not be conflated.

Other shorthand collisions are corrected as follows:

- **Convolution ← filter banks:** a linear convolution layer is exactly a shared local filter operation; the operation itself is not new. But a fixed signal-processing filter bank is not by itself a trained hierarchical CNN with local receptive fields, tied weights, nonlinear stages, and pooling. Fukushima's Neocognitron (1980) is direct architecture prior art for the latter organization, so “filter bank” alone is an inadequate architecture-level argument. [Fukushima (1980)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00344251).
- **LSTM ← gated recurrence:** generic recurrence/gating is not the exact LSTM update. The original LSTM couples a protected linear cell-state path (constant-error carousel) with gates to preserve long-lag error flow; a generic gated RNN does not automatically preserve that transition or gradient guarantee. The LSTM itself is direct prior art for any modern generic gated-memory claim. [Hochreiter & Schmidhuber (1997)](https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/lstm1997-2024head.pdf).
- **GAN ← predictability minimization (1992):** PM's predictor/encoder game seeks factorial or statistically independent codes; that is not the GAN's data-vs-generated-sample discriminator game and density-matching objective. Thus PM is not the same computation. An earlier artificial-curiosity report is a closer generator/predictor adversarial architecture, but its objective is prediction surprise/curiosity in an agent-environment loop, not obviously the same classifier-based distribution-matching objective. The historical priority/equivalence claim is disputed in retrospective sources; the reliable conclusion here is narrower: PM alone does not kill GAN. [Goodfellow et al. (2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.2661); [Schmidhuber, PM (1992)](https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/factorial/); [FKI-129-90 report](https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/FKI-129-90ocr.pdf).
- **Mixture-of-experts ← Jacobs et al. (1991):** this is a direct architecture collision, not merely an ingredient list. The original system has separate experts plus a learned gating network that allocates cases to one or a few experts and localizes updates; generic modern sparse MoE routing inherits that basic computation. New hardware or scale is an engineering advance unless it changes a relevant guaranteed property. [Jacobs et al. (1991)](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/jjnh91.pdf).
- **Attention ← Nadaraya–Watson + associative memory:** same weighted-read operation, not same whole architecture. The old filter is right about the operation but wrong if it concludes that an attention-only, all-position sequence architecture has thereby been reproduced. The attention read is an exact primitive collision; the Transformer organization changes parallel depth and information paths.
- **Residual ← LSTM/Highway:** Highway Networks are a close direct architecture prior. But “all are gated recurrence” is inaccurate: ResNet's ungated additive identity route yields an explicit `I + J_F` gradient path. Whether a particular earlier highway formulation preserves that precise property is the comparison, not a reason to erase the architecture category.
- **Diffusion ← score matching + Langevin:** broad family correspondence is real and later reverse-SDE work formalizes it; finite-step transition rules, objectives, and likelihood guarantees still need exact alignment before declaring identity.

**Neural × symbolic fusion.** The bounded search found no established theorem showing a neural-guided, sound theorem prover or SAT solver p-simulates a stronger proof calculus than the symbolic rules it is allowed to apply. Existing neural theorem-proving systems use networks to rank clauses/tactics, propose steps, or guide tree search while a prover checks the proof; this can change practical search cost but does not itself add inference rules. [Loos et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06972); [Proverbot9001 (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.07794); [AlphaProof (2025)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09833-y). This is **not** proof that no neural-symbolic separation theorem exists; it is an unresolved literature question. A valid future claim would have to define the proof system, soundness checker, neural interface, and resource measure, then prove p-simulation or an explicit separation. Heuristic solve-rate results do not answer that question.

**Re-audit of decomposition-led Codex kills.** Classifications below use the owner's labels. These are architecture-level dispositions, not claims that the systems are useless.

- **C003 Associative Fold Machine — `KILLED — EXISTING MECHANISM`.** State is a segment summary in a monoid; operation is associative composition; transition replaces a sequential fold with a tree/scan; guarantee is parenthesization/chunking invariance and parallel reduction. Monoids, semigroup networks, and parallel prefix scans already perform this exact operation. Implementing learned summaries plus a scan preserves the algebraic guarantee and parallel scaling; there is no additional coupling property in C003. [Learnable Commutative Monoids for GNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08541); [Sequential-Parallel Duality in Prefix-Scannable Models (ICLR 2026)](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2026/hash/4fef2f009c960581664363987fbe34d5-Abstract-Conference.html).
- **C007 Error-Correcting Belief Code — `KILLED — IMPOSSIBLE / NON-IDENTIFIABLE` for epistemic correctness; `KILLED — EXISTING MECHANISM` for hardware fault tolerance.** A parity syndrome can detect some departures from a codeword; it cannot determine that a valid codeword encodes a true or calibrated belief. The proposal supplies no operation-closed semantic code or correction-radius theorem. For numerical state, algorithm-based fault tolerance already encodes data, computes on the encoded form, and preserves checks through matrix addition, multiplication, scalar products, LU, and transpose. Re-encoding after each learned nonlinear operation is a separate cost, not a missing architecture primitive. [Huang & Abraham (1984)](https://graal.ens-lyon.fr/~abenoit/CR02/papers/abft2.pdf); [Judd & Munro (1992)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/1992/hash/c361bc7b2c033a83d663b8d9fb4be56e-Abstract.html); [Zlokapa et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12887).
- **C014 Communication-Budget Machine — `KILLED — EXISTING ARCHITECTURE`.** State is distributed local state plus channel budget; operation chooses message contents/recipients/timing and updates each site; guarantee is bounded communication with joint task behavior. TarMAC learns contents and recipients; ETCNet learns send timing under bandwidth constraints; CommNet and communication-complexity/rate-distortion cover the broad protocol problem. Splitting local computation, a budgeted channel, and a learned scheduler preserves the stated transition and hard cap. The suggested stale-cache/value-of-information extension has no precise rule or guarantee yet and is not promoted. [TarMAC](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/das19a/das19a.pdf); [ETCNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.04978).
- **C017 Global-Workspace Broadcast — `KILLED — EXISTING ARCHITECTURE`.** Limited workspace, specialist proposals, coalition selection, and recurrent broadcast already characterize Global Workspace Theory implementations, LIDA, Soar, and blackboard systems. The candidate's interruption and cross-modal availability properties follow from that organization; no distinct state transition or scaling law is specified.
- **C020 Predictive Delta Ledger — `KILLED — PIPELINE ONLY` (broad claim).** State is cached derived claims plus dependencies; edits trigger invalidation and recomputation of the changed cone; the desired guarantee is exact current outputs with work proportional to affected dependencies. TMS, self-adjusting computation, DRed/differential dataflow, and build/reactive systems already do this when dependencies are explicit. The neural reuse variant is also directly instantiated by Incrementally-Computable Neural Networks, which discretize intermediate values and reuse work after atomic edits (reported 12.1× fewer median operations on one OPT-125M document-classification protocol, without a formal exact-output guarantee). A modular “learn dependency hints → cache → verify → invalidate or fall back” implementation can preserve safety by fallback and preserve the incremental speed property only when its dependency support is valid; if verification must be global, the claimed scaling advantage disappears. No new coupled transition, learning rule, or resource bound was specified. This is a positive application of the new standard: decomposition alone is not the kill; the property check and missing coupling rule are. [Doyle (1977)](https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/77-1/Papers/035.pdf); [Acar et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.0478); [Differential Dataflow](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2013/Papers/CIDR13_Paper111.pdf); [Incrementally-Computable Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.14988).
- **HY-80 reversible residual-to-generator consolidation — `KILLED — PIPELINE ONLY` as an architecture claim.** Its state/update pair is a shared CPPN-like generator plus offsets, with repeated residual motifs absorbed into the generator and reversible rollback. Offset-HybrID already couples generator and offset state; the exact evidence threshold/consolidation/rollback policy is still unspecified, and the cited authors explicitly identify phenotype-to-genotype/epigenetic transfer as a future direction. It remains a possible systems/update-rule study, not evidence that current architecture novelty survives. No new test was run. [Helms & Clune (2017)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5363933/).

**Disposition and exact next action.** No Codex candidate survives initial architecture reduction. The historic controls confirm that the novelty filter must not equate “built from familiar operations” with “same architecture”; CDCL and Strassen are explicit positive controls, while reverse-mode AD and monoid folding are direct-operation negatives. Next, take one concrete candidate from future primitive generation and write `STATE + OPERATION + WRITE/TRANSITION RULE + GUARANTEE`; then find the nearest architecture that preserves each claimed property and explicitly compare the resource law. Do not reopen the broad PDL, generic communication, or coded-belief claims absent a newly specified transition and a property not preserved by their known replacements.

## AR-139 — Native internal coupling: signal-level prior-art collision map (2026-09-27)

### Question and method

The target is the broad proposal class “an architecture gains an important property because a necessary signal, derivation, state write, or feedback path is native to one coupled mechanism.” I treated each named signal as a candidate operation, rather than assuming that modularity is equivalent to a feed-forward pipeline. For each one I asked: what exact value moves, which state receives it, when the write occurs, what claimed property depends on that transition, and which known architecture already runs the same loop?

The decomposition test is intentionally stronger than “another program could emulate it.” Split the candidate at module boundaries, expose the full relevant interface (activation, cotangent, message, belief, route score, reward error, learned clause, proof state, or memory write), preserve the same trigger and schedule, and ask whether the state transition and stated guarantee remain. If a candidate needs a rate, latency, bandwidth, memory, or asymptotic advantage, that is a separate resource claim; equal outputs alone do not settle it. A decomposition that returns a conflict clause into the active SAT database is CDCL, not a counterexample to CDCL's architectural identity.

**Result.** The “native coupling” phrase alone names neither a primitive nor an architecture. All 15 concrete signal families below have a direct historical or modern architecture collision, or a standard interface that preserves the claimed signal. The generic umbrella is killed for lacking a material property. No candidate survives this family-level pass. This is not a proof that no future coupling architecture can exist; it is a closure of the generic claim until a proposal specifies the missing signal and property.

### Collision map

#### 1. Cross-module differentiable programming — KILLED — DECOMPOSITION PRESERVES PROPERTY

- **Candidate name:** end-to-end differentiable composition of otherwise separate learned or scientific modules.
- **Claimed internal signal / native coupling:** a downstream loss supplies cotangents to upstream module inputs and parameters; modules train jointly through the composed computation.
- **Ordinary decomposition and alleged loss:** separately trained modules may not receive a downstream derivative, so locally good modules can be globally misaligned. That is a real loss for a pipeline that stops at an opaque or non-differentiable interface.
- **Strongest restoration:** let each component expose its primal output and vector-Jacobian product (or an equivalent custom pullback); compose the pullbacks in reverse execution order. With the same graph, derivative convention, and optimizer, the interface preserves the same chain-rule signal and parameter update. Differentiable pipelines across heterogeneous frameworks and differentiable solver layers make this explicit, rather than hypothetical.
- **Closest historical prior art:** reverse-mode automatic differentiation and compositional functional differentiation; the 2017 end-to-end differentiable pipeline interface already permits separately implemented primitives to be refined end to end.
- **Closest modern prior art:** differentiable convex optimization layers use an affine-solver-affine decomposition with analytic differentiation; the 2026 JMLR common AD interface explicitly supports modular selection and composition of AD backends. [End-to-end differentiable pipelines (2017)](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/publications/publication14251-abstract.html); [Differentiable Convex Optimization Layers (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.12430); [A Common Interface for Automatic Differentiation (JMLR 2026)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume27/25-1024/25-1024.pdf).
- **Architecture verdict:** **KILLED — DECOMPOSITION PRESERVES PROPERTY.** A hard interface that withholds derivatives changes the training protocol; it does not establish that the property is inseparable from a monolithic architecture.

#### 2. Recurrent, implicit, or equilibrium feedback — KILLED — EXISTING ARCHITECTURE

- **Candidate name:** a coupled recurrent computation whose internal feedback converges to a solution and whose learning signal passes through that solution.
- **Claimed internal signal / native coupling:** hidden state is repeatedly updated by a shared transition; an equilibrium state then drives output and gradient/update.
- **Ordinary decomposition and alleged loss:** a feed-forward stack or finite unroll may stop short of the equilibrium, change the transition, or store activations proportional to effective depth. Those replacements can lose convergence behavior or memory scaling.
- **Strongest restoration:** expose the recurrent state and iterate the same update, or expose the root/equilibrium residual and apply implicit differentiation. The latter restores the fixed-point derivative and constant-memory training property when the assumptions hold; it is the DEQ architecture itself, not an appeal to universal simulation.
- **Closest historical prior art:** recurrent backpropagation and fixed-point networks; Hopfield-style energy relaxation.
- **Closest modern prior art:** Deep Equilibrium Models directly replace depth by a root-found fixed point and report constant activation memory; Equilibrium Propagation uses a second nearby equilibrium to carry the error-dependent learning signal. [Deep Equilibrium Models (NeurIPS 2019)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/hash/01386bd6d8e091c2ab4c7c7de644d37b-Abstract.html); [Equilibrium Propagation (2017)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/computational-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fncom.2017.00024/full); [Equivalence of Equilibrium Propagation and Recurrent Backpropagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.08416).
- **Architecture verdict:** **KILLED — EXISTING ARCHITECTURE.** A naive finite unroll may not preserve the property, but equilibrium architectures already do.

#### 3. Predictive-coding error feedback — KILLED — EXISTING ARCHITECTURE

- **Candidate name:** perception or inference organized around predictions flowing down and residual errors flowing up.
- **Claimed internal signal / native coupling:** each level stores a latent cause and prediction; a lower-level mismatch writes an error that updates higher-level causes and recurrent feedback predictions.
- **Ordinary decomposition and alleged loss:** a one-pass encoder discards iterative correction and error-state dynamics; it can therefore lose the candidate's claimed inference path.
- **Strongest restoration:** make each level a module with explicit latent, prediction, and residual ports, then schedule the same alternating updates. This preserves the local state transitions. The architecture-level question is whether its chosen energy, schedule, and learning rule produce a property beyond a conventional iterative inference graph, not whether it is “coupled.”
- **Closest historical prior art:** Rao–Ballard predictive coding (1999), generalized predictive processing, and recurrent error-correction/inference schemes.
- **Closest modern prior art:** predictive-coding networks trained with local or approximate gradients and Equilibrium Propagation already make the error-bearing state participate in learning. [Rao & Ballard (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1038/4580); [Scellier & Bengio (2017)](https://doi.org/10.3389/fncom.2017.00024).
- **Architecture verdict:** **KILLED — EXISTING ARCHITECTURE.** Replacing it with a feed-forward network is not a preserving decomposition; preserving the latent/error feedback reproduces predictive coding.

#### 4. Learned graph messages and neural algorithmic reasoning — KILLED — DECOMPOSITION PRESERVES PROPERTY

- **Candidate name:** a distributed learner whose reasoning signal travels along internal graph edges rather than through a centralized representation.
- **Claimed internal signal / native coupling:** each node's current state generates edge-indexed messages; neighbors aggregate them and write a new node state, often over repeated rounds.
- **Ordinary decomposition and alleged loss:** isolated per-node networks lose relational context and multi-hop derivations if no edge communication is allowed.
- **Strongest restoration:** make node processors separate modules and expose the exact edge message, reducer, and synchronous/asynchronous update order. This preserves the message-passing transition round by round. If a claim concerns long-range reasoning, specify the number of rounds, graph diameter assumptions, or communication volume; “native” alone supplies no stronger guarantee.
- **Closest historical prior art:** graph neural networks and distributed dataflow/message-passing algorithms.
- **Closest modern prior art:** Message Passing Neural Networks unify many graph-network variants; Neural Algorithmic Reasoning explicitly trains processor networks aligned to classical algorithm steps; 2026 work continues to analyze which algorithms these graph networks can learn. [Gilmer et al. (ICML 2017)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/gilmer17a.html); [Veličković & Blundell, Neural Algorithmic Reasoning (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8276006/); [Which Algorithms Can Graph Neural Networks Learn? (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13106).
